Risk stratification tools for cardiovascular pre-exercise screening include the American heart association (AHA) and the American College of Cardiology (ACC) pre-participation questionnaire, the Duke Activity Status Index, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) for high-risk individuals.

Circadian variation in cardiovascular events presents a clinical paradox: adults face peak SCD risk during early morning Ex, while young athletes are most vulnerable during afternoon/evening training [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR10 "Thompson PD, Funk EJ, Carleton RA, Sturner WQ (1982) Death during jogging in Rhode Island. JAMA 247(18):2535–2538")]. These opposing patterns may reflect different underlying mechanisms; morning catecholamine surges and hypercoagulability in atherosclerotic adults versus exertion-related arrhythmias in structurally abnormal young hearts.

Emerging mechanistic data implicate morning elevations in catecholamines, cortisol, platelet aggregability, and coagulation factors (including plasminogen activator inhibitor type 1 (PAI-1)) as contributing to the increased morning cardiovascular event risk in older atherosclerotic patients. In young athletes, sympathetic-triggered arrhythmias in structurally abnormal myocardium underlie the afternoon/evening risk pattern. Definitive mechanistic studies are lacking.

### Athletic heart syndrome

Long-distance runners show sinus bradycardia, atrioventricular blocks, and premature beats, raising concerns about hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Screening of family members can distinguish training-induced LV hypertrophy from familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is essential since vigorous Ex is contraindicated in the latter [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR11 "Lavie CJ, Milani RV, Marks P, de Gruiter H (2001) Exercise and the heart. Ochsner J 3(4):207–213")].

Detraining helps differentiate between physiological and pathological hypertrophy, elite male athletes with eccentric left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy showed regression of LV mass and wall thickness but 22% had residual LV dilation. Strength-trained athletes with concentric hypertrophy also demonstrated LV hypertrophy regression. The duration required for effective detraining is still unknown [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR12 "Hegde SM, Solomon SD (2015) Physical activity influence on hypertension. Curr Hypertens Rep 17(10):77")].

Exercise induced hypertension (EIH), is defined as elevated systolic BP > 190 mm Hg, and > 210 mmHg for females and males respectively during Ex [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR13 "Mohammed LLM, Dhavale M, Abdelaal MK, Alam AN, Blazin T, Prajapati D et al (2020) Exercise-induced hypertension: alarming sign? Cureus 12(12). 
                  https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.11988
                  
                ")]. Ex can cause a significant spike in BP especially after weight lifting, planks or wall-sits, high-intensity interval training (HIIT), sprinting, squash, skydiving, and SCUBA diving [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR14 "Sharman JE, La Gerche A, Coombes JS (2015) Exercise and cardiovascular risk in hypertension. Am J Hypertens 28(2):147–158")].

Management of EIH: blood pressure should be monitored before, during, and after exercise. Exercise should be terminated if systolic BP exceeds 250 mmHg or diastolic BP exceeds 115 mmHg. For patients on antihypertensives, particularly beta-blockers, the blunted heart rate response should be recognized; Rating of perceived exertion- RPE (Borg scale) is preferable to heart rate targets for exercise intensity guidance [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR15 "Williams N (2017) Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion scale. Occup Med (Lond) 67(5):404–405")].

### Exercise and coronary artery disease

Ex intensity affects progression of coronary artery calcification (CAC). Vigorous Ex slows progression of CAC, while very vigorous Ex accelerates it. Longer Ex durations are linked to higher CAC [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR9 "Corrado D, Basso C, Rizzoli G, Schiavon M, Thiene G (2003) Sudden death and sports activity in adolescents and young adults. J Am Coll Cardiol 42(11):1959–1963")].

### Exercise and abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)

Specific guidance on AAA in Ex guidelines for patients with cardiovascular diseases is limited. Small AAA poses minimal risks during Ex training, and no major adverse events have been reported. The optimal Ex level for AAA remains unclear due to the potential risk of blood pressure-induced rupture, which can be catastrophic [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR16 "Aune D, Sen A, Kobeissi E, Hamer M, Norat T, Riboli E (2020) Physical activity & abdominal aortic aneurysm risk. Sci Rep 10(1):22287")].

### Exercise and valvular heart disease

Asymptomatic individuals with minor valvular abnormalities can participate in competitive sports, but individuals with moderate severity lesions may Ex intensively if an Ex stress test shows good functional capacity. Symptomatic athletes, those with severe heart disease, impaired ventricular function, pulmonary hypertension, and arrhythmias should avoid competitive sports. Athletes with a bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse, and anticoagulation therapy should avoid contact or collision sports to minimize bleeding risks [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR17 "Gati S, Malhotra A, Sharma S (2019) Exercise in valvular heart disease. Heart 105(2):106–110")]. The majority of sudden deaths in patients with aortic stenosis do not take place during strenuous Ex. Therefore, limiting Ex is not well-supported by evidence and should be considered carefully. Patients with significant congenital aortic stenosis are at risk for sudden death. Recommendations are unsettled for Ex restriction after balloon valvuloplasty [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR18 "Rome JJ (2010) Exercise restriction in congenital aortic stenosis. American College of Cardiology Foundation, pp 1947–1948")].

Standard early Ex termination criteria apply in this population [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR19 "Bailey DM, Davies RG, Rose GA, Lewis MH, Aldayem AA, Twine CP et al (2023) Cardiopulmonary exercise testing in abdominal aortic aneurysm. Exp Physiol 108(9):1118–1131")], and condition-specific risks, contraindications, and monitoring parameters relevant to safe cardiovascular training are summarized in Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab1).

## Exercise and respiratory diseases

While Ex improves lung function, quality of life, and reduce number of exacerbations, durability in many chronic respiratory conditions, even in pulmonary embolism [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR20 "Xiong T, Bai X, Wei X, Wang L, Li F, Shi H et al (2023) Exercise rehabilitation in chronic respiratory diseases. Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis 18:1251–1266")], certain situations necessitate caution.

### Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)

The paradigm shift from considering Ex an absolute contraindication in PAH to endorsing supervised training is supported by preliminary randomized controlled (RCT) trial data with small sample size (_n_ = 116), underscoring the need for larger methodological robust trials [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR21 "Garvey C (2011) Guidelines for Pulmonary Rehabilitation Programs. 4th ed. Human Kinetics; In: ZuWallack R, Crouch G, editors"), [22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR22 "Grünig E, MacKenzie A, Peacock AJ, Eichstaedt CA, Benjamin N, Nechwatal R et al (2021) Exercise training in pulmonary hypertension. Eur Heart J 42(23):2284–2295")].

For patients with PAH, supervised Ex is generally recommended only when they are stable on the best standard of pharmacological treatment and meet the criteria for low-risk (Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab1)) [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR23 "Humbert M, Kovacs G, HoeperMM, Badagliacca R, Berger RMF, Brida M et al (2022) 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines. Eur Respir J 43:3618–3731. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022
                  
                ")]. Low-risk PAH criteria (per the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Respiratory Society (ERS) Guidelines 2022): WHO functional class I–II, 6MWT > 440 m, absence of right heart failure signs, NT-proBNP within near-normal range, and hemodynamic stability on optimized pharmacotherapy [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR24 "Humbert M, Kovacs G, Hoeper MM, Badagliacca R, Berger RMF, Brida M et al (2022) 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines. Eur Heart J 43(38):3618–3731")].

Exercise induced PAH; is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial hypertension (mPAP)/cardiac output (CO) slope > 3 mmHg/L/min between rest and Ex. It can be attributed to alterations in pulmonary artery flow affected by cardiac output (CO), pulmonary vascular resistance and left atrial pressures during Ex [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR23 "Humbert M, Kovacs G, HoeperMM, Badagliacca R, Berger RMF, Brida M et al (2022) 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines. Eur Respir J 43:3618–3731. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00879-2022
                  
                ")]. A pathological increase in pulmonary pressure during Ex is associated with impaired prognosis in patients with exertional dyspnea and in several cardiovascular conditions (see Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab2) Exercise induced adverse effects) [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR25 "Ho JE, Zern EK, Lau ES, Wooster L, Bailey CS, Cunningham T et al (2020) Exercise pulmonary hypertension predicts clinical outcomes. J Am Coll Cardiol 75(1):17–26")].

Exercise induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) is defined as airway constriction associated with Ex [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR26 "Parsons JP, Hallstrand TS, Mastronarde JG, Kaminsky DA, Rundell KW, Hull JH et al (2013) Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: guideline. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 187(9):1016–1027")]. EIB typically develops within 15 min, after at least 5 to 8 min of high-intensity aerobic training (Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Fig1)-B) [[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR27 "Anderson SD, Silverman M, König P, Godfrey S (1975) Exercise-induced asthma. Br J Dis Chest 69:1–39")]. Recently, EIB was separated into EIB with asthma and EIB without asthma, the latter being particularly common in athletes after years of intensive training [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR28 "Carlsen K, Anderson S, Bjermer L, Bonini S, Brusasco V, Canonica W et al (2008) Exercise-induced asthma in elite athletes. Allergy 63(4):387–403")]. It is thought to result from Ex-induced airway hyperreactivity and underlying inflammatory processes [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR29 "Bonini M, Silvers W (2018) Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Immunol Allergy Clin North Am 38(2):205–214"), [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR30 "Boulet LP, O’Byrne PM (2015) Asthma & exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. N Engl J Med 372(7):641–648")].

Preventive strategies for EIB, particularly in athletes, include: (1) pre-exercise short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) 15 min before exercise; (2) adequate warm-up (gradual intensity increase for ≥ 10 min); (3) avoidance of cold/dry air and high-pollen environments; (4) use of face masks in cold weather. Leukotriene receptor antagonists and inhaled corticosteroids serve as maintenance strategies for recurrent EIB (Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab2), Preventive Strategies).

Exercise and acute exacerbation of COPD, the effects of initiation of pulmonary rehabilitation in the first 4 weeks after hospital discharge are unclear. Patient characteristics favoring early post-discharge pulmonary rehabilitation initiation include: stable respiratory status, absence of acute infection, adequate oxygenation (SpO2 > 88% at rest), and patient motivation. Those with recent severe exacerbation, significant cardiac comorbidity, or functional dependence may require delayed initiation. Evidence from current trials remains equivocal, and some studies report no significant functional improvement with early initiation in frailer patients [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR31 "Greening NJ, Williams JE, Hussain SF, Harvey-Dunstan TC, Bankart MJ, Chaplin EJ et al (2014) Early rehabilitation in COPD exacerbation. BMJ 349:g4315")]. The most frequently prescribed training modalities were non-treadmill walking, sit-to-stand and non-equipment based lower limb strengthening. Interval training was more often advised than continuous training, with lower limb strengthening, upper limb strengthening and functional training the most frequently prescribed (see Table [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab3) Exercise prescription framework by disease severity) [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR32 "Puhan MA, Gimeno‐Santos E, Cates CJ et al (2016) Pulmonary rehabilitation following exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev (12). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD005305.pub4
                  
                ")].

### Exercise with Interstitial lung disease (ILD)

The safety of Ex in ILD patients has been poorly studied. Development of exertional hypoxemia is common in ILD patients which can lead to adverse responses [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR33 "Garvey C, Tiep B, Carter R, Barnett M, Hart M, Casaburi R (2012) Severe exercise-induced hypoxemia. Respir Care 57(7):1154–1160")]; as premature lactic acidosis accelerates peripheral muscle fatigue and discomfort [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR34 "Vogiatzis I, Zakynthinos S (2012) Exercise tolerance limits in chronic lung disease. Compr Physiol 2(3):1779–1817")], reflex tachycardia and cardiac arrhythmias [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR35 "Park JH, Jegal Y, Shim TS, Lim CM, Lee SD, Koh Y et al (2011) Hypoxemia & arrhythmia in fibrotic ILD. J Korean Med Sci 26(3):372–378")], which may even lead to fatal adverse events [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR36 "Vahdatpour CA, Luebbert JJ, Palevsky HI (2020) Atrial arrhythmias in CLD-associated PAH. Pulm Circ 10(1):2045894020910685")]. The limited efficacy of supplemental oxygen evidenced by the inability of approximately 40% of patients to maintain O2 saturation > 88%, highlights the need for objective individualized monitoring criteria [[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR37 "Martí S, Pajares V, Morante F, Ramón M-A, Lara J, Ferrer J et al (2013) Oxygen-conserving devices in exercise hypoxemia. Respir Care 58(10):1606–1613")].

Monitoring strategies for ILD patients during exercise include continuous pulse oximetry during exercise (target SpO2 ≥ 88%), RPE-guided intensity progression, short-interval or circuit training rather than prolonged continuous aerobic exercise, and supplemental oxygen titration for patients dropping below 88% saturation. The 6-minute walk test (6MWT) with oximetry is recommended for baseline assessment and monitoring [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR38 "Dowman L, Hill CJ, May A, Holland AE (2021) Pulmonary rehabilitation in ILD. Cochrane Database Syst Rev (2). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD006322.pub4
                  
                ")]. Priority research questions for ILD are detailed in Table [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab4).

## Exercise and renal diseases

### Chronic kidney disease (CKD)

Developing an Ex-program for CKD patients is a complex task due to the diversity of CKD stages, variable electrolyte profiles, and different treatment modalities [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR39 "Arazi H, Mohabbat M, Saidie P, Falahati A, Suzuki K (2022) Exercise & kidney diseases. Sports 10(3):42")]. Surpassing an optimal dose of Ex might raise the potential for coronary plaque development, angina, atrial fibrillation, arrhythmia, MI, hypertension, hypotension and SCD [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR40 "Stylemans D, Vandecruys M, Leunis S, Engelborghs S, Gargioli D, Monbaliu D et al (2024) Exercise post solid organ transplant. Transpl Int 37:12448")].

### In non-dialysis CKD patients

The impact of Ex training (aerobic or resistance) on kidney function, estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) or CKD progression lacks definitive evidence. Resistance Ex in CKD presents conflicting evidence. Potential benefits for patients who are intolerant of aerobic Ex, must be weighed against significant LDL elevations and fistula injury risk [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR41 "Chen C-C, Huang Y-Y, Li X-Q, Long Y-Q, Chen Z-W, Jin T (2024) Resistance exercise in CKD. BMC Nephrol 25(1):115")]. However, the clinical significance of Ex-induced LDL increases remains uncertain. Studies showing this effect (_n_< 100 total patients) lacked cardiovascular outcome data and may reflect acute post-Ex lipid fluctuations rather than sustained atherogenic changes. Moreover, LDL elevation may be outweighed by other cardiometabolic benefits (improved insulin sensitivity, reduced inflammation). This equipoise highlights the need for adequately powered trials with cardiovascular endpoints before dismissing resistance Ex in CKD.

In hot and humid climates, Ex leads to the redistribution of cardiac output to the skin. When combined with evaporation-induced dehydration, this can result in an additional 15%–30% reduction in renal blood flow with corresponding decrease in GFR (Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Fig1)-C). Moreover, at high altitudes Ex such as rock climbing and snowshoe hiking, individuals may experience high-altitude renal syndrome, characterized by a combination of polycythemia, hyperuricemia, hypertension, and proteinuria. Prolonged aerobic Ex improves insulin sensitivity hours after Ex cessation, carrying the risk of hypoglycemia. Consumption of more protein than allowed for each CKD stage to build muscle will lead to the same unfortunate result [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR39 "Arazi H, Mohabbat M, Saidie P, Falahati A, Suzuki K (2022) Exercise & kidney diseases. Sports 10(3):42"), [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR40 "Stylemans D, Vandecruys M, Leunis S, Engelborghs S, Gargioli D, Monbaliu D et al (2024) Exercise post solid organ transplant. Transpl Int 37:12448")].

### In dialysis dependent CKD

High levels of inflammatory markers were seen after acute aerobic sessions (40%) compared to regular sessions (25%) [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR42 "Cavalcante PAM, Gregnani MF, Henrique JS, Ornellas FH, Araújo RC (2017) Aerobic but not resistance exercise induces TLR pathways. Sports Med Open 3:1–18")]. Similarly, resistance Ex initially elevates acute inflammation markers due to muscle breakdown. However, this process ultimately contributes to long-term benefits by promoting the rebuilding of stronger muscles [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR43 "Calle MC, Fernandez ML (2010) Resistance training & inflammatory response. Nutr Res Pract 4(4):259–269")]. Nevertheless, these Ex can also lead to adverse musculoskeletal outcomes, including muscle soreness, strains, tears, or even frank avulsion [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR40 "Stylemans D, Vandecruys M, Leunis S, Engelborghs S, Gargioli D, Monbaliu D et al (2024) Exercise post solid organ transplant. Transpl Int 37:12448")].

Specific exercise protocols by CKD stage: CKD Stages 1–3: moderate aerobic exercise 150 min/week at 40–60% VO2max, resistance training 2–3x/week; CKD Stages 4–5: low-to-moderate intensity, 90–150 min/week, supervised, with caution around arteriovenous fistula protection; Dialysis patients: intra-dialytic cycling 30–45 min at low-to-moderate intensity, 3x/week (Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab3)). Monitoring parameters include: serum creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes (potassium, phosphate), hemoglobin, blood pressure pre/post-exercise, and CK levels if rhabdomyolysis is suspected. For dialysis patients, fluid weight and post-dialysis fatigue scores are also recommended (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab1)).

### Kidney transplant recipients

Ex-induced release of noradrenaline during moderate and vigorous-intensity Ex might raise BP to dangerous levels and reduces kidney blood flow by approximately 20% and 52%, respectively. These changes may pose a risk for kidney injury, especially in recipients with estimated GFR below 60 mL/kg/m². Additionally, strenuous Ex can lead to rare conditions such as rhabdomyolysis, which can cause acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia (Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Tab2)) [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR40 "Stylemans D, Vandecruys M, Leunis S, Engelborghs S, Gargioli D, Monbaliu D et al (2024) Exercise post solid organ transplant. Transpl Int 37:12448")].

During strenuous Ex, redistribution of blood supply to muscles can have adverse effects on intestinal health. This includes reduced blood flow and increased permeability, which can impair gut-barrier function and elevate the risk of infection [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR40 "Stylemans D, Vandecruys M, Leunis S, Engelborghs S, Gargioli D, Monbaliu D et al (2024) Exercise post solid organ transplant. Transpl Int 37:12448")]. Ex-induced infectious diarrhea in transplant recipients carries risk of graft failure due to dehydration with negative affect graft perfusion [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR40 "Stylemans D, Vandecruys M, Leunis S, Engelborghs S, Gargioli D, Monbaliu D et al (2024) Exercise post solid organ transplant. Transpl Int 37:12448")].

Exercise in renal transplant recipients: exercise is generally safe and beneficial post-transplantation, but timing relative to immunosuppressive therapy adjustments, infection risk, bone density loss (from corticosteroids), and graft function should be monitored. High-contact or collision sports (e.g., rugby, American football, martial arts, ice hockey, boxing) should be avoided due to risk of graft trauma. Resistance training is beneficial for counteracting steroid-induced myopathy, provided adequate bone density assessment precedes initiation. Kidney transplant recipients on fluoroquinolone therapy face elevated risk of Achilles tendinopathy and overuse injuries [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR40 "Stylemans D, Vandecruys M, Leunis S, Engelborghs S, Gargioli D, Monbaliu D et al (2024) Exercise post solid organ transplant. Transpl Int 37:12448")].

Special Conditions, Patients with polycystic kidney disease should also be refrained from contact Ex due to the potential of direct injury or hemorrhage from renal cysts in enlarged kidneys [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR44 "Courivaud C, Roubiou C, Delabrousse E, Bresson-Vautrin C, Chalopin J, Ducloux D (2014) Polycystic kidney size outcomes. Clin Kidney J 7(2):138–143")].

Ex can induce proteinuria, hematuria and cylindruria in normal individuals. Ex-induced proteinuria is a result of the intensity, rather than the duration, of Ex [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR45 "Peeri M, Kohanpour M-A, Sanavi S, Matinhomaee H, Mirsepasi M (2012) Exercise intensity & proteinuria. Dial Traspl 33(3):84–88")]. In patients with glomerulonephritis, moderate proteinuria, and nephrotic syndrome, Ex causes initial increase in proteinuria that returned to baseline after 2 h, suggesting that Ex can be safely incorporated under appropriate monitoring. (Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#Fig1)-C) [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR46 "Yamagata K, Hoshino J, Sugiyama H, Hanafusa N, Shibagaki Y, Komatsu Y et al (2019) Renal rehabilitation guideline. Ren Replace Ther 5(1):1–19")].

Moderate-intensity Ex may increase the risk of renal stone formation due to enhanced crystallization of uric acid and calcium oxalate. Activities involving jarring or high-impact movements, such as running, jumping, or vigorous aerobic Ex, can potentially elevate the likelihood of kidney stone episodes [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43162-026-00623-0#ref-CR39 "Arazi H, Mohabbat M, Saidie P, Falahati A, Suzuki K (2022) Exercise & kidney diseases. Sports 10(3):42")].

This is a narrative review article published in The Egyptian Journal of Internal Medicine (Volume 38, article 38, 2026) titled "Safety considerations and adverse events associated with exercise across medical disciplines." It is an open-access review by 10+ authors (including Amin Roshdy Soliman, Gehad Maghraby, Farouk Mostafa Faris, and Inass Shaltout) affiliated with Aff1.

PURPOSE: The review synthesizes evidence on exercise (Ex)-related adverse effects across 10 medical subspecialties—cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, hepatic, rheumatic, neurological, psychiatric, endocrine, and pediatric—and provides expert-informed recommendations for individualized exercise prescription.

KEY METHODS: A narrative review of literature from PubMed (MEDLINE), Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, with MeSH terms covering exercise types and adverse events. An expert panel of 10 specialists (cardiology, respiratory, hepatology, rheumatology, nephrology, endocrinology, pediatrics, neurology, psychiatry) contributed. The review follows the SANRA framework. Evidence was categorized into minor, moderate, and severe adverse effects.

KEY FINDINGS BY SYSTEM:
- CARDIOVASCULAR: Regular exercise reduces overall cardiovascular mortality by 30–40%, but sedentary individuals face 50–80x higher MI risk during vigorous exercise. Young athletes may die from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital coronary anomalies, aortic stenosis, arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia, and long QT syndromes. Circadian variation: adults peak SCD risk during early morning exercise; young athletes vulnerable in afternoon/evening. Exercise-induced hypertension (EIH) defined as systolic BP >190 mmHg (females) / >210 mmHg (males); exercise should terminate if systolic >250 or diastolic >115 mmHg. Vigorous exercise slows coronary artery calcification progression while very vigorous exercise accelerates it. Athletic heart syndrome and detraining effects discussed.

- RESPIRATORY: PAH shifted from absolute contraindication to supervised training (RCT n=116, small). Low-risk PAH criteria per ESC/ERS 2022 guidelines: WHO class I-II, 6MWT >440m, no right heart failure signs, near-normal NT-proBNP. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) develops within 15 min after 5–8 min of high-intensity aerobic training; prevention includes pre-exercise SABA, ≥10 min warm-up, avoiding cold/dry air. ILD patients commonly develop exertional hypoxemia (~40% cannot maintain O2 saturation >88% even with supplemental oxygen); monitoring via continuous pulse oximetry targeting SpO2 ≥88%, short-interval training, 6MWT with oximetry.

- RENAL: CKD exercise is complex due to variable stages and electrolytes. Non-dialysis CKD: resistance exercise benefits weighed against LDL elevations and fistula injury risk. Hot/humid climates reduce renal blood flow by 15–30%. Specific protocols: CKD stages 1–3 (150 min/week moderate aerobic, resistance 2–3x/week); stages 4–5 (90–150 min/week, supervised); dialysis (intra-dialytic cycling 30–45 min, 3x/week). Kidney transplant recipients: moderate/vigorous exercise reduces kidney blood flow ~20% and ~52%, respectively; avoid contact/collision sports due to graft trauma risk; fluoroquinolone therapy increases Achilles tendinopathy risk. Polycystic kidney disease patients should avoid contact exercise.

CONCLUSIONS: Exercise is a powerful therapeutic intervention requiring individualized, condition-specific risk stratification. Safe implementation depends on structured pre-exercise evaluation, recognition of absolute/relative contraindications, supervision, and ongoing monitoring. Substantial evidence gaps exist in hepatology, advanced ILD, and rare neurological conditions where RCT data are lacking. Multidisciplinary coordination and improved physician–exercise professional communication are essential. A clinical decision algorithm and structured summary tables are provided.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS: Exercise prescription requires individualized, condition-specific risk stratification; adverse events range from musculoskeletal injury to life-threatening arrhythmias, hypoglycemia, and rhabdomyolysis; special populations (children, transplant recipients, elderly with comorbidities) warrant narrower safety margins; structured pre-exercise evaluation and multidisciplinary coordination are essential.
args.key_excerpts: "Exercise is a powerful therapeutic intervention that requires individualized prescription to maximize benefits and minimize potential risks. Safe implementation depends on structured pre-exercise evaluation, condition-specific risk stratification, recognition of absolute and relative contraindications, appropriate supervision, and ongoing monitoring."

## Abstract

### Objectives

To examine the effects of different protocols of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on VO 2 max improvements in healthy, overweight/obese and athletic adults, based on the classifications of work intervals, session volumes and training periods.

### Design

[Systematic review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/systematic-review) and meta-analysis.

### Methods

PubMed, [Scopus](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/scopus), Medline, and Web of Science databases were searched up to April 2018. Inclusion criteria were [randomised controlled trials](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/randomized-controlled-trial); healthy, overweight/obese or athletic adults; examined pre- and post-training VO 2 max/peak; HIIT in comparison to control or moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) groups.

### Results

Fifty-three studies met the eligibility criteria. Overall, the degree of change in VO 2 max induced by HIIT varied by populations (SMD=0.41–1.81, _p<_ 0.05). When compared to control groups, even short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min) and short-term HIIT (≤4 weeks) elicited clear beneficial effects (SMD=0.79–1.65, _p<_ 0.05) on VO 2 max/peak. However, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min) and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT displayed significantly larger effects on VO 2 max (SMD=0.50–2.48, _p_<0.05). When compared to MICT, only long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min) and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT showed beneficial effects (SMD=0.65–1.07, _p_<0.05).

### Conclusions

Short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min) and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT represent effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO 2 max, especially for the general population. To maximize the training effects on VO 2 max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min) and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended.

This webpage presents a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (Volume 22, Issue 8, August 2019, Pages 941-947) titled "Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials." The study was conducted by Daizong Wen, Till Utesch, Jun Wu, Samuel Robertson, John Liu, Guopeng Hu, and Haichun Chen (DOI: 10.1016/j.jsams.2019.01.013).

OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of different HIIT protocols on VO2max improvements in healthy, overweight/obese, and athletic adults, based on classifications of work intervals, session volumes, and training periods.

METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Medline, and Web of Science databases were searched up to April 2018. Inclusion criteria were randomised controlled trials involving healthy, overweight/obese, or athletic adults, examining pre- and post-training VO2max/peak, with HIIT compared to control or moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) groups.

RESULTS: Of 1,190 articles initially identified, 53 studies met eligibility criteria. The degree of change in VO2max induced by HIIT varied by populations (SMD=0.41–1.81, p<0.05). Compared to control groups, even short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term HIIT (≤4 weeks) elicited clear beneficial effects (SMD=0.79–1.65, p<0.05) on VO2max/peak. However, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT displayed significantly larger effects on VO2max (SMD=0.50–2.48, p<0.05). When compared to MICT, only long-interval, high-volume, and moderate to long-term HIIT showed beneficial effects (SMD=0.65–1.07, p<0.05).

CONCLUSIONS: Short-interval (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT are effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2max, especially for the general population. To maximize training effects on VO2max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended. The study was supported by the Key Laboratory of Physical Motor Function Assessment, General Administration of Sport of China. The article has been cited 218 times and is part of the JSAMS Highlights 2018 and 2019 special issue. The authors reported no conflicts of interest.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791)Abstract

Consensus is lacking regarding whether high-intensity interval training (HIIT) effectively improves VO 2 max (VO 2 peak) in elite athletes (Athlete must be involved in regular competition at the national level). This meta-analysis compared the effects of HIIT and conventional training methods (continuous training, repeated-sprint training, high volume low-intensity training, high-intensity continuous running, sprint-interval training, moderate-intensity continuous training)on VO 2 max in elite athletes. Nine studies were included, comprising 176 elite athletes (80 female). Compared to that with conventional training, VO 2 max was significantly increased after HIIT (overall: 0.58 [0.30, 0.87], I 2=0.49, P=0.03; males: 0.41 [0.06, 0.76], I 2=0%, P=0.89). VO 2 max had positive training effects when the HIIT recovery period had an interval time ≥2 min (0.44 [0.03, 0.84], I 2=0%, P=0.99) and recovery phase intensity ≤40% (0.38 [0.05, 0.71], I 2=0%, P=0.96). Thus, HIIT shows superiority over conventional training methods in improving VO 2 max, promoting aerobic capacity, in elite athletes.

**Keywords:**Meta-Analysis, High-intensity interval training, Elite athlete, VO 2 max

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791)Introduction

1
The ultimate goal of athletes and coaches is to obtain excellent performance. In order to stand on the highest podium, athletes must reach or create their highest level of sports performance. For elite athletes, knowing how to select and combine training programs to improve their sports performance is crucial.

Elite-athletes maintain a high level of training for a long time, at this point, routine training has limited effect on the improvement of capacity, so it is necessary to consider new training methods. Generally, the higher VO 2 max (VO 2 peak), the great aerobic and health. Did HIIT has a positive effect on VO 2 max (VO 2 peak) in elite athletes? If HIIT could enhance VO 2 max, how different HIIT composition methods (such as intensity, the length of intermittent recovery period, and the intensity of intermittent) produced different training effects. Coaches and athletes needed to “convince” of the importance of HIIT for VO 2 max. By study the effect of various possible factors of HIIT on VO 2 max of elite athletes, in order to provide help for high-level training.

In contrast to studies on elite athletes, most studies were conducted on non-elite athletes (adolescent athlete collegiate athlete), healthy adults, patients [[[1]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib1), [[2]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib2), [[3]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib3), [[4]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib4), [[5]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib5), [[6]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib6), [[7]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib7)]. The results showed that HIIT were more easily to traditional training methods in improving VO 2 max, and has nothing to do with HIIT approach.

HIIT has improved anaerobic and aerobic capacity (VO 2 max), physical fitness in highly trained athletes [[[8]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib8), [[9]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib9), [[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib10), [[11]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib11)]. Ravier found that HIIT can significantly improve both the VO 2 max (4.6%) and anaerobic capacity (10.3%) of elite male Karate athletes [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib12)]. During some rowing race, both aerobic and anaerobic energy systems are high demands [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib13)]. For a long time, it was widely believed that aerobic exercise is an effective training method for improving aerobic capacity, while anaerobic exercise is an effective training method for improving anaerobic capacity [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib14)]. However, when humans exercise for 2 min to exhaustion, oxygen deficiency reaches it maximum, which suggests that when the aerobic oxidation energy supply system is fully mobilized, the anaerobic energy supply system is also mobilized to its maximum. When humans exercise for 30 s to exhaustion, about 30% of the energy supply depends on the aerobic energy system; even after 10 s of exhausting exercise, 10% of the energy still comes from the aerobic system [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib15)]. Therefore, when athletes meet a bottleneck in training, they can break through themselves through HIIT to improve their athletic ability.

Accordingly, there is no simple distinction between aerobic and anaerobic exercise [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib15)], and Laursen thought that HIT can be defined as a repeated set of exercises of short to moderate duration completed at an intensity above the anaerobic threshold. In fact, exceeding the anaerobic threshold is an important basis for HIIT [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib16)], which provides the theoretical basis for the popularity of HIIT worldwide. Compared to other training methods, HIIT is characterized by a short duration, time efficiency, high intensity, and small amount of exercise. However, the training effect can reach, or even exceed, that with conventional methods, and its unique training mode meets the training purposes of aerobic and anaerobic oxidation.

Numerous studies have shown that HIIT significantly improves athletic performance, and aerobic and anaerobic capacity [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib17)]. Furthermore, HIIT effectively improves anaerobic capacity [[[18]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib18), [[19]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib19), [[20]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib20)] and maximum oxygen consumption in athletes [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib18),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib21),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib22)], and the lower limb training model of HIIT improves anaerobic and aerobic capacity [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib23),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib24)]. Engel et al. found that HIIT not only improves the aerobic capacity of young athletes, but also promotes anaerobic capacity and sports performance [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib25)]. Laursen and Jenkins reported that HIIT improves VO 2 max by approximately 6%–8% in high-level cyclists [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib26)]. Gunnarsson found that HIIT improves the work efficiency by 3%–6% in elite soccer players [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib27)]. Kinnunen et al. found that HIIT effectively improves neuromuscular efficiency and explosive power in ice hockey players [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib28)]. Other studies found that HIIT improved athletes repeated sprint ability [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib21)], sprint ability [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib22)], ice speed [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib20)], and vertical jump height [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib29)]. Additionally, Monks et al. found that HIIT increased anaerobic capacity by 10.3% and aerobic capacity (VO 2 max) by 4.6% in elite karate athletes [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib2)]. Christensen et al. found that the perfect design of HIIT can effectively improve the performance of elite athletes by 2%–3% [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib9)].

Besides HIIT could promote adaptive changes in physiological indicators. Gibala et al. found that HIIT effectively promotes muscle and cardiovascular adaptive changes in athletes [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib30)]. Clemente-Suárez et al. found HIIT training improves the functioning of the autonomic and parasympathetic nervous systems [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib31)]. Some researchers found that HIIT was to be effective in improving VO 2 max [[[32]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib32), [[33]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib33), [[34]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib34)] and running economy in endurance runners. This may be an increased oxidative capacity and a reduced plasma K+ concentration, which contributes to delay fatigue [[[33]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib33), [[34]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib34), [[35]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib35)]. Compared with continue running, intensive running requires the activation of larger motor units, with increased recruitment of fast oxidative and glycolytic muscle-fiber, which contributes the contractile ability of the muscle [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib36),[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib37)]. Thus, regardless of the type of exercise, both aerobic and anaerobic energy supply systems are involved.

In addition to HIIT has been applied in various sports as an effective training method; specifically, some coaches have used HIIT to improve aerobic capacity [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib26),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib27),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib38)]. However, some studies have suggested that HIIT impairs athletic performance. For example, Kingsley et al. suggested that HIIT could cause muscle damage and pain, as well as increase biomarkers of cell damage and lipid peroxidation [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib39)]. Bloomer and Goldfarb found that HIIT induces lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, and inflammatory responses, causing muscle cell damage and affecting the function of structural and contractile proteins [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib40)]. These muscular disorders can affect the athlete's physiological function and athletic performance [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib41)].

Although there are many studies on HIIT, most of them have focused on adolescents, sedentary populations, and patients. The results showed that HIIT improved the VO 2 max of these subjects more easily than traditional training methods [[[1]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib1), [[2]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib2), [[3]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib3), [[4]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib4), [[5]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib5), [[6]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib6), [[7]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib7)]. Studies on HIIT in elite athletes are limited, and there is some controversy about the training effects of HIIT [[[39]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib39), [[40]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib40), [[41]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib41)]. In addition, HIIT meta-studies on elite, high-level athletes are lacking. Therefore, we conducted a meta-analysis of the HIIT effect on high-level elite athletes in an effort to better understand the aerobic performance of elite athletes after HIIT; explore the possible training and physiological mechanisms of HIIT, to provide theoretical support for HIIT methods, with scientific insights for future studies.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791)Materials and methods

2
### Search strategy

2.1
The systematic review was conducted applying the guidelines of PRISMA [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib42)]. The following databases were searched from the time of their inception to March 2022: LISTA(37), PubMed(512), Web of Science(664), and China National Knowledge Internet(172). The following terms were used in the database searches: “high intensity interval training, high intensity training, intensive interval training, intensity training, sprint interval training, HIIT, HIT, IIT, or SIT” and “athlete”.

Intensity≥ 85%(PPO, HRmax, Pmax, VO 2 peak, MAP, vVO 2 peak).

HR, heart rate; HRmax, maximal HR; MAP, maximal aerobic power; PPO, power-output; Pmax, minimal power output to elicit VO 2 peak; vVO 2 peak, velocity of the VO 2 peak.

### Inclusion criteria

2.2
Studies inclusion criteria were as follows: the study was a published experimental study; the study had a control training group; the study focused on high-level athletes; the HIIT training period was ≥3 weeks and the number of training session per week was ≥2 times; and the study specified the HIIT training intensity.

Elite athlete must be involved in regular competition at the national level.

### Exclusion criteria

2.3
The study exclusion criteria were as follows: the study was a duplicate publication; the study population comprised adolescents and children; the study focused on drug interactions; the study focused on the combined effects of nutrition and tonics; the research object comprised patients; the study was a Masters or Doctoral dissertation; and the language is not English or Chinese.

### Data extraction and risk of bias

2.4
In this paper, the data used are mean value and standard deviation from published journals. In one case, the data was obtained by contacting the corresponding author [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib43)].

The PEDro scale was used to evaluate study quality and risk of bias. Two researchers evaluated the quality and risk of bias of the included studies in accordance with Sherrington C et al. [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib44)]. The deviation risk for 11 items in the PEDro scale was evaluated as “yes”, “unknown”, or “no” for each included study. Differences of opinion were resolved by discussion with a third researcher.

The assessment criteria included: 1. Eligibility criteria were specified; 2. Subjects were randomly allocated to groups (in a crossover study, subjects were randomly allocated an order in which treatments were received); 3. allocation was concealed; 4. The groups were similar at baseline regarding the most important prognostic indicators; 5. There was blinding of all subjects; 6. There was blinding of all therapists who administered the therapy; 7. There was blinding of all assessors who measured at least one key outcome; 8. Measures of at least one key outcome were obtained from more than 85% of the subjects initially allocated to groups; 9. All subjects for whom outcome measures were available received the treatment or control condition as allocated or, where this was not the case, data for at least one key outcome was analyzed by “intention to treat”; 10. The results of between-group statistical comparisons are reported for at least one key outcome; 11. The study provides both point measures and measures of variability for at least one key outcome.

Studies were evaluated by classifying each study criterion as low risk of bias, moderate risk of bias, or high risk of bias. When Score ≦4, “high”, 4＜Score≦6, “moderate”, score≥7, “low”.

### Statistical Analysis

2.5
The meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.3 software. Homogeneity testing was conducted for included studies. The homogeneity was tested by chi-square test. When I 2＜50%, and P>0.05, homogeneity was considered. If the included studies were homogenous, the fixed-effect model was adopted; if there was heterogeneity, the random-effect model was adopted. Subgroup analyses were conducted to exclude heterogeneity. Combined statistical analysis was performed using the weighted mean difference (WMD) and 95% confidence interval (CI). The level of statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

### Effect of HIIT on VO 2 max in elite athletes

3.3

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791)Discussion

4
### HIIT and VO 2 max (VO 2 peak)

4.1
VO 2 max reflects the overall working status of cardiopulmonary and muscle oxidation functions [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib45),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib46)], and is an effective index for evaluating endurance sports. In elite athletes, VO2max has reached a high level because of long-term planned training, and VO2max is greatly affected by genetic factors, so increases in VO2max are very small, however it is urgent for athletes to improve their ability, therefore, it is necessary to carefully select an effective training program to improve the physiological status of VO2max in elite athletes.

In the present meta-analysis, HIIT had a positive effect on VO 2 max in elite athletes ([Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#fig3)). Through the subgroup analysis of gender, intensity, the interval time and exercise program, it was found that the athletes were male, the recovery interval time was ≥2 min, the recovery interval intensity was ≤40%, the routine training intensity was ≤75%, except for taekwondo, tennis and kayaking athlete, VO2max was enhanced ([Figs. 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#fig4)–7,9). When the object of study were taekwondo, tennis and kayaking athletes, Although HIIT was found to have an effect on VO2max in such athletes, it was not statistically significant because the analysis results were heterogeneous, but according to the original literature, HIIT has been shown to increase VO2max such athletes. The reason for the heterogeneity may be that after HIIT training, the VO2max of taekwondo athletes (4.7±1.49 ml/kg/min) increased more than that of tennis(2.8±3.579 ml/kg/min) and kayaking athletes(2.02±5.37 ml/kg/min). From the results, some HIIT scheme could facilitate VO 2 max.Therefor, if athletes can choose the most appropriate HIIT that can promote higher VO 2 max

How did HIIT contribute to the increase VO 2 max? IT is possible that HIIT increased cardiac output, thereby boosting VO 2 max. Fernandez-Fernandez et al. found that achieving and maintaining a high filling pressure in the heart is necessary to improve cardiac function [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib47)]; thus, training at the maximum intensity cardiac output per stroke is important. Studies have found that before fatigue, the cardiac output per stroke reaches its peak during exercise in approximately 1 min [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib48)], 2 min [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib18),[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib49)], or 4 min [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib50)]. Thus, to improve the stroke volume in athletes, the duration of each HIIT interval should not be<60sec. The evidence for short-duration (<60sec) HIIT in improving cardiac stroke volume is limited，however, short-duration HIIT may limit the effectiveness of the venous muscle pump, which in turn limits the maintenance of each stoke volume during the recovery period [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib51)]. Furthermore, Nybo et al. suggested that the difference between the cardiac output and arterial venous oxygen concentration (a-vDO 2) may determine VO 2 max [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib52)]. Macpherson et al. found that although VO 2 max increased by 12% after a 6-week sprint interval training program, the maximum cardiac output did not change, which might underlie improvements in peripheral a-vDO 2 [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib53)]. Above all, HIIT increases the recruitment of rapid oxidation and glycolytic muscle fibers, which contribute to muscle contraction capacity, and changes in muscle contractility promote venous blood return and maintain cardiac output. In addition, varying the type of exercise, intensity, and recovery time during intervals can also help boost cardiac output. Nybo and Warburton found that, in patients and the general population, the maximum stroke volume occurred during the intermittent recovery period of HIIT [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib52),[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib54)]. The results of Buchheit, Racinais, Girard, and Laursen in elite cyclists are consistent with those of Cumming and Takahashi [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib53)]. Similarly, Iaia and Bangsbo found that, regardless of the type of exercise (incremental load test, 3-min pVO2max test, or 15-s sprint run test), the maximum amount of exercise per stroke occurred during the intermittent recovery period [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib55)]. Therefore, the intermittent recovery mode of HIIT can enhance the adaptability of cardiovascular function to sports in athletes. Although VO2max may be determined by the effect of the intensity and form of HIIT intermittent recovery on the stroke volume, Stanley and Buchheit et al. found that the stroke output was the same for HIIT intermittent recovery periods of 0%, 30%, and 60% VO2max intensity in elite cyclists [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib30)]. In addition, during HIIT interval recovery, a long interval (>2 min) is conducive to maximizing the stroke volume [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib30),[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib56)]. The present meta-analysis found that HIIT with interval recovery duration ≥2 min and intensity ≤40% improved the VO 2 max in elite athletes ([Fig. 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#fig5), [Fig. 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#fig6)), which may promote improved cardiac output and peripheral aerobic metabolism capacity.

Illi et al. found that the training intensity promoted the oxidative adaptability of muscle fibers only when the HIIT intensity was close to VO 2 max [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib57)]. Under this condition, the recruitment of motor units, maximum ventilation rate, and cardiac output jointly induced VO 2 max [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib58)]. Laursen and Jenkins found that effective physiological stimulation only occurs when the HIIT training intensity is at least 90% VO 2 max and is sustained for several minutes, which could increase VO 2 max [[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib59),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib60)]. In the present meta-analysis, the HIIT intensities of the studies that showed improvement in VO 2 max included 100% all-out power, >90–95% maximal heart rate (HRmax), minimal power output to elicit VO 2 peak, 85%–100% HRmax, 90%–100% maximal aerobic power, 100% velocity of the VO 2 peak, and ≥90% VO 2 max, with training times that could be>200 s.

Effective training methods can promote improvement in VO2max in athletes. According to specific training theories and the SAID principle, which asserts that the human body adapts specifically to applied demands, specific HIIT protocols can promote improvement in athletes' physiological function for different sports [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib30),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib61)]. Based on this principle, training methods similar to one's own sport should be selected, and athletes should repeatedly-training within their own limits. To promote the adaptability of the physiological system and achieve training effects, HIIT is the perfect method for specific training needs and applications.

### HIIT and aerobic and anaerobic capacity

4.2
HIIT may promote improvement in aerobic capacity via various mechanisms, such as increased ventilation threshold [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib62)]; enhanced mitochondrial enzyme activity [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib50)], lipid oxidation [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib63)], and H+ elimination ability; increased glycogen utilization and reduced lactic acid accumulation [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib50)]; and improved cardiovascular function (enlarged heart, increased blood flow capacity, and arterial dilation) [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib64),[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib65)]. These adaptive changes in human physiology improve the ability of the cardiovascular system to transport oxygen, thus promoting improvements in human aerobic capacity [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib64)].

HIIT can also improve anaerobic capacity in elite athletes. Studies have found that HIIT improves the anaerobic ability of athletes by 12% [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib8),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib17),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib66)]. HIIT may impose greater load intensity on muscles, resulting in the promotion of rapid contraction muscle development [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib29)]; enhanced glycolysis capacity [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib62)] and glycolysis enzyme activity (lactate dehydrogenase, phosphofructokinase, glycogen phosphorylase) [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib67)]; accelerated energy conversion rate of glycolysis [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib47)]; increased number of myo-membrane transporters [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib48)]; and enhanced muscle buffering capacity [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib68)].

From the above we can know that HIIT can not only improve the VO2max of endurance exercise, but also improve the VO2max of anaerobic capacity exercise.

This may be HIIT improves aerobic and anaerobic capacity in different ways. Improvement in aerobic capacity is more about the development of heart function and slow contraction muscle, while the regulation of anaerobic capacity is more about fast twitch contraction muscle. Thus, HIIT may promote improvement in the aerobic capacity of fast twitch muscle and the anaerobic capacity of slow twitch muscle. Suitable HIIT methods can regulate and improve the proportion of ATP and ADP in the body. The accumulation of metabolites and free radicals in muscle; glycogen reserve; and rates of carbohydrate oxidation, mitochondrial content, and fat oxidation, GLUT4 transporter, glycogen content, and oxidative fiber conversion are increased with HIIT [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib17)]. The synthesis efficiency of mitochondrial protein is also improved. All of these features promote both aerobic and anaerobic capacity.

### Possible mechanisms of different HIIT combination modes

4.3
Different HIIT protocols (differing in intensity, duration, number of sessions, number of intervals, and mode of rest) can affect specific metabolic pathways and neuromuscular functions in muscle cells. Buchheit and Laursen suggested that acute physiological changes after different HIIT methods could be described based on three metabolic energy supply modes (ATP/CP, glycolysis, and oxidative metabolism) and the load status of the nervous skeletal muscle system [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib69)]. The oxidase pathway of aerobic metabolism and the glycolytic enzyme system (ATP) of anaerobic metabolism are significantly upregulated after different forms of HIIT [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib68),[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib70),[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791#bib71)]. Therefore, priority should be given to aerobic ability training, with anaerobic ability training as an auxiliary method, which is often the more preferred mode of training for coaches and athletes. The advantage of anaerobic ability training is to promote better resistance against fatigue. The priority with aerobic exercise, with nerve muscle stress as the auxiliary role of training, is to improve the overall physical ability. In practice, in order to achieve the best training effect, the coach must be clear about the training purpose and select the HIIT mode with a clear target.

### Limitations

4.4
This review has several limitations. First, a total of 9 articles were included in this paper, among which 4 articles did not divide the research objects between genders. Moreover, as the research objects were high-level athletes, the sample size of the 7 articles was small (<10). Second, the included studies used different HIIT regimens (exercise style, interval time, intensity, duration). The purpose of this paper is to provide the best evidence in HIIT practice, and our results justify the need for more rigorous research with great methods and larger sample sizes to strengthen the quality of existing evidence and determine HIIT most positively affect VO2max in elite athletes.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791)Conclusions

5
Accumulating studies have evaluated HIIT methods in the training practices of athletes. Compared to that with other training methods, HIIT can slightly improve VO2max and sports performance, and promote improvement in aerobic and anaerobic capacity. Considering the training specificity of elite athletes, the value of HIIT training is worthwhile. During practice, coaches should reasonably select the HIIT form according to the training purpose.

### Practical implications

5.1
This report comprises the first meta-analysis of the HIIT effect in elite athletes. VO2max (VO2peak) was increased after HIIT in elite athletes. For excellent endurance and to better enhance the training effect, athletes should undergo not only aerobic ability training, but also anaerobic ability training. The recovery intensity and duration of HIIT play important roles in the cardiopulmonary function of endurance athletes.

args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in Heliyon (June 1, 2023) examining the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on VO2 max (VO2 peak) in elite athletes. The study, authored by Xianghua Ma, Zhenbo Cao, Zheng Zhu, Xiangru Chen, Donglin Wen, and Ziwei Cao from Shanghai University of Sport and Xi'an Physical Education University, China, was funded by the Science and Technology Department of Shaanxi Province (grant no. 2021JM-529).

METHODOLOGY: A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted across four databases (LISTA, PubMed, Web of Science, and China National Knowledge Internet) from inception to March 2022. Nine studies (8 English, 1 Chinese) met inclusion criteria, comprising 176 elite athletes (80 female) across sports including kayaking, tennis, taekwondo, triathlon, and cycling. Inclusion criteria required published experimental studies with a control group, focus on high-level (national-level competition) athletes, HIIT training period ≥3 weeks, ≥2 sessions per week, and specified training intensity. Study quality was assessed using the PEDro scale (average score 7.2/11; 6 studies low risk, 3 moderate risk). Meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.3 with weighted mean difference and 95% confidence intervals.

KEY RESULTS: Compared to conventional training (continuous training, repeated-sprint training, high-volume low-intensity training, high-intensity continuous running, sprint-interval training, moderate-intensity continuous training), VO2 max was significantly increased after HIIT (overall effect size: 0.58 [0.30, 0.87], P=0.03, I²=0.49). Significant subgroup findings included: males (0.41 [0.06, 0.76], P=0.89, I²=0%), recovery interval ≥2 min (0.44 [0.03, 0.84], P=0.99, I²=0%), recovery phase intensity ≤40% (0.38 [0.05, 0.71], P=0.96, I²=0%), control training intensity ≤75% (0.42 [0.11, 0.73], P=0.008), and taekwondo/tennis/kayaking athletes (0.99 [0.50, 1.48], P<0.0001, though with high heterogeneity I²=80%).

DISCUSSION & MECHANISMS: The study proposes that HIIT improves VO2 max through increased cardiac output (with peak stroke volume occurring during intermittent recovery periods, requiring interval durations not less than 60 seconds), enhanced recruitment of fast oxidative and glycolytic muscle fibers, increased mitochondrial enzyme activity, improved ventilation threshold, enhanced lipid oxidation, and improved cardiovascular function. HIIT intensities that showed improvement included 90-100% of HRmax, VO2 max, MAP, and other maximal parameters. HIIT also improves anaerobic capacity (~12% improvement) through enhanced glycolysis capacity, muscle buffering capacity, and fast-twitch muscle development.

LIMITATIONS: Only 9 articles were included; 4 did not divide subjects by gender; 7 studies had small samples (<10 subjects); and HIIT regimens varied significantly across studies in exercise style, interval time, intensity, and duration.

CONCLUSIONS: HIIT shows superiority over conventional training methods in improving VO2 max and aerobic capacity in elite athletes. This is the first meta-analysis of HIIT effects specifically in elite athletes. Practical implications include that coaches should select HIIT forms according to training purpose, and athletes should undergo both aerobic and anaerobic training. Recovery intensity and duration of HIIT play important roles in cardiopulmonary function of endurance athletes.
