This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
Vol.:(0123456789) European Journal of Applied Physiology https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-025-05975-z ORIGINAL ARTICLE Sprint interval training for cardiovascular prevention: a time‑efficient alternative or an overstated promise? An umbrella review Weibao Liang1,2 · Chuannan Liu6 · Shuting Xu4 · Shuhui Ma3 · Yue Zong5 · Xujie Yan3 Received: 5 July 2025 / Accepted: 30 August 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2025 Abstract Purpose Sprint interval training (SIT) is a time-efficient strategy for improving cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). However, existing systematic reviews show conflicting results and variable quality. This umbrella review synthesizes this evidence to appraise the certainty of SIT’s effects on CRF.
Methods A systematic search was conducted in six databases for systematic reviews with meta-analyses comparing SIT with non-exercise control conditions and other comparator training modalities such as moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT), or high-intensity interval training (HIIT). The methodological quality of included systematic reviews was assessed using AMSTAR-2.
Results Sixteen systematic reviews were included, with a majority (9/16) rated as ‘Low’ or ‘Critically Low’ methodologi-cal quality. The 16 included reviews synthesized data from 393 unique primary studies and more than 8642 participants, encompassing populations from healthy sedentary adults and athletes to individuals with cardiovascular risk factors. Pooled data showed SIT elicited a significant improvement in CRF versus control (Standardized Mean Difference [SMD] = 0.59; 95% CI 0.43–0.74). In contrast, no significant difference was found between SIT and MICT (SMD = 0.07; 95% CI – 0.03 to 0.16). Evidence comparing SIT to HIIT was inconclusive.
Conclusion SIT is an effective intervention for improving CRF compared to no exercise. However, current evidence, espe-cially from higher-quality systematic reviews, does not support SIT’s superiority over MICT. Confidence in these findings is limited by prevalent methodological flaws, underscoring the need for more rigorous primary and secondary research.
Trial registration PROSPERO ID CRD420251074348.
Keywords Sprint interval training · Moderate-intensity continuous training · High-intensity interval training · Cardiorespiratory fitness · VO2max Abbreviations ACSM  American College of Sports Medicine AHA  American Heart Association AMSTAR-2  A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews 2 BJSM  British Journal of Sports Medicine CCA​  Corrected Covered Area CI  Confidence Interval CRF  Cardiorespiratory Fitness CT  Continuous Training CVD  Cardiovascular Disease EAPC  European Association of Preventive Cardiology EJPC  European Journal of Preventive Cardiology Communicated by Michalis G Nikolaidis. * Xujie Yan yanxj0515@126.com 1 School of Physical Education and Sports Science, Hengyang Normal University, Hengyang, China 2 Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Speed Capability Research, Su Bingtian Center for Speed Research and Training, School of Physical Education, Jinan University, Guangzhou, China 3 Present Address: School of Physical Education and Sports Science, South China Normal University, Guangzhou, China 4 The First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University, Guangzhou, China 5 School of Physical Education, Guangdong Technology College, Zhaoqing, China 6 School of Physical Education and Health, Zunyi Mdedical University, Zunyi, China European Journal of Applied Physiology ESC  European Society of Cardiology ET  Endurance Training GRADE  Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations HIIT  High-Intensity Interval Training HRR  Heart Rate Reserve ICC  Intraclass Correlation Coefficient IQR  Interquartile Range; MA, Meta-Analysis MD  Mean Difference MET  Metabolic Equivalent MICT  Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training MSSE  Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise PICO  Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome PRISMA  Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses PROSPERO  International Prospective Register of Sys-tematic Reviews RCT​  Randomized Controlled Trial RoB  Risk of Bias RST  Repeated-Sprint Training SBP  Systolic Blood Pressure SD  Standard Deviation SE  Standard Error SIT  Sprint Interval Training sSIT  Short-Sprint Interval Training SMD  Standardized Mean Difference SR  Systematic Review TT  Time-Trial VO2max  Maximal Oxygen Uptake VO2peak  Peak Oxygen Uptake WMD  Weighted Mean Difference Introduction Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), most commonly quantified by maximal oxygen uptake ­ (VO2max), is well-established as one of the most potent clinical predictors of all-cause mor-tality and cardiovascular events, independent of traditional risk factors such as hypertension and smoking(Kodama 2009; Ross et al. 2016). It reflects the integrated capacity of the body to transport and utilize oxygen during maxi-mal exertion (Gibala et al. 2012). A substantial body of epidemiological evidence indicates that higher levels of CRF are strongly associated with a significantly lower risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular morbidity, with a prognostic power that can surpass that of conventional risk factors like smoking, hypertension, and diabetes (Mandsager et al. 2018). Given that each 1-metabolic equivalent (MET) improvement in CRF corresponds to a 13–15% reduction in mortality risk, the American Heart Association (AHA) has advocated for the assessment of CRF as a clinical vital sign(Ross et al. 2016). Consequently, implementing effec-tive interventions to improve CRF is a primary objective in preventive cardiology and clinical practice (Blair 2009).
Traditionally, moderate-intensity continuous train-ing (MICT) is the cornerstone of recommendations from authoritative bodies such as the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM 2025) and the European Society of Car-diology (ESC) for improving CRF and promoting health (Garber et al. 2011; Pelliccia et al. 2021). However, MICT protocols typically require a substantial time commitment. “Lack of time” is one of the most frequently cited barriers to regular physical activity engagement among the general population (Trost et al. 2002; Bull et al. 2020), which signifi-cantly limits the adherence to and effectiveness of exercise prescriptions in real-world settings (Mezzani et al. 2013).
To address this challenge, time-efficient training para-digms such as high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and sprint interval training (SIT) have garnered considerable attention and are increasingly viewed as having therapeu-tic potential (Weston et al. 2014). HIIT is generally defined as intermittent exercise performed at submaximal intensi-ties (e.g., > 80% ­ VO2max) for relatively prolonged dura-tions (e.g., > 60 s), whereas SIT represents the apex of the intensity spectrum. SIT is characterized by repeated, brief bouts (typically ≤ 30 s) of “all-out” or supramaximal effort, interspersed with longer, often passive, recovery periods (Buchheit and Laursen 2013). A large body of seminal research has demonstrated that despite a substantially lower total training volume and time commitment, SIT can induce comparable, or even superior, adaptations in skeletal muscle mitochondria and improvements in CRF, establishing it as an attractive time-efficient training paradigm (Burgomaster et al. 2008; Gibala et al. 2012; Sloth et al. 2013a; Vollaard et al. 2017).
With the rapid proliferation of research on SIT, numer-ous systematic reviews (SRs) and meta-analyses (MAs) have sought to summarize its effects, generally confirming its efficacy in improving CRF (Gist et al. 2014; Vollaard et al. 2017). However, the existing body of SRs and MAs has several limitations. First, there is significant heterogeneity in the SIT protocols included in these reviews, encompassing wide variations in sprint duration, recovery time, number of repetitions, and total training period. This heterogeneity may lead to inconsistent conclusions and obscures the identifica-tion of optimal SIT protocols. Second, many earlier meta-analyses often aggregated SIT and HIIT, failing to clearly distinguish the unique physiological adaptations associated with “all-out” sprinting. More recent systematic reviews that directly compare these two high-intensity modalities have yielded nuanced and sometimes conflicting conclusions. For instance, some meta-analyses (de Oliveira-Nunes et al. 2021; Boullosa et al. 2022) concluded that there are no signifi-cant overall differences in VO₂max improvements between European Journal of Applied Physiology SIT and HIIT. However, the picture is complicated by other findings. The meta-analysis by Rosenblat (Rosenblat et al. 2020), while finding no overall difference in VO₂max in trained athletes, noted that long-duration HIIT (i.e., inter-vals ≥ 4 min) may be superior for enhancing endurance time-trial performance. Furthermore, a large meta-analysis (Mattioni Maturana et al. 2021) provided indirect evidence suggesting HIIT’s potential superiority, as their subgroup analysis found HIIT to be significantly more effective than MICT for improving VO₂max, whereas SIT was not. This complex landscape of direct equivalence, potential perfor-mance-specific advantages for HIIT, and indirect evidence of HIIT’s greater efficacy highlights the uncertainty in the field. Furthermore, the populations in some reviews are narrowly focused, limiting the generalizability of their findings. For instance, several reviews concentrated specifically on on ath-letic or highly active populations (Yang et al. 2021; Boullosa et al. 2022; Thurlow et al. 2024). Others targeted distinct demographic groups, such as middle-aged and older adults (Poon et al. 2021) or reproductive-age women (Aparecido et al. 2022). Conversely, some reviews explicitly excluded certain groups (Rugbeer et al. 2021; Hall et al. 2023), such as athletes or individuals with obesity, further complicating the synthesis of evidence for the general population.
These factors limit the synthesis and reliability of the cur-rent evidence, providing uncertain guidance for clinical and practical application. While numerous reviews exist, there is a clear need for a higher-level evidence synthesis—an umbrella review—to systematically collate, appraise, and synthesize the findings from all available systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Such a review can provide a broader and more robust overview of the state of the evidence, resolve inconsistencies between reviews, and, crucially, evaluate the methodological rigor of the secondary evidence base itself.
To clearly delineate the contribution of our study, Table 1 contrasts the key features of our umbrella review with the typical characteristics of the systematic reviews it syn-thesizes. As illustrated, our work expands upon previous reviews by providing a more comprehensive scope—simul-taneously assessing all major training comparators across a broad range of populations. Most importantly, it introduces a higher level of methodological scrutiny by systematically appraising the quality of the existing secondary evidence itself, a critical step for determining the certainty of the cur-rent evidence base.
Therefore, the aims of this umbrella review are: (1) to systematically collate and synthesize the evidence from all available systematic reviews and meta-analyses on the effects of SIT on cardiorespiratory fitness; (2) to provide an updated evidence hierarchy on the effects of SIT relative to different comparator interventions (control, MICT, and HIIT) by conducting secondary meta-analyses of homog-enous studies; and (3) to rigorously appraise the methodo-logical quality of the existing systematic reviews using the AMSTAR-2 tool to determine the certainty of the current evidence base.
Methods Protocol and reporting This umbrella review was conducted and is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for System-atic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Page et al. 2021). The review protocol was pre-registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO ID CRD420251074348).
Search strategy A systematic literature search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, the Cochrane Library, and Embase, from their inception to April 30, 2025. To ensure a com-prehensive search, we employed a strategy that combined Table 1 Distinguishing features of the present umbrella review compared to typical systematic reviews on the topic This table contrasts the key features of the current umbrella review with the generalized characteristics of the 16 systematic reviews it synthe-sizes, highlighting differences in review type, scope of comparisons, population focus, and the level of methodological appraisal. SR systematic review, MA meta-analysis, MICT moderate-intensity continuous training, HIIT high-intensity interval training, AMSTAR-2 A MeaSurement tool to assess systematic reviews 2 Feature Typical included systematic reviews Present umbrella review Review type Systematic review & meta-analysis (of primary studies) Umbrella review (of systematic reviews) Scope of comparators Focused on a single comparator (e.g., MICT only) or a pairwise comparison (e.g., SIT vs. Control) Comprehensive synthesis across all three major compara-tors (Control, MICT, and HIIT) Population focus Often narrow, focusing on specific populations (e.g., athletes, older adults, women) or health statuses Broad synthesis across diverse populations (from healthy to at-risk) Methodological appraisal Appraisal of included primary studies using various tools (e.g., PEDro, Cochrane RoB) Higher-level appraisal of systematic reviews themselves using the standardized AMSTAR-2 tool European Journal of Applied Physiology controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH, Emtree) with free-text keywords. Example search terms included, but were not lim-ited to, ‘sprint interval training’, ‘all-out interval exercise’, ‘repeated sprint training’, ‘cardiorespiratory fitness’, ‘maxi-mal oxygen uptake’, ‘VO2max’, ‘systematic review’, and ‘meta-analysis’. The search strategy was structured around three core concepts: (1) the intervention (sprint interval training), (2) the outcome (cardiorespiratory fitness), and (3) the study design (systematic review and meta-analysis). The detailed search strategy is provided in Supplementary Table S1.
Study eligibility criteria Peer-reviewed articles published in English that met the fol-lowing eligibility criteria, structured according to the PICOS framework, were included.
Types of studies Eligible articles were required to be systematic reviews that included a meta-analysis.
Population Reviews were deemed eligible if their study populations consisted of adults (mean age ≥ 18 years). To ensure compre-hensiveness, no strict limitations were placed on participant characteristics (e.g., health or training status), encompassing populations ranging from sedentary individuals and healthy adults to trained athletes and specific groups with cardiovas-cular risk factors (e.g., overweight/obese, prehypertensive/ hypertensive). Baseline population characteristics were con-sidered a potential moderating variable for subgroup analysis or discussion. Reviews focusing exclusively on populations with specific clinical pathologies (e.g., heart failure, coro-nary artery disease, COPD, stroke, spinal cord injury, dia-betes, or cancer) were excluded.
Intervention The intervention of interest was required to be Sprint Inter-val Training (SIT). SIT was operationally defined as a training protocol involving repeated bouts of "all-out" or supramaximal intensity exercise (i.e., ≥ 100% of ­ VO2max or peak power output). The total intervention period was required to be a minimum of two weeks. Reviews of inter-ventions where the independent effects of SIT could not be isolated (e.g., combined with specific nutritional supple-ments or resistance training) were excluded.
Comparator To comprehensively evaluate the effects of SIT, eligible comparators were divided into two distinct categories: other training modalities and non-exercise control conditions.
1. Comparator training modalities: These included other forms of structured exercise used to assess the relative efficacy of SIT: • Moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT): Defined as continuous exercise performed at a steady, moderate intensity (e.g., 60–80% of maximal effort) for a pro-longed duration.
• High-intensity interval training (HIIT): Defined as inter-mittent exercise involving repeated bouts of high, but submaximal, intensity (e.g., > 80% of maximal effort) interspersed with recovery periods.
2. Control conditions: These were used to assess the abso-lute effects of SIT compared to a non-SIT baseline and were sub-categorized as: • Inactive/No-Exercise control: A condition where partici-pants maintained a sedentary lifestyle or did not engage in any structured exercise intervention.
• Active control: A condition where participants contin-ued their usual sport-specific training or habitual physical activity without the addition of the SIT intervention.
Additionally, reviews that only reported pre-post inter-vention changes but provided a separate pooled effect size for SIT (Vollaard et al. 2017) were also included for the qualitative synthesis of SIT’s overall effects and the influ-ence of moderating variables.
Outcomes The primary outcome of interest was cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). Included systematic reviews were required to report CRF as maximal oxygen uptake ­ (VO2max) or peak oxygen uptake ­ (VO2peak), directly measured via gas analysis.
Data extraction Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers (WL and SX) using a pre-designed, standardized European Journal of Applied Physiology data extraction form. Any discrepancies encountered dur-ing this process were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, arbitration by a third reviewer (YZ).
The following key information was extracted from each included systematic review and meta-analysis: (1) General Characteristics: First author, year of publication, and the number and type of primary studies included (e.g., rand-omized controlled trials [RCTs]); (2) Participant Charac-teristics: Key characteristics of the participants in the pri-mary studies, including mean age, sex composition, health status, and training level (e.g., sedentary, active, trained athletes); (3) Training Protocol Details: Core variables for both the SIT intervention and all comparator groups (MICT, HIIT, control) were recorded, including: exercise mode, intensity, bout duration, recovery time and modal-ity, weekly frequency, and total intervention duration; (4) Outcome and Effect Size Data: For the quantitative synthesis of this umbrella review, the following core data related to CRF were extracted: the pooled effect size for each comparison (e.g., SIT vs. MICT), specified as either a Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) or a Weighted/ Mean Difference (WMD/MD); its corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI); the between-study heterogeneity statistic (e.g., ­ I2); and the number of primary studies con-tributing to the pooled estimate; (5) Methodological Qual-ity Information: The quality assessment tool used by each systematic review (e.g., AMSTAR-2, PEDro, Cochrane RoB) and their overall conclusions on the quality of their included studies.
Risk of bias assessment The methodological quality of each included review was assessed independently and in duplicate by two reviewers (CL, SM) using the AMSTAR-2 (A MeaSurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews) tool (Shea et al. 2017). Disagreements were resolved by consensus or arbitration by a third reviewer (XY).
The AMSTAR-2 tool consists of 16 items, of which 7 are considered critical domains for assessing the quality of a review: protocol registration (Q2), adequacy of the literature search (Q4), justification for excluded studies (Q7), risk of bias assessment of primary studies (Q9), appropriateness of meta-analytical methods (Q11), con-sideration of risk of bias in the interpretation of results (Q13), and assessment of publication bias (Q15). Based on the number of weaknesses identified in these critical and non-critical domains, the overall confidence in the results of each review was rated as ‘High’, ‘Moderate’, ‘Low’, or ‘Critically Low’. The results of the methodological quality assessment are presented in Table 2.
Statistical analyses The degree of overlap in the primary studies included across all eligible reviews was assessed using the Corrected Cov-ered Area (CCA) formula: CCA = (N − r) / (rc − r), where N is the sum of the total number of primary studies, r is the number of unique primary studies, and c is the total number of reviews (Pieper et al. 2014). CCA was categorized as slight (0–5%), moderate (6–10%), high (11–15%), or very high (> 15%) overlap.
All statistical analyses were performed using R (Version 4.5.0) within the RStudio environment, and the results of each meta-analysis are presented using forest plots. The pooled effect size and its 95% CI were extracted from each included review. Due to the anticipated heterogeneity in populations and intervention protocols, all quantitative syntheses were conducted using a random-effects model. Between-study statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane’s Q-test and quantified with the ­ I2 statistic, with values of < 25%, 25–75%, and > 75% considered as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively(Higgins et al. 2003).
To assess the robustness of the pooled estimates, a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was performed for each meta-analysis. Publication bias was evaluated visually through Egger’s linear regression test (Egger et al. 1997). We acknowledge that the statistical power of these tests is lim-ited when fewer than 10 studies are included in a meta-anal-ysis, and the results were therefore interpreted with caution.
Results Study selection From an initial yield of 1,284 records identified through the database search, 16 articles (Gist et al. 2013; Sloth et al. 2013b; Vollaard et al. 2017; Rosenblat et al. 2020, 2022; Rugbeer et al. 2021; de Oliveira-Nunes et al. 2021; Mat-tioni Maturana et al. 2021; Bonafiglia et al. 2021; Poon et al. 2021; Yang et al. 2021; Boullosa et al. 2022; Aparecido et al. 2022; Hall et al. 2023; Liang et al. 2024; Thurlow et al. 2024) were included after the removal of duplicates and the screening of titles, abstracts, and full texts. The complete literature search and selection process is illustrated in the PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1).

Regarding the scale of evidence, the number of primary studies included within each systematic review was highly variable, ranging from 6 to 55. The median number of included studies was 19 (Interquartile Range [IQR]: 12–33), indicating that most reviews synthesized a moderate volume of primary evidence (Fig. 2c). Similarly, the total participant sample size synthesized by each review varied substantially, from 125 to over 1,500 participants. The median sample size was 440 participants (IQR: 344–769), with the violin plot revealing a right-skewed distribution. This suggests the field is composed of a few large-scale reviews alongside many of more modest size (Fig. 2b).
Participant characteristics The included reviews encompassed a broad spectrum of pop-ulations (Fig. 2d). A subset of reviews focused primarily on healthy, recreationally active or sedentary adults (Gist et al. 2013; Sloth et al. 2013b; Vollaard et al. 2017; de Oliveira-Nunes et al. 2021; Bonafiglia et al. 2021), while several oth-ers specifically targeted trained athletes to investigate the effects of SIT in competitive populations (Rosenblat et al. 2020; Yang et al. 2021; Boullosa et al. 2022; Thurlow et al. 2024). Furthermore, a considerable body of evidence was derived from populations with specific cardiovascular risk factors, such as overweight or obese individuals (Rugbeer et al. 2021; Hall et al. 2023), middle-aged and older adults (Poon et al. 2021), reproductive-age women (Aparecido et al. 2022), and patients with prehypertension or hyperten-sion (Liang et al. 2024). A few large-scale reviews covered a range of populations from health to disease, aiming to provide a broader evidence summary (Mattioni Maturana et al. 2021). This population diversity provides a varied evidence base for assessing the effects of SIT in different contexts but also constitutes a primary source of between-study heterogeneity.
Intervention and comparator characteristics The operational definitions of SIT, while centered on “all-out” or supramaximal efforts, varied across the included reviews. Sprint duration was a key variable, with some reviews specifically analyzing short-duration sprints (≤ 10 s) (Boullosa et al. 2022; Thurlow et al. 2024), whereas more classic protocols focused on 20–30 s Wingate-style sprints (Gist et al. 2013; Hall et al. 2023). The comparator groups were equally diverse. The most frequent comparator was traditional MICT (Gist et al. 2013; Rugbeer et al. 2021; Bonafiglia et al. 2021). The second most common comparison was against other high-inten-sity modalities, primarily HIIT (Rosenblat et al. 2020; de Oliveira-Nunes et al. 2021). A large number of studies also compared SIT against active (e.g., usual training) or inactive control conditions to establish its absolute efficacy (Yang et al. 2021; Hall et al. 2023; Thurlow et al. 2024) (Table 3).
Quality assessment characteristics To understand the landscape of quality appraisal within the included literature, we extracted the methodological quality assessment tools used by each systematic review to evaluate its primary studies. These details are summarized in Table 4. A notable diversity in the choice of assessment tools was observed across the 16 reviews. The Cochrane Risk of Bias tool was the most frequently utilized instrument, employed by six reviews (Mattioni Maturana et al. 2021; Bonafiglia et al. 2021; Poon et al. 2021; Yang et al. 2021; Aparecido et al. 2022; Liang et al. 2024), followed by the PEDro scale, which was used in four reviews (Rosenblat et al. 2020, 2022; Rugbeer et al. 2021; Boullosa et al. 2022). Other instru-ments, such as the TESTEX scale and modified Downs and Black checklists, were also applied in some reviews Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram of the study selection process European Journal of Applied Physiology (de Oliveira-Nunes et al. 2021; Hall et al. 2023; Thurlow et al. 2024). This heterogeneity in assessment tools reflects the diverse methodological standards within the field but also presents a challenge for directly comparing the quality-related conclusions across the reviews.
Quality of studies The methodological quality of the 16 included systematic reviews, as assessed by the AMSTAR-2 tool, was variable. The detailed item-by-item results are presented in a heatmap (Fig. 3a), with an aggregate summary of the field’s over-all performance shown in Fig. 3b. Overall, only one review (Rugbeer et al. 2021) was rated as ‘High’ confidence, two as ‘Moderate’(Aparecido et al. 2022; Hall et al. 2023), four as ‘Low’(Rosenblat et al. 2020; Poon et al. 2021; Boullosa et al. 2022; Liang et al. 2024), and the remaining nine were rated as ‘Critically Low’ confidence.
As visually summarized in Fig. 3b, common methodo-logical strengths included a clear definition of the PICO ele-ments (Item 1), justification for the choice of study design (Item 3), appropriate statistical methods for quantitative syn-thesis (Item 11), and an explanation of between-study het-erogeneity (Item 14), all of which were addressed by 100% of the reviews. Most reviews also provided an adequate description of their included studies (Item 8, 94%) and used a satisfactory tool to assess the risk of bias in the primary studies (Item 9, 81%).
However, several critical weaknesses were prevalent. A universal limitation was the failure to report the fund-ing sources of the included primary studies (Item 10, 0%). Regarding the critical domains, only 75% of reviews reported an a priori registered protocol (Item 2). The com-prehensiveness of the literature search (Item 4) and the pro-vision of a list of excluded studies (Item 7) were also com-mon shortcomings, with only 44% of reviews fully satisfying these criteria. Furthermore, despite most reviews assess-ing risk of bias, only four (25%) adequately discussed the potential impact of these risks on the overall meta-analytic results (Item 12) (Rugbeer et al. 2021; de Oliveira-Nunes et al. 2021; Bonafiglia et al. 2021; Aparecido et al. 2022).

This is an umbrella review published in the European Journal of Applied Physiology (2025) by Liang et al. that systematically synthesizes evidence on the effects of Sprint Interval Training (SIT) on cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) for cardiovascular prevention. The study was pre-registered (PROSPERO ID CRD420251074348) and conducted per PRISMA guidelines.

METHODS: A systematic search of six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase) from inception to April 30, 2025, identified 1,284 records, of which 16 systematic reviews with meta-analyses were included. These reviews synthesized data from 393 unique primary studies and more than 8,642 participants, spanning populations from healthy sedentary adults and athletes to individuals with cardiovascular risk factors (overweight/obese, prehypertensive/hypertensive, middle-aged/older adults, and reproductive-age women). Methodological quality of included reviews was assessed using AMSTAR-2. The intervention was defined as SIT (repeated bouts of "all-out" or supramaximal intensity, ≥100% VO2max/peak power, minimum 2 weeks duration). Comparators included MICT, HIIT, and control conditions. Secondary meta-analyses were conducted using random-effects models.

KEY RESULTS:
- 9 of 16 (56%) included systematic reviews were rated 'Low' or 'Critically Low' methodological quality via AMSTAR-2; only 1 review (Rugbeer et al. 2021) was rated 'High' confidence, 2 'Moderate', 4 'Low', and 9 'Critically Low'.
- SIT vs. control: SIT produced a significant, moderate-to-large improvement in CRF (SMD = 0.59; 95% CI 0.43–0.74; p < 0.001; I² = 15.2%) based on meta-analysis of 5 reviews.
- SIT vs. MICT: No significant difference found based on standardized effects (SMD = 0.07; 95% CI −0.03 to 0.16; p = 0.17; I² = 0.0%) from 3 reviews; however, a meta-analysis of 4 reviews reporting weighted mean differences showed a small significant effect favoring SIT (WMD = 0.81 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; 95% CI 0.05–1.57; I² = 55.4%).
- SIT vs. HIIT: Evidence was inconclusive (only 2 reviews directly compared them; one found no significant difference in VO2max).
- Individual reviews showed conflicting results: some found SIT superior to MICT (Rugbeer 2021 in overweight/obese; Poon 2021 in middle-aged/older adults), others found SIT inferior (Aparecido 2022 in reproductive-age women; Liang 2024 in prehypertensive/hypertensive individuals).
- Common methodological weaknesses across reviews: universal failure to report funding sources of primary studies (Item 10, 0%), only 75% reported a priori registered protocols, only 44% satisfied comprehensive literature search criteria and provided excluded study lists, and only 25% adequately discussed risk of bias impact on results.
- The Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (6 reviews) and PEDro scale (4 reviews) were the most common quality assessment tools used within the included reviews.

CONCLUSION: SIT is an effective time-efficient intervention for improving CRF compared to no exercise. However, current evidence—especially from higher-quality systematic reviews—does not support SIT's superiority over MICT for improving CRF. Confidence in findings is limited by prevalent methodological flaws in the secondary evidence base, underscoring the need for more rigorous primary and secondary research. The review does not provide support for SIT as an "overstated promise," but rather positions it as a time-efficient alternative to MICT rather than a superior one.
args.key_excerpts: "Pooled data showed SIT elicited a significant improvement in CRF versus control (Standardized Mean Difference [SMD] = 0.59; 95% CI 0.43–0.74). In contrast, no significant difference was found between SIT and MICT (SMD = 0.07; 95% CI – 0.03 to 0.16)."

## Abstract

### Background

Prior studies show significant increases in cardiorespiratory fitness (V̇O 2 max) and other health-related outcomes in response to reduced exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT), yet these studies are characterized by small sample sizes which casts doubt on the true efficacy of this form of physical activity for enhancing fitness and health. We propose a definitive randomized controlled exercise training study in a large sample of inactive adults to examine the effects of REHIT on outcomes related to cardiometabolic health in comparison to a non-exercise control group.

### Methods

After baseline testing, 120 inactive men and women ages 18–64 years will be randomized to a non-exercising control group or undergo 12 weeks of REHIT. Participants will be healthy, weight stable, and have BMI < 35 kg/m 2 and be required to maintain their habitual physical activity and dietary patterns during the study. Training will be supervised and performed 2 days per week. Changes in V̇O 2 max, body composition, and substrate metabolism will be monitored to assess adaptations in cardiometabolic health in response to REHIT. To assess the feasibility of REHIT, various perceptual measures including RPE, affective valence, and enjoyment will be recorded, and quality of life will be measured.

### Discussion

Data from the current study will advance physical activity research by bolstering the implementation of REHIT, which will contribute to reduced risk factors of cardiovascular disease and, in turn, improved public health.

### Trial registration

OSF (osf.io/wvcz4). Registered on November 3, 2025.

## Background

Low levels of physical activity (PA) and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) are significant issues for societal health. Current public health guidelines for adults recommend performing at least 150 min of moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) or 75 min of vigorous exercise per week, and strength training on 2 or more days per week [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR1 "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Physical activity guidelines for Americans. 2nd ed. 2018:8.")]. However, self-report data suggest that in 2020, more than 75% of adult Americans did not meet these minimum PA recommendations [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR2 "Elgaddal N, Kramarow EA, Reuben C. Physical activity among adults aged 18 and over: United States, 2020. NCHS Data Brief, no 443. Hyattsville, MD: National Center for Health Statistics; 2022.")]. This is a major concern given that physical inactivity is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR3 "Kohl HW 3rd, Craig CL, Lambert EV, Inoue S, Alkandari JR, Leetongin G, et al. The pandemic of physical inactivity: global action for public health. Lancet. 2012;380(9838):294–305.")]. It is well-documented that inactivity increases the risk of 40 chronic conditions or diseases [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR4 "Ruegsegger GN, Booth FW. Health benefits of exercise. Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med. 2018;8(7):a029694.")], and that low maximal oxygen uptake (V̇O 2 max; the gold standard measure of CRF) is strongly associated with increased risk of future morbidity and all-cause mortality [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR5 "Lang JJ, Prince SA, Merucci K, Cadenas-Sanchez C, Chaput JP, Fraser BJ, et al. Cardiorespiratory fitness is a strong and consistent predictor of morbidity and mortality among adults: an overview of meta-analyses representing over 20.9 million observations from 199 unique cohort studies. Br J Sports Med. 2024;58(10):556–66."), [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR6 "Ross R, Blair SN, Arena R, Church TS, Després JP, Franklin BA, et al. Importance of assessing cardiorespiratory fitness in clinical practice: a case for fitness as a clinical vital sign: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2016;134(24):e653–99.")]. Importantly, many large-scale studies have reported V̇O 2 max to be a more powerful predictor of risk for future morbidity and all-cause mortality than more traditional risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, obesity, high cholesterol, and insulin resistance [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR7 "Fogelholm M. Physical activity, fitness and fatness: relations to mortality, morbidity and disease risk factors. A systematic review. Obes Rev. 2010;11(3):202–21."),[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR8 "Kodama S, Saito K, Tanaka S, Maki M, Yachi Y, Asumi M, et al. Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women: a meta-analysis. JAMA. 2009;301(19):2024–35."),[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR9 "Kokkinos P, Myers J. Exercise and physical activity: clinical outcomes and applications. Circulation. 2010;122(16):1637–48."),[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR10 "Myers J, Prakash M, Froelicher V, Do D, Partington S, Atwood JE. Exercise capacity and mortality among men referred for exercise testing. N Engl J Med. 2002;346(11):793–801.")]. For population-level health, the largest benefits from improved PA and CRF are gained by the least fit individuals, with even small increases in fitness shown to improve health [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR8 "Kodama S, Saito K, Tanaka S, Maki M, Yachi Y, Asumi M, et al. Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women: a meta-analysis. JAMA. 2009;301(19):2024–35.")]. Despite exercise being the only viable means to improve V̇O 2 max, it remains underutilized for primary disease prevention [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR11 "Ekkekakis P. Why is exercise underutilized in clinical practice despite evidence it is effective? Lessons in pragmatism from the inclusion of exercise in guidelines for the treatment of depression in the British National Health Service. Kinesiol Rev. 2021;10:29–50."), [12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR12 "Hanssen H, Boardman H, Deiseroth A, Moholdt T, Simonenko M, Kränkel N, et al. Personalized exercise prescription in the prevention and treatment of arterial hypertension: a consensus document from the European Association of Preventive Cardiology (EAPC) and the ESC Council on Hypertension. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2022;29(1):205–15.")].

## Applicability of high intensity interval training (HIIT)

Reported barriers to exercise include lack of time, lack of knowledge about exercise, poor local facilities, lack of transportation, costs, and inclement weather [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR13 "Trost SG, Owen N, Bauman AE, Sallis JF, Brown W. Correlates of adults’ participation in physical activity: review and update. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2002;34(12):1996–2001."),[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR14 "Kimm SY, Glynn NW, McMahon RP, Voorhees CC, Striegel-Moore RH, Daniels SR. Self-perceived barriers to activity participation among sedentary adolescent girls. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2006;38(3):534–40."),[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR15 "Korkiakangas EE, Alahuhta MA, Laitinen JH. Barriers to regular exercise among adults at high risk or diagnosed with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review. Health Promot Int. 2009;24(4):416–27.")]. Of these barriers, the most commonly reported is perceived lack of time. Consequently, there has been increasing interest in identifying effective, time-efficient exercise interventions compared to current PA recommendations. In the last 20 years, interventions involving submaximal high-intensity interval training (HIIT; typically ~10 × 1-min efforts) and supramaximal sprint interval training (SIT; typically 4–6 × 30-s “all-out” cycle sprints) [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR16 "Astorino TA, Causer E, Hazell TJ, Arhen BB, Gurd BJ. Change in central cardiovascular function in response to intense interval training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022;54(12):1991–2004.")] have been proposed as time-efficient alternatives to MICT. The generation of high intensities during HIIT and SIT provides a potent metabolic stimulus which enables substantial adaptive responses with a reduced volume of exercise versus MICT [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR17 "Metcalfe RS, Vollaard NBJ. Reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT): a feasible approach for improving health and fitness ? Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2024;49(7):984–92.")]. Hundreds of studies have examined changes in health and fitness to HIIT and SIT in healthy, active, and sedentary adults and patients with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, stroke, hypertension, and cancer [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR18 "Poon ET, Li HY, Gibala MJ, Wong SH, Ho RS. High-intensity interval training and cardiorespiratory fitness in adults: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34(5):e14652.")]. These data show that HIIT and SIT significantly improve key health markers including V̇O 2 max, insulin sensitivity and glycemic control, blood pressure, body composition, and blood lipids [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR19 "Coates AM, Joyner MJ, Little JP, Jones AM, Gibala MJ. A perspective on high-intensity interval training for performance and health. Sports Med. 2023;53(Suppl 1):85–96.")]. Several meta-analyses demonstrate that HIIT and SIT can provide health benefits similar to, or better than, MICT [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR20 "Milanovic Z, Sporis G, Weston M. Effectiveness of high-intensity interval training (hit) and continuous endurance training for VO2max improvements: a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials. Sports Med. 2015;45(10):1469–81."),[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR21 "Sloth M, Sloth D, Overgaard K, Dalgas U. Effects of sprint interval training on VO2max and aerobic exercise performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2013;23(6):e341-52."),[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR22 "Weston M, Taylor KL, Batterham AM, Hopkins WG. Effects of low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIT) on fitness in adults: a meta-analysis of controlled and non-controlled trials. Sports Med. 2014;44(7):1005–17.")], further supporting the efficacy of these protocols.

### Criticisms of HIIT and SIT

Despite the many health benefits of HIIT and SIT shown in lab-based studies, criticisms concern the suitability of such protocols to be implemented as real-world exercise interventions for improving general health and wellbeing [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR23 "Biddle SJ, Batterham AM. High-intensity interval exercise training for public health: a big HIT or shall we HIT it on the head? Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2015;12:95."),[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR24 "Ekkekakis P, Vallance J, Wilson PM, Ewing Garber C. Extraordinary claims in the literature on high-intensity interval training (HIIT): III. Critical analysis of four foundational arguments from an interdisciplinary lens. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2023;66:102399."),[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR25 "Hardcastle SJ, Ray H, Beale L, Hagger MS. Why sprint interval training is inappropriate for a largely sedentary population. Front Psychol. 2014;5:1505.")]. First, most studies examining effects of HIIT and SIT used small sample sizes, questioning the reliability of these findings [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR26 "Ekkekakis PE, Swinton PP, Tiller NB. Extraordinary claims in the literature on high-intensity interval training (HIIT): I. bonafide scientific revolution or a looming crisis of replication and credibility? Sports Med. 2023;53(10):1865–90.")]. Second, while the total volume of exercise in HIIT or SIT sessions is low, the need for recovery periods following each interval means that the total time commitment of the most commonly studied HIIT and SIT protocols is ~66–93 min/week [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR17 "Metcalfe RS, Vollaard NBJ. Reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT): a feasible approach for improving health and fitness ? Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2024;49(7):984–92.")] which is not a time-efficient alternative to current vigorous PA recommendations. Third, the multiple intense efforts make most HIIT and SIT protocols demanding, resulting in high ratings of perceived exertion [[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR27 "Little JP, Gillen JB, Percival ME, Safdar A, Tarnopolsky MA, Punthakee Z, et al. Low-volume high-intensity interval training reduces hyperglycemia and increases muscle mitochondrial capacity in patients with type 2 diabetes. J Appl Physiol. 2011;111(6):1554–60.")] and reductions in affective valence (i.e., this exercise makes you “feel bad”) [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR28 "Metcalfe RS, Williams S, Fernandes GS, Astorino TA, Stork MJ, Phillips SM, et al. Affecting effects on affect: the impact of protocol permutations on affective responses to sprint interval exercise; a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled individual participant data. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2022;4:815555.")]. These effects have been proposed to result in reduced enjoyment and consequently reduced uptake of, and adherence to, these protocols [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR29 "Brand R, Ekkekakis P. Affective–reflective theory of physical inactivity and exercise: foundations and preliminary evidence. Germ J Exerc Sport Res. 2018;48:48–58.")].

### The case for reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT)

Surprisingly, despite the fact that time efficiency is widely stated as the main rationale for studying the health benefits of HIIT and SIT, few studies have determined if protocols with fewer and/or shorter sprints are effective. Prior data demonstrated that mechanisms mediating improved glycemic control and insulin sensitivity with SIT [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR30 "Babraj JA, Vollaard NB, Keast C, Guppy FM, Cottrell G, Timmons JA. Extremely short duration high intensity interval training substantially improves insulin action in young healthy males. BMC Endocr Disord. 2009;9:3.")] may be related to the rapid glycogenolysis occurring during the first half of the first two 30-s sprint repetitions [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR31 "Parolin ML, Chesley A, Matsos MP, Spriet LL, Jones NL, Heigenhauser GJ. Regulation of skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase and PDH during maximal intermittent exercise. Am J Physiol. 1999;277(5):E890-900.")]. These authors created a protocol having two 20-s all-out sprints within a 10-min exercise session called “reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training” (REHIT) [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR32 "Metcalfe RS, Babraj JA, Fawkner SG, Vollaard NBJ. Towards the minimal amount of exercise for improving metabolic health: beneficial effects of reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2012;112(7):2767–75.")]. In a small RCT (_n_ = 15 REHIT/_n_ = 14 control), there was a significant 28% improvement in the Cederholm Index of insulin sensitivity in men [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR32 "Metcalfe RS, Babraj JA, Fawkner SG, Vollaard NBJ. Towards the minimal amount of exercise for improving metabolic health: beneficial effects of reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2012;112(7):2767–75.")] as well as a significant increase in V̇O 2 max in both men (+15%) and women (+12%).

Subsequently, the efficacy of the 10-min REHIT protocol to improve V̇O 2 max has been confirmed by these authors [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR33 "Thomas G, Songsorn P, Gorman A, Brackenridge B, Cullen T, Fitzpatrick B, et al. Reducing training frequency from 3 or 4 sessions/week to 2 sessions/week does not attenuate improvements in maximal aerobic capacity with reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT). Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2020;45(6):683–5."),[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR34 "Ruffino JS, Songsorn P, Haggett M, Edmonds D, Robinson AM, Thompson D, et al. A comparison of the health benefits of reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) and moderate-intensity walking in type 2 diabetes patients. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2017;42(2):202–8."),[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR35 "Nalçakan G, Songsorn P, Fitzpatrick BL, Yüzbasioglu Y, Brick NE, Metcalfe RS, et al. Decreasing sprint duration from 20 to 10 s during reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) attenuates the increase in maximal aerobic capacity but has no effect on affective and perceptual responses. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2017;43(4):338–44."),[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR36 "Metcalfe RS, Tardif N, Thompson D, Vollaard NBJ, et al. Changes in aerobic capacity and glycaemic control in response to reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) are not different between sedentary men and women. BMC Public Health. 2020;20(1):313.")] and in other independent laboratories [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR38 "Gillen JB, Percival ME, Skelly LE, Martin BJ, Tan RB, Tarnopolsky MA, et al. Reduced exertion high-intensity interval training is more effective at improving cardiorespiratory fitness and cardiometabolic health than traditional moderate-intensity continuous training. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2019;16(3):483.")]. On average, V̇O 2 max increases ~10% following 6 weeks of REHIT and by ~19% after 12 weeks (Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#Tab1)). Such improvements in V̇O 2 max are associated with risk reductions of 30 and 38% for all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality, respectively, if maintained [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR41 "Lee DC, Sui X, Artero EG, Lee IM, Church TS, McAuley PA, et al. Reducing training frequency from 3 or 4 sessions/week to 2 sessions/week does not attenuate improvements in maximal aerobic capacity with reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT). With a total time commitment as low as 20 min/week, REHIT is a genuinely time-efficient intervention, circumventing the most commonly reported perceived barrier to exercise of lack of time. Moreover, REHIT may enable other barriers to exercise to be addressed. First, a common criticism of HIIT and SIT protocols is that, even if they are associated with health benefits, they are unlikely to be taken up and adhered to by the general public because the high exercise intensities may be associated with a rapid decrease in affective valence (e.g., exercise makes you “feel bad”), which will cause low exercise enjoyment [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR26 "Ekkekakis PE, Swinton PP, Tiller NB. Extraordinary claims in the literature on high-intensity interval training (HIIT): I. bonafide scientific revolution or a looming crisis of replication and credibility? Sports Med. 2023;53(10):1865–90."),[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR27 "Little JP, Gillen JB, Percival ME, Safdar A, Tarnopolsky MA, Punthakee Z, et al. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2022;4:815555."),[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR29 "Brand R, Ekkekakis P. Affective–reflective theory of physical inactivity and exercise: foundations and preliminary evidence. Germ J Exerc Sport Res. 2018;48:48–58.")]. Although the association between decreases in affective valence and exercise enjoyment is tenuous [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR28 "Metcalfe RS, Williams S, Fernandes GS, Astorino TA, Stork MJ, Phillips SM, et al. Affecting effects on affect: the impact of protocol permutations on affective responses to sprint interval exercise; a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled individual participant data. A systematic review and meta-analysis of affective responses to acute high intensity interval exercise compared with continuous moderate- and high-intensity exercise. Health Psychol Rev. 2021;15(4):540–73.")], as is the link between changes in affective valence and future exercise behavior [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR43 "Stork MJ, Santos A, Locke SR, Little JP, Jung ME. Can in-task affect during interval and continuous exercise predict 12-month physical activity behavior? Findings from a randomized trial. Affecting effects on affect: the impact of protocol permutations on affective responses to sprint interval exercise; a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled individual participant data. However, we demonstrated that the interaction between sprint intensity and sprint volume determines the magnitude of the affective response to HIIT and SIT [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR28 "Metcalfe RS, Williams S, Fernandes GS, Astorino TA, Stork MJ, Phillips SM, et al. Affecting effects on affect: the impact of protocol permutations on affective responses to sprint interval exercise; a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled individual participant data. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2022;4:815555.")]. For SIT, the typical reduction in affective valence is substantially attenuated by reducing sprint duration and repetitions. In fact, the in-task decrease in affective valence with REHIT is similar to that observed following a duration and intensity of MICT commensurate with current PA guidelines, and the majority of our research participants have a preference for REHIT versus MICT [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR28 "Metcalfe RS, Williams S, Fernandes GS, Astorino TA, Stork MJ, Phillips SM, et al. Affecting effects on affect: the impact of protocol permutations on affective responses to sprint interval exercise; a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled individual participant data. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2022;4:815555."), [35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR35 "Nalçakan G, Songsorn P, Fitzpatrick BL, Yüzbasioglu Y, Brick NE, Metcalfe RS, et al. All exercise including REHIT is associated with some risk, but current data do not show that HIIT/SIT or REHIT increase risk for the population of insufficiently active adults without clear contraindications to exercise in general.

Overall, there is accumulating evidence for the sizable health benefits of REHIT and the acceptability and safety of the intervention. Other commonly studied HIIT and SIT protocols have major disadvantages that prevent real-world implementation (i.e.: not time-efficient, too strenuous, induce feelings of displeasure), but REHIT may circumvent most or all of these barriers. REHIT is at least as efficacious at improving key health markers as MICT, as enjoyable as MICT, and not associated with more negative affective responses during exercise versus MICT. We acknowledge that it is unlikely that any single intervention can remove the perceived barriers to exercise for all adults, but REHIT has the potential to enable a meaningful proportion of adults to reap the health benefits of exercise through a manageable, time-efficient intervention. REHIT represents a promising protocol for further study and subsequent inclusion in PA recommendations as a feasible alternative or adjunct to moderate or vigorous-intensity exercise as currently promoted. Thus, there is a strong justification to conduct a fully powered RCT to provide a definitive answer to the question whether REHIT induces a clinically meaningful improvement in V̇O 2 max and is perceived as feasible/acceptable.

### Objectives

The study objectives included (1) to examine changes in V̇O 2 max in response to 12 weeks of REHIT in inactive adults; (2) to examine changes in the metabolic response to 12 weeks of REHIT in inactive adults, which has yet to be studied; and (3) to examine the feasibility and acceptability of REHIT in inactive adults. It was hypothesized that compared to a control group, a significant increase in V̇O 2 max will occur, which will be identified through incremental exercise testing performed before and after training. It is also hypothesized that compared to a control group, a significant increase in exercise fat oxidation will occur, and that REHIT will be well-tolerated, safe, and perceived as enjoyable.

## Methods

### Experimental design

This study is a definitive randomized controlled trial using a repeated measures design, as participant responses to 12 weeks of REHIT will be compared to those in a non-exercising control group. Baseline testing will consist of assessments of body composition, VO 2 max, and substrate metabolism. After baseline testing, participants will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio to REHIT or control by a statistician who will use a computer-generated random sequence program. REHIT will consist of 2 days/week of training on a cycle ergometer for 12 weeks, with reassessment of VO 2 max performed during week 6 and at the end of training. Participants randomized to the control group will be re-tested in weeks 6 and 12 and be given the option to subsequently undergo REHIT. During the study, habitual physical activity and dietary patterns will be monitored and participants will be required not to change these behaviors. The study protocol was approved by the CSU—San Marcos Institutional Review Board (#2313242−2 on September 12, 2025) and has been registered with OSF (osf.io/wvcz4) on November 3, 2025 and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07328568) on January 7, 2026. The study design is consistent with the SPIRIT guidelines [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR46 "Chan AW, Tetzlaff JM, Gøtzsche PC, Altman DG, Mann H, Berlin J, et al. SPIRIT 2013 explanation and elaboration: guidance for protocols of clinical trials. BMJ. 2013;346:e7586.")] and a SPIRIT figure is included below as Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#Fig1). At this time, there are no plans to change this study protocol, although if needed, formal procedures will be followed and submitted to the campus IRB for approval. In addition, there is no plan to conduct additional studies using data acquired in this study.

### Study setting and oversight

All participant interactions in this study will be completed in the Department of Kinesiology at California State University—San Marcos. Data collection will begin in January 2026, and up to 60 adults will undergo REHIT during the 3-year study duration.

The Principal Investigator Dr. Todd A. Astorino will be responsible for oversight including management of all facets of the study, such as participant enrollment, training of study staff, data collection and analysis, and data storage and dissemination. Dr. Michael Joyner from the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, MN is serving as the NIH appointed Safety Officer who will perform annual reviews of safety issues and adverse events related to the study. The PI’s Institution does not have a Data Safety Monitoring Board, yet one will be developed if the funder requests this.

### Participant recruitment and pre-screening

Recruitment will be initially performed through word-of-mouth and ads placed on campus as well as in local and regional schools, newspapers, workplaces, physician offices, and on Facebook and Instagram. A website will be developed to describe the study. If recruitment is poor in the early stages of the study, the Investigators will employ services including Trialfacts or Wayturn to enhance participant recruitment. Because of the long duration of participation equal to 12 weeks, recruitment and eventual enrollment in the study will need to be appropriately timed to prohibit the possibility of absences from training or missed assessments due to holiday breaks, summer vacation, etc.

Granting of informed consent and pre-screening will be overseen by the Primary Investigator and will include acquisition of demographic traits and review of study requirements including time commitment, maintenance of habitual diet and activity, and participant inclusion/exclusion criteria. These data will be maintained by the Primary Investigator using codes to preserve anonymity.

### Randomization

After baseline testing, the Principal Investigator will provide each participant’s age, sex, and code to the statistician. Participant randomization to REHIT or control will be computer generated and performed by the study statistician who will have no interaction with participants or role in exercise training or testing. Participants will be randomized using simple randomization according to the NIH Clinical Trial Randomization tool. All research personnel will not have access to this randomization sequence. Once randomized, the statistician will provide the Principal Investigator with the group assignment for each participant via email who will use this information to enroll participants. The Principal Investigator and all Research personnel who interact with participants will not be blinded to group allocation.

### Participants

We will recruit healthy, low-active men and women aged 18–64 years until 120 participants (60 controls and 60 who undergo REHIT) have completed the study, whose protocol is shown in Fig. [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#Fig2). Eligible participants will be free of disease and will not have been involved in structured exercise training in the last year. Adults over 64 years old are excluded as the NIA and CDC classify “older adults” as >65 years, and there is increased risk of adverse events of exercise testing in participants 65 years and older [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR47 "ACSM. ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2021.")]. Activity status will be verified using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR48 "Craig CL, Marshall AL, Sjöström M, Bauman AE, Booth ML, Ainsworth BE, et al. International physical activity questionnaire: 12-country reliability and validity. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2003;35(8):1381–95.")]. Based on our experience in similar studies, we expect a dropout rate of 10–15%. Control participants will complete assessments at baseline and again at 6 and 12 weeks, after which they will be offered the opportunity to partake in 12 weeks of REHIT if they choose. Exclusion criteria include answering “yes” to any question on a standard Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire (PARQ), onset of type 2 diabetes, CVD, blood pressure > 160/100 mm Hg at rest, pregnant or plans to become pregnant, use of medications altering our outcomes, and severe medical conditions that contraindicate exercise training. We will exclude adults who diet or plan to lose weight and those with BMI > 35 kg·m−2, which may reduce the V̇O 2 max response to training [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#ref-CR49 "Clark A, De La Rosa AB, DeRevere JL, Astorino TA. Effects of various interval training regimes on changes in maximal oxygen uptake, body composition, and muscular strength in sedentary women with obesity. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019;119(4):879–88.")].

### Trial outcomes

Figure [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x#Fig1) shows the main outcomes acquired in this study. The primary outcome is the change in V̇O 2 max measured using indirect calorimetry, which will be assessed at baseline and then at 6 and 12 weeks of the protocol. The overall change in V̇O 2 max will be compared between the REHIT and control groups. args.summary:
This is a study protocol published in the journal Trials (Springer Nature) for a definitive randomized controlled trial examining the effect of low-volume sprint interval training (specifically reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training, REHIT) on cardiorespiratory fitness in inactive adults.

**Background and Rationale:** Low physical activity and low cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max) are major public health concerns, with over 75% of adult Americans not meeting minimum PA recommendations in 2020. Physical inactivity is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide. Traditional HIIT and SIT protocols are criticized for being too time-consuming (~66-93 min/week), too strenuous, and producing negative affective responses. REHIT, consisting of two 20-second all-out sprints within a 10-minute session, 2 days per week (20 min/week total), addresses these barriers. Prior studies show VO2max increases ~10% after 6 weeks and ~19% after 12 weeks of REHIT, with no serious adverse events observed. Improvements in VO2max of this magnitude are associated with 30% and 38% risk reductions for all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality, respectively.

**Methods:** The study will recruit 120 inactive men and women aged 18-64 years (60 controls, 60 REHIT), who are healthy, weight-stable, with BMI < 35 kg/m². Participants will be randomized 1:1 to a non-exercising control group or 12 weeks of supervised REHIT performed 2 days/week on a cycle ergometer. Primary outcome is change in VO2max (measured via indirect calorimetry using incremental cycling test), assessed at baseline, week 6, and week 12. Secondary outcomes include body composition (bioelectrical impedance analysis), substrate metabolism, cardiac output, and perceptual measures (RPE, affective valence, enjoyment), plus quality of life. Expected dropout rate is 10-15%. The study is set at California State University—San Marcos (Department of Kinesiology), with data collection beginning January 2026 over a 3-year period. PI is Dr. Todd A. Astorino; Dr. Michael Joyner (Mayo Clinic) serves as NIH-appointed Safety Officer.

**Registration and Approval:** Approved by CSU—San Marcos IRB (#2313242−2 on September 12, 2025). Registered with OSF (osf.io/wvcz4) on November 3, 2025, and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07328568) on January 8, 2026. Study design follows SPIRIT guidelines. Published 23 March 2026, Volume 27, article number 340.

**Hypotheses:** Compared to control, REHIT will produce a significant increase in VO2max and exercise fat oxidation, and will be well-tolerated, safe, and perceived as enjoyable.

**Discussion:** This study aims to provide a definitive answer on whether REHIT induces clinically meaningful improvements in VO2max and is feasible/acceptable, advancing physical activity research and potentially contributing to reduced cardiovascular disease risk factors and improved public health.
args.key_excerpts: "We propose a definitive randomized controlled exercise training study in a large sample of inactive adults to examine the effects of REHIT on outcomes related to cardiometabolic health in comparison to a non-exercise control group."

<webpage_content>
See discussions, stats, and author profiles for this publication at: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257839214 Sprint Interval Training Effects on Aerobic Capacity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Article in Sports Medicine · October 2013 DOI: 10.1007/s40279-013-0115-0 · Source: PubMed CITATIONS 329 READS 19,202 4 authors, including: Nicholas H Gist United States Military Academy West Point 11 PUBLICATIONS 810 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE Michael V Fedewa University of Alabama 132 PUBLICATIONS 2,095 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE Kirk J Cureton University of Georgia 225 PUBLICATIONS 9,017 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE All content following this page was uploaded by Kirk J Cureton on 03 June 2014.
