Ann Phys Rehabil Med. 2017;60(1):50–7."), [32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR32 "Rognmo Ø, Hetland E, Helgerud J, Hoff J, Slørdahl SA. High intensity aerobic interval exercise is superior to moderate intensity exercise for increasing aerobic capacity in patients with coronary artery disease. Eur J Cardiovasc Prev Rehabil. 2004;11(3):216–22.")].

Accordingly, HIIT in CR is now a burgeoning area of interest within the field of clinical exercise physiology. To illustrate the escalating number of reports on this topic, a 2021 PubMed search for the key terms “high-intensity interval training/cardiac rehabilitation” yielded > 200 citations, with an exponential increase starting in 2017.

This editorial provides an overview of the benefits and risks of HIIT in varied patient populations, including atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD) and heart failure (HF), with specific reference to atrial fibrillation (AF) and cardiometabolic health. A relevant brief case report is also included.

## Training Studies in Varied Populations

### Healthy Individuals

In healthy individuals, HIIT has been reported to elicit comparable or greater increases in CRF or aerobic capacity as compared with MICT and in a shortened training duration [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR33 "Ross LM, Porter RR, Durstine JL. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) for patients with chronic disease. J Sport Health Sci. 2016;5(2):139–44.")]. The superiority of HIIT in improving CRF was particularly apparent when total work and training frequency are matched [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR16 "Helgerud J, Hoydal K, Wang E, Karlsen T, Berg P, Bjerkaas M, Simonsen T, Helgesen C, Hjorth N, Bach R, Hoff J. Aerobic high-intensity intervals improve VO2max more than moderate training. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(4):665–71.")].

### Atherosclerotic CVD

In one of the early studies, researchers randomized patients with coronary artery disease into either HIIT or MICT groups for 10 weeks to evaluate changes in exercise capacity, expressed as VO 2peak [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR32 "Rognmo Ø, Hetland E, Helgerud J, Hoff J, Slørdahl SA. High intensity aerobic interval exercise is superior to moderate intensity exercise for increasing aerobic capacity in patients with coronary artery disease. Eur J Cardiovasc Prev Rehabil. 2004;11(3):216–22.")]. Between-group analyses indicate that the HIIT group’s 17.9% increase in VO 2peak was significantly greater than the 7.9% improvement noted for the MICT group. Moreover, none of the patients in either the HIIT or MICT experienced an acute cardiac event during the training program.

Comparative trials of HIIT and MICT in patients with atherosclerotic CVD have yielded conflicting findings, noting greater improvements in CRF with HIIT [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR23 "Moholdt T, Amundsen BH, Rustad LA, Wahba A, Løvø KT, Gullikstad LR, Bye A, Skogvoll E, Wisløff U, Slørdahl SA. Aerobic interval training versus continuous moderate exercise after coronary artery bypass surgery: a randomized study of cardiovascular effects and quality of life. Am Heart J. 2009;158(6):1031–7.")], and no difference in benefits between HIIT and MICT from a multisite, RCT in patients with coronary artery disease after 12 months [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR26 "Pattyn N, Vanhees L, Cornelissen VA, Coeckelberghs E, De Maeyer C, Goetschalckx K, Possemiers N, Wuyts K, Van Craenenbroeck EM, Beckers PJ. The long-term effects of a randomized trial comparing aerobic interval versus continuous training in coronary artery disease patients: 1-year data from the SAINTEX-CAD study. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2016;23(11):1154–64.")]. On the other hand, a meta-analysis of 10 studies in patients with coronary disease (_n_ = 472) revealed that MICT was associated with a more marked decline in patients’ average resting heart rate and body weight when compared with HIIT [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR19 "Liou K, Ho S, Fildes J, Ooi SY. High intensity interval versus moderate intensity continuous training in patients with coronary artery disease: a meta-analysis of physiological and clinical parameters. Heart Lung Circ. 2016;25:116–74.")], whereas another similar analysis found no differences in QoL outcomes between these training methods [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR13 "Gomes-Neto M, Durấes AR, Reis HFCD, Neves VR, Martinez BP, Carvalho VO. High-intensity interval training versus moderate-intensity continuous training on exercise capacity and quality of life in patients with coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2017;24(16):1696–707.")].

### Heart Failure

More than a decade ago, researchers evaluated the impact of an 8-week CR program of HIIT versus MICT in patients with chronic HF [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR11 "Freyssin C, Verkindt T, Prieur F, Benaich P, Maunier S, Blanc P. Cardiac rehabilitation in chronic heart failure: effect of an 8-week, high-intensity interval training versus continuous training. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2012;93(8):1359–64.")]. HIIT used stationary cycling up to ~ 80% of maximal power output, whereas MICT used either the cycle ergometer or treadmill at the heart rate corresponding to the ventilatory threshold. The HIIT group demonstrated a significant increase in aerobic capacity and oxygen consumption at the ventilatory threshold, whereas for the MICT, these variables remain unchanged. No cardiac events were reported in either group over the relatively brief intervention.

A RCT including 19 HF patients with preserved ejection fraction (mean age, 60 years; 63% women) found that HIIT elicited a significantly greater increase in aerobic capacity or VO 2peak compared with MICT over 12 weeks, with HIIT demonstrating a 22% increase versus 11% in MICT [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR8 " Donelli da Silveira A, Beust de Lima J, da Silva Piardi D, Dos Santos Macedo D, Zanini M, Nery R, Laukkanen JA, Stein R. High-intensity interval training is effective and superior to moderate continuous training in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a randomized clinical trial. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2020;27(16):1733–1743.")]. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found that HIIT generally improved CRF or VO 2peak more effectively than MICT in patients with HF [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR5 "Chen X, Zhang T, Hu X, Wen Z, Lu W, Jiang W. High-intensity interval training programs versus moderate-intensity continuous training for individuals with heart failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2025;106(1):98–112.")]. In contrast, another RCT evaluated the effects of HIIT and MICT on exercise capacity in 180 patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction and found no significant difference in VO 2peak improvement between HIIT and MICT after 3 months [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR25 "Mueller S, Winzer WB, Duvinage A, Gevaert AB, Edelmann F, Haller B, Pieske-Kraigher E, Beckers P, Bobenko A, Hommel J, Van de Heyning CM, Esefeld K, von Korn P, Christle JW, Haykowsky MJ, Linke A, Wisløff U, Adams V, Pieske B, van Craenenbroeck EM, Halle M; OptimEx-Clin Study Group. Effect of high-intensity interval training, moderate continuous training, or guideline-based physical activity advice on peak oxygen consumption in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2021;325(6):542–51.")]. Accordingly, due to these conflicting reports, additional research is needed to clarify whether HIIT is superior to MICT in improving aerobic capacity or CRF.

## Adherence to Supervised and Home-Based HIIT vs. MICT

Adherence to exercise-based preventive and rehabilitative regimens is critical to achieving program effectiveness and favorable outcomes. To date, supervised secondary prevention interventions in patients with coronary artery disease reported similar adherence rates between patients assigned to HIIT or MICT [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR6 "Conraads VM, Pattyn N, De Maeyer C, Beckers PJ, Coeckelberghs E, Cornelissen VA, Denollet J, Frederix G, Goetschalckx K, Hoymans VY, Possemiers N, Schepers D, Shivalkar B, Voigt JU, Van Craenenbroeck EM, Vanhees L. Aerobic interval training and continuous training equally improve aerobic exercise capacity in patients with coronary artery disease: the SAINTEX-CAD study. Int J Cardiol. 2015;179:203–10."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR26 "Pattyn N, Vanhees L, Cornelissen VA, Coeckelberghs E, De Maeyer C, Goetschalckx K, Possemiers N, Wuyts K, Van Craenenbroeck EM, Beckers PJ. The long-term effects of a randomized trial comparing aerobic interval versus continuous training in coronary artery disease patients: 1-year data from the SAINTEX-CAD study. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2016;23(11):1154–64."), [34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR34 "Taylor JL, Holland DJ, Keating SE, Leveritt MD, Gomersall SR, Rowlands A, Bailey TG, Coombes JS. Short-term and long-term feasibility, safety, and efficacy of high-intensity interval training in cardiac rehabilitation: the FITR heart study randomized clinical trial. JAMA Cardiol. 2020;5(12):1382–9.")]. On the other hand, investigators examined self-reported exercise adherence to home-based HIIT and found that it was only 58% [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR24 "Moholdt T, Bekken Vold M, Grimsmo J, Slørdahl SA, Wisløff U. Home-based aerobic interval training improves peak oxygen uptake equal to residential cardiac rehabilitation: a randomized, controlled trial. PLoS One. 2012;7(7):e41199.")]. Moreover, a recent home-based investigation of MICT found that self-reported adherence rates exceeded 81% at 6 months post discharge [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR35 "Torri A, Panzarino C, Scaglione A, Modica M, Bordoni B, Redaelli R, De Maria R, MFerratini . Promotion of home-based exercise training as secondary prevention of coronary heart disease: a pilot web-based intervention. J Cardiopulm Rehabil Prev. 2018;38(4):253–8.")]. Collectively, these findings suggest that supervised, early outpatient exercise adherence is similar for HIIT vs. MICT, whereas dropouts are more likely to occur in patients assigned to home-based HIIT programs. Others have reported that high intensity regimens are less likely to retain participants who are exercising on their own [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR15 "Haskell WL, Lee IM, Pate KE, Powell KE, Blair SN, Franklin BA, Macera CA, Heath GW, Thompson PD, Bauman A; ACSM; AHA. Physical activity and public health: updated recommendation for adults from the American College of Sports Medicine and the American Heart Association. Circulation 2007;116(9):1081–1093.")]. Finally, a recent investigation that evaluated the feasibility of implementing HIIT in varied CR settings found slightly higher dropout rates in women, as compared with men [[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR37 "Way KL, Vidal-Almela S, Keast ML, Hans H, Pipe AL, Reed JL. The feasibility of implementing high-intensity interval training in cardiac rehabilitation settings: a retrospective analysis. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2020;12:38.")]. The authors concluded that additional studies are needed to clarify the causative factors underlying this finding.

## Impact of HIIT on Cardiometabolic Health and Chronic Diseases

An early review examined the effectiveness and safety of HIIT in patients with chronic diseases, including cardiovascular, pulmonary, and type 2 diabetes [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR33 "Ross LM, Porter RR, Durstine JL. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) for patients with chronic disease. J Sport Health Sci. 2016;5(2):139–44.")]. Results indicated that HIIT was superior to MICT for increasing exercise capacity in patients with coronary artery disease as well as those with HF, and none of the patients in either group experienced cardiac events during exercise training. Other favorable adaptations in the HF population undergoing HIIT included the reversal of left ventricular remodeling and significant improvements in ejection fraction, stroke volume, and ventricular relaxation, suggesting increased myocardial contractility. Similarly, in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or type 2 diabetes, HIIT was at least as effective as MICT in improving exercise tolerance, peak power output, QoL scores, selected indices of pulmonary function, breathlessness at a standard submaximal workload, and in reducing percent body fat.

Subsequently, another report involved an umbrella systematic review to identify existing reviews pertaining to the impact of HIIT on reducing cardiometabolic disease risk [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR4 "Campbell W, Kraus W, Powell KE, Haskell WL, Janz KF, Jakicic JM, Troiano RP, Sprow K, Torres A, Piercy KL, Bartlett DB; 2018 Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee. High-intensity interval training for cardiometabolic disease prevention. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(6):1220–6.")]. Databases yielded suitable information from one systematic review and two meta-analyses. Participants included men and women whose mean ages ranged from ~ 20 to 77 years. Subcommittee members graded scientific evidence strength into one of four categories: strong, moderate, limited, or not assignable. Moderate evidence indicated that HIIT improved insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and body composition in adults comparable to MICT. Moreover, these improvements were more likely to occur in overweight/obese adults and those at greater risk of CVD and diabetes, as compared with healthy adults. Insufficient evidence precluded the determination whether a dose-response relationship exists between the quantity of HIIT and selected risk factors for CVD and diabetes, and whether the effects of HIIT on cardiometabolic risk factors are influenced by age, sex, race/ethnicity, or socioeconomic status.

More recently, researchers conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate changes in cardiometabolic risk factors following HIIT versus MICT [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR21 "Maturana FM, Martus P, Zipfel S, Neib AM. Effectiveness of HIIE versus MICT in improving cardiometabolic risk factors in health and disease: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(3):559–73.")]. Overall, HIIT was more effective in improving CRF or VO 2max and cardiovascular health, specifically flow-mediated dilation, whereas MICT was superior in improving long-term glucose metabolism (hemoglobin A1c). No differences between exercise groups were observed in body mass index, body mass, percent body fat, systolic/diastolic blood pressure, HDL-cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, triglycerides, total cholesterol, fasting insulin, fasting glucose, and insulin resistance. The authors concluded that both HIIT and MICT exhibit varied adaptations, that the health enhancing effectiveness of these exercise training regimens may be improved by considering the individual risk factor profile, and that a combined program of HIIT and MICT may offer the greatest promise in favorably modifying comprehensive health outcomes.

Finally, in a just-published systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 RCTs involving 790 patients (50% men, 50% women; age 59.8 ± 12.9 years, body mass index 28.9 ± 4.2 kg/m² with type 2 diabetes mellitus and concomitant overweight/obesity [diabesity]), investigators compared the effectiveness of HIIT and MICT on indices of cardiometabolic health [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR1 "Al-Mhanna SB, Poon ET-C, Franklin BA. Comparative effectiveness of high-intensity interval training and moderate-intensity continuous training on cardiometabolic health in patients with diabesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Diabetol Metabolic Syndrome. 2025;17:331.")]. Results indicated that HIIT offers modest additional benefits over MICT for specific cardiometabolic outcomes, including fasting insulin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance, and CRF, regardless of changes in body composition. In contrast, other cardiometabolic variables, such as body composition, lipid profile, fasting blood glucose, glycosylated hemoglobin, and blood pressure showed comparable effects between HIIT and MICT.

In closing, the authors urged caution when initiating HIIT in previously inactive adults with diabesity—an “at risk” population that is often affected by underlying CVD [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR9 "Franklin BA, Quindry J. High level physical activity in cardiac rehabilitation: implications for exercise training and leisure-time pursuits. Prog Cardiovasc Dis. 2022;70:22–32."), [28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR28 "Quindry JC, Franklin BA, Chapman M, Humphrey R, Mathis S. Benefits and risks of high-intensity interval training in patients with coronary artery disease. Am J Cardiol. 2019;123(8):1370–7.")]. Recommendations included a thorough medical evaluation in this patient population prior to embarking on medically supervised HIIT, or initiating HIIT only after the individual with diabesity has completed a moderate-to-vigorous exercise program without adverse signs, symptoms, or complications.

## High-Intensity Interval Training in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common heart rate rhythm irregularity in older adults (generally > 65 years) that manifests as extremely fast and irregular heartbeats from the upper chambers of the heart. It may occur periodically, or it can be persistent or permanent. Common symptoms of AF include: chest pain, dizziness, fainting (syncope), unusual fatigue, palpitations, weakness and shortness of breath.

When the atria get out of sync with the ventricles, blood can pool in the atrium, which can lead to blood clots which can travel to the head, triggering a stroke. In fact, persistent AF increases the risk of stroke by about 5-fold. For these patients, doctors commonly prescribe a blood thinner (e.g., apixaban or Eliquis®) to reduce the risk of stroke.

In the first study to examine the impact of HIIT in patients with nonpermanent AF, investigators reported significant decreases in time in AF, AF symptom frequency and severity, and increases in CRF, QoL, and physical activity levels following HIIT compared with a control group [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR20 "Malmo V, Nes BM, Amundsen BH, Tjonna AE, Stoylen A, Rossvoll O, Wisloff U, Loennechen JP. Aerobic interval training reduces the burden of atrial fibrillation in the short term: a randomized trial. Circulation. 2016;133(5):466–73.")]. More recently, in a RCT, researchers evaluated 86 patients (age = 69 ± 7 years, 66% men, mean baseline exercise capacity, 5.1 METs), who underwent 12 weeks of HIIT or MICT-based CR. Twice weekly 23-min HIIT was as effective as 60-min MICT in improving 6-min walk test distance, general and disease specific QoL, and resting heart rate in patients with persistent and permanent AF, despite a substantial difference in total exercise time of 336 min between groups [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR29 "Reed JL, Terada T, Vidal-Almela S, Tulloch HE, Mistura M, Birnie DH, Wells GA, Nair GM, Hans H, Way KL. Effect of high-intensity interval training in patients with atrial fibrillation. JAMA Netw Open. 2022;5(10):e2239380.")]. The investigators concluded that although HIIT offers a more time efficient option to improve exercise capacity and QoL, dropouts were significantly higher in the HIIT group (_n_ = 11) versus the MICT group (_n_ = 4; _P_ = 0.047), likely due to more exercise-related complications (e.g., joint injuries).

## Current Limitations Regarding HIIT in Cardiac Rehabilitation

The fact of the matter is that, to date, few RCTs comparing HIIT and MICT in CR settings have been conducted. Furthermore, most of these investigations have been conducted in medically supervised, electrocardiographically (ECG)-monitored settings, in low-risk patients and male-centric populations.

Although the existing data suggests that HIIT may offer some advantages over MICT relative to improvements in CRF or aerobic capacity, approximating an additional average gain in VO 2peak of 1.71 mL/kg/min (~ 0.5 METs) [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR28 "Quindry JC, Franklin BA, Chapman M, Humphrey R, Mathis S. Benefits and risks of high-intensity interval training in patients with coronary artery disease. Am J Cardiol. 2019;123(8):1370–7.")], these increases in aerobic capacity are not universally observed in RCT comparisons of HIIT vs. MICT. Gains in CRF in patients who perform HIIT are also tempered by the observation that improvements are comparable to MICT when normalized for the associated caloric expenditure [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR13 "Gomes-Neto M, Durấes AR, Reis HFCD, Neves VR, Martinez BP, Carvalho VO. High-intensity interval training versus moderate-intensity continuous training on exercise capacity and quality of life in patients with coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2017;24(16):1696–707.")].

Finally, the patient hours amassed during HIIT within the current literature fall short of statistical estimates for the anticipated number of observational hours likely needed to trigger an acute cardiac event, previously reported at 23,182 h [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR31 "Rognmo Ø, Moholdt T, Bakken H, Hole T, Mølstad P, Myhr NE, Grimsmo J, Wisløff U. Cardiovascular risk of high-versus moderate-intensity aerobic exercise in coronary heart disease patients. Circulation. 2012;126(12):1436–40.")]. Accordingly, patient hours collectively observed in the HIIT-MICT trials published to date represent only a fraction of those expected to result in a cardiac event. Thus, it is currently premature to conclude that HIIT is a safe and/or superior CR intervention compared to MICT.

## Risk of High-Intensity Interval Training

A concern in using HIIT in cardiac patients is the increased potential to trigger an exertion-related fatal cardiac event. A systematic review reported an adverse event rate of 8% using HIIT in patients with cardiometabolic diseases [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR18 "Levinger I, Shaw CS, Stepto NK, Cassar S, McAinch AJ, Cheetham C, Maiorana AJ. What doesn’t kill you makes you fitter: a systematic review of high-intensity interval exercise for patients with cardiovascular and metabolic diseases. Clin Med Insights Cardiol. 2015;9:53–63.")]. Another review, analyzing the safety of HIIT in patients with CVD in CR settings, found that the overall adverse rate was 1 event per 3417 sessions for HIIT and 1 event per 7134 sessions for MICT [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR38 "Wewege MA, Ahn D, Yu J, Liou K, Keech A. High-intensity interval training for patients with cardiovascular disease-is it safe? A systematic review. J Am Heart Assoc. 2018;7(21):e009305.")]. Other investigators compared the cardiovascular event rates during HIIT and MICT in 4846 coronary patients participating in exercise-based CR programs [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR31 "Rognmo Ø, Moholdt T, Bakken H, Hole T, Mølstad P, Myhr NE, Grimsmo J, Wisløff U. Cardiovascular risk of high-versus moderate-intensity aerobic exercise in coronary heart disease patients. Circulation. 2012;126(12):1436–40.")]. The absolute risk was low for HIIT (1 event per 23,182 patient-hours) and MICT (1 event per 129,456 patient-hours), but 5.6 times higher in the HIIT group.

In our previous review of 11 RCTs that compared the safety (untoward event rate) of HIIT vs. MICT in patients with coronary disease, none reported acute cardiac events [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR28 "Quindry JC, Franklin BA, Chapman M, Humphrey R, Mathis S. Benefits and risks of high-intensity interval training in patients with coronary artery disease. Am J Cardiol. 2019;123(8):1370–7.")], a finding that is supported by a meta-analysis of interval training in patients with coronary artery disease [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR7 "Cornish AK, Broadbent S, Cheema BS. Interval training for patients with coronary artery disease: a systematic review. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2011;111:579–89.")]. However, nearly all comparative HIIT-MICT investigations in our review as well as those in the meta-analysis were conducted on patients classified as either low or low-to-moderate risk for an acute cardiac event. Thus, the perceived safety of HIIT must be interpreted with caution since the cumulative patient exercise hours completed for the 11 studies we reviewed is only a fraction of the calculated event rate of 1 of 23,182 per patient hours of high intensity exercise [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR31 "Rognmo Ø, Moholdt T, Bakken H, Hole T, Mølstad P, Myhr NE, Grimsmo J, Wisløff U. Cardiovascular risk of high-versus moderate-intensity aerobic exercise in coronary heart disease patients. Circulation. 2012;126(12):1436–40.")]. Anecdotally, in an investigation of home-based aerobic HIIT, one patient died during the warm-up [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR24 "Moholdt T, Bekken Vold M, Grimsmo J, Slørdahl SA, Wisløff U. Home-based aerobic interval training improves peak oxygen uptake equal to residential cardiac rehabilitation: a randomized, controlled trial. PLoS One. 2012;7(7):e41199.")].

_Relevant Case Report_. A few years ago, I (B.F.) was asked to review a legal case, regarding a 38-year-old male nurse, non-smoker, whose body mass index was 36 kg/m 2 who wanted to get “in shape” after an extended layoff from regular exercise; he enrolled in a HIIT program. His client intake form was unremarkable with 6 “No” responses to the following questions:

*   Has your doctor ever told you that you have a heart condition, seizure disorder, dizziness, or fainting disorder (syncope)?

*   Do you feel pain in your chest during physical activity or at any other time?

*   Are there any other reasons that you should not perform, or limitations that could prevent you from performing physical activity?

*   Do you have any muscle, tendon, ligament, bone or joint problems that will be exacerbated by an increase in activity?

*   Are you currently pregnant?

*   Are you currently taking any medications or supplements that may affect your heart rate or blood pressure?

The intake form also required the client to sign off on the following disclaimer, listed below:

> “I understand that it is my complete right to decrease or stop any use of or physical activity in the Facility and that it is my obligation to inform Facility staff of any symptoms or other medical issues should any develop.”

During the client’s _first session_, he wore a proprietary heart rate monitor sold to him by the gym and participated in four consecutive circuits (treadmill, floor exercise, rowing, and treadmill); total time ~ 25–30 min. His heart rate during exercise was monitored by staff at a console. Twice during the exercise session staff approached him to readjust the heart rate monitor (due to perceived artifact versus atypical heart rate responses).

Heart rates during exercise were erratic and ranged from ~ 120 to 170 beats/min, and went as high as over 200 beats/min. Estimated highest exercise intensity was on the last treadmill station, corresponding to jogging at 5.0 to 5.5 miles per hour, equivalent to ~ 7 to 9 METs – which may have represented maximal or supramaximal effort. It was during this last treadmill station that he collapsed, experiencing sudden cardiac death (SCD). If symptoms occurred during exercise, it appeared that these were not conveyed to staff during his exercise session. He was immediately treated at the fitness facility with cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and with an automated external defibrillator, and was shocked twice. Emergency medical service (EMS) arrived and applied immediate CPR, the patient was intubated without difficulty, and was treated with 3–4 doses of epinephrine. He was in asystole and remained in asystole throughout their entire treatment of ~ 30 min in the field. When he arrived in the emergency room there were no signs of life. The final EMS report confirmed that this was the patient’s first day at this fitness facility. A subsequent review of the patient’s heart rate monitor at the gym that day suggested frequent atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, including possible atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia.

The patient’s autopsy report revealed mid-left anterior descending coronary artery intimal thickening and luminal narrowing (~ 65%), signifying moderate single vessel atherosclerotic coronary artery disease, with circumferential dystrophic calcification and cholesterol clefts. The final diagnoses also listed marked cardiac hypertrophy, as the heart weighed 490 g (normal weight ~ 300 g). The cause of death was listed as: “atherosclerotic and hypertensive cardiovascular disease”. Although the manner of death was listed as “natural”, unaccustomed vigorous to high intensity interval training likely triggered this fatal cardiac event [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR22 "Mittleman MA, Maclure M, Tofler GH, Sherwood JB, Goldberg RJ, Muller JE. Triggering of acute myocardial infarction by heavy physical exertion. Protection against triggering by regular exertion. Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study Investigators.N Engl J Med. 1993;329(23):1677–83.")]. Interestingly, although this 38-year-old patient had never been diagnosed with heart disease, he had both atherosclerotic and structural heart disease.

## Exercise, Heart Disease, and Acute Cardiac Events: the Protection Versus Provocation Conundrum

Think relatively young to middle-aged people cannot have heart disease? Think again! In a classic study conducted at the Cleveland Clinic using intravascular ultrasound, investigators evaluated the presence of coronary atherosclerosis in young and middle-aged adults [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR36 "Tuzcu EM, Kapadia SR, Tutar E, Ziada KM, Hobbs RE, McCarthy PM, Young JB, Nissen SE. High prevalence of coronary atherosclerosis in asymptomatic teenagers and young adults: evidence from intravascular ultrasound. Circulation. 2001;103(22):2705–10.")]. Sites with intimal thickness ≥ 0.5 mm were defined as atherosclerotic. The prevalence of atherosclerosis approximated 60% and 71% in individuals whose age ranged from 30 to 39 and 40 to 49 years, respectively. Those people 50 and older had an 85% likelihood of coronary atherosclerosis! For all age groups, the prevalence of coronary atherosclerosis was similar in men and women, 52%. More recently, using coronary computed tomography angiography on > 25,000 people in Sweden aged 50 to 64 without diagnosed heart disease, 42% had silent coronary atherosclerosis [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR2 "Bergström G, Persson M, Adiels M, Björnson E, Bonander C, Ahlström H, Alfredsson J, Angerås O, Berglund G, Blomberg A, Brandberg J, Börjesson M, Cederlund K, de Faire U, Duvernoy O, Ekblom Ö, Engström G, Engvall JE, Fagman E, Eriksson M, Erlinge D, Fagerberg B, Flinck A, Gonçalves I, Hagström E, Hjelmgren O, Lind L, Lindberg E, Lindqvist P, Ljungberg J, Magnusson M, Mannila M, Markstad H, Mohammad MA, Nystrom FH, Ostenfeld E, Persson A, Rosengren A, Sandström A, Själander A, Sköld MC, Sundström J, Swahn E, Söderberg S, Torén K, Östgren CJ, Jernberg T. Prevalence of subclinical coronary artery atherosclerosis in the general population. Circulation. 2021;144(12):916–29.")].

The incidence of cardiac arrest increases acutely with vigorous-to-high intensity exercise, especially in those who are unaccustomed to this level of physical exertion [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR22 "Mittleman MA, Maclure M, Tofler GH, Sherwood JB, Goldberg RJ, Muller JE. Triggering of acute myocardial infarction by heavy physical exertion. Protection against triggering by regular exertion. Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study Investigators.N Engl J Med. 1993;329(23):1677–83.")]. Genetic and structural cardiac disease is usually the cause of exercise-related SCD in young athletes, most notably hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR14 "Harmon KG, Asif IM, Maleszewski JJ, Owens DS, Prutkin JM, Salerno JC, Zigman ML, Ellenbogen R, Rao AL, Ackerman MJ, Drezner JA. Incidence, cause, and comparative frequency of sudden cardiac death in National Collegiate Athletic Association athletes. Circulation. 2015;132(1):10–9.")]. However, in older athletes > 35 years of age, SCD is primarily due to atherosclerotic CVD, especially during very strenuous exercise. This is likely due to plaque rupture, myocardial ischemia induced threatening ventricular arrhythmias, or combinations thereof [[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR27 "Pelliccia A, Sharma S, Gati S, Bäck M, Börjesson M, Caselli S, Collet JP, Corrado D, Drezner JA, Halle M, Hansen D, Heidbuchel H, Myers J, Niebauer J, Papadakis M, Piepoli MF, Prescott E, Roos-Hesselink JW, Graham Stuart A, Taylor RS, Thompson PD, Tiberi M, Vanhees L, Wilhelm M; ESC Scientific Document Group. 2020 ESC guidelines on sports cardiology and exercise in patients with cardiovascular disease. Eur Heart J. 2021;42(1):17–96.")].

Epidemiologic and clinical studies strongly support a cause-and-effect relationship between increased levels of physical activity or CRF and a reduced incidence of atherosclerotic CVD and acute cardiac events. On the other hand, sudden strenuous physical exertion (e.g., running to catch a bus, racquetball, snow shoveling), particularly when performed by inactive, deconditioned individuals with known or occult CVD, can acutely increase the risk of SCD and/or acute myocardial infarction [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR10 "Franklin BA, Thompson PD, Al-Zaiti SS, Albert CM, Hivert MF, Levine BD, Lobelo F, Madan K, Sharrief AZ, Eijsvogels TMH; American Heart Association Physical Activity Committee of the Council on Lifestyle and Cardiometabolic Health; Council on Cardiovascular and Stroke Nursing; Council on Clinical Cardiology; Stroke Council. Exercise-related acute cardiovascular events and potential deleterious adaptations following long-term exercise training: placing the risks into perspective- an update: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2020;141(13):e705-36.")].

In summary, recognize that if you are in your mid-to-upper 30’s or older, it’s very possible that you have underlying CVD – even if you’re symptom-free and haven’t been diagnosed with it. Accordingly, this population cohort, when initiating an exercise program, should begin slowly, generally with a walking program, and gradually increase the intensity and duration of exercise as their tolerance permits. Why? Because it is the combination of unfamiliar, strenuous physical exertion in habitually sedentary, unfit individuals with a diseased or susceptible heart, rather than the exercise itself, that seems to present the hazardous milieu for exercise-triggered acute cardiac events.

WARNING: For inactive, unfit individuals aged ~ 35 years and older, starting a physical conditioning program with vigorous exercise or high-intensity interval training may be hazardous to your health.

## Conclusions

Although vigorous-to-high-intensity exercise training precipitates acute cardiac events more frequently than MICT [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR22 "Mittleman MA, Maclure M, Tofler GH, Sherwood JB, Goldberg RJ, Muller JE. Triggering of acute myocardial infarction by heavy physical exertion. Protection against triggering by regular exertion. Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study Investigators.N Engl J Med. 1993;329(23):1677–83."), [31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR31 "Rognmo Ø, Moholdt T, Bakken H, Hole T, Mølstad P, Myhr NE, Grimsmo J, Wisløff U. Cardiovascular risk of high-versus moderate-intensity aerobic exercise in coronary heart disease patients. Circulation. 2012;126(12):1436–40.")], RCT comparisons of relatively short-term HIIT versus MICT, indicates the absolute risk for cardiovascular events and musculoskeletal injury remains low. One factor is that most early published investigations of the safety and effectiveness of HIIT utilized clinically stable, low risk cardiac patients who were generally medically supervised and/or ECG monitored.

Based on varied health and performance outcomes, HIIT seems to offer patients with coronary disease some distinct advantages, including comparable or even greater benefits, with a shortened training time investment. For example, HIIT appears superior to MICT in improving CRF or aerobic capacity (expressed as mL O 2/kg/min or peak METs), indices of submaximal exercise performance, and possibly cardiac performance, including left ventricular ejection fraction [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR39 "Wisløff U, Støylen A, Loennechen JP, Bruvold M, Rognmo Ø, Haram PM, Tjønna AE, Helgerud J, Slørdahl SA, Lee SJ, Videm V, Bye A, Smith GL, Najjar SM, Ellingsen Ø, Skjaerpe T. Superior cardiovascular effect of aerobic interval training versus moderate continuous training in heart failure patients: a randomized study. Circulation. 2007;115(24):3086–94.")]. Moreover, excess post exercise oxygen consumption is the most recognized link between exercise intensity and weight loss potential. HIIT elicits a sustained increase in post exercise oxygen consumption, often exceeding 24 h in duration [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR12 "Gibala MJ, Little JP, Macdonald MJ, Hawley JA. Physiological adaptations to low-volume, high-intensity interval training in health and disease. J Physiol. 2012;590:1077–84.")]. It also has independent effects on appetite suppression.

With regard to the contemporary CR setting, there is no consensus regarding staffing approaches, HIIT prescriptive guidelines, or criteria for prematurely stopping exercise due to abnormal signs or symptoms. Because of the higher risk of exercise-related acute cardiac events during HIIT, medical supervision in the immediate training area appears prudent. Clearly, additional long-term training studies are needed to assess safety, adherence, and morbidity and mortality following HIIT in varied population subsets as well as in real-life medically supervised and unsupervised settings [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR28 "Quindry JC, Franklin BA, Chapman M, Humphrey R, Mathis S. Benefits and risks of high-intensity interval training in patients with coronary artery disease. Am J Cardiol. 2019;123(8):1370–7.")].

How the risk of HIIT applies to varied CVD diagnoses, including patients with HF and reduced or preserved ejection, and in those with potentially threatening atrial or ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., exercise-induced atrial fibrillation, bundle branch block, ventricular couplets/triplets), are also understudied. Similarly, the benefits of HIIT as applied to under-represented populations, based on age, sex, race, and ethnicity, are largely unknown and further highlight the need to withhold conclusions about the safety and effectiveness as compared to MICT [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w#ref-CR9 "Franklin BA, Quindry J. High level physical activity in cardiac rehabilitation: implications for exercise training and leisure-time pursuits. Prog Cardiovasc Dis. 2022;70:22–32.")]. In the interim, we recommend that clinicians use caution when implementing HIIT in conventional, exercise-based CR programs, by providing direct medical supervision and continuous ECG monitoring, at least during the initial weeks of the intervention.

This is an editorial published in the Journal of Science in Sport and Exercise (Volume 8, pages 1–8, published January 23, 2026) by Barry A. Franklin and Weimo Zhu, titled "High-Intensity Interval Training: Benefits, Risks, and Clinical Implications." The article provides a comprehensive overview of the benefits and risks of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) across varied patient populations, including healthy individuals, those with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD), heart failure (HF), atrial fibrillation (AF), and cardiometabolic conditions.

KEY FINDINGS BY POPULATION:
- **Healthy individuals**: HIIT elicits comparable or greater increases in cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) vs. MICT in shortened training duration, especially when total work and frequency are matched.
- **Atherosclerotic CVD**: One early study showed HIIT produced a 17.9% increase in VO2peak vs. 7.9% for MICT over 10 weeks in coronary artery disease patients. However, results are conflicting—some trials found no difference, and a meta-analysis of 10 studies (n=472) found MICT was associated with more marked declines in resting heart rate and body weight.
- **Heart failure**: Studies generally show HIIT improves aerobic capacity more than MICT (e.g., 22% vs. 11% increase in VO2peak in HF with preserved ejection fraction over 12 weeks; one RCT of 180 patients found no difference). A systematic review/meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found HIIT generally superior for CRF in HF patients.
- **Adherence**: Supervised adherence is similar between HIIT and MICT, but home-based HIIT adherence was only 58% (vs. >81% for home-based MICT), with higher dropout rates in home-based HIIT and slightly higher dropout rates in women.
- **Cardiometabolic health**: A meta-analysis found HIIT more effective for CRF and flow-mediated dilation, while MICT was superior for long-term glucose metabolism (hemoglobin A1c). No differences in BMI, blood pressure, lipids, or insulin resistance. A recent meta-analysis of 26 RCTs (790 patients with "diabesity") found HIIT offered modest additional benefits for fasting insulin, insulin resistance, and CRF.
- **Atrial fibrillation**: In 86 patients with persistent/permanent AF, twice-weekly 23-min HIIT was as effective as 60-min MICT in improving 6-min walk test, QoL, and resting heart rate, despite a 336-min difference in total exercise time. However, HIIT had significantly higher dropout rates (11 vs. 4, P=0.047) likely due to exercise-related complications like joint injuries.

SAFETY/RISK DATA:
- Adverse event rate of 8% reported for HIIT in cardiometabolic disease patients in one review.
- Another review found 1 event per 3,417 sessions for HIIT vs. 1 per 7,134 sessions for MICT.
- In 4,846 coronary patients, absolute risk was 1 event per 23,182 patient-hours for HIIT vs. 1 per 129,456 for MICT—5.6 times higher in HIIT.
- A home-based HIIT study reported one patient death during warm-up.
- The cumulative patient-hours in existing HIIT trials fall far short of the ~23,182 hours statistically estimated to trigger an acute cardiac event, so it is premature to conclude HIIT is safe/superior.

CASE REPORT: The authors describe a 38-year-old male nurse (BMI 36 kg/m²) who enrolled in a HIIT program after an extended exercise layoff. He collapsed and died of sudden cardiac death during his first session's last treadmill station (jogging at 5.0–5.5 mph, ~7–9 METs). His intake form was unremarkable. Autopsy revealed moderate single-vessel atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (~65% luminal narrowing), marked cardiac hypertrophy (heart weighed 490g vs. ~300g normal), and cause of death listed as "atherosclerotic and hypertensive cardiovascular disease."

PREVALENCE OF SILENT CVD: Cleveland Clinic intravascular ultrasound study showed coronary atherosclerosis in ~60% of those aged 30–39 and 71% aged 40–49; a Swedish study of >25,000 people aged 50–64 found 42% had silent coronary atherosclerosis.

CONCLUSIONS: HIIT appears superior to MICT in improving CRF/aerobic capacity with shorter training time, and elicits sustained post-exercise oxygen consumption exceeding 24 hours with appetite suppression effects. However, there is no consensus on HIIT prescriptive guidelines, staffing, or stopping criteria in cardiac rehabilitation. The authors recommend direct medical supervision and continuous ECG monitoring at least during initial weeks, caution when initiating HIIT in previously inactive adults, and warn that starting a conditioning program with vigorous exercise for inactive, unfit individuals aged ~35+ may be hazardous to health. Additional long-term studies are needed to assess safety, adherence, and outcomes across varied populations.

**Keywords:**High-intensity interval training, Older adults, Seniors, Chronic disease

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951)Key Points

High-intensity interval training, though increasingly popular, has not been well-studied in older adults.Early research suggests that HIIT may confer health benefits over moderate-intensity continuous training (traditional endurance exercise) and is generally well-tolerated in older adults.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951)Introduction

Globally, the number of people aged 65 years or older is expected to more than double in the next 30 years, making it the fastest growing age demographic [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR1)]. It has been estimated that these older adults experience 23% of the global burden of disease and that this number increases to nearly 50% in high-income countries and is about 20% in low- and middle-income countries [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR2)]. Chronic non-communicable diseases make up the majority of this burden [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR2)]. This accounts for a significant and growing financial burden on our health care systems and the UN National Assembly (2012) has acknowledged the urgent need for governments to scale up and transition towards universal, affordable, and quality health-care services [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR3)]. Exercise is known to be an important part of healthy aging and is useful in preventing and managing chronic disease [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR4)]. The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR5)] recommend that adults over 65 years of age achieve at least 150 min of moderate- or 75 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity per week, in addition to muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 2 days per week. They also highlight that in this population, exercise can be done to improve both health outcomes and functional abilities and that they should include multicomponent training that incorporates balance and flexibility training [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR5)]. As such, identifying modes of exercise which achieve these goals and are tolerable and feasible in older adults is an important step towards improving the health of these populations.

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is an increasingly popular form of aerobic exercise which includes bouts of high-intensity exercise, typically lasting seconds to minutes, interspersed with periods of rest [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR6)]. HIIT has been proposed to be equal or advantageous to continuous endurance training both in terms of physiologic results [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR7), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR8)] and in enjoyability [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR9)]. However, the health benefits, risks, and optimal design of HIIT are still unclear. Further, most of the research on the effects and benefits of HIIT has been done in younger and middle-aged adults, and as such, the tolerability and effects in older populations are less well-known.

The purpose of this scoping review is to identify and characterize existing research on the effects of HIIT in older adults to assist in knowledge translation and recommend further areas of study. Specifically, it aims to describe which study populations are included, the training protocol designs, whether this training is feasible and/or tolerable for older adults, the main outcomes being addressed, and to identify gaps in the current knowledge.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951)Methodological Framework

According to Arksey and O’Malley [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR10)], the purpose of a scoping review is to examine the extent, range, and nature of research activity, to summarize research findings, or to identify gaps in the existing literature. To achieve this, they established a 5-step framework which was used in the undertaking of this review. The steps are detailed below and include the following: 1. Identifying the research question, 2. Identifying relevant studies, 3. Study selection, 4. Charting the data, 5. Collating, summarizing, and reporting the results [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR10)].

The research question was as follows: What is known in the literature about HIIT in older adults, including which protocols are used, outcomes measured, its feasibility and safety in this population, and what are the gaps in the current knowledge?

A full description of the study protocol including search strategy and detailed reasons for article exclusion are available in the [supplemental materials](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#MOESM1). In summary, five databases were searched (Scopus, Medline (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), CINAHL, and SportDiscus) for articles published up to February 2021. Search terms included combinations and variations of the following: “high-intensity interval training,” “interval aerobic training,” “HIIT,” “older adult,” and “senior.” A description of the complete search strategy is included in the [supplemental materials](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#MOESM1)_._ These searches identified 4644 potential studies. Of these, 2019 references were removed as duplicates. The non-duplicate titles and abstracts were read by authors CM and AP to determine if the studies were relevant to the research question. Initial exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) published before 2009 (as it was not feasible for the authors to screen all of the potential studies and the authors wanted to include the most recent and relevant studies), (2) review papers or not peer-reviewed, (3) did not include high-intensity exercise protocols, (4) did not use human subjects, or (5) the mean age of the study subjects was less than 50 years old.

In keeping with the iterative nature of scoping review methods, inclusion criteria were then developed in collaboration with author RP. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) the mean age of all participants was at least 65 years of age or older, or one mean cohort age was at least 65 years and was not statistically different from the other groups, (2) the study was an experimental or semi-experimental trial, (3) the study was an original source (for example, letters to the editor, correspondences, and editorials were not included) published as full-text in English, and (4) the exercise protocol used was exclusively high-intensity interval aerobic training, and was not combined with another intervention, such as resistance training (RT). Many exercise training modalities which have some similarities to HIIT were excluded from this review. These included RT or high-intensity resistance training, which primarily aims to overload the musculoskeletal system by causing the muscles to contract against an external force [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR11)], circuit training and body-weight interval training (which includes RT), moderate-intensity interval training (MIT), and moderate-intensity continuous training (MCT). Additionally, high-intensity functional exercise is a form of functional weight-bearing exercise training designed for the elderly populations dependent on activities of daily living. This type of training more closely resembles RT than HIIT, and as such, it was also excluded from this review [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR12)]. Exercise intensity is often measured using heart rate (HR), heart rate reserve (HRR), or oxygen uptake (VO 2). “High-intensity” was defined and categorized as vigorous effort (70–89% of peak HR; 60–84% of HRR; 60–79% of peak VO 2) or “very hard” effort (≥ 90% of peak HR; ≥ 85% of HRR; ≥ 80% of peak VO 2) [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR13), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR14)]. The anaerobic threshold (VT 2) was included as high-intensity, but the aerobic threshold (VT 1) was not [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR15)]. The percentage of peak power output (%PPO) is occasionally used to measure and report exercise intensity. There are reports that %PPO does not correlate with the same percentage of HR max in different exercise modalities/patient populations [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR16)]. To illustrate this point, Hood et al. [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR17)] used a target intensity of 60% PPO which correlated with approximately 80% HRR and increased over time to 95% HRR. Where a range of target intensities was described in the study protocols, the average intensity was used to determine eligibility. For example, if the study had participants exercise at 60–70% HR peak, it was excluded as the average intensity was presumed to be 65% HR peak. Sprint interval training (SIT) is an interval exercise involving maximal or supramaximal intensity activity for short periods of time (typically seconds) [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR7)]. Though different from HIIT, SIT treatment groups were included in this review as they may offer further insight into the tolerability, safety, and acceptance of similar interval protocols. The remaining articles were read in full by authors CM and AP to assess for eligibility. Any discrepancy was discussed by these authors until consensus was achieved.

The eligible studies were read and grouped by clinical populations. Data from these studies were extracted and charted by CM, including the population(s) studied, the study design, and the main outcomes measured. Details of the HIIT protocol intervention were also charted and included exercise frequency, intensity and duration of interval, intensity and duration of the rest period, and modality (such as treadmill, cycling, etc.). If it was noted in the publication, information on whether the HIIT was feasible and/or tolerated by study participants was also extracted. This was done by measuring outcomes such as attendance, adherence, drop-outs/withdrawals, “enjoyability” or acceptance of protocol, and adverse events. These data were validated by research assistant, EM. In charting the study design, the HIIT interventions were summarized to allow for ease of comparison between studies. Controls or other treatment groups compared to HIIT in the literature were noted and included RT and MCT. MCT was defined as an intensity of 55–69% HR max or 40–59% VO 2max and is representative of typical endurance training [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR13)]. RT was defined as exercise primarily aiming to overload the musculoskeletal system by causing the muscles to contract against an external force [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#CR11)]. Data were summarized and reported as per the emerging themes.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951)Results

The search yielded 4644 references. Duplicates were removed and inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied. Age was a common reason for exclusion. As such, if the mean age was not provided in the abstract, this information was found in the full text as part of the screening process. In the papers assessed for eligibility, resistance or circuit training were often combined with HIIT. However, as many papers focused exclusively on HIIT, these combined programs were excluded from the final subset. This left 69 studies to be included in the review (Fig. [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#Fig1)). Fig. 1Flow chart of the study selection process

The studies included were classified by clinical population. The largest grouping was of non-clinical populations (_n_ = 30), followed by cardiovascular diseases (_n_ = 12), cardiac disease (_n_ = 9), metabolic disease (_n_ = 8), and other (_n_ = 10). Study design, sample size, population(s) included, and baseline characteristics of included studies, grouped by clinical cohort, are reported in Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8289951#Tab1). These studies had sample sizes ranging from 10 to 473 (mean [SD] = 47.0 [65.2]) and included a total of 3243 individuals. The mean ages of the study participants ranged from 61.4 to 80.8 years (mean [SD] = 67.9 [3.4] years). Forty-eight studies were randomized controlled or crossover designs; 21 were quasi-experimental. args.summary:
This is a scoping review published in Sports Medicine - Open (July 19, 2021) titled "High-Intensity Interval Training in Older Adults: A Scoping Review" by Catherine F. S. Marriott and colleagues from Western University and the University of British Columbia. The review aims to characterize existing research on HIIT in older adults, including study populations, training protocols, feasibility/tolerability, outcomes, and knowledge gaps.

METHODOLOGY: The authors used the Arksey and O'Malley 5-step scoping review framework. Five databases (Scopus, Medline, Embase, CINAHL, SportDiscus) were searched for articles published up to February 2021, yielding 4,644 potential studies. After removing duplicates and applying inclusion/exclusion criteria (including requiring mean participant age ≥65 years, experimental or semi-experimental designs, original research, and exclusively high-intensity interval aerobic training not combined with resistance training), 69 studies were included. "High-intensity" was defined as 70-89% of peak HR, 60-84% of HRR, or 60-79% of peak VO2 (vigorous), or ≥90% peak HR, ≥85% HRR, ≥80% peak VO2 (very hard). Sprint interval training (SIT) groups were also included.

RESULTS: The 69 studies included 3,243 individuals with sample sizes ranging from 10 to 473 (mean 47.0 ± 65.2). Mean participant ages ranged from 61.4 to 80.8 years (mean 67.9 ± 3.4 years). Studies were classified by clinical population: non-clinical (n=30), cardiovascular diseases (n=12), cardiac disease (n=9), metabolic disease (n=8), and other (n=10). 48 studies were randomized controlled or crossover designs; 21 were quasi-experimental. Interventions ranged from a single session to 6 months (mean 7.9 ± 7.0 weeks), with session frequency of 2-5 per week. The most common modality was cycle ergometer (n=46), followed by treadmills/walking, water-based training, all-extremity ergometers, and recumbent steppers. The review included 12 SIT studies, 3 short-interval studies (<1 min), and 57 long-interval studies (≥1 min).

KEY FINDINGS: HIIT was generally reported as well-tolerated in older adults across most studies, with high compliance rates (e.g., 85-100% attendance) and few adverse events. HIIT showed benefits in cardiorespiratory fitness, blood pressure reduction, body composition, functional ability, and in some studies cognitive outcomes, often comparable or superior to moderate-intensity continuous training (MCT). The review notes HIIT is increasingly popular but has not been well-studied in older adults compared to younger populations, and early research suggests it may confer health benefits over traditional endurance exercise while being generally well-tolerated.
args.key_excerpts: "High-intensity interval training, though increasingly popular, has not been well-studied in older adults. Early research suggests that HIIT may confer health benefits over moderate-intensity continuous training (traditional endurance exercise) and is generally well-tolerated in older adults."

## Abstract

**Background:** Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, with approximately 17.9 million lives lost each year, and has an incidence of 77-80% amongst those 60-80 years old. HIIT is not the initial treatment of choice in those with CVD among physical therapists because of the fear and concern relating to the patient’s response to high-intensity exercise.

**Objective:** The purpose of this systematic review was to determine the effectiveness of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on older adults with cardiovascular disease and, if it was effective, find the proper protocol for this population. This systematic review intends to find the proper frequency, intensity, time, and type (FIIT) of HIIT for these patients to receive the maximal benefits in the safest way possible.

**METHODS:** The search for this systematic review took place from September of 2024 to January of 2025 and used CINAHL, PubMed, and Medline databases. The search terms within these databases included: high intensity interval training, HIIT, older adults, protocol, cardiovascular, elderly, and heart disease. The inclusion criteria of these searches included participants with cardiovascular diseases, HIIT interventions, peer-reviewed, randomized controlled trials, English language, and published within the last 10 years. After a thorough review of the mentioned databases using these criteria, 12 studies were chosen to be included in this systematic review.

**RESULTS:** The results of the chosen articles showed that HIIT was more beneficial for older adults with cardiovascular disease compared to interventions of moderate-continuous training (MCT) and control groups with no adjustments to their current exercise regimen. HIIT showed greater improvements in older adults' peak VO2 max and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), as well as increases in 6 MWT and QOL scales. Of the HIIT protocols examined, the most beneficial protocols were the 4x4, consisting of 4 minute high-intensity training, followed by 3 minutes of active/passive rest for 4 sets total, as well as the 2x8, using 8 minutes of high intensity training with 30 seconds of high intensity training, followed by 30 seconds of active rest, for 2 sets. There were also some benefits seen with the M-ullevaal protocol, which is 3 HIIT sets at 90% maxHR, combined with 2 moderate-continuous training (MCT) sets at 70% max HR. These protocols were performed through various activities, including walking, cycling, elliptical, and muscle strengthening exercises.

**CONCLUSION:** There were significant physiological and psychological benefits seen amongst the older adults participating in HIIT training. Throughout a review of the 12 studies, there was little to no increase in adverse events amongst the HIIT group compared to the MCT or control groups, helping to emphasize the fact that these protocols can be performed in a safe and effective manner for this patient population. There was also an overall beneficial frequency, intensity, time, and type that can be used as a baseline for future intervention within this population. In the future, studies can be done to evaluate the difference between males and females with HIIT training, as well as studies to determine the proper intensity thresholds to reach HIIT.

**Abstract summary:**
- **Background:** Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide (~17.9 million lives lost annually), with 77-80% incidence among those aged 60-80. Physical therapists often avoid HIIT for CVD patients due to concerns about high-intensity exercise responses.
