## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064)Abstract

Engaging in regular exercise results in a range of physiological adaptations offering benefits for exercise capacity and health, independent of age, gender or the presence of chronic diseases. Accumulating evidence shows that lack of time is a major impediment to exercise, causing physical inactivity worldwide. This issue has resulted in momentum for interval training models known to elicit higher enjoyment and induce adaptations similar to or greater than moderate-intensity continuous training, despite a lower total exercise volume. Although there is no universal definition, high-intensity interval exercise is characterized by repeated short bursts of intense activity, performed with a “near maximal” or “all-out” effort corresponding to ≥90% of maximal oxygen uptake or >75% of maximal power, with periods of rest or low-intensity exercise. Research has indicated that high-intensity interval training induces numerous physiological adaptations that improve exercise capacity (maximal oxygen uptake, aerobic endurance, anaerobic capacity etc.) and metabolic health in both clinical and healthy (athletes, active and inactive individuals without any apparent disease or disorder) populations. In this paper, a brief history of high-intensity interval training is presented, based on the novel findings of some selected studies on exercise capacity and health, starting from the early 1920s to date. Further, an overview of the mechanisms underlying the physiological adaptations in response to high-intensity interval training is provided.

**Keywords:**exercise, intermittent training, physical endurance, health benefits, physiological adaptation

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064)1. Introduction

Exercise is a cornerstone in the primary prevention of chronic diseases including diabetes mellitus, cancer, obesity, hypertension, coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease, and depression [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B1-ijerph-18-07201),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B2-ijerph-18-07201),[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B3-ijerph-18-07201)]. For centuries, exercise has long been prescribed by physicians as a medicine for their patients [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B4-ijerph-18-07201)], and quotes attributed to Hippocrates, the father of Western medicine, include: “Walking is man’s best medicine” and “if there is a deficiency in food and exercise, the body will fall sick [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B5-ijerph-18-07201),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B6-ijerph-18-07201)].” Evidence-based scientific guidelines suggest that exercise is a novel non-pharmacological strategy in the prevention and management of chronic diseases [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B7-ijerph-18-07201),[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B8-ijerph-18-07201),[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B9-ijerph-18-07201),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B10-ijerph-18-07201),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B11-ijerph-18-07201)]. Despite these well-documented benefits of exercise, a third of adults and four-fifths of adolescents—approximately 1.4 billion people—do not meet public health guidelines for recommended levels of exercise [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B7-ijerph-18-07201)], making physical inactivity a global problem [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B12-ijerph-18-07201)]. The recently updated World Health Organization 2020 Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B13-ijerph-18-07201)] recommend performing at least 150 to 300 min of moderate-intensity physical activity, or 75 to 150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise, per week to achieve substantial health benefits [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B14-ijerph-18-07201)]. However, the lack of sufficient time is the most common barrier to adhering to regular exercise [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B15-ijerph-18-07201)]. Therefore, research has recently focused on interval training models, which consist of brief periods of intense activity performed with a “near-maximal” or “all-out” effort corresponding to ≥90 of maximal oxygen uptake ($\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max) [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)] or >75% of maximal power [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B17-ijerph-18-07201)], interspersed with passive or active recovery periods, that can induce similar or even greater physiological adaptations when compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B17-ijerph-18-07201),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B18-ijerph-18-07201),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B19-ijerph-18-07201)], which generally consists of 30–60 min of moderate-intensity exercise at 40% to <60% of oxygen consumption reserve [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B20-ijerph-18-07201),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B21-ijerph-18-07201)]. There are numerous excellent reviews on the effects of interval training on exercise capacity and general health in healthy and clinic populations as well as the mechanisms underlying these effects [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B15-ijerph-18-07201),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B18-ijerph-18-07201),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B22-ijerph-18-07201),[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B23-ijerph-18-07201),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B24-ijerph-18-07201)]. However, to the best of our knowledge, no study to date has applied a historical approach. In this review, after defining the types of different interval-training models, the findings of some selected high-intensity interval-training studies that have received considerable interest due to their novel findings on exercise capacity and health, which can be considered milestone studies in the related literature, are presented. Finally, a brief overview of the mechanisms underlying the physiological adaptations in response to high-intensity interval training is presented.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064)2. Interval Training

Interval training is characterized by short bursts of intense activities that elicit ≥90% of $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)], >75% of maximal power [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B17-ijerph-18-07201)] or supra-maximal effort [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B17-ijerph-18-07201),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B18-ijerph-18-07201)], with periods of rest or low-intensity exercise for recovery. The most used types of interval training models are: (1) the high-intensity interval training (HIIT) model with submaximal efforts that elicit ≥90% of $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)] or >75% of maximal power [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B18-ijerph-18-07201),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B25-ijerph-18-07201)]; (2) the sprint interval training (SIT) model, a more intense version of HIIT that involves maximal or supramaximal efforts greater than $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max or maximal power; and (3) the repeated-sprint training (RST) model, which is characterized by performing a high number of sprints lasting less than 10 s interspersed with relatively shorter recoveries (<60 s) compared to the recovery periods of SIT [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B26-ijerph-18-07201)].

Interval training has been an integral part of training for coaches and athletes to enhance performance for over a century, and it has received considerable scientific inquiry due to its ability to induce remarkable physiological adaptations and health benefits that resemble MICT with less time commitment [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B27-ijerph-18-07201)]. Besides, it should be noted that from a mechanistic standpoint, physiological adaptations elicited by interval training is not only attributable to intensity per se but also the intrinsic nature of the intermittent exercise.

It is well documented that HIIT provides a robust stimulus for central cardiovascular adaptations and metabolic stress [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B28-ijerph-18-07201)], while MICT mainly triggers peripheral adaptations contributing to muscular oxygen extraction and metabolic efficiency [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B29-ijerph-18-07201),[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B30-ijerph-18-07201),[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B31-ijerph-18-07201)]. HIIT is known to elicit higher enjoyment than MICT, as reported by original research [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B32-ijerph-18-07201)] and meta-analysis [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B33-ijerph-18-07201)], making the interval training model a practical and enjoyable exercise mode for the general population. Furthermore, a meta-analysis by Reljic et al. [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B34-ijerph-18-07201)] reported that following HIIT-based interventions, there were lower dropout rates than traditional exercise programs in previously sedentary individuals, showing that HIIT is tolerable and acceptable. However, a single bout of high-intensity interval exercise performed at a strenuous intensity with a low resting period likely results in decreased enjoyment, and thus, adequate resting intervals between high-intensity sessions are essential in preventing negative affective responses for long-term exercise maintenance.

Due to its time-saving nature and the induced physiological adaptations similar to MICT, HIIT has been ranked first in 2018 [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B35-ijerph-18-07201)] and third in 2019 in Worldwide Fitness Trends [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B36-ijerph-18-07201)]. Growing evidence-based research, both original research and meta-analysis studies, shows that interval training programs ranging from 5 days to 12 months are effective in improving $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B37-ijerph-18-07201)], endurance capacity [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B38-ijerph-18-07201),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B39-ijerph-18-07201)], resting metabolic rate [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B40-ijerph-18-07201)], substrate metabolism [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B41-ijerph-18-07201),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B42-ijerph-18-07201)], body composition [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B43-ijerph-18-07201)], insulin sensitivity [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B44-ijerph-18-07201),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B45-ijerph-18-07201)], and cognitive functions [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B46-ijerph-18-07201),[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B47-ijerph-18-07201),[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B48-ijerph-18-07201)]. Besides, interval training has been shown to decrease the risk for cardiovascular diseases [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B15-ijerph-18-07201),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B25-ijerph-18-07201)], breast cancer [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B49-ijerph-18-07201)], metabolic syndrome [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B50-ijerph-18-07201)], osteoarthritis [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B51-ijerph-18-07201),[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B52-ijerph-18-07201)], and rheumatoid arthritis known to cause lower back pain [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B53-ijerph-18-07201),[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B54-ijerph-18-07201),[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B55-ijerph-18-07201),[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B56-ijerph-18-07201),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B57-ijerph-18-07201)] ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#ijerph-18-07201-f001)). In the following subheadings, the definition, as well as health and performance benefits, of different interval trainings models are presented.

### 2.1. High-Intensity Interval Training

High-intensity interval exercise is characterized by relatively short bursts of vigorous activity performed at a high relative workload corresponding to ≥90% of $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)], >75% of maximal power [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B17-ijerph-18-07201)], ≥90% minimal running speed required to elicit VO 2max [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)], and at a range of “hard” to “very hard” rate of perceived exertion (≥6 on a 10 Borg scale and ≥15 on a 6–20 scale) [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)]. Each single effort generally lasts from a few seconds to several minutes, dependent on exercise intensity, with multiple efforts interspersed by up to a few minutes of rest or less exertion. Although some research has determined the exercise intensity of high-intensity work based on the HR in the absence of equipment and expertise for determining $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B21-ijerph-18-07201),[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B58-ijerph-18-07201)], it is not consistently reliable due to the heterogeneous character of the heart rate (HR), such as people with cardiovascular disease, who can have an upward deflection of the HR performance curve [[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B59-ijerph-18-07201)]; using maximal HR (HR max) for exercise intensity can result in an overestimation of the individual training HR up to 40% in single cases [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B60-ijerph-18-07201),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B61-ijerph-18-07201)], and true HR max can not be obtained in untrained subjects using incremental exercise tests on a treadmill or a cycle ergometer, because of local leg fatigue that is likely to cause tests to end prematurely before cardiopulmonary endpoints [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B62-ijerph-18-07201)].

Despite having various sub-categories, HIIT is generally sub-categorized into low—less than 15 min—and high-volume (greater than 15 min) HIIT based on the total time spent in active intervals [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B63-ijerph-18-07201)]. These HIIT protocols have been shown to lead to similar, and sometimes greater, health and performance benefits despite less time commitment [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B43-ijerph-18-07201),[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B64-ijerph-18-07201),[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B65-ijerph-18-07201),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B66-ijerph-18-07201),[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B67-ijerph-18-07201)]. Moreover, as highlighted by a recent review [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B63-ijerph-18-07201)] and meta-analysis [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B43-ijerph-18-07201)], it is evident that low-volume HIIT, involving less than 15 min of active high-intensity training per session, is a time-efficient exercise strategy to improve cardiometabolic health and cardiovascular endurance [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B63-ijerph-18-07201)].

Inevitably, strong motivation is required due to the high-exertion nature of the classic interval training model, which is very fatiguing and too strenuous for sedentary individuals [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B19-ijerph-18-07201)]. In addition, the total time commitment of classic HIIT protocols include warm-up, recovery intervals, and cool-down, which is typically more than 20 min and therefore reduces the time efficiency [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B64-ijerph-18-07201)]. In this sense, the findings of studies involving low-volume protocols are promising to determine whether the levels of exertion and time-commitment of the current HIIT protocols can be reduced while maintaining the associated health and performance benefits.

### 2.2. Sprint Interval Training

SIT is a more intense form of HIIT performed at an intensity that exceeds the workload required to elicit $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max or maximal power. Each bout of high-intensity work lasts short periods of activity (≤30 s), separated by relatively long recovery periods between intervals (~4 min) [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B68-ijerph-18-07201)]. The target exercise intensities during SIT are usually workloads greater than the pace that elicits $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max or maximal power, including ‘all-out’ or ‘supramaximal’ efforts [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B68-ijerph-18-07201)]. The minimal intensities suggested for SIT are >100% of maximal power [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B17-ijerph-18-07201)], ≥85% maximal sprinting speed, and ≥160% minimal running speed required to elicit VO 2max [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)]. The most used SIT protocol is performed on a cycle ergometer and consists of 4 × 30 s all-out maximal intervals, pedaling against a high force corresponding to approximately 170% of $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max with rest intervals or light exercise [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B69-ijerph-18-07201)].

Ample evidence has shown that 2 and 6 weeks of SIT was effective in increasing skeletal muscle oxidative capacity and endurance capacity as well as inducing key molecules associated with mitochondrial biogenesis in healthy individuals [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B70-ijerph-18-07201),[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B71-ijerph-18-07201),[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B72-ijerph-18-07201)], which was comparable to that observed after MICT, despite robust difference in training volume. Besides, some research has reported improved insulin sensitivity in young healthy men [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B45-ijerph-18-07201),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B73-ijerph-18-07201)] and increased resting fat oxidation in overweight/obese individuals following 2 weeks [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B41-ijerph-18-07201)], as well as reduced fat mass following 12 and 15 weeks of SIT in normal weight and overweight individuals [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B74-ijerph-18-07201),[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B75-ijerph-18-07201)]. However, it is worth noting that SIT requires maximal effort and may not be well-tolerated or appealing for many individuals, including people with chronic diseases or obesity in particular. Hence, although current findings seem interesting from the perspective of health and performance benefits, it would not be an easy translation into physical activity recommendations for the general population, suggesting the need for further research into SIT that can establish acceptable and effective protocols.

### 2.3. Repeated-Sprint Training

RST is characterized by performing repeated sprints (10–20 maximal or shuttle sprints lasting ≤10 s), interspersed with short recoveries (<60 s) [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B76-ijerph-18-07201),[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B77-ijerph-18-07201)]. The minimal intensity suggested for RST is ≥120% minimal running speed required to elicit VO 2max [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B16-ijerph-18-07201)]. This training model is widely utilized in the physical preparation of athletes for many sports [[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B78-ijerph-18-07201),[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B79-ijerph-18-07201),[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B80-ijerph-18-07201)]. The published literature is not, however, as abundant for RST studies as for SIT or HIIT. The SIT and HIIT models are repeatedly performed with recovery periods long enough to allow for near full recovery of sprint performance, whilst the recovery duration between repeated sprints during RST is minimal, thus there is inevitably performance decrement during RST. Research has shown that RST can improve endurance, sprint, repeated-sprint ability, and aerobic capacity in healthy and fit subjects [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B26-ijerph-18-07201),[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B77-ijerph-18-07201)]. A meta-analysis by Taylor et al. [[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B81-ijerph-18-07201)] reviewed controlled and non-controlled trials investigating the effect of RST on athletic-performance variables, including counter-movement jump, 10 m sprint, 20 m sprint, 30 m sprint, repeated-sprint ability, and high-intensity intermittent-running performance, and documented RST to be effective in improving power, speed, repeated-sprint ability, and endurance.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064)3. Effects of HIIT on Exercise Capacity and Health Based on Selected Studies

In this section, early attempts applying interval training and the main findings of selected HIIT studies are summarized. Since the early 2000s, the number of HIIT studies has gained momentum and increased exponentially. A quick search on PubMed now yields about 300 research articles per year containing “high-intensity interval training”, “sprint interval training”, “repeated sprint training” and “HIIT” in the title ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#ijerph-18-07201-f002)). Some HIIT studies to date have significantly contributed to the literature, by showing the physiological and molecular adaptations in response to high-intensity interval exercise intervention in healthy and clinical populations. The training studies included in this section are described in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#ijerph-18-07201-t001).

### 3.1. Most Early Attempts at Applying Interval Training Model

Despite the momentum in the number of studies indicating the effectiveness of HIIT in improving health and exercise performance over the last 20 years, it is well known that this training model dates back a hundred years and was the key strategy behind important sporting successes observed in the early 20th century [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B27-ijerph-18-07201)]. During this early period, HIIT significantly evolved through the contributions of innovative athletes and trainers [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B27-ijerph-18-07201),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B51-ijerph-18-07201)], such as Lauri Pikhala, who coached champion runners in Finland, including Hannes Kolehmainen and Paavo Nurmi. Paavo Nurmi was the world’s most successful distance runner between 1920 and 1930, earning his place in sporting history with nine Olympic gold medals; his training program mainly consisted of 20 × 60 s of high-intensity intervals, separated by short rest periods.

In the 1930s, a German physician and coach Woldemar Gerschler, together with cardiologist Herbert Reindel, designed a training model performed at a specific HR with rest periods. In this model, the athletes performed a short-distance run with a target HR of 180 beats/min, followed by a rest period until their HR decreased to 120 beats/min, before starting the next repetition [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B102-ijerph-18-07201)]. As reviewed by Gibala and Hawley [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B102-ijerph-18-07201)], Gerschler and Reindel proposed that the rest period between high-intensity bouts was the most important aspect of this training model, during which the heart adapted, allowing it to grow larger and stronger. This notion was supported by a study they conducted, in which 21 days of HIIT elicited a 20% increase in heart volume and improvement in the endurance capacity of middle- and long-distance runners [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B102-ijerph-18-07201)]. Perhaps the most notable athletes in history to adopt the interval training model is Sir Roger Bannister, who first ran 1.6 km (1 mile) in less than 4 min. His training protocol involved 10 × 400 m of running under 60 s, separated by 2 min rest [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B102-ijerph-18-07201)].

### 3.2. Studies on Exercise Capacity and Health in Healthy Populations

Although trainers and athletes have long known the effectiveness of interval training since the early 20th century, the effects of interval training models on human physiology did not get enough attention until the early 1960s [[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B103-ijerph-18-07201)]. In the following years, the effects of this type of exercise model on health and exercise performance gained popularity [[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B82-ijerph-18-07201),[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B83-ijerph-18-07201),[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B95-ijerph-18-07201),[104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B104-ijerph-18-07201)]. For example, in 1973, the Bengt Saltin group reported approximately 20% increase in $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max in young military conscripts following only 2 months of an interval training program consisting of 15 s exercise, followed by 15 s rest or 3 min exercise, followed by 3 min rest (3 times/wk) [[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B82-ijerph-18-07201)]. In 1975, Fox et al. reported [[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B83-ijerph-18-07201)] that the improvement in $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max in young healthy males was dependent on training intensity and attributed to increased stroke volume (SV) and arteriovenous oxygen difference (a-vO 2 diff) following 7 and 13 weeks of interval training program performed on an indoor oval track. In 1976, Henriksson and Reitman aimed to reveal if the effects of HIIT with MICT on oxidative and glycolytic enzyme activities were muscle-fiber-specific [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B84-ijerph-18-07201)]. To address this, nine young healthy subjects were divided into HIIT (5 × 4 min cycling at 101% $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max, separated by 2 min rest) or MICT (27 min of continuous cycling at 79% $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max) groups for 7–8 weeks [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B84-ijerph-18-07201)]. The authors reported an increase in $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max and the type II-succinate-dehydrogenase activity only in the HIIT group, while the MICT group showed an average 32% increase in type I-succinate-dehydrogenase activity [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B84-ijerph-18-07201)]. This paper showed that the enhancement of the $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max and the physiological adaptations observed in skeletal-muscle-fiber types following exercise were dependent on exercise intensity and fiber recruitment during exercise. Following these studies, Roberts et al. investigated in early 1980 the effects of HIIT on the anaerobic metabolism of skeletal muscle in young active males [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B85-ijerph-18-07201)]. The training program consisted of eight 200 m runs at 90% of maximal speed with 2 min rest periods over 5 weeks [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B85-ijerph-18-07201)]. They reported an improved anaerobic metabolism, as evidenced by the increased activities of key enzymes associated with glycogenolysis and anaerobic glycolysis in skeletal muscle [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B85-ijerph-18-07201)], indicating that a short-term interval training program was a potent stimulus to improve anaerobic metabolism.

In 1986, Sharp et al. documented that 8 weeks of SIT involving 8 × 30 s all-out training (4 times/week) increased the buffering capacity and $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max by 37% and 8%, respectively, in young healthy men [[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B86-ijerph-18-07201)]. This paper was the first to show SIT increased muscle buffer capacity [[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B86-ijerph-18-07201)]. Furthermore, in 1996 Tabata et al. [[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B87-ijerph-18-07201)] compared the effects of 6 weeks of HIIT (8 × 20 s at 170% PPO, separated by 10 s rest, 5 days/week) and MICT (70% $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max, 60 min/day, 5 days/week) on both aerobic and anaerobic exercise capacity in active individuals. This novel research showed that despite the robust difference in time commitment between the exercise protocols administered (43 min/week versus 300 min/week), HIIT was more effective in simultaneously upregulating oxidative and glycolytic energy systems, in turn producing an improved energy state in the exercising muscle and preserving high-energy phosphates [[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B87-ijerph-18-07201)].

Following this study, interest in the potential value of different interval training models that could be applied as an alternative to traditional MICT gained momentum. For example, MacDougall et al. in 1998 reported an increase in $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max and glycolytic and oxidative enzyme activity, including citrate synthase (CS), succinate-dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase, following 7 weeks of SIT involving 4 to 10 × 30 s all-out with 2 to 4 min of recovery (3 times/week) in young healthy men [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B89-ijerph-18-07201)]. In 2006, a landmark study by Gibala et al. was published, which compared SIT with traditional MICT on exercise performance and skeletal-muscle adaptations [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B71-ijerph-18-07201)]. Despite completing ~90% less total training volume (630 kJ vs. 6500 kJ), six sessions of SIT (30 s × 4–6 repeats) resulted in similar improvement in time trial performance to that observed following MICT [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B71-ijerph-18-07201)]. Analyses of skeletal-muscle samples showed similar increases in muscle oxidative capacity, muscle buffering capacity, and glycogen content between the two groups [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B71-ijerph-18-07201)]. The authors, therefore, concluded that SIT was a time-efficient strategy for rapid adaptations in exercise performance and skeletal muscle [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B71-ijerph-18-07201)], showing SIT to be as effective as MICT in improving cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle buffering capacity, and glycogen content, despite less time commitment.

Notably, in 2007, Helgerud et al. compared four training methods in young healthy males (2 interval training versus 2 continuous training) performed at different intensities, matched for total work and frequency (3 days/week for 8 weeks) [[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B90-ijerph-18-07201)]. The interval groups performed either 15/15 interval running (15 s of running at 90–95% HR max followed by 15 s of active resting at 70% HR max) or 4 × 4 min of interval running at 90–95% HR max followed by 3 min of active resting at 70% HR max. The continuous training involved either slow long-distance running at 70% HR max or lactate threshold running at 85% HR max. The authors reported an increase in $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max and left ventricular SV in the two HIIT groups, but no changes in the continuous running groups [[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B90-ijerph-18-07201)]. The authors, therefore, concluded that HIIT was more effective in improving $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max and SV than performing the same total work at either lactate threshold or at 70% HR max [[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B90-ijerph-18-07201)]. This paper revealed for the first time that increases in $\overset{\cdot}{V}$O 2max in response to interval training corresponded with changes in SV, showing a close link between the two.

On the other hand, until a study by Little et al. [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B91-ijerph-18-07201)], the majority of HIIT studies applied “all out” protocol that is not practical and is poorly tolerated by certain individuals; thus, there was a necessity to design a more practical and attainable protocol capable of inducing similar adaptations as classic HIIT models for the general population. To address this, in 2010, Little et al. [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B91-ijerph-18-07201)] designed a practical model of low-volume high-intensity interval exercise (8 to 12 × 60 s intervals at ~100% of PPO, separated by 75 s of recovery) [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B91-ijerph-18-07201)]. Similar to previous studies, they reported that performing this new training model over 2 weeks increased exercise capacity, as shown by improvements in cycling time trial performance [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B91-ijerph-18-07201)]. Additionally, the protein content and maximal activity of CS and cytochrome C oxidase in skeletal muscle increased, together with the protein content of mitochondrial transcription factor A and sirtuin 1, as well as the nuclear abundance of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 alpha (PGC-1α) [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B91-ijerph-18-07201)], which mediated skeletal-muscle mitochondrial adaptations. This is the first study to document that this new exercise model is a potent stimulus for improving endurance performance, skeletal muscle mitochondrial capacity, sirtuin 1, mitochondrial transcription factor A, and nuclear PGC-1α, which were previously reported to increase in response to the repeated SIT protocols of earlier studies [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B76-ijerph-18-07201),[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B77-ijerph-18-07201),[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B99-ijerph-18-07201),[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B100-ijerph-18-07201)].

The following years have witnessed some novel research involving mechanistic examinations carried out with muscle biopsies. These studies have allowed researchers to both investigate the effects of different types of interval training models on mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial biogenesis as well as distinguish the effects of training volume and training intensity. For example, in 2016, one of these several HIIT studies by Granata et al. compared three different training methods on skeletal-muscle mitochondrial content and mitochondrial respiration: SIT (4–10 × 30 s all-out bouts at ~200% of PPO), HIIT (4–7 × 4 min intervals at ~90% PPO), or sub-lactate threshold continuous training (20–36 min at ~65% PPO)), performed 3 sessions/wk for 4 weeks [[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B92-ijerph-18-07201)]. Unlike previously published data, PPO improved in the HIIT and SIT groups, while the time trial performance only improved in sub-lactate threshold continuous training and HIIT groups, remaining unchanged after SIT [[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B92-ijerph-18-07201)]. Only SIT increased mass-specific mitochondrial respiration in skeletal muscle, as well as the protein content of PGC-1α, protein p53, and plant homeodomain finger-containing protein 20 [[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B92-ijerph-18-07201)], which modulate mitochondrial biogenesis [[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B105-ijerph-18-07201)]. The authors concluded that training intensity was an important factor that determines changes in mitochondrial respiration, suggesting that SIT promotes greater and faster mitochondrial adaptations in skeletal muscle. Further, an elegant follow-up study by the same group was conducted to ascertain how different training volumes would affect mitochondrial respiration and markers of mitochondrial biogenesis [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B93-ijerph-18-07201)]. To address this, ten healthy men performed high-intensity interval cycling during 3 consecutive training phases, 4 weeks of normal-volume training (3 days/week), followed by 20 days of high-volume training (2 sessions/day) and 2 weeks of reduced-volume training (5 sessions) [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B93-ijerph-18-07201)]. The main finding of the study was that mitochondrial parameters did not change following normal-volume training, while there were improvements in mitochondrial respiration, the maximal activity of CS, and PGC-1α after high-volume training [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B93-ijerph-18-07201)]. Similarly, the protein content of mitochondrial complex I, II, III, IV, and V, and mass-specific mitochondrial respiration were elevated after high-volume training but dropped quickly after 2 weeks of reduced-volume training [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B93-ijerph-18-07201)]. The authors concluded that there would be a rapid reversal of human skeletal-muscle adaptations to a reduction in training volume, and that training volume plays a key role in training-induced mitochondrial adaptations.

Finally, in the growing HIIT literature, most studies examining the effects of HIIT on health and performance involved high-intensity interval exercise performed once a day for various durations [[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B106-ijerph-18-07201),[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B107-ijerph-18-07201),[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B108-ijerph-18-07201),[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B109-ijerph-18-07201),[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B110-ijerph-18-07201),[111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B111-ijerph-18-07201),[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B112-ijerph-18-07201),[113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B113-ijerph-18-07201),[114](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B114-ijerph-18-07201)]. This has led Andrade-Souza and colleagues to wonder whether the effects of “twice a day” and “once a day” HIIT on mitochondrial biogenesis were identical. To address this, this research group designed a novel protocol that allowed the authors to manipulate the recovery duration between the first muscle glycogen-depleting exercise and the second exercise session, either 2 h (twice-a-day) or 15 h (once-daily) after the first exercise session [[115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B115-ijerph-18-07201)]. In both approaches, the second exercise session (10 × 2 min intervals corresponding to an intensity of 20% of the difference between the lactate threshold and PPO) started with reduced muscle glycogen content [[115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B115-ijerph-18-07201)]. The authors reported greater mRNA expression of PGC-1α, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta, and greater nuclear abundance of PGC-1α and protein p53 after twice-a-day high-intensity interval exercise [[115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B115-ijerph-18-07201)]. On the other hand, muscle glycogen decreased similarly between the two exercise approaches [[115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B115-ijerph-18-07201)]. A notable finding in this study is that performing two exercise sessions separated by a short recovery period might be more effective at inducing adaptations related to mitochondrial biogenesis and fat oxidation than the once-daily exercise, which in turn helps improve endurance performance.

A landmark study by Stensvold et al. [[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B94-ijerph-18-07201)], published in 2020, compared the effects of five years of supervised exercise training, including HIIT and MICT, with recommendations for physical activity on mortality in older adults [[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064#B94-ijerph-18-07201)]. A total of 1567 older adults were randomized into one of three groups: twice-a-week high-intensity interval exercise sessions (4 × 4 min at 85–95% peak HR (HR peak) with 3 min active recovery 60–70% HR peak); twice-a-week MICT sessions (50 min of continuous cycling at 70% HR peak); and a control group of generally active people who followed the Norwegian physical activity guidelines recommending 30 min of moderate-leve

args.summary:
This is a scientific review article published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2021 Jul 05;18(13):7201; doi: 10.3390/ijerph18137201) titled "Evidence-Based Effects of High-Intensity Interval Training on Exercise Capacity and Health: A Review with Historical Perspective." The authors are Muhammed Mustafa Atakan (Hacettepe University, Turkey), Yanchun Li (Beijing Sport University, China), Şükran Nazan Koşar (Hacettepe University), Hüseyin Hüsrev Turnagöl (Hacettepe University), and Xu Yan (Victoria University, Australia). The article is open access under a CC BY license (PMCID: PMC8294064, PMID: 34281138).

KEY FINDINGS AND CONTENT:

**Context and Rationale:** Lack of time is a major barrier to exercise worldwide, with approximately 1.4 billion people (a third of adults and four-fifths of adolescents) not meeting public health exercise guidelines. WHO 2020 guidelines recommend 150-300 min of moderate or 75-150 min of vigorous aerobic activity weekly. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) offers similar or greater physiological adaptations than moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) with lower total exercise volume.

**Definitions of Interval Training Models:**
- HIIT: repeated short bursts at ≥90% of VO2max or >75% of maximal power
- Sprint Interval Training (SIT): maximal or supramaximal efforts exceeding VO2max or maximal power; typical protocol is 4×30s all-out intervals at ~170% of VO2max
- Repeated-Sprint Training (RST): 10-20 maximal sprints lasting ≤10s with recoveries <60s

**Historical Development:**
- Lauri Pikhala coached Finnish runners Hannes Kolehmainen and Paavo Nurmi (9 Olympic gold medals, 1920-1930), whose training included 20×60s high-intensity intervals
- In the 1930s, German physician Woldemar Gerschler and cardiologist Herbert Reindel designed a HR-based interval model (target 180 beats/min, rest until HR drops to 120); 21 days of HIIT elicited 20% increase in heart volume
- Sir Roger Bannister ran the first sub-4-minute mile using 10×400m intervals under 60s with 2 min rest

**Key Studies and Findings:**
- 1973 (Saltin group): ~20% increase in VO2max in young military conscripts after 2 months of interval training
- 1975 (Fox et al.): VO2max improvement depended on training intensity, attributed to increased stroke volume and arteriovenous oxygen difference
- 1976 (Henriksson & Reitman): HIIT increased type II-succinate-dehydrogenase activity while MICT increased type I-succinate-dehydrogenase activity (32% increase)
- 1986 (Sharp et al.): 8 weeks of SIT (8×30s all-out, 4×/week) increased muscle buffering capacity by 37% and VO2max by 8% — first study showing SIT increases muscle buffer capacity
- 1996 (Tabata et al.): HIIT (8×20s at 170% PPO) was more effective than MICT in upregulating both oxidative and glycolytic energy systems despite much less time (43 vs 300 min/week)
- 2006 (Gibala et al., landmark study): Six sessions of SIT with ~90% less total training volume (630 kJ vs 6500 kJ) produced similar improvements in time trial performance, muscle oxidative capacity, buffering capacity, and glycogen content compared to MICT
- 2007 (Helgerud et al.): HIIT improved VO2max and left ventricular stroke volume while continuous training at 70% or 85% HR max did not — first to show VO2max increases correspond with stroke volume changes
- 2010 (Little et al.): Designed a practical low-volume HIIT protocol (8-12×60s at ~100% PPO) that improved exercise capacity and increased CS, cytochrome C oxidase, mitochondrial transcription factor A, sirtuin 1, and nuclear PGC-1α
- 2016 (Granata et al.): Only SIT increased mass-specific mitochondrial respiration, PGC-1α, protein p53, and plant homeodomain finger-containing protein 20; training intensity was key for mitochondrial adaptations
- 2020 (Stensvold et al.): Five-year randomized trial of 1567 older adults comparing twice-weekly HIIT (4×4 min at 85-95% HR peak), MICT, and Norwegian physical activity guidelines

**Mechanistic Insights:** HIIT provides robust central cardiovascular adaptations and metabolic stress, while MICT mainly triggers peripheral adaptations. HIIT elicits higher enjoyment than MICT and lower dropout rates in previously sedentary individuals. HIIT has been shown to improve VO2max, endurance capacity, resting metabolic rate, substrate metabolism, body composition, insulin sensitivity, and cognitive functions, while decreasing risk for cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, metabolic syndrome, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis. HIIT ranked first in 2018 and third in 2019 Worldwide Fitness Trends. The paper also notes that muscle glycogen depletion and "twice-a-day" training separated by short recovery may enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and fat oxidation adaptations.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Exercise strategy

This article is about the cardiovascular exercise made popular in the 2010s. For the 1970s weight training, see [High intensity training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_intensity_training "High intensity training").

"HIIT" redirects here. For other uses, see [HIIT (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIIT_(disambiguation) "HIIT (disambiguation)").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/HIIT_Workout.jpg/250px-HIIT_Workout.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HIIT_Workout.jpg)

HIIT with dumbbells

**High-intensity interval training** (**HIIT**) is a training protocol alternating short periods of intense or explosive [anaerobic exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaerobic_exercise "Anaerobic exercise") with brief recovery periods until the point of exhaustion.[[1]](#cite_note-Tabata_Nishimura_|first2=Kouji_Kouzaki_1996-1) HIIT involves exercises performed in repeated quick bursts at maximum or near maximal effort with periods of rest or low activity between bouts. The very high level of intensity, the interval duration, and number of bouts distinguish it from [aerobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerobic_exercise "Aerobic exercise") (cardiovascular) activity, because the body significantly recruits anaerobic energy systems (although not completely to the exclusion of aerobic pathways).[[1]](#cite_note-Tabata_Nishimura_|first2=Kouji_Kouzaki_1996-1) The method thereby relies on "the anaerobic energy releasing system almost maximally".[[1]](#cite_note-Tabata_Nishimura_|first2=Kouji_Kouzaki_1996-1)

Although there are varying forms of HIIT-style workouts which may involve exercises associated with both cardiovascular activity and also [resistance training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strength_training "Strength training"), HIIT's crucial features of maximal effort, duration, and short rest periods (thereby triggering the anaerobic pathways of energy production) materially differentiate it from being considered a form of cardiovascular exercise.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Though there is no universal HIIT session duration, a HIIT workout typically lasts under 30 minutes in total as it uses the anaerobic energy systems which are typically used for short, sharp bursts. The times vary, based on a participant's current fitness level.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Traditional HIIT initially had been designed to be no longer than 20 seconds on with no more than 10 seconds off; however, intervals of exercise effort tend to range from 20 to 45 seconds but no longer than 75 seconds, at which point the aerobic system would then kick in.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

HIIT workouts provide improved athletic capacity and [condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_exercise "Physical exercise") as well as improved [glucose metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate_metabolism "Carbohydrate metabolism").[[5]](#cite_note-5) Compared with longer sessions typical of other regimens, HIIT may not be as effective for treating [hyperlipidemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperlipidemia "Hyperlipidemia") and [obesity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obesity "Obesity"), or improving muscle and bone mass.[[6]](#cite_note-6) However, research has shown that HIIT regimens produced reductions in the fat mass of the whole-body in young women comparable to prolonged moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT).[[7]](#cite_note-7) Some researchers also note that HIIT requires "an extremely high level of subject motivation" and question whether the general population could safely or practically tolerate the extreme nature of the exercise regimen.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

**Sprint interval training** (**SIT**) is an exercise conducted in a similar way to HIIT, but instead of using "near maximal" effort for the high-intensity periods, "supramaximal" or "all-out" efforts are used in shorter bursts. In physiological terms, "near maximal" means reaching 80–100% [HRmax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HRmax "HRmax"), while "supramaximal" means a pace that exceeds what would elicit [VO2 peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VO2_peak "VO2 peak"). SIT regimens generally include a lower volume of total exercise compared with HIIT ones as well as longer, lower activity recovery periods and creates a greater homeostatic disturbance.[[9]](#cite_note-9) Both HIIT and SIT fall into the larger class of [interval training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_training "Interval training").[[10]](#cite_note-pmid27748956-10) Distinction between the two is not always maintained, even in academia: for example, Tabata describes his 170% VO2 max regimen as "supermaximal", but does not use the term SIT.[[11]](#cite_note-pmid29151442-11)

## Procedure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Procedure")]

HIIT exercise sessions generally consist of a [warm-up period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warming_up "Warming up") followed by repetitions of high-intensity exercises separated by medium intensity exercises for recovery, then a cool-down period. The high-intensity exercise should be done at near maximum intensity. The medium exercise should be about 50% intensity. The number of repetitions and length of each depends on the exercise, but may be as little as three repetitions with just 20 seconds of intense exercise.[[12]](#cite_note-NYT_Well_Blog-12) The specific exercises performed during the high-intensity portions vary. Most of the research on HIIT has been done using a cycling ergometer, but other exercises like a rowing ergometer, running, stair climbing and uphill walking can also be effective.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

There is no specific formula for HIIT. Depending on one's level of cardiovascular development, the moderate-level intensity can be as slow as walking. A typical HIIT session uses a 2:1 work-to-rest ratio, for example, 30–40 seconds of hard sprinting alternated with 15–20 seconds of jogging or walking, repeated to failure.

The entire HIIT session may last between four and 30 minutes, meaning that it is considered to be an excellent way to maximize a workout limited by time constraints.[[14]](#cite_note-Forbes-14) Use of a clock or timer is recommended to keep accurate times, the number of rounds, and intensity.

An alternative form of HIIT, designed for [heart rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_rate "Heart rate") training, involves a 30-minute period of cardio followed by 30 minutes of full-body resistance training to help maximize [calorie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calorie "Calorie") burning.[[15]](#cite_note-15) The idea is to combine [aerobic exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerobic_exercise "Aerobic exercise") with intense [weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weight_training "Weight training") and [resistance training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strength_training "Strength training") to achieve a high level heart rate for an extended period of time, in order to maximize strength and [endurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance "Endurance").

## Branches

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Branches")]

### Peter Coe regimen

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Peter Coe regimen")]

In the 1970s a type of high-intensity interval training with short recovery periods was used by the athletics coach [Peter Coe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Coe "Peter Coe") when setting sessions for his son [Sebastian Coe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastian_Coe "Sebastian Coe"). Inspired by the principles propounded by the German coach and university professor [Woldemar Gerschler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woldemar_Gerschler "Woldemar Gerschler") and the Swedish physiologist [Per-Olof Åstrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per-Olof_Åstrand "Per-Olof Åstrand"), Coe set sessions involving repeated fast 200 meter runs with only 30 seconds recovery between each fast run.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

### Tabata regimen

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Tabata regimen")]

A version of HIIT is based on a 1996 study[[1]](#cite_note-Tabata_Nishimura_|first2=Kouji_Kouzaki_1996-1) by [Ritsumeikan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritsumeikan_University "Ritsumeikan University") Professor [Izumi Tabata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izumi_Tabata "Izumi Tabata") (田畑泉) et al. initially involving [Olympic speedskaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedskating "Speedskating"). The study used 20 seconds of ultra-intense exercise (at an intensity of about 170% of [VO2max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VO2_max "VO2 max")) followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated continuously for 4 minutes (8 cycles). The exercise was performed on a mechanically braked [cycle ergometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_ergometer "Cycle ergometer"). Tabata called this **the IE1 protocol**.[[17]](#cite_note-pmid9139179-17) In the original study, athletes using this method trained 4 times per week, plus another day of steady-state training, for 6 weeks and obtained gains similar to a group of athletes who did [steady state training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_training "Continuous training") (70% VO2max) 5 times per week. The steady state group had a higher VO2max at the end (from 52 to 57 mL/(kg•min)). The Tabata group had achieved comparable aerobic improvements but only exercised 4 minutes per day on their 4 HIIT days compared to 60 minutes for the aerobic group. The Tabata group also started lower and gained more overall (from 48 to 55 mL/(kg•min)). Also, only the Tabata group had gained [anaerobic capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaerobic_exercise "Anaerobic exercise") benefits (As Tabata's protocol is "supermaximal",[[11]](#cite_note-pmid29151442-11) his regimen technically falls into the scope of SIT).

### Gibala regimen

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Gibala regimen")]

Professor Martin Gibala and his team at [McMaster University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMaster_University "McMaster University") in Canada have been researching high-intensity exercise for several years. Their 2010 study on students[[18]](#cite_note-pmid20100740-18) uses 3 minutes for warming up, then 60 seconds of intense exercise (at 95% of VO2max) followed by 75 seconds of rest, repeated for 8–12 cycles (sometimes referred to as "The Little Method"). Subjects using this method training 3 times per week on a stationary bicycle obtained gains similar to what would be expected from subjects who did steady-state (50–70% VO2max) training five times per week.

Gibala's group published a less intense version of their regimen in a 2011 paper in *[Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine_&_Science_in_Sports_&_Exercise "Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise")*. This was intended as a gentler option for sedentary people who had done no exercise for over a year. It included 3 minutes of warm-up, 10 repetitions of 60-second bursts at 60% peak power (80–95% of [heart rate reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_rate#Heart_rate_reserve "Heart rate")) each followed by 60 seconds of recovery, and then a 5-minute cool-down.[[19]](#cite_note-Hood2011-19)

### Zuniga regimen

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Zuniga regimen")]

In 2011 Jorge Zuniga, assistant professor of exercise science at [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University"), set out to determine how to fit the highest volume of work and oxygen consumption into the smallest amount of time. He found that intervals of 30 seconds at 90% of power output at VO2 max followed by 30 seconds of rest allowed for the highest VO2 consumption and the longest workout duration at specified intensity. Alternative protocols considered included 100% of maximum power output on the same interval schedule, similar to the Coe regimen, and 90% of maximum power output for three minutes, similar to traditional interval training.[[20]](#cite_note-Zuniga-20)

Zuniga's protocol has been implemented with great success by students of his who were participating in Creighton's Army [ROTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ROTC "ROTC") program. Cadets completing the protocol twice a week saw greater improvements in [APFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Physical_Fitness_Test "United States Army Physical Fitness Test") scores than in years past.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Zuniga's protocol typically consists of 10 repetitions.

### Vollaard regimen

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Vollaard regimen")]

Dr Niels Vollaard at the [University of Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Stirling "University of Stirling") proposed that when high-intensity intervals are done at "all-out" intensities, associated health benefits plateau after performing 2 or 3 sprint repetitions. This led to the development of a 10-minute exercise routine consisting of easy pedalling interspersed with two 20-second "all-out" cycling sprints.[[21]](#cite_note-Metcalfe-21) In a 2017 meta-analysis, Vollaard indeed showed that common protocols with as many as 6 to 10 repetitions of 30-second "all-out" sprints do not improve aerobic fitness more than the "2×20-s" protocol. He shifted the terminology for his to SIT.[[22]](#cite_note-Vollaard-22) It is claimed that this short protocol may remove many of the drawbacks that make other high-intensity interval training protocols unsuitable for the general population.[[23]](#cite_note-Vollaard/Metcalfe-23)

In a BBC *[Horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizon_(BBC_TV_series) "Horizon (BBC TV series)")* program in February 2012, Jamie Timmons, professor of systems biology at the [University of Loughborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Loughborough "University of Loughborough"), led [Michael Mosley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Mosley "Michael Mosley") through this exercise bike regimen, each time using three sprints instead of two. This protocol was performed three times a week for a total of 30 minutes of exercise per week (3 minutes of intense exercise), plus warm-up and recovery time.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

## Regimen comparison

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Regimen comparison")]

A study compared HIIT of eight 1-minute bouts at 85% maximum Watts (Wmax) interspersed with 1-minute active recovery at 25% Wmax, to SIT of eight 30-second bouts at 130% Wmax interspersed with 90-second active recovery at 25% Wmax (Total time-matched at 24 minutes including warm-up & cooldown). Its conclusion was "HIIT is the recommended routine" but "the magnitude of differences in various parameters between regimens was small; therefore, preference for either modality may be up to the individual".[[25]](#cite_note-25)

## Health effects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Health effects")]

### Cardiovascular effects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Cardiovascular effects")]

HIIT training and traditional endurance training both lead to significantly improved [cardiovascular fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_fitness "Cardiovascular fitness") in healthy adults ages 18–45 but HIIT leads to greater improvements in VO2 max.[[26]](#cite_note-Milanovic2015-26) HIIT regimens of one month or longer effectively improve cardiovascular fitness in adolescents and lead to moderate improvements in body composition.[[27]](#cite_note-Costigan2015-27) Notably, prolonged HIIT programs are similarly effective to short term low volume ones.[[28]](#cite_note-28) HIIT (when defined as four intervals of four minutes at 85–95% of max heart rate with three-minute intervals at 60–70% of max heart rate) is also more effective than moderate-intensity continuous training at improving blood vessel function and markers of blood vessel health.[[29]](#cite_note-Ramos2015-29)

Comparing HIIT to moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) in people with [coronary artery disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_disease "Coronary artery disease"), HIIT leads to greater improvements in VO2 max but MICT leads to greater reductions in body weight and heart rate.[[30]](#cite_note-Liou2015-30) Improvement to [cardiorespiratory fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiorespiratory_fitness "Cardiorespiratory fitness"), as measured by VO2 max, of individuals with lifestyle-induced chronic cardiovascular or metabolic diseases (including [high blood pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertension "Hypertension"), obesity, [heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_failure "Heart failure"), coronary artery disease, or [metabolic syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolic_syndrome "Metabolic syndrome")) who completed a HIIT exercise program can be nearly double that of individuals who completed a MICT exercise program (19.4% increase and 10.3% increase, respectively).[[31]](#cite_note-Weston2014-31)

### Rehabilitative effects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Rehabilitative effects")]

For people suffering from [coronary artery disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_disease "Coronary artery disease"), [heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_failure "Heart failure") or [myocardial infarction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocardial_infarction "Myocardial infarction") survivors, a HIIT regimen is beneficial for substantially improving VO2 max and overall exercise capacity; with more intense HIIT leading to the greatest cardiovascular improvements.[[32]](#cite_note-:1-32)[[33]](#cite_note-33) A combination of a proper HIIT program with active recovery instead of passive recovery is most beneficial to improving heart contractibility in people with heart failure.[[32]](#cite_note-:1-32)

### Metabolic effects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Metabolic effects")]

HIIT significantly lowers [insulin resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin_resistance "Insulin resistance") compared to continuous training or control conditions and leads to modestly decreased fasting blood [glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose "Glucose") levels and increased weight loss compared to those who do not undergo a physical activity intervention.[[34]](#cite_note-Jelleyman2015-34)

### Fat oxidation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Fat oxidation")]

HIIT can result in modest reductions of subcutaneous fat in young and healthy individuals, but greater reductions for overweight individuals.[[35]](#cite_note-35) HIIT, particularly running, is a time-efficient strategy in decreasing abdominal and visceral fat-mass deposits.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

A 2021 systematic review examined the effects of HIIT combined with [resistance training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strength_training "Strength training") in teens (ages 10–19), without providing a nutritional plan. The study found that 8 to 12 weeks of HIIT combined with resistance training can substantially reduce waist size and [body fat percentage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_fat_percentage "Body fat percentage"). However the study did not find conclusive evidence of HIIT and resistance training being an effective solitary treatment for [type 2 diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_2_diabetes "Type 2 diabetes") or arterial [hypertension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertension "Hypertension"), but did find HIIT has the potential to reduce future cardiovascular problems in teens.[[37]](#cite_note-:3-37)

### Cognitive effects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Cognitive effects")]

HIIT can elicit short term cognitive improvements similar to those usually observed with aerobic exercise.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

### Youth

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Youth")]

HIIT has been shown to increase muscle mass in adolescent populations, especially in the mid-to-late teenage years.[[39]](#cite_note-:03-39)[[40]](#cite_note-:23-40)[[41]](#cite_note-:13-41) In cases of pediatric obesity, HIIT training can be used as both a treatment and a preventative measure, as it can help decrease BMI (body mass index), decrease body fat mass percentage, decrease insulin resistance, and decrease the count of low-density lipoproteins across the body.[[41]](#cite_note-:13-41) The reduction in fat mass and BMI at a young age create effects against obesity that are also tantamount in preventing other health issues such as diabetes, coronary heart disease, and cancer.[[40]](#cite_note-:23-40) It has been shown to increase full body strength, and thereby improve full-body movement capability, which can reduce sedentariness.[[39]](#cite_note-:03-39)[[40]](#cite_note-:23-40)[[41]](#cite_note-:13-41)

## Dangers

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Dangers")]

The [American College of Sports Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_College_of_Sports_Medicine "American College of Sports Medicine") suggests consulting one's doctor before starting a HIIT regimen, particularly if there is a history of [coronary heart disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_heart_disease "Coronary heart disease"). This is to ascertain its safety and allow the patient to build up the intensity of exercise without causing harm.[[42]](#cite_note-42) It is advised to start a lower intensity and go at one's own pace.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

High-intensity exercise has the potential to elicit rapid increases in systemic blood pressure that may be transmitted to the brain, which could lead to hyper-perfusion injury in at-risk populations such as sedentary adults.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

There is a risk of injury due to fatigue and [overtraining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtraining "Overtraining"), so it is advised to allow time for recovery.[[45]](#cite_note-45)[[46]](#cite_note-46) Research from [Rutgers University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University") demonstrated that the knees, shoulders, and ankles were the most commonly involved injuries. More specifically, knee and ankle [sprains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprain "Sprain") were very common. Based on that, [neuromuscular training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromuscular_training "Neuromuscular training") and pre-strengthening programs are recommended to improve [flexibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexibility_(anatomy) "Flexibility (anatomy)"), particularly before exercise.[[47]](#cite_note-47)

## Research

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=High-intensity_interval_training&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Research")]

A 2007 study examined HIIT's physiological effects on fat oxidation in moderately active women. The participants in the study performed HIIT (defined as ten sets of 4-minute cycling bursts at an intensity of 90% VO2max separated by 2 minutes of rest) every other day over a 2-week period. The study found that seven sessions of HIIT over a 2-week period improved whole body fat oxidation and the capacity for skeletal muscle to oxidize fat in moderately active women.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

A 2008 research study found that HIIT was more effective than moderate-intensity continuous training at lowering fasting insulin levels (31% decrease and 9% decrease, respectively).[[49]](#cite_note-49)

A 2011 study compared 3 different HIIT training programs, 4×4 min, 4×8 min, and 4×16 min. The workouts were performed twice per week, at an average of 94%, 90% and 88% of the [maximum heart rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_heart_rate "Maximum heart rate"), respectively. The 4×8 min regimen (4 times 8 minutes of intense work separated by 2 minutes of recovery time) was found to provide the greatest improvements in VO2 max (~11% after 7 weeks).[[50]](#cite_note-50)

A 2017 study examined the effect of HIIT on cognitive performance among a group of children. The authors show that HIIT is beneficial to cognitive control and working memory capacity when compared against "a blend of board games, computer games, and trivia quizzes" and that this effect is mediated by the [BDNF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain-derived_neurotrophic_factor "Brain-derived neurotrophic factor") polymorphism. They conclude that the study "suggests a promising alternative to enhance cognition, via short and potent exercise regimens".[[51]](#cite_note-51)

A 2019 [clinical trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_trial "Clinical trial") assessed the effects of HIIT on [vascular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_vessel "Blood vessel") health in inactive people and found that HIIT has beneficial vascular effects, based on observed decreases in [arterial wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arterial_wall "Arterial wall") thickness and increase in [endothelial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endothelium "Endothelium") function. The trial also found that HIIT had stronger effects than medium intensity continuous training (MICT) in enhancing [flow mediated dilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow-mediated_dilation "Flow-mediated dilation") and lowering [pulse wave velocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse_wave_velocity "Pulse wave velocity") in inactive adults from the greater blood flow and [vasodilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasodilation "Vasodilation") of blood vessels stimulated by HIIT. Increased flow mediated dilation allows for greater opening of an artery and increased blood flow, allowing for more oxygen to be supplied throughout the body during activity. Pulse wave velocity is used to monitor [arterial stiffness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arterial_stiffness "Arterial stiffness"); which increases with age and high blood pressure, leading to a higher probability of cardiovascular problems including hypertension or a stroke.[[52]](#cite_note-:02-52)

A 2019 study on the relevance of exercise intensity in lower back rehabilitation, demonstrated higher intensity had a greater effectiveness with back [therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therapy "Therapy") than moderate intensity exercise. Participants in the HIIT group had a decrease in back pain intensity and an increase in [back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_back "Human back") muscle strength.[[53]](#cite_note-:2-53) In 2020, a similar study explained the strong effectiveness of cardiorespiratory HIIT in treating lower back pain, when combined with other forms of HIIT or mobility exercises.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

A 2020 study examined the impact of HIIT and moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) on overweight individuals by measuring the effect on cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). The study found that both forms of training were effective in improving CRF with an increase in VO2 max, however there was no evidence that either training method was more effective than the other in improving cardiorespiratory fitness.[[54]](#cite_note-:4-54)

According to a 2020 study HIIT could be used as [prehabilitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehabilitation "Prehabilitation") for men awaiting surgery for urological cancer and it may improve [heart and lung fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiorespiratory_fitness "Cardiorespiratory fitness") within a month before their surgery.[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-56)
