## Abstract

### Background

Exercise is an established non-pharmacological strategy for lowering blood pressure (BP), but the comparative effectiveness and optimal dose of different exercise modalities in middle-aged and older adults remain unclear.

### Objective

This study aimed to systematically compare the effects of different exercise modalities and doses on resting systolic and diastolic BP (SBP/DBP) in middle-aged and older adults (≥ 45 years).

### Methods

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified from six electronic databases from inception to May 2025. Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis was used to compare BP-lowering effects across exercise modalities. Model-based dose–response analyses were conducted to examine associations between exercise dose, expressed as metabolic equivalent of task minutes per week (METs-min/week), and SBP reduction. Network meta-regression was used to explore potential effect modifiers.

### Results

A total of 159 RCTs (_n_ = 10,821) were included. All exercise modalities were associated with significant reductions in SBP and DBP compared with control. Circuit-based training (CBT) showed the largest estimated SBP reduction (mean difference [MD] − 13.52 mmHg; 95% credible interval [CrI] − 18.59 to − 8.44), followed by combined training (CT), high-intensity interval training, moderate-intensity continuous training, dynamic resistance training, and isometric exercise. CBT and CT generally remained among the highest-ranked modalities across sensitivity analyses, supporting the potential value of integrated aerobic–resistance training (IART). Higher baseline SBP was associated with greater SBP reductions (_β_ = − 2.49 mmHg per 10-mmHg increase; 95% CrI − 3.73 to − 1.24). Dose–response analyses suggested a nonlinear association between exercise dose and SBP reduction, with the largest model-estimated reduction occurring around 1200 METs-min/week, corresponding to the upper range of World Health Organization (WHO) physical activity recommendations. CBT showed a model-estimated peak effect at approximately 580 METs-min/week, close to the lower range of WHO recommendations.

### Conclusions

All exercise modalities were associated with significant BP reductions in middle-aged and older adults, although effect magnitude, certainty, and robustness varied. IART, including CBT and CT, appeared to be a promising approach for BP management. CBT showed the largest estimated effect and may offer a time-efficient option, but its apparent superiority over CT should be interpreted cautiously given the limited CBT-specific evidence, low-to-very-low certainty of evidence, and sensitivity analysis findings. Given that no network comparison was rated as high confidence and many included studies had some concerns or high risk of bias, comparative rankings should be interpreted cautiously and should not be considered definitive evidence of superiority.

FormalPara Key Points 

Exercise training was associated with lower resting blood pressure in middle-aged and older adults across all included modalities, although effect magnitude, certainty, and robustness varied across modalities.
Integrated aerobic-resistance training appeared promising for blood pressure management, with circuit-based training and combined training generally ranking highly.
The overall dose–response curve suggested that systolic blood pressure reduction increased up to approximately 1200 METs-min/week and then plateaued.
Circuit-based training showed the largest primary-analysis estimate, but this finding was based on limited evidence and was sensitive to study quality and sample size restrictions; combined training surpassed circuit-based training in some sensitivity analyses.

## 1 Introduction

By 2050, the global population aged over 60 years is projected to account for 22% of the total population, reflecting an accelerating trend of population aging [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR1 "Kanasi E, Ayilavarapu S, Jones J. The aging population: demographics and the biology of aging. Periodontol 2000. 2000;72(1):13–8.")]. Aging is often accompanied by increases in blood pressure (BP) and arterial stiffness [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR2 "Wu S, Jin C, Li S, Zheng X, Zhang X, Cui L, et al. Aging, arterial stiffness, and blood pressure association in Chinese adults. Hypertension. 2019;73(4):893–9."), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR3 "Steen B. Body composition and aging. Nutr Rev. 1988;46(2):45–51.")]. Elevated BP, or hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular complications and is associated with approximately 10.8 million deaths globally each year [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR4 "Hassen N, Lacaille D, Xu A, Alandejani A, Sidi S, Mansourian M, et al. National burden of rheumatoid arthritis in Canada, 1990–2019: findings from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 – a GBD collaborator-led study. RMD Open. 2024;10(1):e003533."), [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR5 "Roth GA, Mensah GA, Johnson CO, Addolorato G, Ammirati E, Baddour LM, et al. Global burden of cardiovascular diseases and risk factors, 1990–2019. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2020;76(25):2982–3021.")]. Elimination of major cardiovascular diseases (CVD) could increase global life expectancy by approximately 5.5 years [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR6 "Arias E, Heron MP, Tejada-Vera B. United States life tables eliminating certain causes of death, 1999–2001. 2013.")], significantly reducing the burden on healthcare systems [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR7 "Control CfD, Prevention. Trends in aging--United States and worldwide. MMWR Morbid Mortal Wkly Rep 2003;52(6):101–6.")].

To date, discrepancies remain among international guidelines regarding the diagnostic threshold for hypertension. The 2017 European Society of Cardiology/European Society of Hypertension (ESC/ESH) guidelines [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR8 "Cuspidi C, Tadic M, Grassi G, Mancia G. Treatment of hypertension: The ESH/ESC guidelines recommendations. Pharmacol Res. 2018;128:315–21.")] recommend initiating antihypertensive treatment at systolic/diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP) ≥ 140/90 mmHg, a criterion reaffirmed in the latest 2024 guideline update [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR9 "McEvoy JW, McCarthy CP, Bruno RM, Brouwers S, Canavan MD, Ceconi C, et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension. Eur Heart J. 2024;45(38):3912–4018.")]. This threshold aligns with the recommendations issued by Chinese [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR10 "Li–Sheng L. 2018 Chinese guidelines for prevention and treatment of hypertension—a report of the revision committee of Chinese guidelines for prevention and treatment of hypertension. J Geriatr Cardiol 2019;16(3):182–241.")] and Japanese [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR11 "Umemura S, Arima H, Arima S, Asayama K, Dohi Y, Hirooka Y, et al. The Japanese Society of Hypertension Guidelines for the Management of Hypertension (JSH 2019). Hypertens Res. 2019;42(9):1235–481.")] hypertension guidelines. In contrast, the 2017 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guideline adopts a lower threshold, defining hypertension as SBP/DBP ≥ 130/80 mmHg [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR12 "Whelton PK, Carey RM, Aronow WS, Casey DE, Collins KJ, Dennison Himmelfarb C, et al. 2017 ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA guideline for the prevention, detection, evaluation, and management of high blood pressure in adults. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2018;71(19):e127–248.")].

While 24-h ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) and central aortic BP provide stronger prognostic value [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR9 "McEvoy JW, McCarthy CP, Bruno RM, Brouwers S, Canavan MD, Ceconi C, et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension. Eur Heart J. 2024;45(38):3912–4018."), [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR13 "Hanssen H, Pescatello LS. Is isometric exercise training the best FIT for exercise prescription in the prevention and treatment of arterial hypertension? Br J Sports Med. 2024;58(4):231–2.")], their limited availability and higher cost restrict widespread clinical use [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR9 "McEvoy JW, McCarthy CP, Bruno RM, Brouwers S, Canavan MD, Ceconi C, et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension. Eur Heart J. 2024;45(38):3912–4018.")]. Importantly, ABPM uses a lower diagnostic threshold (≥ 130/80), which may introduce systematic bias and increase between-study heterogeneity in meta-analyses if baseline BP classification is not consistently accounted for. Given this, the present study focuses exclusively on resting peripheral BP measurements, the most widely used and standardized approach in clinical trials.

Exercise, as a non-pharmacological intervention, is widely recognized as an essential component in the primary prevention, treatment, and control of hypertension [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR14 "Pescatello LS, Franklin BA, Fagard R, Farquhar WB, Kelley GA, Ray CA. Exercise and hypertension. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2004;36(3):533–53."), [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR15 "Pelliccia A, Sharma S, Gati S, Bäck M, Börjesson M, Caselli S, et al. 2020 ESC Guidelines on sports cardiology and exercise in patients with cardiovascular disease. Eur Heart J. 2021;42(1):17–96.")]. In recent years, numerous pairwise meta-analyses have demonstrated the blood pressure-lowering effects of aerobic training [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR16 "Whelton SP, Chin A, Xin X, He J. Effect of aerobic exercise on blood pressure. Ann Intern Med. 2002;136(7):493–503."), [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR17 "Kelley GA, Kelley KS. Aerobic exercise and resting blood pressure in older adults: a meta-analytic review of randomized controlled trials. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2001;56(5):M298–303.")], dynamic resistance training (DRT) [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR18 "Cornelissen VA, Fagard RH, Coeckelberghs E, Vanhees L. Impact of resistance training on blood pressure and other cardiovascular risk factors. Hypertension. 2011;58(5):950–8."), [19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR19 "Lemes ÍR, Ferreira PH, Linares SN, Machado AF, Pastre CM, Netto J. Resistance training reduces systolic blood pressure in metabolic syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Br J Sports Med. 2016;50(23):1438–42.")], and combined aerobic and resistance training (CT) [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR20 "Al-Mhanna SB, Batrakoulis A, Wan Ghazali WS, Mohamed M, Aldayel A, Alhussain MH, et al. Effects of combined aerobic and resistance training on glycemic control, blood pressure, inflammation, cardiorespiratory fitness and quality of life in patients with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PeerJ. 2024;12:e17525."), [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR21 "Wewege MA, Thom JM, Rye K-A, Parmenter BJ. Aerobic, resistance or combined training: A systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise to reduce cardiovascular risk in adults with metabolic syndrome. Atherosclerosis. 2018;274:162–71.")]. Emerging evidence has also highlighted the hypotensive effect of isometric exercise (IE) [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR22 "Edwards J, De Caux A, Donaldson J, Wiles J, O’Driscoll J. Isometric exercise versus high-intensity interval training for the management of blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(9):506–14."),[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR23 "Edwards J, Jalaludeen N, Marciniak A, Sharma R, O’Driscoll J. Haemodynamic and cardiac mechanical adaptations following isometric exercise training in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Imaging. 2025;26(Supplement 1):i438."),[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR24 "Edwards JJ, Wiles J, O’Driscoll J. Mechanisms for blood pressure reduction following isometric exercise training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Hypertens. 2022;40(11):2299–306.")] and circuit-based training (CBT) [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR25 "Hu C, Xia Y, Zeng D, Ye M, Mei T. Effect of resistance circuit training on comprehensive health indicators in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2024. 
                https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-59386-9
                
              ."),[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR26 "Hu Z, Jiang S, Hu C, Shen B, Gu J. The effects of circuit-based resistance training on blood pressure, arterial stiffness, and body composition in community-dwelling older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2025. 
                https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2025.1609013
                
              ."),[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR27 "Ramos-Campo DJ, Andreu Caravaca L, Martínez-Rodríguez A, Rubio-Arias JÁ. Effects of resistance circuit-based training on body composition, strength and cardiorespiratory fitness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Biology. 2021;10(5):377.")]. Comparisons between moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) and high-intensity interval training (HIIT) suggest that HIIT may offer superior BP reductions [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR28 "Li L, Liu X, Shen F, Xu N, Li Y, Xu K, et al. Effects of high-intensity interval training versus moderate-intensity continuous training on blood pressure in patients with hypertension: a meta-analysis. Medicine. 2022;101(50):e32246."), [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR29 "Way KL, Sultana RN, Sabag A, Baker MK, Johnson NA. The effect of high Intensity interval training versus moderate intensity continuous training on arterial stiffness and 24 h blood pressure responses: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. 2019;22(4):385–91.")]. However, direct comparisons between most exercise modalities remain scarce in original trials.

Although two recent network meta-analyses [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR30 "Edwards JJ, Deenmamode AH, Griffiths M, Arnold O, Cooper NJ, Wiles JD, et al. Exercise training and resting blood pressure: a large-scale pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(20):1317–26."), [31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR31 "Batrakoulis A, Jamurtas AZ, Metsios GS, Perivoliotis K, Liguori G, Feito Y, et al. Comparative efficacy of 5 exercise types on cardiometabolic health in overweight and obese adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of 81 randomized controlled trials. Circulation: Cardiovasc Qual Outc 2022;15:6.")] compared a wide range of exercise modalities, they did not restrict inclusion to age-specific populations. Consequently, evidence on the comparative efficacy of exercise interventions for BP improvement in middle-aged and older adults remains limited. Furthermore, to our knowledge, no published network meta-analysis to date has explored the dose–response relationship between exercises and blood pressure reduction.

Current World Health Organization (WHO) physical activity guidelines recommend 150–300 min/week of moderate-intensity, or 75–150 min/week of vigorous-intensity physical activity for adults, corresponding approximately to 600–1200 metabolic equivalent of task minutes per week (METs-min/week) [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR32 "Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, Borodulin K, Buman MP, Cardon G, et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med. 2020;54(24):1451–62."), [33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR33 "Organization WH. Global physical activity questionnaire (GPAQ) analysis guide. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2012. p. 1–22.")]. However, whether the BP-lowering dose–response relationship differs across exercise modalities, and whether the optimal dose aligns with this recommended range, remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to conduct a comprehensive and up-to-date systematic review and Bayesian model-based network meta-analysis (NMA) of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of various exercise modalities on resting SBP and DBP. In addition, a Bayesian model-based dose–response analysis was also performed to explore the relationship between exercise dose (in METs-min/week) and blood pressure reduction for each exercise modality. One metabolic equivalent of task (MET) is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed (approximately 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min) during seated rest, and represents the energy cost of physical activity (PA) as a multiple of the resting metabolic rate [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR34 "Jetté M, Sidney K, Blümchen G. Metabolic equivalents (METS) in exercise testing, exercise prescription, and evaluation of functional capacity. Clin Cardiol. 1990;13(8):555–65.")].

## 2 Methods

This study was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR35 "Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM, Boutron I, Hoffmann TC, Mulrow CD, et al. statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ. 2020;2021:n71.")]. The current review was also pre-registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251123349). Since only publicly available data from published literature were used, no ethics approval or informed consent was required.

### 2.1 Search Strategy

Six electronic databases—PubMed (Medline), Cochrane library, Web of Science, EMBASE, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus—were systematically searched using a combination of both medical subject heading (MeSH) terms (if applicable) and free-text entry terms with Boolean logic terms ‘OR’ and ‘AND’. A filtered search was applied (RCTs only). Additionally, the search was restricted to English-language publications from inception to May 2025 (Table [S1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#MOESM1), see Electronic Supplementary Material [ESM]).

### 2.2 Eligibility Criteria

The inclusion criteria were constructed according to the PICOS framework [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR35 "Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM, Boutron I, Hoffmann TC, Mulrow CD, et al. statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ. 2020;2021:n71.")]. Studies were considered eligible if they met the following criteria:

1.   1.
Participants: Adults with a study-level mean age of ≥ 45 years. For multi-arm trials reporting separate mean ages by arm, eligibility was assessed using the average of the arm-level mean ages to represent the study-level mean age. Participants with stable chronic diseases, such as controlled hypertension or diabetes, were eligible if they were able to engage in exercise interventions.

2.   2.
Intervention: The study implemented at least one of the following exercise modalities as an intervention arm: HIIT, MICT, DRT, IE, CT, and CBT, with a minimum intervention duration of 4 weeks.

3.   3.
Comparators: The study compared the intervention with usual care, no intervention, placebo, or any other eligible exercise intervention listed above.

4.   4.
Outcomes: The study reported pre- and post-intervention SBP and/or DBP data, change scores, or sufficient summary statistics to derive mean differences (MDs) and corresponding standard errors (SEs) for exercise and control arms.

5.   5.
Study design: RCTs published in English were included. The search was restricted to English-language publications because of resource limitations for translation and to ensure accurate extraction and interpretation of intervention and outcome data.

Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria:

1.   1.
Blood pressure outcomes were reported solely as 24-h ABPM or central aortic pressure, without reporting resting peripheral blood pressure.

2.   2.
Interventions involved multiple treatments (e.g., exercise combined with diet, supplements, or other eligible exercise modalities) in which the independent effect of a single exercise modality on blood pressure could not be isolated.

3.   3.
Cross-over trials and other non-parallel designs were excluded because of potential carryover effects from chronic exercise-induced adaptations and their incompatibility with the arm-based network meta-analysis framework used in this review.

### 2.3 Outcomes

The primary outcome was resting SBP and the secondary outcome was resting DBP.

### 2.4 Study Selection and Data Extraction

Two independent reviewers (HZX and GJF) screened all retrieved records and extracted data using a standardized Microsoft Excel form, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR35 "Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM, Boutron I, Hoffmann TC, Mulrow CD, et al. statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ. 2020;2021:n71.")], to minimize potential selection bias. During the selection process, titles and abstracts were first screened to exclude clearly irrelevant records, followed by full-text review to determine final eligibility. Any disagreements during study selection or data extraction were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached.

The extracted information included study characteristics (first author, year of publication, and country), participant characteristics (sample size per group at baseline, endpoint, and final analysis, and arm-level mean age), intervention characteristics (exercise modality, intervention period, weekly training frequency, session duration, weekly exercise duration, descriptions of exercise intensity monitoring, and progression), and outcome-related information. Outcome-related information included pre- and post-intervention SBP and/or DBP means, change scores, SEs, SDs, or other summary statistics required to derive the corresponding MDs and SEs, as well as blood pressure measurement position. The procedures used to derive change scores, SDs, and SEs for quantitative synthesis are described in Sect. [2.6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#Sec9). For studies with incomplete or unclear outcome data, attempts were made to contact the corresponding authors to obtain the missing information. If the required data could not be obtained from the study, supplementary materials, or author contact, the study was excluded from the quantitative synthesis for that specific outcome.

### 2.5 Exercise Modality Classification and Dose Coding

Informed by the 2020 ESC Guidelines on sports cardiology [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR15 "Pelliccia A, Sharma S, Gati S, Bäck M, Börjesson M, Caselli S, et al. 2020 ESC Guidelines on sports cardiology and exercise in patients with cardiovascular disease. Eur Heart J. 2021;42(1):17–96.")], aerobic training was categorized as moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) or high-intensity interval training (HIIT), whereas resistance training was classified as dynamic resistance training (DRT) or isometric exercise (IE).

Additionally, IART was also considered an intervention of interest and was classified into two subtypes according to the temporal organization of aerobic and resistance components. Combined training (CT) was defined as a sequential format in which aerobic and resistance exercises were performed as distinct components within the same session or programme [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR36 "Dalgas U, Stenager E, Ingemann-Hansen T. Review: Multiple sclerosis and physical exercise: recommendations for the application of resistance-, endurance- and combined training. Mult Scler J. 2008;14(1):35–53.")]. In contrast, CBT was operationally defined as a station-based circuit format in which multiple exercises were performed successively with short inter-station recovery intervals and longer rest between completed circuits. This format typically involves whole-body or large-muscle-group movements and was considered to generate sustained aerobic or metabolic demand within the same session [[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR37 "Gettman LR, Pollock ML. Circuit weight training: a critical review of its physiological benefits. Phys Sportsmed. 1981;9(1):44–60."), [38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR38 "Muñoz-Martínez FA, Rubio-Arias JÁ, Ramos-Campo DJ, Alcaraz PE. Effectiveness of resistance circuit-based training for maximum oxygen uptake and upper-body one-repetition maximum improvements: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2017;47(12):2553–68.")]. The classification of training types and sub-modalities is presented in Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#Tab1).

**Table 1 Classification of exercise modalities**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5/tables/2)

For dose coding, two independent reviewers (HZX and XXY) selected the most appropriate activity code and corresponding MET value for each intervention arm based on the intervention characteristics extracted from the included RCTs. These characteristics included exercise modality, activity type, prescribed intensity descriptors (e.g., %VO₂peak [peak oxygen consumption], %VO₂max [maximal oxygen consumption], %HRmax [maximal heart rate], %HRR [heart rate reserve], %1RM [one repetition maximum], %MVC [maximum voluntary contraction], and RPE [rate of perceived exertion]), weekly exercise duration, and progression. Code selection and MET assignment were guided by the 2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR39 "Herrmann SD, Willis EA, Ainsworth BE, Barreira TV, Hastert M, Kracht CL, et al. 2024 adult compendium of physical activities: a third update of the energy costs of human activities. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):6–12.")] and the 2024 Older Adult Compendium of Physical Activities [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR40 "Willis EA, Herrmann SD, Hastert M, Kracht CL, Barreira TV, Schuna JM, et al. Older adult compendium of physical activities: energy costs of human activities in adults aged 60 and older. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):13–7.")], according to the mean age of the intervention arm.

Exercise-specific MET values were sourced from the 2024 Older Adult Compendium when a corresponding activity code was available for participants aged ≥ 60 years. However, because the Older Adult Compendium includes a more limited range of activity types, MET values for activities not listed in this compendium were sourced from the 2024 Adult Compendium [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR39 "Herrmann SD, Willis EA, Ainsworth BE, Barreira TV, Hastert M, Kracht CL, et al. 2024 adult compendium of physical activities: a third update of the energy costs of human activities. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):6–12."), [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR40 "Willis EA, Herrmann SD, Hastert M, Kracht CL, Barreira TV, Schuna JM, et al. Older adult compendium of physical activities: energy costs of human activities in adults aged 60 and older. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):13–7.")]. In such cases, adult METs 18-59 values were converted to older-adult METs 60+ values because older adults generally have a lower resting metabolic rate and therefore incur a higher relative metabolic cost when performing the same physical activity. Specifically, adult MET values based on the conventional 1 MET value of 3.5 mL/kg/min were adjusted using 2.7 mL/kg/min, the updated estimate of 1 MET in older adults [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR39 "Herrmann SD, Willis EA, Ainsworth BE, Barreira TV, Hastert M, Kracht CL, et al. 2024 adult compendium of physical activities: a third update of the energy costs of human activities. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):6–12."), [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR40 "Willis EA, Herrmann SD, Hastert M, Kracht CL, Barreira TV, Schuna JM, et al. Older adult compendium of physical activities: energy costs of human activities in adults aged 60 and older. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):13–7.")]:

$${METs}_{60+}= {METs}_{18-59} \times 3.5\div 2.7$$

When prescribed intensity was reported, the assigned MET value was not mathematically adjusted from the intensity descriptor; rather, the reported intensity was used to select the closest corresponding Compendium activity code and MET value. For example, when a trial reported stationary cycling at 60–70% HRmax as MICT, the activity was coded as “Bicycling, stationary, moderate effort” (Code: 0101160; 4.3 METs) [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR40 "Willis EA, Herrmann SD, Hastert M, Kracht CL, Barreira TV, Schuna JM, et al. Older adult compendium of physical activities: energy costs of human activities in adults aged 60 and older. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):13–7.")]. When intensity information was not clearly reported, the activity code was selected based on the reported exercise modality and activity type using the closest generic or moderate-effort Compendium category. Any discrepancies in code selection or dose estimation were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. The activity codes, MET values, and extracted intensity descriptors for each intervention arm are provided in Table S17 (see ESM).

The weekly exercise dose (in METs-min/week) was calculated using the following equation:

$$Exercise Dose=METs value \times Weekly sessions \times Session duration$$

Weekly sessions refer to the number of training sessions per week, and session duration denotes the length of the primary exercise component of the intervention, excluding warm-up, stretching, or cool-down periods.

For progressive interventions or interventions reporting intensity or duration as a range, average intensity and/or duration values were used when they could be calculated. When duration was reported as a range, the midpoint was used. When intensity was reported as a range or progression without sufficient phase-specific details for precise averaging, the midpoint or the closest representative intensity category across the intervention period was selected by consensus between the two reviewers.

For IART, CT and CBT were handled according to their intervention structure. For CT, when aerobic and resistance components were reported separately, component-specific MET values and component-specific durations were used, and the component-specific doses were summed to estimate the total weekly exercise dose. When component-specific duration or intensity was not clearly reported, the closest representative activity code and intensity category were selected according to the rules described above. For CBT, the total duration of the main circuit component was used, excluding warm-up and cool-down where possible, and the MET value was assigned using the closest circuit-training code according to the reported activity type and intensity.

Finally, to ensure network connectivity, exercise doses across studies were standardized using six predefined dose nodes: 0 (control), 250, 500, 750, 1250, and 1750 METs-min/week [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR41 "Higgins JPT, Jackson D, Barrett JK, Lu G, Ades AE, White IR. Consistency and inconsistency in network meta-analysis: concepts and models for multi-arm studies. Res Synth Methods. 2012;3(2):98–110.")]. The original exercise doses were then matched to the nearest predefined node using the nearest-value mapping method.

### 2.6 Data Synthesis

Treatment effects were analyzed as MDs in pre- to post-intervention changes in SBP and DBP, with corresponding SEs. Change scores were extracted directly when reported; otherwise, they were calculated from baseline and post-intervention means. If baseline or post-intervention means were not directly reported, they were estimated from medians with interquartile ranges or ranges using established methods [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR42 "Higgins JP, Li T, Deeks JJ. Choosing effect measures and computing estimates of effect. In: Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions. 2019. p. 143–76."),[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR43 "Wan X, Wang W, Liu J, Tong T. Estimating the sample mean and standard deviation from the sample size, median, range and/or interquartile range. BMC Med Res Methodol. 2014;14(1):135."),[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR44 "Luo D, Wan X, Liu J, Tong T. Optimally estimating the sample mean from the sample size, median, mid-range, and/or mid-quartile range. Stat Methods Med Res. 2018;27(6):1785–805.")]. When change-score SEs were directly reported, they were extracted and used in the meta-analysis. For studies without directly reported change-score SEs, change-score SDs were used as the intermediate variability measure. These SDs were extracted directly when reported or estimated from other available summary statistics, including 95% confidence intervals, _p-_ values, ranges, or interquartile ranges, where possible [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR42 "Higgins JP, Li T, Deeks JJ. Choosing effect measures and computing estimates of effect. In: Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions. 2019. p. 143–76."),[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR43 "Wan X, Wang W, Liu J, Tong T. Estimating the sample mean and standard deviation from the sample size, median, range and/or interquartile range. BMC Med Res Methodol. 2014;14(1):135."),[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR44 "Luo D, Wan X, Liu J, Tong T. Optimally estimating the sample mean from the sample size, median, mid-range, and/or mid-quartile range. Stat Methods Med Res. 2018;27(6):1785–805.")]. If change-score SDs were not available, they were calculated from baseline and post-intervention SDs using an assumed correlation coefficient of 0.5 [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR42 "Higgins JP, Li T, Deeks JJ. Choosing effect measures and computing estimates of effect. In: Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions. 2019. p. 143–76.")]. SEs were then calculated from the available or estimated change-score SDs and sample sizes. The same correlation coefficient was applied when synthesizing subgroup data. If the required data could not be obtained or derived, the study was excluded from the quantitative synthesis for that specific outcome.

### 2.7 Risk of Bias and Certainty of Evidence

Two independent reviewers (XXY and GJF) assessed the risk of bias for the included studies using the Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR45 "Higgins JP, Savović J, Page MJ, Elbers RG, Sterne JA. Assessing risk of bias in a randomized trial. In: Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions. 2019. p. 205–28.")]. The quality of evidence for ranking outcomes based on the network meta-analyses was evaluated using CINeMA (Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis) [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR46 "Nikolakopoulou A, Higgins JP, Papakonstantinou T, Chaimani A, Del Giovane C, Egger M, et al. CINeMA: an approach for assessing confidence in the results of a network meta-analysis. PLoS Med. 2020;17(4):e1003082.")]. Any discrepancies were discussed until consensus was reached; if necessary, a third reviewer (MW) was consulted.

### 2.8 Statistical Analysis

#### 2.8.1 Network Meta-Analysis

The transitivity assumption was initially evaluated by comparing key study and participant characteristics across the different exercise comparisons, including baseline blood pressure, age, and intervention duration. Only studies involving comparable populations and intervention definitions were included to support valid indirect comparisons.

To enable comparisons between exercise modalities that have not been directly evaluated in RCTs and to enhance the precision of effect estimates by incorporating both direct and indirect evidence, a Bayesian NMA was conducted using the web-based MetaInsight tool (version 6.4.0) [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR47 "Owen RK, Bradbury N, Xin Y, Cooper N, Sutton A. MetaInsight: An interactive web-based tool for analyzing, interrogating, and visualizing network meta-analyses using R-shiny and netmeta. Res Synth Methods. 2019;10(4):569–81.")], which implements the ‘_gemtc’_ and ‘_BUGSnet’_ packages in R. The analysis was performed within a Bayesian framework using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR48 "Van Valkenhoef G, Lu G, De Brock B, Hillege H, Ades AE, Welton NJ. Automating network meta-analysis. Res Synth Methods. 2012;3(4):285–99.")], involving four parallel chains and a total of 25,000 iterations (first 5000 iterations discarded as burn-in). Non-informative priors were applied to all parameters. Subsequently, the Brooks–Gelman–Rubin diagnostic was used to assess model convergence [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR49 "Brooks SP, Gelman A. General methods for monitoring convergence of iterative simulations. J Comput Graph Stat. 1998;7(4):434–55.")]. Between-study heterogeneity was evaluated using the standard deviation (τ) and the 95% credible interval (CrI). Global inconsistency was assessed by comparing model fit, deviance information criterion (DIC), and variance parameters between the consistency and unrelated mean effects models [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR50 "Dias S, Welton NJ, Sutton AJ, Caldwell DM, Lu G, Ades AE. Evidence synthesis for decision making 4. Med Decis Making. 2013;33(5):641–56.")]. The node-splitting method was employed to examine inconsistencies between direct and indirect comparisons within the network (_p_-values < 0.05 were considered to indicate significant inconsistency in the network) [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR50 "Dias S, Welton NJ, Sutton AJ, Caldwell DM, Lu G, Ades AE. Evidence synthesis for decision making 4. Med Decis Making. 2013;33(5):641–56.")].

Ranking probability analyses were also conducted via MetaInsight [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR47 "Owen RK, Bradbury N, Xin Y, Cooper N, Sutton A. MetaInsight: An interactive web-based tool for analyzing, interrogating, and visualizing network meta-analyses using R-shiny and netmeta. Res Synth Methods. 2019;10(4):569–81.")], and the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values were generated for each exercise modality. SUCRA values range from 0 to 100%, with higher values indicating greater treatment effectiveness [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR51 "Salanti G, Ades AE, Ioannidis JPA. Graphical methods and numerical summaries for presenting results from multiple-treatment meta-analysis: an overview and tutorial. J Clin Epidemiol. 2011;64(2):163–71.")].

#### 2.8.2 Dose–Response Network Meta-Analysis

We conducted a random-effects Bayesian model-based network meta-analysis [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR52 "Mawdsley D, Bennetts M, Dias S, Boucher M, Welton N. Model‐based network meta‐analysis: a framework for evidence synthesis of clinical trial data. CPT Pharmacomet Syst Pharmacol. 2016;5(8):393–401.")] to examine the dose–response relationship between exercise dose and SBP. Non-informative priors were applied to all parameters. The Bayesian estimation was performed using four Markov chains with 25,000 iterations and a burn-in period of 5000. No violations of the key assumptions underlying network meta-analysis were identified, including network connectivity [[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR53 "Ter Veer E, Van Oijen MGH, Van Laarhoven HWM. the use of (network) meta-analysis in clinical oncology. Front Oncol. 2019;9.")], data consistency [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR41 "Higgins JPT, Jackson D, Barrett JK, Lu G, Ades AE, White IR. Consistency and inconsistency in network meta-analysis: concepts and models for multi-arm studies. Res Synth Methods. 2012;3(2):98–110."), [54](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR54 "White IR, Barrett JK, Jackson D, Higgins JPT. Consistency and inconsistency in network meta‐analysis: model estimation using multivariate meta‐regression. Res Synth Methods. 2012;3(2):111–25.")], and transitivity [[55](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR55 "Wheeler DC, Hickson DA, Waller LA. Assessing local model adequacy in Bayesian hierarchical models using the partitioned deviance information criterion. Comput Stat Data Anal. 2010;54(6):1657–71.")]. Effect sizes were expressed as MDs, and 95% CrIs were used to assess the confidence of the estimates [[56](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-026-02521-5#ref-CR56 "Etzioni RD, Kadane JB. This is a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis published in Sports Medicine (open access, published 18 August 2026) examining the optimal exercise modality and dose for blood pressure management in middle-aged and older adults (≥45 years). The study was conducted by Zhongxu Hu and colleagues, pre-registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251123349).

METHODS: 159 randomized controlled trials (n=10,821) were identified from six electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane, Web of Science, EMBASE, Scopus, SPORTDiscus) from inception to May 2025. Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis compared six exercise modalities: high-intensity interval training (HIIT), moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT), dynamic resistance training (DRT), isometric exercise (IE), combined training (CT), and circuit-based training (CBT). Dose-response analyses used metabolic equivalent task minutes per week (METs-min/week), with doses standardized to six nodes (0, 250, 500, 750, 1250, 1750 METs-min/week). Resting systolic BP (SBP) was the primary outcome; resting diastolic BP (DBP) was secondary. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 tool and certainty of evidence via CINeMA.

KEY RESULTS: All exercise modalities significantly reduced SBP and DBP versus control. Circuit-based training (CBT) showed the largest estimated SBP reduction (mean difference -13.52 mmHg; 95% CrI -18.59 to -8.44), followed by combined training (CT), HIIT, MICT, DRT, and isometric exercise. Higher baseline SBP was associated with greater reductions (β=-2.49 mmHg per 10-mmHg increase; 95% CrI -3.73 to -1.24). Dose-response analysis revealed a nonlinear association, with the largest model-estimated reduction around 1200 METs-min/week (upper range of WHO physical activity recommendations). CBT showed a peak effect at approximately 580 METs-min/week (lower range of WHO recommendations).

CONCLUSIONS: Integrated aerobic-resistance training (IART), including CBT and CT, appeared most promising for BP management. CBT showed the largest effect and may be time-efficient, but its apparent superiority over CT should be interpreted cautiously given limited CBT-specific evidence, low-to-very-low certainty of evidence, and sensitivity analyses (CT surpassed CBT in some sensitivity analyses). No network comparison was rated as high confidence, and many included studies had some concerns or high risk of bias, so rankings should not be considered definitive evidence of superiority.

--- SOURCE 1: HIIT vs. MICT to Improve Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Exercise Capacity in Older Adult ---
URL: https://clinmedjournals.org/articles/ijsem/international-journal-of-sports-and-exercise-medicine-ijsem-9-256.php?jid=ijsem

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the International Journal of Sports and Exercise Medicine (2023, Vol 9:256) by Yang Yang, Cao Youxiang, Chen Jiacheng, Hu Guangxuan, Chang Bo, and Yi Xuejie, examining whether High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) is more effective than Moderate-Intensity Continuous Exercise (MICT) for improving cardiorespiratory fitness and exercise capacity in older adults.

**Methods:** The review searched five electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, and Cochrane Library) up to September 10, 2022, and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022302359). Inclusion criteria required supervised HIIT and MICT interventions, mean subject age ≥55 years, intervention duration ≥2 weeks, and exercise modalities of running, cycling, or elliptical. The search identified 6,709 articles from databases plus 3 additional manual finds; after removing 2,317 duplicates, screening titles and abstracts, and full-text review, 30 studies met inclusion criteria, involving 1,973 subjects. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool, and statistical analyses were performed using REVMAN software.

**Key Results:**
- HIIT significantly improved VO2max compared to MICT (weighted mean difference = 1.80, 95% CI: 1.25-2.35, p < 0.001), and HIIT improved VO2peak over controls (WMD = 2.97, 95% CI: 2.39-3.56, p < 0.001)
- Subgroup analysis showed the greatest effects on VO2 peak with: training period <12 weeks (WMD = 3.59), 3 sessions/week (WMD = 4.46), 20 min per intervention (WMD = 3.57), <80% intensity VO2 peak (WMD = 4.47), >4 repetitions (WMD = 4.51), >60s per training session (WMD = 3.34), and ≤90s rest time (WMD = 4.04)
- Sick patients had a larger effect on VO2 peaks in older adults compared to healthy subjects (WMDs of 3.85 vs 2.47)
- HIIT significantly improved maximal heart rate (WMD = 2.68, HIIT vs MICT), ventilation (VE/VO2), and peak power output (PPO; WMD = 16.54, HIIT vs MICT)
- 16 studies showed reduction in systolic blood pressure (WMD = -2.59) and diastolic blood pressure (WMD = -1.40) after HIIT, though SBP reduction was not statistically superior to MICT; longer interventions (≥12 weeks) showed better SBP reduction
- HIIT significantly improved 6-minute walk test (WMD = 51.60), time up and go test, METs, and peak power output

**Conclusions:** HIIT is more effective than MICT in improving cardiorespiratory fitness and exercise capacity in older adults. The optimal HIIT protocol suggested was approximately 8 × ≤60s HIIT at <80% VO2 peak with ≤90s recovery, 3 times per week for <20 minutes for <12 weeks. No serious adverse events were reported. The study aligns with ACSM recommendations of 20 minutes of vigorous exercise 3 days per week and demonstrates HIIT can achieve results in shorter time than moderate-intensity exercise. The authors note limitations including the lack of subgroup confirmation for blood pressure effects and insufficient studies on muscle area metrics.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"HIIT significantly improved VO2max (HIIT vs. MICT) (weighted mean difference = 1.80, 95% confidence interval: 1.25-2.35, p < 0.001) and maximal heart rate, ventilation maximal power output compared to the MICT protocol."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The effects of HIIT and MICT on body fat composition and cardiopulmonary fitness in adults: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12911145

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (2026 Jan 24;18:94, doi: 10.1186/s13102-025-01519-2, PMID: 41580784, PMCID: PMC12911145) examining the effects of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) versus Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training (MICT) on body fat composition and cardiorespiratory fitness in adults. The study was conducted by Hongling Cheng (Tianjin Police Institute, China) and colleagues from the University of Birmingham (UK), Guangxi Science and Technology Normal University (China), Shanghai University of Sport, and Beijing Academy.

METHODS: The authors searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (January 1, 2000 to December 31, 2024) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing HIIT cycling's effects on fat reduction and cardiorespiratory fitness. A total of 1,326 articles were identified from databases plus 841 via citation searching; 19 RCTs met inclusion criteria, comprising 527 participants (HIIT: n=267; MICT: n=260). All studies used cycling-based interventions lasting 2–24 weeks, 3–5 sessions/week. Data were pooled using standardized mean differences (SMD) in Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 18, with subgroup analyses stratified by population (disease, obese, sedentary). GRADE assessment was performed.

KEY RESULTS:
- BMI: HIIT significantly reduced BMI overall (SMD = −0.25 kg/m², 95% CI: −0.45 to −0.06, P=0.012). Subgroup: reduced BMI in obese populations (SMD = −0.59, 95% CI: −0.84 to −0.34, P<0.001), increased BMI in disease populations (SMD = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.77, P=0.042), no effect in sedentary populations.
- Body fat percentage: No significant difference between HIIT and MICT overall (SMD = −0.17%, 95% CI: −0.39 to 0.06, P=0.160).
- Fat mass: No significant difference (SMD = −0.18 kg, 95% CI: −0.43 to 0.06, P=0.134).
- Lean body mass: No significant difference (SMD = −0.11 kg, 95% CI: −0.38 to 0.16, P=0.461).
- VO₂peak: HIIT significantly improved VO₂peak overall (SMD = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.08 to 0.44, P=0.007), with significant improvements in obese (SMD = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.45, P=0.041) and sedentary populations (SMD = 6.21, 95% CI: 4.68 to 7.74, P<0.001), but no significant effect in clinical populations.

GRADE assessment rated BMI, lean body mass, and VO₂peak as MODERATE certainty, while body fat and fat mass were rated LOW. Sensitivity analysis (leave-one-out) confirmed findings were robust; no single study exerted dominant influence.

DISCUSSION AND MECHANISMS: HIIT's BMI reduction in obese individuals may result from enhanced fat oxidation via AMPK pathway activation and increased resting metabolic rate. Increased BMI in clinical populations (diabetes, fibromyalgia) may stem from metabolic compensatory mechanisms, chronic hyperglycemia-induced inflammatory stress, compensatory eating, or exercise-induced muscle damage/tissue edema. VO₂peak improvements are attributed to cardiovascular adaptive remodeling, improved cardiac output, erythropoietin release, and mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α/NRF-1 pathway activation. Clinical populations showed no VO₂peak improvement due to disease-imposed cardiopulmonary limitations.

CLINICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: For obese individuals, HIIT on a cycle ergometer (4-min intervals at 90% VO₂peak with 3-min active recovery at 50% VO₂peak, 3–4 times/week for >12 weeks) is recommended. For those with comorbidities, modified low-intensity HIIT three times weekly with an initial 6-week shortened period is advised. For sedentary individuals, a progressive approach starting with lower-intensity HIIT (3 min at 75% VO₂peak/3 min at 50% VO₂peak) five times/week for >12 weeks, potentially extended to 24 weeks.

LIMITATIONS: Gender differences not accounted for; no age or comorbidity stratification; notable protocol variations between HIIT and MICT interventions.

CONCLUSION: HIIT cycling demonstrates comparable efficacy to MICT for improving body composition (body fat percentage, fat mass, lean body mass) in adults, while outperforming MICT in reducing BMI among obese individuals and enhancing cardiorespiratory fitness (VO₂peak) across obese and sedentary populations. Given its time efficiency, HIIT offers a viable exercise option for adults seeking fat reduction and cardiopulmonary endurance improvement.
</summary>

"Compared to MICT, HIIT significantly reduced BMI in obese populations (SMD = -0.59 kg/m2, 95% CI: -0.84 to -0.34, P<0.001), but slightly increased BMI in disease populations (SMD = 0.40 kg/m2, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.77, P = 0.042)."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.ajmc.com/view/hiit-improves-cardiorespiratory-fitness-more-than-low-intensity-exercise-review-says

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from The American Journal of Managed Care (AJMC), published September 26, 2021, authored by Hayden E. Klein. The article reports on a review published in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine (September 3, 2021; doi:10.3389/fcvm.2021.734278) by Taylor JL, Bonikowske AR, and Olson TP, titled "Optimizing outcomes in cardiac rehabilitation: the importance of exercise intensity."

KEY FINDINGS:
- High intensity interval training (HIIT) produces greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness than moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) or low-intensity exercise for patients with heart failure and cardiovascular disease.
- Investigators recommend slowly introducing and progressing HIIT on a case-by-case basis to reduce musculoskeletal discomfort while maximizing safety, adherence, enjoyment, and physiological outcomes.
- Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a class 1 clinical practice recommendation for patients with select cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).
- Systematic reviews on coronary heart disease (2004-2011) showed exercise-based CR reduced hospitalizations by 31%, cardiovascular mortality by 26%, and all-cause mortality by 20% compared with standard medical care. However, the RAMIT (Rehabilitation After Myocardial Infarction Trial) results later questioned these benefits.
- Guidelines recommend aerobic exercise prescription based on relative indices of peak exercise capacity, including: percentage of peak workload (Wpeak), percentage of peak heart rate (%HRpeak), percentage of VO2peak, percentage of HR reserve (%HRR), and percentage of VO2 reserve (%VO2R).

STUDY DETAILS:
- Moholdt et al: HIIT improved VO2peak and HR recovery more than MICT at 6 months in post-coronary artery bypass patients; similar QOL and adiponectin improvements in both groups.
- SAINTEX-CAD and FITR Heart studies: Similar improvements between HIIT and MICT at 12 months in CAD patients for VO2peak, CVD risk factors, QOL, body composition, and physical activity; no dietary intake changes. FITR Heart Study showed HIIT numerically higher VO2peak improvement (2.9 mL/kg/min vs 1.8 mL/kg/min for MICT).
- Adherence data: FITR Heart Study reported 53% adherence for HIIT and 41% for MICT; OptimEx-Clin reported 56% for HIIT and 60% for MICT. After excluding nonadherent participants, HIIT showed greater VO2peak improvement (5.2 mL/kg/min vs 2.2 mL/kg/min for MICT).
- SMARTEX HF (HFrEF patients) and OptimEX-Clin (HFpEF patients) both showed regression of supervised training improvements at 12 months regardless of exercise intensity.
- Moholdt et al: After 5 months of home-based training, 35% of participants stopped HIIT in favor of MICT, while only 4% of MICT participants increased intensity; 74% of HIIT and 68% of MICT participants performed 3 sessions/week.

CONCLUSION: While short-duration HIIT protocols can improve peripheral mitochondrial adaptations and provide similar VO2peak improvements to MICT, longer-duration and higher-volume HIIT protocols appear superior for eliciting stroke volume and vascular adaptations, and greater VO2peak improvements. High-intensity exercise also improves VO2 at submaximal exercise, important for daily activities.

The article is categorized under Heart Failure and Payers on the AJMC site.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Home-based high-intensity interval training improves cardiorespiratory fitness: a systematic review and meta-analysis ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13102-023-00777-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published on December 5, 2023, in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (Volume 15, article number 166), titled "Home-based high-intensity interval training improves cardiorespiratory fitness: a systematic review and meta-analysis." The study was conducted by Katsunori Tsuji, Yosuke Tsuchiya, Hisashi Ueda, and Eisuke Ochi.

BACKGROUND: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is an effective method to improve maximal oxygen uptake (VO2 peak), but there was no definitive conclusion about the specific effectiveness of home-based HIIT. Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is strongly associated with reduced risk of all-cause mortality, cancer mortality, and cardiovascular morbidity. An improvement in VO2 peak of 1 ml/kg/min can reduce all-cause mortality risk by 9%.

METHODS: The systematic review searched four electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Igaku Chuo Zasshi) for studies through March 25, 2023. Inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials of home-based HIIT in adult people regardless of disease or handicap. Comparisons were made against non-exercise controls, laboratory-based HIIT, and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). The primary outcome was cardiorespiratory fitness; secondary outcomes were patient-reported outcomes. The standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was calculated, and a random-effects model was used. The PRISMA 2020 checklist was used, and the protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42021260812). The Cochrane risk of bias 1 tool was used to assess internal validity. HIIT was defined as multiple repetitions of short bursts (≤4 min) of high-intensity (≥80% of HRmax) exercise; MICT was defined as prolonged moderate-intensity (40-70% of HRmax) continuous exercise.

RESULTS: 643 articles were identified from the four databases; after removing duplicates and screening, 15 studies satisfied inclusion criteria (12 included in the quantitative meta-analysis). Five studies involved healthy adults and 10 involved patients. Comparisons included: lab-based HIIT (4 studies), MICT (7 studies), resistance training (1 study), and non-exercise controls (3 studies). Exercise modalities included weight-bearing exercise (6 studies), stationary cycling/treadmill (6 studies), and outdoor/indoor equipment (3 studies).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Home-based HIIT was superior to non-exercise controls for cardiorespiratory fitness (SMD 0.61, 95% CI: 0.21, 1.02).
- No significant difference in cardiorespiratory fitness was observed between home-based HIIT and lab-based HIIT (SMD: -0.35, 95% CI: -0.73, 0.03).
- No significant difference was observed between home-based HIIT and MICT (SMD 0.34, 95% CI: -0.05, 0.73).

CONCLUSION: Home-based HIIT is an effective intervention for improving cardiorespiratory fitness in healthy adults and patients, with comparable effectiveness to laboratory-based HIIT and MICT, making it a practical and valuable exercise intervention. The article has 6462 accesses, 18 citations, and 10 Altmetric mentions.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1594574/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Physiology (June 13, 2025) comparing the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on cardiopulmonary function, body composition, and physical function in cancer survivors. 

METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, the authors systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and EBSCOhost up to February 2025. Twelve eligible RCTs were included: 7 breast cancer, 3 colorectal cancer, and 2 mixed cancer type studies. Studies were conducted in New Zealand (1), Australia (6), Canada (1), Iran (2), US (1), and Germany (1), spanning 2015-2023, with sample sizes of 7-47 participants and ages 39-75 years. Exercise durations ranged from 3-12 weeks, 2-5 days/week (mostly 3 days/week), 10-75 min/session. Meta-analysis used Cochrane's Review Manager 5.4; sensitivity analysis used Stata MP 14.0; Egger's test assessed publication bias. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420250654968.

KEY RESULTS:
- VO2 peak (primary outcome, 7 studies, 92 HIIT vs 78 MICT participants): HIIT significantly superior [SMD = 0.53, 95% CI (0.21, 0.84), Z = 3.30, P = 0.001, I² = 0%]. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness; Egger's test showed no publication bias (P = 0.75).
- Subgroup analysis: Breast cancer (5 studies, 100 subjects) showed improvement but not significant [SMD = 0.39, P = 0.06]; colorectal cancer (2 studies, 70 subjects) showed significant improvement [SMD = 0.74, P = 0.004].
- Heart rate (2 studies): No significant difference [SMD = -0.55, P = 0.14].
- Resting heart rate (3 studies): No significant difference [SMD = -0.11, P = 0.63].
- Body composition: No significant differences between HIIT and MICT for body mass, total fat mass, lean body mass, fat percentage, BMI, waist circumference, or hip circumference.
- Physical function: No significant differences in Sit-to-Stand test (STS) or 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT).

RISK OF BIAS: 8 studies at high risk of bias, 4 with some concerns. Main issues included lack of blinding (performance bias), unclear randomization/allocation concealment, and unblinded outcome assessors.

DISCUSSION/CONCLUSION: HIIT appears superior to MICT in enhancing VO2 peak and cardiopulmonary function in cancer survivors, particularly breast and colorectal cancer. Both modalities produce comparable outcomes in body composition and physical function. Proposed mechanisms for HIIT's VO2 peak advantage include AMPK-PGC-1α pathway activation (mitochondrial biogenesis) and catecholamine-mediated cardiorespiratory adaptations. Limitations include small number of studies/participants, heterogeneity in intervention protocols, uneven cancer type distribution, lack of long-term follow-up, unavoidable performance bias, and absence of direct survival/recurrence analysis. The authors call for larger, well-designed RCTs with standardized protocols, diverse cancer subgroups, long-term follow-up, and modern technologies (remote monitoring, AI personalized prescriptions).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Effect of high-intensity interval training versus moderate intensity continuous training in heart failure patients on cardiorespiratory fitness and quality of life: a systematic review and meta-analysis ---
URL: https://www.resmedjournal.com/article/S0954-6111(26)00030-2/fulltext

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published as an open-access Review Article in Respiratory Medicine (Volume 253, Article 108662, March 2026) examining the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on cardiorespiratory fitness and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in heart failure patients. 

Authors: Lino Sergio Rocha Conceição (corresponding author, linosergiorocha@gmail.com), Mansueto Gomes-Neto, Camila Souza Gama Rocha, Acauã Oliveira Coelho, and Vitor Oliveira Carvalho, affiliated with Universidade Federal de Sergipe (Brazil) and related institutions.

Key methods: The review followed PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD42025636762), searching PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and PEDro databases up to April 2025, plus gray literature (Google Scholar, OpenThesis). Eligibility used PICOT criteria including HFrEF (LVEF <40%), HFmrEF (40-49%), and HFpEF (≥50%) patients. HIIT was defined as 70-85% peak VO2, 75-90% max heart rate, or Borg 14-16; MICT as 40-69% peak VO2, 55-74% max heart rate, or Borg 12-13. Only randomized controlled trials with programs at least twice weekly and ≥4 weeks duration were included. Methodological quality was assessed via PEDro scale, certainty of evidence via GRADE.

Key results: 18 studies were included. HIIT improved VO2peak by 1.49 mL/kg/min (95% CI: 0.74-2.24; I²=61.2%; N=682) compared to MICT overall. However, subanalysis of isocaloric exercise protocols accounting for left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) showed no statistically significant difference between HIIT and MICT. No significant differences in HRQoL were observed between the two. HIIT improved 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) in HFrEF patients compared to MICT.

Conclusion: While HIIT appears superior to MICT for VO2peak improvement when HFrEF and HFpEF patients are considered collectively, this superiority disappears when protocols are matched for isocaloric conditions and LVEF is considered. The limited number of isocaloric studies involving HFpEF precludes definitive conclusions for this subgroup. Publication history: Received July 8, 2025; Revised December 12, 2025; Accepted January 14, 2026; Published online January 23, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.rmed.2026.108662. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

--- SOURCE 7: The effect of high-intensity interval training and moderate-intensity continuous training on cardiorespiratory function in healthy elderly individuals: Systematic review and meta-analysis ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12795074

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Medicine (Baltimore) on January 9, 2026 (PMCID: PMC12795074, PMID: 41517714), examining the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on cardiorespiratory function in healthy elderly individuals.

**Background and Methods:**
- Cardiorespiratory fitness, measured by maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max), is the gold standard for assessing cardiorespiratory endurance and is positively correlated with all-cause mortality and chronic disease risk.
- After age 30, VO2max declines 5-15% per decade, reaching up to 50% decline by age 70.
- A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar (through March 2025) identified 2,798 relevant studies; after screening, 16 randomized controlled trials (n=1,434) were included.
- The protocol was registered at PROSPERO (Registration No. CRD420251037775).
- Data were analyzed using RevMan 5.4 and Stata 15.1 with a random-effects model; weighted mean difference (WMD) with 95% CI was used as the effect size.
- Quality assessment used an adapted 8-item PRISMA-based risk checklist: 4 studies were low risk, 10 moderate risk, and 2 high risk.

**Key Results:**
- **MICT (12 studies, n=535):** Significantly improved VO2max (MD = 1.22, 95% CI: 0.90–1.53, P<.01), with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%).
- **HIIT (11 studies, n=483):** More pronounced improvement in VO2max (MD = 1.62, 95% CI: 1.10–2.13, P<.01), no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). Some publication bias detected (Egger test P=.003), but trim-and-fill analysis confirmed stability (corrected MD = 1.48).
- **Direct comparison (7 studies, n=610):** HIIT demonstrated significantly superior improvements compared to MICT (MD = 1.17, 95% CI: 0.52–1.82, P<.01), though with significant heterogeneity (I² = 70%).

**Optimal Training Protocols (Subgroup Analysis):**
- **HIIT optimal protocol:** Duration >3 months and <6 months, 4 sessions per week, session duration of 21–39 minutes.
- **MICT optimal protocol:** Duration >3 months and <6 months, 3 sessions per week, session duration ≥60 minutes.
- HIIT showed "short-duration, high-efficiency" characteristics with significant improvements even within ≤3 months (MD = 2.56), while MICT required mid-cycle periods to show significant effects.
- MICT at high frequency (4×/week) significantly declined in effectiveness (MD = 0.20), likely due to fatigue accumulation.

**Conclusion:** Both HIIT and MICT effectively improve cardiovascular and pulmonary function in elderly individuals, with HIIT yielding more favorable results. MICT is suitable for long-term training in individuals with good tolerance, while HIIT is better suited for short-term interventions for those able to tolerate high-intensity exercise. Clinical selection should be based on individual health status.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a peer-reviewed systematic review and meta-analysis published in Sports Medicine (2015) by Zoran Milanović, Goran Sporiš, and Matthew Weston, titled "Effectiveness of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max improvements: A Systematic review and Meta-Analysis of controlled trials."

**Study Objective & Methods:** The authors meta-analysed the effects of endurance training and high-intensity interval training (HIT) on maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) in healthy, young to middle-aged adults (aged 18-45 years). Six electronic databases were searched (MEDLINE, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and Google Scholar) using terms including 'high intensity', 'HIT', 'sprint interval training', 'endurance training', 'peak oxygen uptake', and 'VO2max'. Inclusion criteria were controlled trials, healthy adults aged 18-45 years, training duration ≥2 weeks, and VO2max assessed pre- and post-training. Twenty-eight studies met inclusion criteria, totaling 723 participants (mean age 25.1 ± 5 years; initial fitness 40.8 ± 7.9 mL•kg-1•min-1).

**Key Results:**
- Endurance training vs. no exercise: possibly large beneficial effect on VO2max (4.9 mL•kg-1•min-1; ±1.4), with additional moderate increases for younger subjects (2.4) and longer interventions (2.2), and small improvement for lower baseline fitness (1.4).
- HIT vs. no exercise: likely large beneficial effect (5.5 mL•kg-1•min-1; ±1.2), with likely moderate greater increases for lower baseline fitness (3.2) and longer interventions (3.0), but a small lesser effect for longer HIT repetitions (-1.8).
- HIT vs. endurance training: possibly small beneficial effect for HIT (1.2 mL•kg-1•min-1; ±0.9), with small additional improvements for longer HIT repetitions (2.2), older subjects (1.8), longer interventions (1.7), greater work:rest ratio (1.6), and lower baseline fitness (0.8).
- Modifying effects of age and work:rest ratio were unclear in some comparisons.

**Conclusion:** Both endurance training and HIT elicit large improvements in VO2max among healthy young to middle-aged adults, with greater gains following HIT compared to endurance training.

The article has a DOI of 10.1007/s40279-015-0365-0 and was published in 2015 in Sports Medicine (ISSN 0112-1642). Supplementary files including the full text and tables are available under a CC BY-NC-ND license.
</summary>

"Endurance training and HIT both elicit large improvements in the VO2max of healthy, young to middle-aged adults with the gains in VO2max being greater following HIT, when compared to endurance training."

--- SOURCE 9: The Impact of High-Intensity Interval Training Versus Moderate ... ---
URL: https://paulogentil.com/pdf/The%20impact%20of%20high-intensity%20interval%20training%20versus%20moderate-intensity%20continuous%20training%20on%20vascular%20function%20-%20a%20systematic%20review%20and%20meta-analysis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Sports Medicine (DOI 10.1007/s40279-015-0321-z) by Ramos, Dalleck, Tjonna, Beetham, and Coombes (2015) examining the impact of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on vascular function.

METHODOLOGY: Three electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE) were searched until May 2014 for randomized trials comparing at least 2 weeks of HIIT and MICT. Vascular function was assessed via brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD). The PEDro scale (score ≥6 required) was used for quality assessment, and meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5 with a random-effects model.

RESULTS: Seven randomized trials including 182 patients (with heart failure, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, post-menopausal women, and obese adults) met inclusion criteria. Mean PEDro score was 7.29/10. The most common HIIT prescription was 4×4-minute intervals at 85-95% of maximum/peak heart rate, interspersed with 3 minutes of active recovery at 60-70% HRmax/peak, three times per week for 12-16 weeks. Brachial artery FMD improved by 4.31% following HIIT and 2.15% following MICT, resulting in a significant mean difference of 2.26% (p<0.05, I²=68%). When the 2-week outlier study was removed, the mean difference increased to 2.45%.

KEY FINDINGS:
- HIIT improved FMD more than MICT (pre vs. post: 5.14% to 9.45% for HIIT; 5.12% to 7.27% for MICT)
- No change in GTN-mediated (vascular-independent) dilation in either group, indicating FMD improvements reflect endothelial-level restoration
- HIIT had greater tendency to positively affect cardiorespiratory fitness (14-46% vs. 5-16% improvement), traditional CVD risk factors, oxidative stress, inflammation, and insulin sensitivity
- Longer-interval HIIT (4×4 min) appeared more effective than shorter-interval HIIT (1-min bouts)
- PGC-1α protein increased 47-138% following HIIT, with no change in MICT groups
- No significant between-group differences in body fat reduction, hsCRP, or shear rate
- 4×4 HIIT significantly reduced ambulatory systolic blood pressure more than MICT (12 vs. 4.5 mmHg)

CONCLUSION: HIIT is more effective than MICT at improving brachial artery vascular function, potentially due to its greater influence on CRF, CVD risk factors, oxidative stress, inflammation, and insulin sensitivity. The review suggests 4×4 HIIT (three times per week for at least 12 weeks) is a powerful exercise form to enhance vascular function, though variability in secondary outcomes and small sample sizes limit the findings.

LIMITATIONS: Most participants were on medications known to improve vascular function; four studies came from the same laboratory in Norway; substantial heterogeneity was detected (I²=68%).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Brachial artery FMD improved by 4.31 and 2.15 % following HIIT and MICT, respectively. This resulted in a significant (p<0.05) mean difference of 2.26 %."

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1440244018309198

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (Volume 22, Issue 8, August 2019, Pages 941-947) titled "Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials." The study was conducted by Daizong Wen, Till Utesch, Jun Wu, Samuel Robertson, John Liu, Guopeng Hu, and Haichun Chen (DOI: 10.1016/j.jsams.2019.01.013).

OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of different HIIT protocols on VO2max improvements in healthy, overweight/obese, and athletic adults, based on classifications of work intervals, session volumes, and training periods.

METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Medline, and Web of Science databases were searched up to April 2018. Inclusion criteria were randomised controlled trials involving healthy, overweight/obese, or athletic adults, examining pre- and post-training VO2max/peak, with HIIT compared to control or moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) groups.

RESULTS: Of 1,190 articles initially identified, 53 studies met eligibility criteria. The degree of change in VO2max induced by HIIT varied by populations (SMD=0.41–1.81, p<0.05). Compared to control groups, even short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term HIIT (≤4 weeks) elicited clear beneficial effects (SMD=0.79–1.65, p<0.05) on VO2max/peak. However, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT displayed significantly larger effects on VO2max (SMD=0.50–2.48, p<0.05). When compared to MICT, only long-interval, high-volume, and moderate to long-term HIIT showed beneficial effects (SMD=0.65–1.07, p<0.05).

CONCLUSIONS: Short-interval (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT are effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2max, especially for the general population. To maximize training effects on VO2max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended. The study was supported by the Key Laboratory of Physical Motor Function Assessment, General Administration of Sport of China. The article has been cited 218 times and is part of the JSAMS Highlights 2018 and 2019 special issue. The authors reported no conflicts of interest.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min) and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT represent effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2 max, especially for the general population. To maximize the training effects on VO2 max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min) and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended."
</key_excerpts>
