## Discussion

The major novel finding from the present study was that 12 weeks of SIT in previously inactive men improved insulin sensitivity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and skeletal muscle mitochondrial content to the same extent as MICT, despite a five-fold lower exercise volume and training time commitment. SIT involved 1 minute of intense intermittent exercise, within a time commitment of 10 minutes per session, whereas MICT consisted of 50 minutes of continuous exercise at a moderate pace. A few previous studies have reported similar improvements in skeletal muscle remodeling and markers of health status after SIT and MICT lasting up to 6 weeks [[10](#pone.0154075.ref010),[11](#pone.0154075.ref011),[13](#pone.0154075.ref013)]. The present work was intended to be more ambitious in scope as compared to previous studies that compared SIT versus MICT. Specifically, it involved a SIT protocol that required less total time commitment than in previous studies (i.e., 10 vs ~25 min), a training program that was twice as long (i.e., 12 vs 6 wk), a more robust measure of insulin sensitivity (i.e., an IVGTT vs OGTT and fasting blood measures of insulin sensitivity), and inclusion of a non-training control group.

### Cardiorespiratory fitness

Low cardiorespiratory fitness is a strong independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality [[25](#pone.0154075.ref025),[26](#pone.0154075.ref026)]. It has been known for decades that interval training involving brief hard efforts is a potent stimulus to improve cardiorespiratory fitness [[27](#pone.0154075.ref027),[28](#pone.0154075.ref028)]. Recent studies have shown that protocols involving as little as one minute of sprint interval training per session can be very effective in this regard [[15](#pone.0154075.ref015)–[17](#pone.0154075.ref017)]. Prior to the present work, no study had directly compared this type of SIT protocol with traditional endurance training as reflected in public health guidelines. We found a strikingly similar 19% improvement in VO2peak after 12 weeks of SIT and MICT, which compares favorably with the typical change reported after several months of traditional endurance training [[29](#pone.0154075.ref029),[30](#pone.0154075.ref030)].

Exercise intensity is generally regarded to be the more critical factor in the trainability of VO2peak, with higher intensity exercise conferring larger improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness when exercise is matched for total energy expenditure [[31](#pone.0154075.ref031)–[34](#pone.0154075.ref034)]. This message was recently reinforced by Ross et al. [[35](#pone.0154075.ref035)], who found that low-intensity exercise (50% VO2peak) performed for about 150 minutes per week, over 24 weeks, may not be sufficient to improve cardiorespiratory fitness for a substantive proportion of adults. In contrast, the present data show it is possible for previously sedentary individuals to markedly improve VO2peak by performing a total of 3 minutes per week of short intense bursts of exercise, within a 30-minute time commitment, over 12 weeks. The absolute change in relative VO2peak was ~6 ml/kg/min in both SIT and MICT, which corresponds to ~1.7 metabolic equivalents (METs). These findings are noteworthy given that a 1-MET increase in cardiorespiratory is comparable to a 7 cm decrease in waist circumference, a 5 mmHg lowering of systolic blood pressure or a 1 mmol/L reduction in fasting plasma glucose, in terms of relative risk reduction in all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality [[25](#pone.0154075.ref025)]. Unfit individuals also have twice the risk of death regardless of BMI, while fit and overweight/obese adults have similar mortality risk as their normal weight counterparts [[26](#pone.0154075.ref026)].

The precise mechanisms responsible for the improved cardiorespiratory fitness observed after SIT and MICT in the present study are unknown. The increase in VO2peak after traditional endurance training is generally attributed to an enhanced cardiac output owing to a greater stroke volume, although numerous factors may contribute to this adaptive response [[3](#pone.0154075.ref003)]. A limited number of studies have assessed cardiovascular adaptations to SIT and these have yielded equivocal results, likely due in part to differences in experimental design as well as the specific analytical procedures employed [[36](#pone.0154075.ref036),[37](#pone.0154075.ref037)]. Increases in resting stroke volume have been observed after 7 weeks of SIT using cardiac MRI [[38](#pone.0154075.ref038)], as has stroke volume during submaximal exercise based on the CO2-rebreathing technique following 4 weeks of SIT [[36](#pone.0154075.ref036)]. Conversely, MacPherson et al. [[37](#pone.0154075.ref037)] reported no changes in maximal cardiac output based on the acetylene non-rebreathing technique after 6 weeks of run-based SIT. It has also been suggested that peripheral factors that enhance oxygen extraction may contribute to SIT-induced improvements in VO2peak, at least over the short-term [[39](#pone.0154075.ref039)]. Additional studies are warranted to clarify both the time course and precise mechanisms responsible for the improved cardiorespiratory fitness after SIT compared to MICT.

### Insulin sensitivity

Perhaps the most striking and novel finding form the present work was the similar increase in insulin sensitivity after SIT and MICT. It has previously been shown that SIT improves indices of glycemic control, as determined by the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp method [[40](#pone.0154075.ref040)], continuous glucose monitoring [[17](#pone.0154075.ref017)] and oral glucose tolerance tests [[13](#pone.0154075.ref013),[41](#pone.0154075.ref041)]. In the present investigation, we employed a 50-minute IVGTT (CSI), which was recently validated by Tura and colleagues as a robust marker of insulin sensitivity [[19](#pone.0154075.ref019)]. The technique was shown to be highly correlated with the gold standard glucose infusion rate obtained during a hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp [[19](#pone.0154075.ref019)], and have greater reproducibility than MISI derived from OGTTs [[20](#pone.0154075.ref020)].

Houmard et al. [[42](#pone.0154075.ref042)], using the IVGTT method, previously reported that a continuous training protocol involving 170 minutes of exercise per week improved insulin sensitivity to a greater extent than 115 minutes per week, regardless of exercise intensity and volume. Several recent reports, however, suggest that when exercise is matched for total volume or energy expenditure, higher-intensity exercise training confers larger improvements in insulin sensitivity in individuals with obesity [[43](#pone.0154075.ref043)], metabolic syndrome [[33](#pone.0154075.ref033)] and type 2 diabetes [[31](#pone.0154075.ref031),[34](#pone.0154075.ref034)]. Our findings support this general concept and demonstrate that a surprisingly small amount of high-intensity exercise can be as effective as a large volume of moderate-intensity continuous exercise for improving insulin sensitivity.

The potential mechanisms that mediate exercise training-induced increases in whole-body insulin sensitivity are obviously complex [[1](#pone.0154075.ref001)]. With respect to potential changes in skeletal muscle that might in part explain the improved insulin sensitivity, we found similar increases in GLUT4 protein content after the two training protocols despite large differences in exercise volume. SIT and MICT have also been shown to similarly increase skeletal muscle microvascular density [[44](#pone.0154075.ref044)], which is associated with improved glucose transport and insulin sensitivity [[44](#pone.0154075.ref044),[45](#pone.0154075.ref045)]. It is also possible that the improvement in mitochondrial content [[1](#pone.0154075.ref001)] or an increased capacity for intramuscular triglyceride utilization [[12](#pone.0154075.ref012)] could be involved.

### Mitochondrial content

Reduced skeletal muscle mitochondrial content is associated with aberrant lipid handling, poor insulin sensitivity and an impaired metabolic health profile [[46](#pone.0154075.ref046)]. Physical activity increases mitochondrial content and insulin sensitivity, but it remains unclear whether these effects are directly linked [[1](#pone.0154075.ref001),[46](#pone.0154075.ref046)]. The maximal activity of citrate synthase is a commonly measured marker that is strongly associated with mitochondrial content in human skeletal muscle [[47](#pone.0154075.ref047)]. A novel finding from the present work was the similar increase in citrate synthase maximal activity after 12 weeks of SIT and MICT, despite the large difference in total exercise volume. We also observed similar increases in the protein content of various subunits from complexes in the electron transport chain, highlighting similar mitochondrial adaptation in both groups. We did not examine the time course of skeletal muscle remodeling, but the mean increase in CS maximal activity after training was similar to the 30–40% increase that we previously observed after 2 [[48](#pone.0154075.ref048)] and 6 weeks [[10](#pone.0154075.ref010),[17](#pone.0154075.ref017)] of both SIT and MICT. Consistent with the recent observations by Egan et al. [[49](#pone.0154075.ref049)], who examined the time course of increased mitochondrial content in response to 14 sessions of endurance training, these data seem to imply that much of the increase in mitochondrial content occurs relatively early in response to training. Given the much lower exercise volume involved with SIT, these data also seemingly suggest that training intensity, rather than volume, may be the more critical determinant of the improvement in mitochondrial content. As recently reviewed by Bishop et al. [[50](#pone.0154075.ref050)], a surprisingly small number of studies have investigated the impact of varying training intensity and volume on changes in mitochondrial function and content in human skeletal muscle, and additional work in this regard is warranted.

### Efficacy versus Effectiveness

While the present study and work by others highlights the efficacy of SIT for improving indices of cardiometabolic health, the potential effectiveness of interval training in its various forms and likely impact on public health remains contentious [[51](#pone.0154075.ref051)]. Research in the field of exercise behavior has demonstrated a negative relationship between exercise intensity and affect, particularly in less trained individuals, which suggests people are less likely to adhere to a program of vigorous exercise since it is deemed aversive [[52](#pone.0154075.ref052),[53](#pone.0154075.ref053)]. However, in a recent study by Jung et al [[54](#pone.0154075.ref054)], subjects reported greater enjoyment of, and a preference to engage in, a high-intensity intermittent exercise protocol as compared to continuous moderate- or vigorous-intensity exercise. The interval protocol involved 20 minutes of alternating 60-second periods of exercise at 100% and 20% Wpeak, whereas the continuous protocols involved exercise at 40% Wpeak for 40 minutes or 80% Wpeak for 20 minutes. Other work by the same authors showed that adherence to a 4-week high-intensity interval training program, assessed by self-report in free-living conditions, was greater than for moderate-intensity continuous exercise in people with prediabetes [[55](#pone.0154075.ref055)]. These findings highlight the potential utility of intense interval training as an alternative exercise strategy that could bolster exercise adherence, but longer and more comprehensive studies are warranted in this regard.

## Conclusion

In summary, we report that a SIT protocol involving 3 minutes of intense intermittent exercise per week, within a total time commitment of 30 minutes, is as effective as 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity continuous training for increasing insulin sensitivity, cardiorespiratory fitness and skeletal muscle mitochondrial content in previously inactive men. This investigation represents the longest comparison of SIT and MICT to date and demonstrates the efficacy of brief, intense exercise to improve indices of cardiometabolic health. While SIT is clearly a potent stimulus to elicit physiological adaptations, this type of exercise requires a very high level of motivation and is clearly not suited for everyone. Future studies should examine the potential for interval training protocols that involve relatively intense but not “all out” efforts to elicit changes like that shown in the present study. Considering that a large number of individuals do not meet the current physical activity recommendations [[56](#pone.0154075.ref056),[57](#pone.0154075.ref057)], there is value in exploring the potential benefits of exercise strategies that involve reduced time commitment. Large-scale randomized clinical trials are needed to advance the field.

## PLOS ONE Research Article Summary

**Title:** Twelve Weeks of Sprint Interval Training Improves Indices of Cardiometabolic Health Similar to Traditional Endurance Training despite a Five-Fold Lower Exercise Volume and Time Commitment

**Authors:** Gillen JB, Martin BJ, MacInnis MJ, Skelly LE, Tarnopolsky MA, Gibala MJ (Department of Kinesiology, McMaster University, Hamilton, ON, Canada)

**Citation:** PLoS ONE 11(4): e0154075. Published April 26, 2016.

### Study Overview
This randomized controlled trial compared the effects of 12 weeks of sprint interval training (SIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on insulin sensitivity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and skeletal muscle mitochondrial content in sedentary men. The SIT protocol involved only 1 minute of intense exercise within a 10-minute session, while MICT involved 50 minutes of continuous exercise per session—a five-fold difference in exercise volume and time commitment.

### Methodology
- **Participants:** 27 sedentary men (age 27±8y; BMI 26±6 kg/m²), randomized to SIT (n=9), MICT (n=10), or non-training control (n=6)
- **SIT protocol:** 3×20-second 'all-out' cycle sprints (~500W) interspersed with 2 minutes of cycling at 50W; sessions were 10 minutes including warm-up/cool-down
- **MICT protocol:** 45 minutes of continuous cycling at ~70% maximal heart rate (~110W); sessions were 50 minutes
- **Frequency:** 3 sessions per week for 12 weeks
- **Outcome measures:** Insulin sensitivity (CSI from 50-min IVGTT), VO2peak, skeletal muscle mitochondrial content (citrate synthase maximal activity), body composition, GLUT4 protein, electron transport chain protein subunits

### Key Results
1. **Cardiorespiratory fitness:** VO2peak increased by 19% in both training groups (SIT: 32±7 to 38±8; MICT: 34±6 to 40±8 ml/kg/min; p<0.001 for both). The absolute change was ~6 ml/kg/min (~1.7 METs).
2. **Insulin sensitivity (CSI):** Increased by 53% after SIT (4.9±2.5 to 7.5±4.7, p=0.002) and 34% after MICT (5.0±3.3 to 6.7±5.0, p=0.013).
3. **Mitochondrial content:** Citrate synthase maximal activity increased by 48% after SIT (p<0.0001) and 27% after MICT (p=0.004). Similar increases in electron transport chain protein subunits (Complex II, III, COX IV, ATP Synthase) were observed.
4. **GLUT4 protein:** Increased by ~50% in both training groups.
5. **Body composition:** Percent body fat decreased after both SIT (p=0.011) and MICT (p=0.011); body mass remained unchanged.
6. **Control group:** Showed minimal changes in VO2peak (p=0.99), CSI (p=0.63), and citrate synthase (p=0.97).

### Training Characteristics
- SIT: mean HR 79±4% HRmax; mean RPE 16±1; ~60 kJ work per session
- MICT: mean HR 71±5% HRmax; mean RPE 13±1; ~310 kJ work per session

### Conclusions
Twelve weeks of brief intense interval exercise (3 minutes of sprinting per week within a 30-minute weekly time commitment) improved cardiometabolic health indices to the same extent as traditional endurance training (150 minutes per week) in previously sedentary men. This is the longest direct comparison of SIT and MICT to date. The authors suggest that training intensity, rather than volume, may be the more critical determinant of improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness and mitochondrial content. However, they note that SIT requires high motivation and is not suited for everyone, and that large-scale randomized clinical trials are needed.

### Funding & Ethics
Supported by NSERC (grant RGPIN/227858-2010) and McMaster University. Approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board. Open access under Creative Commons Attribution License.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Rates of compliance and adherence to high-intensity interval training ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10664287

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analyses published in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity (2023 Nov 21;20:134; DOI: 10.1186/s12966-023-01535-w) examining rates of compliance and adherence to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) among insufficiently active adults and adults with medical conditions.

**Study Purpose:**
- To determine rates of compliance (supervised intervention attendance) and adherence (unsupervised physical activity completion) to HIIT
- To determine whether compliance and adherence rates differ between HIIT and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)

**Methods:**
- Searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsychINFO, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, and Web of Science from inception until October 3, 2022
- 188 unique studies included with 8,928 total participants
- Risk of bias assessed using RoB 2.0 (for RCTs) and ROBINS-I (for quasi-experimental studies)
- Meta-analyses conducted using random-effects models with Hedge's g as the effect size
- Registered in PROSPERO (identifier CRD42019103313)
- Followed PRISMA 2020 reporting standards

**Key Results:**
- Compliance to HIIT interventions averaged 89.4% (SD: 11.8%)
- Adherence to HIIT averaged 63% (SD: 21.1%)
- Compliance to MICT averaged 92.5% (SD: 10.6%)
- Adherence to MICT averaged 68.2% (SD: 16.2%)
- Based on 65 studies in the meta-analysis, compliance rates were NOT significantly different between supervised HIIT and MICT [Hedge's g = 0.015 (95%CI: -0.088–0.118), p = .78]
- Based on 10 studies, adherence rates were NOT significantly different between unsupervised HIIT and MICT [Hedge's g = -0.313 (95%CI: -0.681–0.056), p = .096]
- Quality of evidence for compliance rated as MODERATE (concerns about directness)
- Quality of evidence for adherence rated as VERY LOW (interpret with caution)
- Results for compliance were robust with low risk of publication bias

**Study Characteristics:**
- 82.4% were randomized controlled trials; 16.5% quasi-experimental
- 73.9% of studies included individuals with at least one medical condition (46 different conditions; most common: cancer 11.2%, obesity 10.1%, coronary artery disease 6.9%, type 2 diabetes 6.9%)
- 26.1% included insufficiently active but otherwise healthy individuals
- 30 different countries represented (Canada 16.5%, US 12.8%, Norway 11.7%)
- Majority of articles published between 2016-2022 (69.7%)
- Most studies were single-centre (93.6%)
- Mean age of HIIT participants: 46.6 years; MICT: 47.3 years

**Conclusions:**
- Compliance to both HIIT and MICT was high among insufficiently active adults and adults with medical conditions
- Adherence was relatively moderate with high heterogeneity and very low quality of evidence
- Sub-group analysis suggested adherence rates depend on the method of outcome measurement

The review follows the SANRA framework. Evidence was categorized into minor, moderate, and severe adverse effects.

KEY FINDINGS BY SYSTEM:
- CARDIOVASCULAR: Regular exercise reduces overall cardiovascular mortality by 30–40%, but sedentary individuals face 50–80x higher MI risk during vigorous exercise. Young athletes may die from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital coronary anomalies, aortic stenosis, arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia, and long QT syndromes. Circadian variation: adults peak SCD risk during early morning exercise; young athletes vulnerable in afternoon/evening. Exercise-induced hypertension (EIH) defined as systolic BP >190 mmHg (females) / >210 mmHg (males); exercise should terminate if systolic >250 or diastolic >115 mmHg. Vigorous exercise slows coronary artery calcification progression while very vigorous exercise accelerates it. Athletic heart syndrome and detraining effects discussed.

- RESPIRATORY: PAH shifted from absolute contraindication to supervised training (RCT n=116, small). Low-risk PAH criteria per ESC/ERS 2022 guidelines: WHO class I-II, 6MWT >440m, no right heart failure signs, near-normal NT-proBNP. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) develops within 15 min after 5–8 min of high-intensity aerobic training; prevention includes pre-exercise SABA, ≥10 min warm-up, avoiding cold/dry air. ILD patients commonly develop exertional hypoxemia (~40% cannot maintain O2 saturation >88% even with supplemental oxygen); monitoring via continuous pulse oximetry targeting SpO2 ≥88%, short-interval training, 6MWT with oximetry.

- RENAL: CKD exercise is complex due to variable stages and electrolytes. Non-dialysis CKD: resistance exercise benefits weighed against LDL elevations and fistula injury risk. Hot/humid climates reduce renal blood flow by 15–30%. Specific protocols: CKD stages 1–3 (150 min/week moderate aerobic, resistance 2–3x/week); stages 4–5 (90–150 min/week, supervised); dialysis (intra-dialytic cycling 30–45 min, 3x/week). Kidney transplant recipients: moderate/vigorous exercise reduces kidney blood flow ~20% and ~52%, respectively; avoid contact/collision sports due to graft trauma risk; fluoroquinolone therapy increases Achilles tendinopathy risk. Polycystic kidney disease patients should avoid contact exercise.

CONCLUSIONS: Exercise is a powerful therapeutic intervention requiring individualized, condition-specific risk stratification. Safe implementation depends on structured pre-exercise evaluation, recognition of absolute/relative contraindications, supervision, and ongoing monitoring. Substantial evidence gaps exist in hepatology, advanced ILD, and rare neurological conditions where RCT data are lacking. Multidisciplinary coordination and improved physician–exercise professional communication are essential. A clinical decision algorithm and structured summary tables are provided.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS: Exercise prescription requires individualized, condition-specific risk stratification; adverse events range from musculoskeletal injury to life-threatening arrhythmias, hypoglycemia, and rhabdomyolysis; special populations (children, transplant recipients, elderly with comorbidities) warrant narrower safety margins; structured pre-exercise evaluation and multidisciplinary coordination are essential.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Effects of very low volume high intensity versus moderate intensity interval training in obese metabolic syndrome patients: a randomized controlled study | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-82372-4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Scientific Reports (volume 11, Article 2836, 2021) examining the effects of very low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity interval training (MIIT) in obese patients with metabolic syndrome (MetS). The study was a 12-week randomized controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT03306069) conducted at Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nürnberg, Germany.

**Study Design and Methods:** A total of 117 obese MetS patients (average age 49.8±13.6 years, BMI 38.2±6.2 kg/m²) were randomized to HIIT (n=40), MIIT (n=37), or an inactive control group (CON, n=40). All groups received nutritional counseling (500 kcal daily deficit) to support weight loss. Both exercise protocols involved only <30 minutes of total time effort per week—specifically 14-minute sessions twice weekly consisting of 2-min warm-up, 5 interval bouts of 1 minute, and 3-min cool-down. HIIT required 80–95% of HRmax intensity (progressively increased every 4 weeks), while MIIT required 65–80% HRmax. Outcomes measured included maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max), MetS severity (MetS z-score), body composition, and quality of life (QoL).

**Key Results:**
- 87 participants completed the study (HIIT: n=32, MIIT: n=22, CON: n=33)
- All groups significantly reduced body weight (~3%; HIIT: −3.9 kg, MIIT: −2.0 kg, CON: −2.8 kg), with no significant between-group differences
- Only exercise groups improved VO2max, MetS z-score, and QoL
- VO2max improved in an intensity-dependent manner: HIIT +3.1 mL/kg/min (p<0.001), MIIT +1.2 mL/kg/min (p<0.05)
- MetS z-score improved: HIIT −1.8 units (p<0.001), MIIT −1.2 units (p<0.01)
- HIIT showed significantly greater improvements in absolute VO2max, maximal power output (Wmax), and waist circumference compared to both MIIT and CON
- Both exercise groups showed greater blood pressure reductions than CON
- No adverse events occurred during any training sessions
- Adherence was high (HIIT: 94.6%, MIIT: 91.7%)
- HIIT was rated more enjoyable (6.1 vs 5.3 on 7-point scale, p=0.001), with 97% of HIIT participants intending to continue the protocol vs 58% in MIIT

**Conclusions:** Extremely low-volume interval training (<30 min/week), even at moderate intensity, is sufficiently effective to improve cardiometabolic health in obese MetS patients. The authors conclude that the findings underpin the crucial role of exercise in treating obesity and MetS, and that even this minimal time commitment produces meaningful health benefits, addressing the primary barrier of time commitment to physical activity in this population.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In conclusion, extremely low-volume interval training, even when done at moderate intensity, is sufficiently effective to improve cardiometabolic health in obese MetS patients. These findings underpin the crucial role of exercise in the treatment of obesity and MetS."

--- SOURCE 2: High-Intensity Interval Training Elicits Higher Enjoyment ... ---
URL: https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/31cd/fd543303598ea9ae834ac4adaa81bc5bc8aa.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This peer-reviewed research article, published in PLOS ONE on January 11, 2017 (DOI:10.1371/journal.pone.0166299), examined differences in enjoyment, affect, and perceived exertion between high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and moderate-intensity continuous exercise (MICT). The study was conducted by researchers at the Department of Kinesiology, California State University San Marcos.

Twelve recreationally active men (n=8) and women (n=4), aged 25.5±10.7 years (range 18-49), with VO2max of 41.3±4.9 mL/kg/min and BMI of 23.1±3.0 kg/m², completed three sessions: an initial VO2max test on a cycle ergometer, followed by two randomized exercise trials. HIIT consisted of eight 1-minute bouts of cycling at 85% maximal workload (Wmax) with 1-minute active recovery at 25% Wmax between bouts (total 16 min). MICT consisted of 20 minutes of continuous cycling at 45% Wmax. During exercise, RPE, affect (Feeling Scale), heart rate, and blood lactate concentration (BLa) were measured. The Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale (PACES) was completed post-exercise.

Key findings:
- Enjoyment was significantly higher in HIIT (103.8±9.4) versus MICT (84.2±19.1) (p=0.013, d=1.54)
- Eleven of 12 participants (92%) preferred HIIT to MICT
- Affect was significantly lower (less positive) during HIIT versus MICT
- Heart rate, RPE (1.5-2.7 units higher), and blood lactate were significantly higher during HIIT versus MICT
- Peak intensity of MICT was 77% HRmax versus 89% HRmax for HIIT

The authors attributed greater HIIT enjoyment to: (1) intermittent recovery intervals providing breaks from aversive affective responses, (2) MICT being perceived as monotonous while HIIT provides an ever-changing stimulus, and (3) a sense of accomplishment experienced during HIIT. The study supports the Dual-Mode Theory, showing affect declines with increasing anaerobic metabolism reliance. Previous research by Bartlett et al., Jung et al., and Martinez et al. showed similar results supporting HIIT enjoyment, while noting that lower-intensity HIIT (~78% Wpeak) elicits more positive affect than higher-intensity protocols (85-100% Wpeak). The authors concluded that HIIT's time efficiency and greater enjoyment may support its integration into exercise routines of healthy, active individuals, though further research in larger, more heterogeneous populations is needed.
</summary>

"Results showed higher enjoyment (p = 0.013) in response to HIIT (103.8 ± 9.4) versus MICT (84.2 ± 19.1). Eleven of 12 participants (92%) preferred HIIT to MICT.", "Although HIIT is more physically demanding than MICT, individuals report greater enjoyment due to its time efficiency and constantly changing stimulus.", "Three potential factors explain this response. First, the intermittent nature of HIIT provides participants with multiple recovery intervals which may provide a 'break' from less positive affective responses. Second, many participants viewed MICT as quite monotonous and did not enjoy maintaining a moderate effort for 20 min. In contrast, HIIT provides an ever changing stimulus that breaks the entire session up into small increments of work interspersed with recovery. Third, there is a certain level of accomplishment that is experienced during HIIT which is not apparent in MICT.", "Data reveal that HIIT requiring a shorter time commitment than MICT led to greater enjoyment in a small sample of active men and women. Despite greater metabolic stress, over 90% of participants preferred HIIT versus MICT.", "The greatest barrier to regular physical activity is lack of time, which questions the practicality of MICT in the overall adult population considering its relatively large time commitment."

--- SOURCE 3: Rates of compliance and adherence to high-intensity interval training: a systematic review and Meta-analyses ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01535-w

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity (Volume 20, article 134) on November 21, 2023, examining rates of compliance and adherence to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) among insufficiently active adults and adults with medical conditions.

**Background and Purpose:** Physical inactivity affects an estimated 27.5% of the global population. The study aimed to: (1) synthesize compliance (supervised intervention attendance) and adherence (unsupervised physical activity completion) rates to HIIT, and (2) determine whether these rates differ between HIIT and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT).

**Methods:** 188 unique studies (n=8,928 participants) were included. Databases searched included MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, and Web of Science (searched from inception to October 3, 2022). Two independent reviewers completed screening and data extraction. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2.0 (for RCTs) and ROBINS-I (for quasi-experimental studies). Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted using Hedge's g.

**Key Results:**
- Compliance to HIIT averaged 89.4% (SD: 11.8%); adherence to HIIT averaged 63% (SD: 21.1%)
- Compliance to MICT averaged 92.5% (SD: 10.6%); adherence to MICT averaged 68.2% (SD: 16.2%)
- Based on 65 studies, compliance rates were NOT significantly different between supervised HIIT and MICT [Hedge's g = 0.015 (95%CI: -0.088 to 0.118), p = .78]; results were robust with low risk of publication bias
- Based on 10 studies, adherence rates were NOT significantly different between unsupervised HIIT and MICT [Hedge's g = -0.313 (95%CI: -0.681 to 0.056), p = .096]
- Sub-group analysis indicated adherence rates differed depending on the method of outcome measurement
- Quality of evidence for compliance was rated as moderate; for adherence it was rated as very low quality

**Conclusions:** Compliance to both HIIT and MICT was high among insufficiently active adults and those with medical conditions. Adherence was relatively moderate with high heterogeneity and very low quality of evidence. Further research should consider exercise protocols, methods of outcome measurement, and measurement timepoints.

**Registration:** The review was registered in PROSPERO (identifier CRD42019103313).

The study addresses ongoing debate about whether HIIT is a feasible exercise modality in real-world settings compared to MICT, with some arguing HIIT is time-efficient and enjoyable while others argue it elicits more negative affective responses that may lead to exercise disengagement.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Compliance to HIIT interventions averaged 89.4% (SD:11.8%), while adherence to HIIT averaged 63% (SD: 21.1%). Compliance and adherence to MICT averaged 92.5% (SD:10.6%) and 68.2% (SD:16.2%), respectively."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Frontiers | Is low-volume high intensity interval training a time-efficient strategy for improving body composition and cardiovascular health in children and adolescents? Evidence from a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1736441/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Physiology (19 December 2025, Volume 16) titled "Is low-volume high intensity interval training a time-efficient strategy for improving body composition and cardiovascular health in children and adolescents?" The study was conducted by Zheng et al. from multiple institutions in China, Australia, and Sweden, and registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/exhjm/).

**Purpose:** To assess the impact of low-volume high-intensity interval training (LV-HIIT) on body composition and cardiovascular health in children and adolescents, and to explore moderating factors. LV-HIIT was defined as training with a total session duration ≤30 minutes (including warm-up, recovery, cool-down) with total vigorous exercise time ≤10 minutes.

**Methods:** A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL), and CNKI was conducted from inception to April 2025. A three-level random-effects model was used (accounting for within-study effect size dependency), with subgroup analyses and meta-regression for moderators. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and certainty of evidence via GRADE. From 5,707 records after duplicate removal, 23 studies (996 participants, 246 female) were included—6 studies on normal-weight and 17 on overweight/obese individuals.

**Key Results (LV-HIIT vs. control):**
- BMI: significantly reduced (g = −1.24, K=17, moderate heterogeneity, moderate GRADE)
- Fat mass: significantly reduced (g = −0.99, K=8, low GRADE)
- Body fat: significantly reduced (g = −0.89, K=11, very low heterogeneity, low GRADE)
- Waistline: significantly reduced (g = −0.42, K=7, low GRADE)
- Weight: significantly reduced (g = −0.34, K=13, moderate GRADE)
- SBP: significantly reduced (g = −0.37, K=10, low GRADE)
- VO2max: significantly improved (g = 1.35, K=10, low GRADE)
- No significant effects for fat-free mass (g = −0.03) or DBP (g = −0.35)

No significant differences were observed between LV-HIIT and MICT. Descriptive (narrative) findings indicated LV-HIIT had comparable effects to small-sided games (SSG) and sprint interval training (SIT), but greater benefits than moderate-intensity interval training (MIIT).

**Subgroup findings:** Weight status, age, intervention duration, training frequency, repetitions, and per-repetition time altered effects. Specifically, LV-HIIT had greater effects on weight reduction in overweight/obese participants (g = −0.50, p<0.01, subgroup difference p=0.039); greater SBP improvement in children (≤12 years, g = −0.65, p<0.01, p=0.024); interventions >8 weeks produced greater SBP improvement (g = −0.59, p<0.01, p=0.027) and DBP reduction (g = −0.61, p<0.01, p=0.014); and VO2max improved more in overweight/obese participants (g = 1.68, p<0.01, p=0.047).

**Study characteristics:** Running was the most common modality, followed by cycling, Tabata-style bodyweight training, and game-based interval protocols. Intervention duration ranged from 4–16 weeks (12 weeks most common, K=12). Training frequency varied from 2–4 sessions/week (3 sessions most common, K=17).

**Conclusion:** LV-HIIT can effectively and time-efficiently improve body composition and cardiovascular health in children and adolescents, with overall effects comparable to MICT. Exercise prescriptions should consider weight status, age, and intervention characteristics. Conclusions should be interpreted with caution given the limited number of studies and potential bias. The trim-and-fill method for publication bias was not applied due to methodological controversy.
</summary>

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8294064

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2021 Jul 05;18(13):7201, doi: 10.3390/ijerph18137201) titled "Evidence-Based Effects of High-Intensity Interval Training on Exercise Capacity and Health: A Review with Historical Perspective." The article was authored by Muhammed Mustafa Atakan, Yanchun Li, Şükran Nazan Koşar, Hüseyin Hüsrev Turnagöl (from Hacettepe University, Ankara, Turkey and Beijing Sport University, China), and Xu Yan (from Victoria University, Australia). The paper presents a historical overview of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) from the early 1920s to date, along with mechanisms underlying physiological adaptations.

KEY DEFINITIONS AND TYPES OF INTERVAL TRAINING:
- HIIT: repeated short bursts of intense activity at ≥90% of maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) or >75% of maximal power, with periods of rest or low-intensity exercise. Subcategorized into low-volume (<15 min of active intervals) and high-volume (>15 min) HIIT.
- Sprint Interval Training (SIT): more intense form with all-out or supramaximal efforts (≤30 s bouts, ~4 min recovery); the most common protocol is 4×30s all-out cycling at ~170% VO2max.
- Repeated-Sprint Training (RST): 10-20 maximal sprints lasting ≤10 s with short recoveries (<60 s).

HISTORICAL BACKGROUND:
- Paavo Nurmi (1920-1930), nine-time Olympic gold medalist, trained with 20×60s high-intensity intervals separated by short rests.
- In the 1930s, German physician Woldemar Gerschler and cardiologist Herbert Reindel designed a HR-based interval model (run at 180 beats/min, rest until HR dropped to 120); 21 days of HIIT elicited a 20% increase in heart volume.
- Sir Roger Bannister, first to run a mile under 4 minutes, used 10×400m under 60s with 2 min rest.

KEY STUDY FINDINGS:
- 1973 (Saltin group): ~20% increase in VO2max in military conscripts after 2 months of interval training.
- 1976 (Henriksson & Reitman): HIIT increased VO2max and type II succinate-dehydrogenase activity; MICT increased type I enzyme activity - showing adaptations are intensity- and fiber-type-dependent.
- 1986 (Sharp et al.): 8 weeks of SIT increased buffering capacity by 37% and VO2max by 8%.
- 1996 (Tabata et al.): HIIT (43 min/week) was more effective than MICT (300 min/week) in simultaneously upregulating oxidative and glycolytic energy systems.
- 2006 (Gibala et al. landmark study): Six SIT sessions (~90% less training volume: 630 kJ vs 6500 kJ) produced similar improvements in time trial performance and muscle adaptations as MICT.
- 2007 (Helgerud et al.): HIIT improved VO2max and left ventricular stroke volume more than continuous training matched for total work.
- 2010 (Little et al.): Designed practical low-volume HIIT (8-12×60s intervals at ~100% PPO with 75s recovery) that increased exercise capacity and mitochondrial markers (CS, cytochrome C oxidase, PGC-1α).
- 2016 (Granata et al.): SIT promoted greater and faster mitochondrial adaptations than HIIT or continuous training; training intensity is a key determinant of mitochondrial respiration changes.
- 2020 (Stensvold et al.): Five-year randomized trial of 1567 older adults comparing HIIT vs MICT vs physical activity guidelines on mortality.

KEY MECHANISMS AND BENEFITS:
- HIIT induces central cardiovascular adaptations and metabolic stress, while MICT mainly triggers peripheral adaptations (muscular oxygen extraction and metabolic efficiency).
- HIIT elicits higher enjoyment than MICT and lower dropout rates in previously sedentary individuals.
- Benefits include improved VO2max, endurance capacity, resting metabolic rate, substrate metabolism, body composition, insulin sensitivity, and cognitive functions, plus reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, metabolic syndrome, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis.
- Low-volume HIIT (<15 min active time) is a time-efficient strategy to improve cardiometabolic health.
- Twice-daily HIIT sessions (separated by 2h) may be more effective at inducing mitochondrial biogenesis and fat oxidation adaptations than once-daily exercise.
- Lack of time is the most common barrier to exercise adherence; ~1.4 billion people (a third of adults and four-fifths of adolescents) do not meet physical activity guidelines.
- SIT may not be well-tolerated by individuals with chronic diseases or obesity; RST is widely used in athletic preparation.
</summary>

"High-intensity interval exercise is characterized by repeated short bursts of intense activity, performed with a 'near maximal' or 'all-out' effort corresponding to ≥90% of maximal oxygen uptake or >75% of maximal power, with periods of rest or low-intensity exercise."

- MICT prescription: 20-50 minutes continuous activity at ~65% HRpeak

--- SOURCE 10: Narrative Review of High-Intensity Interval Training: Positive Impacts on Cardiovascular Health and Disease Prevention ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2308-3425/12/4/158

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a peer-reviewed open-access narrative review article titled "Narrative Review of High-Intensity Interval Training: Positive Impacts on Cardiovascular Health and Disease Prevention," published in the Journal of Cardiovascular Development and Disease (J. Cardiovasc. Dev. Dis. 2025, 12(4), 158; DOI: 10.3390/jcdd12040158). The article was authored by Jae-Myun Ko (Yonsei University), Wi-Young So (Korea National University of Transportation), and Sung-Eun Park (University of Seoul), with So and Park serving as corresponding authors. It was submitted on 12 March 2025, revised 11 April 2025, accepted 15 April 2025, and published 17 April 2025.

METHODS: The review followed the Whittemore and Knafl integrative review framework. A PubMed search (concluded 10 February 2024) using MeSH terms for high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and cardiovascular diseases yielded 257 articles. After applying inclusion/exclusion criteria (experimental designs, diverse populations including healthy individuals, obese, metabolic syndrome, CVD patients, cancer survivors, and animal studies; excluding single-bout studies, reviews, meta-analyses, conference abstracts, and non-English publications), 138 studies passed preliminary screening, and a quality assessment scored on a 0-2 scale per criterion reduced this to 39 studies for final analysis.

KEY RESULTS: 
- Vascular function: HIIT reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure, improved flow-mediated dilation (FMD), decreased pulse wave velocity (PWV) and peripheral vascular resistance, indicating reduced arterial stiffness.
- Cardiac function: Increased left ventricular wall thickness, cardiac output, heart rate variability (HRV), and sympathetic nerve efficiency.
- Lipid/metabolic profiles: Decreased LDL, total cholesterol, and triglycerides while increasing HDL; reduced hemoglobin A1c, increased insulin sensitivity, and improved fasting blood glucose.
- Body composition: Significant reductions in body fat mass, waist circumference, BMI, and body fat percentage.
- Cardiorespiratory fitness: Most studies reported significant increases in VO2peak after HIIT.
- Safety/mental health: HIIT was safely applied to high-risk populations (obesity, metabolic syndrome, CVD, cancer survivors) with minimal serious adverse effects, and reduced stress, depression, and anxiety while improving quality of life.

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS: HIIT proved equal or superior to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) for CRF, vascular health, and blood pressure despite shorter sessions, making it time-efficient. However, long-term effectiveness showed limitations—Berglund et al.'s 5-year twice-weekly HIIT study (the longest intervention included) showed protective effects only against HDL-C decline with no significant changes in other markers. Protocol heterogeneity (e.g., 4×4 min, 10×1 min, or 30 s sprint intervals) and varying definitions of "high intensity" (VO2max 85-90%, HRmax, RPE) complicate comparisons. Healthy adults improved after just 6 weeks, whereas patients with diabetes, hypertension, or cancer required at least 8 weeks. Long-term HIIT may cause muscle damage and fatigue accumulation.

CONCLUSIONS: HIIT is an effective, safe, and time-efficient exercise modality for improving cardiovascular health, metabolic indicators, body composition, mental health, and quality of life across diverse populations. An individualized approach is essential, particularly for high-risk groups, with adjustments to intensity and frequency. Future research should focus on standardizing HIIT protocols, including more diverse populations, evaluating long-term effects, and developing tailored programs with motivational approaches to enhance adherence.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"HIIT significantly improved vascular function, evidenced by reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure and enhanced flow-mediated dilation. Improvements in cardiac function were observed through increased cardiac output and heart rate variability."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42978-025-00352-w

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an editorial published in the Journal of Science in Sport and Exercise (Volume 8, pages 1–8, published January 23, 2026) by Barry A. Franklin and Weimo Zhu, titled "High-Intensity Interval Training: Benefits, Risks, and Clinical Implications." The article provides a comprehensive overview of the benefits and risks of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) across varied patient populations, including healthy individuals, those with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD), heart failure (HF), atrial fibrillation (AF), and cardiometabolic conditions.

KEY FINDINGS BY POPULATION:
- **Healthy individuals**: HIIT elicits comparable or greater increases in cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) vs. MICT in shortened training duration, especially when total work and frequency are matched.
- **Atherosclerotic CVD**: One early study showed HIIT produced a 17.9% increase in VO2peak vs. 7.9% for MICT over 10 weeks in coronary artery disease patients. However, results are conflicting—some trials found no difference, and a meta-analysis of 10 studies (n=472) found MICT was associated with more marked declines in resting heart rate and body weight.
- **Heart failure**: Studies generally show HIIT improves aerobic capacity more than MICT (e.g., 22% vs. 11% increase in VO2peak in HF with preserved ejection fraction over 12 weeks; one RCT of 180 patients found no difference). A systematic review/meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found HIIT generally superior for CRF in HF patients.
- **Adherence**: Supervised adherence is similar between HIIT and MICT, but home-based HIIT adherence was only 58% (vs. >81% for home-based MICT), with higher dropout rates in home-based HIIT and slightly higher dropout rates in women.
- **Cardiometabolic health**: A meta-analysis found HIIT more effective for CRF and flow-mediated dilation, while MICT was superior for long-term glucose metabolism (hemoglobin A1c). No differences in BMI, blood pressure, lipids, or insulin resistance. A recent meta-analysis of 26 RCTs (790 patients with "diabesity") found HIIT offered modest additional benefits for fasting insulin, insulin resistance, and CRF.
- **Atrial fibrillation**: In 86 patients with persistent/permanent AF, twice-weekly 23-min HIIT was as effective as 60-min MICT in improving 6-min walk test, QoL, and resting heart rate, despite a 336-min difference in total exercise time. However, HIIT had significantly higher dropout rates (11 vs. 4, P=0.047) likely due to exercise-related complications like joint injuries.

SAFETY/RISK DATA:
- Adverse event rate of 8% reported for HIIT in cardiometabolic disease patients in one review.
- Another review found 1 event per 3,417 sessions for HIIT vs. 1 per 7,134 sessions for MICT.
- In 4,846 coronary patients, absolute risk was 1 event per 23,182 patient-hours for HIIT vs. 1 per 129,456 for MICT—5.6 times higher in HIIT.
- A home-based HIIT study reported one patient death during warm-up.
- The cumulative patient-hours in existing HIIT trials fall far short of the ~23,182 hours statistically estimated to trigger an acute cardiac event, so it is premature to conclude HIIT is safe/superior.

CASE REPORT: The authors describe a 38-year-old male nurse (BMI 36 kg/m²) who enrolled in a HIIT program after an extended exercise layoff. He collapsed and died of sudden cardiac death during his first session's last treadmill station (jogging at 5.0–5.5 mph, ~7–9 METs). His intake form was unremarkable. Autopsy revealed moderate single-vessel atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (~65% luminal narrowing), marked cardiac hypertrophy (heart weighed 490g vs. ~300g normal), and cause of death listed as "atherosclerotic and hypertensive cardiovascular disease."

PREVALENCE OF SILENT CVD: Cleveland Clinic intravascular ultrasound study showed coronary atherosclerosis in ~60% of those aged 30–39 and 71% aged 40–49; a Swedish study of >25,000 people aged 50–64 found 42% had silent coronary atherosclerosis.

CONCLUSIONS: HIIT appears superior to MICT in improving CRF/aerobic capacity with shorter training time, and elicits sustained post-exercise oxygen consumption exceeding 24 hours with appetite suppression effects. However, there is no consensus on HIIT prescriptive guidelines, staffing, or stopping criteria in cardiac rehabilitation. The authors recommend direct medical supervision and continuous ECG monitoring at least during initial weeks, caution when initiating HIIT in previously inactive adults, and warn that starting a conditioning program with vigorous exercise for inactive, unfit individuals aged ~35+ may be hazardous to health. Additional long-term studies are needed to assess safety, adherence, and outcomes across varied populations.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scoping review published in Sports Medicine - Open (July 19, 2021) titled "High-Intensity Interval Training in Older Adults: A Scoping Review" by Catherine F. S. Marriott and colleagues from Western University and the University of British Columbia. The review aims to characterize existing research on HIIT in older adults, including study populations, training protocols, feasibility/tolerability, outcomes, and knowledge gaps.

METHODOLOGY: The authors used the Arksey and O'Malley 5-step scoping review framework. Five databases (Scopus, Medline, Embase, CINAHL, SportDiscus) were searched for articles published up to February 2021, yielding 4,644 potential studies. After removing duplicates and applying inclusion/exclusion criteria (including requiring mean participant age ≥65 years, experimental or semi-experimental designs, original research, and exclusively high-intensity interval aerobic training not combined with resistance training), 69 studies were included. "High-intensity" was defined as 70-89% of peak HR, 60-84% of HRR, or 60-79% of peak VO2 (vigorous), or ≥90% peak HR, ≥85% HRR, ≥80% peak VO2 (very hard). Sprint interval training (SIT) groups were also included.

RESULTS: The 69 studies included 3,243 individuals with sample sizes ranging from 10 to 473 (mean 47.0 ± 65.2). Mean participant ages ranged from 61.4 to 80.8 years (mean 67.9 ± 3.4 years). Studies were classified by clinical population: non-clinical (n=30), cardiovascular diseases (n=12), cardiac disease (n=9), metabolic disease (n=8), and other (n=10). 48 studies were randomized controlled or crossover designs; 21 were quasi-experimental. Interventions ranged from a single session to 6 months (mean 7.9 ± 7.0 weeks), with session frequency of 2-5 per week. The most common modality was cycle ergometer (n=46), followed by treadmills/walking, water-based training, all-extremity ergometers, and recumbent steppers. The review included 12 SIT studies, 3 short-interval studies (<1 min), and 57 long-interval studies (≥1 min).

KEY FINDINGS: HIIT was generally reported as well-tolerated in older adults across most studies, with high compliance rates (e.g., 85-100% attendance) and few adverse events. HIIT showed benefits in cardiorespiratory fitness, blood pressure reduction, body composition, functional ability, and in some studies cognitive outcomes, often comparable or superior to moderate-intensity continuous training (MCT). The review notes HIIT is increasingly popular but has not been well-studied in older adults compared to younger populations, and early research suggests it may confer health benefits over traditional endurance exercise while being generally well-tolerated.

--- SOURCE 17: HIIT for older adults: How to use intervals safely and effectively ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from ACE Fitness (American Council on Exercise) is an article from the Certified™ magazine (June 2026 issue) titled "How to Safely Use High-Intensity Interval Training With Older Adult Clients," written by Pete McCall, a Health and Fitness Expert.

**Main Topic:** The article examines whether HIIT is appropriate and safe for older adults (50+), presenting scientific evidence, safety considerations, and practical implementation guidelines.

**Key Points:**

1. **Core Argument:** Age alone should not be the deciding factor for HIIT suitability. Training history, health status, medications, movement skill, balance, musculoskeletal capacity, recovery and personal preference all matter. The question should be "What version of interval training is appropriate for this person today?" rather than "Is this person too old for HIIT?"

2. **Benefits of Lifelong Exercise:** A study of lifelong exercisers in their 70s found that more than 50 years of aerobic exercise fully preserved skeletal muscle capillarization and aerobic enzymes, regardless of intensity. However, programming should be based on current readiness, not just exercise history.

3. **Recent Research Findings:**
   - A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis in Sports Medicine-Open (44 RCTs, 1,863 participants ages 60.5–81.2) found HIIT significantly improved resting heart rate, systolic blood pressure, cardiorespiratory fitness, body-fat percentage, muscular strength, muscular endurance and balance compared to non-exercise controls.
   - A 2024 meta-analysis in Archives of Gerontology and Geriatrics (29 trials, 1,227 participants age 60+) found HIIT and moderate-intensity continuous training produced similar changes in most markers, though cardiorespiratory fitness gains were greater with HIIT in higher-quality trials.
   - A 2025 review in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (11 RCTs) found HIIT improved six-minute walk test performance, VO2peak and quality of life; gait speed did not change significantly.

4. **Chronic Health Conditions:** HIIT can be appropriate for clients with stable hypertension, coronary artery disease (a 2023 trial of 382 cardiac rehab patients showed greater cardiorespiratory fitness gains with HIIT), and type 2 diabetes (using all-extremity ergometers to reduce balance/impact demands). Uncontrolled conditions require medical clearance first.

5. **Safety Considerations:** Preparticipation screening, informed consent, medication awareness (especially beta blockers affecting heart-rate response), use of perceived exertion over heart-rate monitors, and mode selection that accounts for balance, joint health and movement skill.

6. **Practical Implementation Guidelines:**
   - Start with low volume: 10–30 second intervals with 1–3 minutes recovery; 1–2 intervals for new clients
   - Choose appropriate mode (stationary/recumbent cycle, rowing, elliptical, walking inclines, aquatic exercise, step-ups)
   - Consider REHIT (reduced-exertion HIIT) — one study showed two 20-second sprints in sessions under 9 minutes improved cardiorespiratory fitness
   - Warm up 5–10 minutes; cool down adequately
   - Start with one HIIT session per week; progress to two for well-conditioned clients (not on consecutive days)
   - Hold off on full Tabata protocols; regress to shorter segments first

7. **Expert Quote:** Robert Linkul, MS, owner of Training the Older Adult (Shingle Springs, Calif., average client age 68): "We use intervals of truly challenging work and inform our clients to exercise to a point of 'discomfort'... We see a great benefit in training strength and conditioning components at the same time."

8. **Multicomponent Program:** HIIT should complement (not replace) resistance training, balance work, mobility and moderate-intensity aerobic activity. Strength and balance are prerequisites for safe conditioning.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | Affective and Enjoyment Responses to Sprint Interval Training in Healthy Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.820228/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Psychology (March 9, 2022) examining affective and enjoyment responses to Sprint Interval Training (SIT) in healthy individuals. The study was conducted by researchers from the University of Macau, University of British Columbia, and Macao Polytechnic Institute.

**Purpose**: SIT is characterized by "all-out" effort intensity and superior time-efficiency compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT), but its supramaximal intensity has been feared to induce adverse psychological feelings. The review aimed to synthesize studies on affective and enjoyment responses to SIT and compare them with MICT and other high-intensity interval training (HIIT) protocols.

**Methods**: A systematic search of 7 databases (Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, NCBI, Cochrane, Medline) was conducted up to March 22, 2021. Twenty-five studies met inclusion criteria (675 healthy adults, 337 men and 338 women). Affect was measured via the Feeling Scale (FS) and enjoyment via the Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale (PACES) or Exercise Enjoyment Scale (EES). Random effects meta-analyses were conducted using Review Manager 5.4. SIT protocols were categorized into four groups: classic SIT (4-6 × 30-s sprints), REHIT (2-3 × 20-s sprints), RST (≥10 × ≤10-s sprints), and Tabata SIT (7-8 × 20-s sprints with 10-s rest). The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021284898).

**Key Results**:
- Affective responses decreased to negative valences during SIT in most studies (lowest scores ranged from -2.8 to 1.5), with declines observed in all studies recording in-task affect.
- Meta-analyses showed SIT induced similar post-exercise affective valences during training compared to MICT and HIIT, but LOWER affective valences immediately post-exercise compared to MICT.
- SIT showed a large adverse effect on affect in the lowest score compared to HIIT.
- Low-volume SIT protocols (REHIT and RST) with shorter sprint durations and fewer repetitions induced more positive affective responses.
- Enjoyment after SIT was positive (PACES scores ranged 51-81%) and comparable to MICT or HIIT, with no significant differences in meta-analyses.
- Most SIT protocols had total training durations under 20 minutes, significantly shorter than MICT (30-65 min) or HIIT (20-60 min).
- Self-reported tolerance (measured via PRETIE-Q) influenced affective responses, with lower tolerance associated with more negative affect or higher post-exercise fatigue.

The article, published as part of the Certified™: Innovative Training Techniques issue (June 2021), examines REHIT (reduced-exertion high-intensity training), a modified form of HIIT that uses fewer and shorter interval bouts.

**Key Content:**
- REHIT shortens traditional HIIT workouts by using fewer/shorter intervals while still providing effective fitness benefits. Traditional HIIT involves 4-10 bouts of 20 seconds to 5 minutes at 80-100% peak heart rate, while SIT (sprint interval training) involves 6-10 all-out 20-30 second sprints at >100% VO2max.

**ACE-Commissioned Research Findings:**
1. 2018 study (8-week REHIT program, 32 participants): REHIT produced nearly double the improvement in cardiorespiratory fitness (12.3%) compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (6.9%). Systolic blood pressure reductions were 3x greater in the REHIT group. Participants completed 89% of assigned workouts. Used CAR.O.L cycle ergometer, 3-4 days/week.
2. 2019 study (10 sedentary volunteers, 6-week crossover design): After just 3 weeks of REHIT (8 min 40 sec sessions, 3x/week, including 2 all-out sprints separated by 3-min recovery), cardiometabolic health improved. **Science of REHIT:** REHIT creates sudden energy demand with ATP regeneration up to 100-fold greater than rest. The "master regulator" PGC-1α (via AMPK activation) drives mitochondrial biogenesis. Research shows AMPK is maximally activated with just two 20-second all-out sprints and doesn't increase further with more reps.

**F.I.T.T. Recommendations for REHIT:**
- Frequency: 2-3 days per week
- Intensity: All-out effort (RPE 9-10 on 0-10 scale)
- Time: 2 interval bouts, 20 seconds each, with 3 minutes light active recovery between
- Type: Running, cycling, jumping rope, elliptical; cycling has lower dropout rates than running/walking

**Additional Research:** A study found reducing training frequency from 3-4 sessions to 2 sessions/week did not diminish improvements (2 sessions: +10.2%, 3 sessions: +8.1%, 4 sessions: +7.3% cardiorespiratory fitness).

**Safety Considerations:** Exercise is generally safe; absolute risk of sudden death during vigorous activity is ~1 per 15,000-18,000 people per year. Individuals with diagnosed cardiovascular, metabolic, or renal disease should receive medical clearance. Preparticipation health screening is recommended.

**Practical Applications:** REHIT is recommended during vacations/holidays (especially between Thanksgiving and New Year), for shift workers, and as at-home workouts during COVID-19. Periodization of REHIT is encouraged rather than exclusive use. "Lack of time" is the most cited reason clients don't exercise regularly, making REHIT particularly valuable for adherence.
</summary>
