# Effects of low-volume High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) on fitness in adults: A meta-analysis of controlled and non-controlled trials

* Matthew Weston
* , Kathryn Weston
* , Alan Batterham
* , William G. Hopkins

Research output: Contribution to journal › Article › peer-review

330 Downloads (Pure)

## Abstract

Background: Low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIT) appears to be an efficient and practical way to develop physical fitness.  
Objective: Our objective was to estimate meta-analysed mean effects of HIT on aerobic power (maximum oxygen consumption [VO2max] in an incremental test) and sprint fitness (peak and mean power in a 30-s Wingate test).  
Data Sources: Five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, BIOSIS and Web of Science) were searched for original research articles published up to January 2014. Search terms included ‘high intensity’, ‘HIT’, ‘sprint’, ‘fitness’ and ‘VO2max’.  
Study Selection: Inclusion criteria were fitness assessed pre- and post-training; training period C2 weeks; repetition duration 30–60 s; work/rest ratio\1.0; exercise intensity described as maximal or near maximal; adult subjects aged [18 years.  
Data Extraction: The final data set consisted of 55 estimates from 32 trials for VO2max, 23 estimates from 16 trials for peak sprint power, and 19 estimates from 12 trials for mean sprint power. Effects on fitness were analysed as percentages via log transformation. Standard errors calculated from exact p values (where reported) or imputed from errors of measurement provided appropriate weightings. Fixed effects in the meta-regression model included type of study (controlled, uncontrolled), subject characteristics (sex, training status, baseline fitness) and training parameters (number of training sessions, repetition duration, work/rest ratio). Probabilistic magnitude-based inferences for meta-analysed effects were based on standardized thresholds for small, moderate and large changes (0.2, 0.6 and 1.2, respectively) derived from between-subject standard deviations (SDs) for baseline fitness.  
Results: A mean low-volume HIT protocol (13 training sessions, 0.16 work/rest ratio) in a controlled trial produced a likely moderate improvement in the VO2max of active non-athletic males (6.2 %; 90 % confidence limits ±3.1 %), when compared with control. There were possibly moderate improvements in the VO2max of sedentary males (10.0 %; ±5.1 %) and active non-athletic females (3.6 %; ±4.3 %) and a likely small increase for sedentary females (7.3 %; ±4.8 %). The effect on the VO2max of athletic males was unclear (2.7 %; ±4.6 %). A possibly moderate additional increase was likely for subjects with a 10 mLkg-1min-1 lower baseline VO2max (3.8 %; ±2.5 %), whereas the modifying effects of sex and difference in exercise dose were unclear. The comparison of HIT with traditional endurance training was unclear (-1.6 %; ±4.3 %). Unexplained variation between studies was 2.0 % (SD). Meta-analysed effects of HIT on Wingate peak and mean power were unclear.  
Conclusions: Low-volume HIT produces moderate improvements in the aerobic power of active non-athletic and sedentary subjects. More studies are needed to resolve the unclear modifying effects of sex and HIT dose on aerobic power and the unclear effects on sprint fitness.

This webpage is a research publication record for a peer-reviewed meta-analysis article published in Sports Medicine (Volume 44, pages 1005-1017, 2014) by Matthew Weston, Kathryn Weston, Alan Batterham, and William G. Hopkins from Teesside University's Research Portal. The article examines the effects of low-volume High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) on fitness in adults.

METHODOLOGY: The authors searched five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, BIOSIS, and Web of Science) for studies published up to January 2014. Inclusion criteria required: fitness assessed pre- and post-training; training period of at least 2 weeks; repetition duration of 30-60 seconds; work/rest ratio <1.0; maximal or near-maximal exercise intensity; and adult subjects aged 18+ years. The final dataset included 55 estimates from 32 trials for VO2max, 23 estimates from 16 trials for peak sprint power, and 19 estimates from 12 trials for mean sprint power. Effects were analyzed as percentages via log transformation, with a meta-regression model incorporating type of study, subject characteristics (sex, training status, baseline fitness), and training parameters.

KEY RESULTS: A mean low-volume HIT protocol (13 training sessions, 0.16 work/rest ratio) in controlled trials produced a likely moderate improvement in VO2max for active non-athletic males (6.2%; 90% CL ±3.1%). Possibly moderate improvements were seen in sedentary males (10.0%; ±5.1%) and active non-athletic females (3.6%; ±4.3%), with a likely small increase for sedentary females (7.3%; ±4.8%). The effect on athletic males was unclear (2.7%; ±4.6%). Subjects with a 10 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ lower baseline VO2max showed a likely possibly moderate additional increase (3.8%; ±2.5%), while the modifying effects of sex and exercise dose were unclear. The comparison of HIT with traditional endurance training was unclear (-1.6%; ±4.3%), and meta-analysed effects on Wingate peak and mean power were also unclear. Unexplained variation between studies was 2.0% (SD).

CONCLUSIONS: Low-volume HIT produces moderate improvements in aerobic power for active non-athletic and sedentary subjects. More studies are needed to resolve unclear modifying effects of sex and HIT dose on aerobic power, and the unclear effects on sprint fitness.

The DOI is 10.1007/s40279-014-0180-z, and the full text is available with a CC BY-NC-ND license.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568)Abstract

### Aim

Although reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) confers well-documented health benefits, most supporting evidence derives from laboratory studies that rely on specialized equipment. This study examined the real-world efficacy of equipment-free REHIT using burpees (BIT) in sedentary young adults.

### Methods

A 12-week randomized controlled trial (n=319 inactive men, age 20.5±1.1 years, maximal oxygen uptake [VO 2max] 37.7±1.4 ml/min/kg) compared four cohorts: supervised BIT (n=79), unsupervised BIT in real-world conditions (BIT-RW; n=79), supervised cycling-based sprint interval training (SIT; n=82), and a non-exercising control (CON; n=79). Exercise groups performed 2×20s all-out effort sessions 3–5 times weekly. Training and affective responses were monitored throughout the intervention. Pre- and post-intervention outcomes included body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness, and mental health (stress, depression, anxiety, sleep quality, resilience, and health-related quality of life [QoL]).

### Results

The supervised BIT achieved 91%–94% of maximal heart rate (HR max), compared to ∼90% HR max in BIT-RW. All exercise groups exhibited significant physiological improvements: 6%–8% body mass reduction, 8%–13% VO 2max increase (_η_ _2_ _p_=0.7–0.8, _p_<0.001). Additionally, exercise training resulted in significant reductions in stress (49–61%, _p_<0.001), anxiety (37–86%, _p_<0.001), depression (14–48%, _p_<0.001), as well as improvements in resilience (22–27%, _p_<0.001) and QoL (14–27%, _p_<0.001). Supervised BIT matched SIT in VO 2max gains (5.0±0.6 ml/min/kg), while BIT-RW showed smaller physiological benefits (3.0±0.6 ml/min/kg) but 10% greater improvements in affective responses (_p_<0.05).

### Conclusions

This study demonstrates that a 40-s equipment-free REHIT protocol utilizing burpees improves both physical and mental health outcomes, even when implemented in unsupervised free-living settings. These findings suggest that BIT is an accessible and time-efficient training option for individuals constrained by limited access to equipment or professional oversight.

**Keywords:**High-intensity interval training, Real-world setting, Cardiorespiratory fitness, Mental health, Physical inactivity

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568)Introduction

1
Sprint Interval Training (SIT), an exceptionally rigorous form of high-intensity interval training (HIIT), is distinguished by repeated bouts of brief, intermittent exercise performed at maximal or supramaximal intensities. These intensities could reach or exceed an individual's maximal aerobic capacity (VO 2max) and rely predominantly on anaerobic metabolic pathways.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib1) SIT has been employed as a method to enhance athletic performance since the mid-20th century.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib1),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib2) Over the past decade, scientific inquiry has increasingly shifted towards investigating the broader applicability of SIT in improving health outcomes among untrained individuals, sedentary populations, and those suffering from chronic conditions.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib3), [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib5), [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib6), [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib7) The traditional SIT protocol, typically involving four bouts of 30-s sprints interspersed with 3–4 min of recovery, can be exceedingly challenging for non-athletic or inactive populations, often resulting in difficulties with adherence. In response, low-volume SIT protocols, featuring shorter sprint durations and fewer repetitions (e.g., two 20-s sprints), have emerged as potentially more feasible alternatives.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib8),[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib9) These protocols, often referred to as reduced-exertion HIIT (REHIT), aim to retain the physiological benefits of classic SIT while ameliorating the discomfort and adverse affective responses associated with supramaximal intensity.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib10),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib11) However, combing extremely high intensities with low training volumes raises concerns about practicality and true efficacy of such protocols. Although some studies have demonstrated that as little as 40 s of total sprint time may significantly enhance cardiorespiratory and cardiovascular fitness,[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib12), [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib13), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib14), [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib15) discrepancies exist within the literature regarding the actual intensity achieved during REHIT sessions. Specifically, inconsistent or inadequate reporting of intensity metrics, such as peak heart rate, maximal oxygen uptake, and elevated ratings of perceived exertion (RPE), raises uncertainties about whether participants consistently engage in vigorous or supramaximal intensities as intended.[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib16),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib17) Moreover, methodological limitations in prior studies (e.g., small sample sizes, non-randomized designs, and short intervention periods) further compromise the reliability of the reported outcomes. Consequently, despite the apparent appeal of performing only two 20-s “all-out” sprints as a time-efficient strategy, rigorous research is still needed to validate these promising yet tentative results.

Despite the ongoing skepticism, the remarkable time efficiency of REHIT renders it an attractive exercise modality for individuals who face time constraints or lack a consistent window for regular physical activity. However, previous REHIT studies demonstrating beneficial outcomes have employed cycling ergometers. In real-world scenarios, individuals who lack access to such equipment at home or at work must travel to fitness facilities even for brief REHIT sessions (e.g., two 20-s sprints), which demands additional time, effort and expense. Therefore, an equipment-free REHIT protocol would hold substantial practical value by eliminating the need for specialized equipment or designated venues, ultimately better serving individuals constrained by limited time or restricted access to training facilities. The Burpee, a compound, full-body calisthenic movement that engages multiple muscle groups and requires minimal space and equipment, emerges as a viable exercise modality for individuals lacking access to traditional gym facilities or ample workout areas.[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib18) Moreover, Burpees typically elicit high physiological responses (heart rate, VO 2, muscle activation), allowing researchers to reliably measure and report these key variables.[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib19) Therefore, this training modality may address concerns regarding whether REHIT can consistently achieve vigorous intensity.

Recent investigations into acute (single-session) or short-term (multi-session, lasting 5–8 weeks) SIT protocols involving Burpee exercises have demonstrated comparable enhancements in aerobic fitness and larger gains in neuromuscular performance compared to those achieved through traditional modalities such as running or cycling.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib20), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib21), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib22) Such effects likely result from the physiological characteristics of Burpee, including substantial full-body engagement, greater neuromuscular activation, and recruitment of multiple muscle groups.[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib23) Moreover, Burpee-based protocols elicited more positive affective responses compared to cycling or running SIT of matched work-rest structure.[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib24) Nevertheless, some studies suggests high-intensity calisthenics could increase discomfort and negative affective responses.[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib25) These discrepancies may be explained by moderating factors such as the degree of supervision, prior high-intensity training experience, or demographic characteristics such as age and fitness background.[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib26) Furthermore, the relatively small sample sizes employed in these studies necessitate cautious interpretation and highlight the need for future research considering these moderating variables explicitly. More importantly, no investigations have yet examined the effectiveness of a Burpee-based protocol incorporating the principles of REHIT (i.e., Burpee Interval Training: BIT), involving only two 20-s sprints, conducted over an extended intervention period under free-living condition. As a result, several critical questions remain unanswered. These include whether individuals can consistently achieve the requisite supramaximal intensities with this modality outside laboratory settings without supervision; whether there are potential adverse events associated with BIT such as joint strain or musculoskeletal discomfort, issues that may also be present in traditional SIT protocols[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib27); the extent to which they find the exercise enjoyable or tolerable, given that positive affective responses (e.g., enjoyment, reduced discomfort) have been suggested to strongly linked to sustained exercise participation and long-term adherence[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib25),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib28); their capacity for sustained adherence over the long term; and the magnitude of health and fitness improvements that can be realistically expected from such interventions.

Therefore, the present study aimed to determine the feasibility, practicability, and efficacy of BIT as a time-efficient, accessible training modality capable of mitigating the barriers faced by individuals with demanding schedules and limited access to conventional training facilities. Specifically, we examined the effects of a 12-week BIT protocol, incorporating two 20-s all-out sprints, performed either under supervision or individually in real-world settings, on affective responses, physical fitness, and mental health in a large cohort of male inactive individuals. It was hypothesized that BIT would induce lower physiological strain and more favorable affective responses than the cycling-SIT protocol. Moreover, it was further posited that the BIT intervention would enhance physical fitness and mental health outcomes to a degree comparable to the cycling-SIT protocol.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568)Method

2
### Participants

2.1
Health male individuals who were physically inactive were recruited for this randomized controlled trial. By focusing on male participants, we controlled for potential gender differences in the responses, thereby enhancing the internal validity of the study. The exclusion criteria encompassed a medical history of chronic conditions, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, or any other illnesses or abnormalities that could potentially impact exercise performance. Additionally, individuals with obesity (defined as a BMI exceeding 30 kg/m 2) or those classified as highly active according to the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) were excluded from participation. Sample size was determined using a power calculation performed with G∗Power software,[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib29) assuming a medium effect size (_f_=0.25), statistical power of 0.90, and an alpha level of 0.05 30. The selected effect size was informed by previous exercise science literature, which reports similar magnitudes of effect in interventions targeting both physical and mental health outcomes, such as VO 2max and psychological well-being.[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib31),[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib32) This calculation indicated that a total sample size of 280 participants was required. Considering an anticipated dropout rate of approximately 40%, based on a meta-analysis reporting a real-world adherence rate of 63% for HIIT interventions,[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib33) we aimed to recruit a total of 392 participants.

A total of 415 male participants were recruited via targeted advertisements within a local university community in Tianjin, China. All participants voluntarily consented to participate in the study. After initial screening, 63 individuals were excluded for not meeting the predefined inclusion criteria, resulting in a final sample of 352 eligible participants. Participants were randomly allocated into four groups, each consisting of 88 individuals. The groups were as follows: a control group (CON), a SIT group, and two BIT groups (i.e., BIT, BIT-RW). Out of the original cohort of 352 participants, thirty-three participants (nine from each group, except for six from the SIT group) withdrew from the study due to factors extraneous to the research, such as scheduling conflicts (n=22), illness (n=11), personal commitments (n=7), and unforeseen travel (n=3). Consequently, their data were excluded from the final analysis, leaving a total sample of 319 participants included in the analysis.

All allocations were concealed from both the participants and the research team until the commencement of the exercise sessions. Ethical approval of this registered study was obtained from the ethics committee, and the experiment was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

### Experimental design

2.2
The 12-week randomized control intervention involved three exercise groups and one control group. Two of the exercise groups performed a BIT protocol, either under direct supervision in an office setting (BIT) or independently in a real-world environment (BIT-RW) without supervision. This is to investigate whether the protocol performed in the real-world setting can be as effective as which performed under supervision. The third exercise group participated in sprint interval training (SIT) on cycle ergometers under supervision in a laboratory, utilizing the same interval protocol as the burpee groups. This comparison aimed to discern whether the mode of exercise (burpee versus cycling) would influence the efficacy of the identified protocol.

During the intervention, participants were instructed to abstain from making any dietary alterations or engaging in physical activity programs outside of the prescribed experimental protocol. Physical activity levels were tracked using the IPAQ, completed on the final day of each week over the two-week period. Additionally, an activity tracker recorded daily step counts on the training days.

Data collection during the study involved several assessments at specified time points. During each session, affective responses, ratings of perceived exertion (RPE), and heart rate measurements were recorded. Assessments of physiological parameters and mental health status were performed 72 h prior to the intervention period (pre-intervention) and 72 h after its completion (post-intervention). All testing sessions were conducted within a controlled laboratory environment maintained at a consistent temperature of 20–22°C and a relative humidity of 40–50%.

### Training protocol

2.3
All exercise sessions began with a low-intensity warm-up (e.g., walking or jogging) for 1 min. Participants in both the BIT and BIT-RW groups performed two 20-s burpee-jump intervals, separated by a 10-s passive recovery period. This extremely short REHIT protocol leverages the principle that high-intensity exercise can trigger significant physiological adaptations, such as improved cardiovascular fitness and enhanced mitochondrial function, by maximizing muscle fiber recruitment and energy system engagement during the intense 20-s sprints, performed at supramaximal effort.[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib34),[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib35) Unlike earlier REHIT studies, which prescribe 2–3 min of recovery and approximately 10 min of total exercise, our protocol trims the rest interval to 10 s. As a result, the entire session can be completed in approximately 2 min, greatly enhancing time-efficiency. [Supplementary Fig. S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#appsec1) illustrates the specific movements involved in performing the burpee exercise. Briefly, the burpee is a dynamic, full-body exercise that moves through a squat, a plank, a push-up, and an explosive jump, targeting multiple muscle groups simultaneously. Participants were instructed to perform each bout in an “all-out” manner, aiming to complete as many repetitions of burpee as possible.

The exercise protocol implemented in the SIT group during the intervention was identical to that of the BIT groups (2×20 s sprints interspersed with 10-s passive recovery), with the primary distinction being that the SIT group performed the exercise on a cycle ergometer. The initial resistance of SIT was set at 1 kg, and if participants maintained a cycling cadence exceeding 100 rpm across all exercise bouts for two consecutive training sessions, the resistance was incrementally increased by 0.5 kg. This progression continued until the workload reached 5% of the participant's individual body mass.

Participants in the BIT and SIT groups were trained under supervision five times per week, in an office setting and on laboratory cycle ergometers, respectively, while participants in the BIT-RW group followed the same BIT protocol independently in a setting of their choice, targeting five (minimum three) sessions weekly. Supervised sessions included standardized verbal encouragement (e.g., clapping and cheering), to motivate participants to perform at maximum effort. The verbal incentives were standardized across all sessions. Heart rate (HR) was recorded every 5 s during the supervised sessions using a Polar H10 heart rate sensor (Polar, Finland) connected to the “Polar Beat” app on a tablet. Rating of perceived exertion (Brog 0–10; RPE) (21) were measured before, at the recovery interval, and immediately after the training.

Participants in the BIT-RW were required to maintain an exercise log for each self-administered session, documenting the exercise duration, the actual number of jumps performed, HR, RPE, and their affective responses before, at the recovery interval and immediately after the training session. Both HR and RPE were utilized to verify the intensity, with thresholds set at HR max> 85% and RPE >8.

Training load was calculated using the data of HR and attendance by Banister TRIMP[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib36): Banister TRIMP=D×HR R×A×e B×HRR, where D=the session duration, A=0.64 for men, B=1.92 for men, e=the Napierian natural logarithm having a value of 2.712, and HRR was calculated using the equation: HR R = HR mean−HR rest/HR max−HR rest, where HR mean=mean HR during exercise, HR rest=resting HR, and HR max=maximal HR.

### Measurements

2.4
#### Physiological parameters

2.4.1
##### Cardiorespiratory fitness

2.4.1.1
Maximal incremental exercise tests were administered to evaluate each participant's cardiorespiratory fitness, quantified as maximal oxygen uptake (VO 2 max). The assessments were conducted on a cycle ergometer (Monark 839E, Varberg, Sweden) with real-time, breath-by-breath oxygen uptake measurements obtained via a calibrated online gas analyzer (Swansea: Jaeger Vyntus, Vyaire Medical; Stirling: Cortex Metalyzer, Cortex). Participants initiated the protocol with a warm-up at a workload of 25 W for 3 min, after which the workload commenced at 50 W and incrementally increased by 25 W every 3 min. They were instructed to maintain a cadence of 60±5 rpm until volitional exhaustion, defined by the attainment of at least two of the following criteria: (1) a respiratory exchange ratio (RER)≥1.15; (2) a rating of perceived exertion (RPE)≥18; or (3) a peak heart rate (HRpeak)≥90% of the age-predicted maximum (220−age). VO2max was determined as the highest value derived from a 15-breath rolling average.[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib37)

##### Anthropometric parameters and resting blood pressure

2.4.1.2
Body mass index (BMI), expressed in kg·m−2, was derived from measurements of body weight (kg) and stature (m), obtained using standardized procedures (i.e., participants wore light clothing and were barefoot). Blood pressure was assessed in triplicate using an electronic sphygmomanometer (Microlife 3BTO-A, Taipei, Taiwan) while participants were seated, following a 10-min period of undisturbed rest. The two closest readings were averaged to determine systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP). Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was subsequently computed using the formula: (SBP+2×DBP)/3.

#### Affective responses

2.4.2
##### Affect and arousal

2.4.2.1
To assess affective valence, the 11-point Feeling Scale (FS) was introduced to participants, providing context on mood fluctuations and positive or negative feelings experienced during exercise with ratings ranging from “very bad” at −5 to “very good” at +5.[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib38) Arousal levels were evaluated using the Felt Arousal Scale (FAS).[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib39) Participants rated their perceived activation or level of excitement on a scale from low activation (1 point) to high activation (6 points). Both scales were administered prior to exercise, at the recovery interval, and immediately post-exercise in every session throughout the 12-week intervention.

##### Enjoyment

2.4.2.2
Enjoyment was measured using the Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale (PACES) weekly immediately post-exercise (scores 18–126) and the Exercise Enjoyment Scale (EES) assessed during each training session (scores 1–7).[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib40) The PACES is an 18-item scale in which respondents rate their enjoyment levels about the physical activity they have just performed. Responses are given on a 7-point bipolar scale, with two reversed descriptors at the ends, such as “I felt bored” and “I felt interested.” The Exercise Enjoyment Scale (EES) is a single-item, 7-point scale intended for rapid administration during physical activity, wherein participants assess “the degree of enjoyment experienced during the exercise session.”

#### Mental health and psychosocial parameters

2.4.3
All measures for mental health and psychosocial parameters were administered at baseline and post-intervention.

##### Mental health symptoms

2.4.3.1
The assessment of symptoms related to stress, anxiety, and depression was conducted using self-reported scales: the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10; scores: 0–40),[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib41) the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-7; scores: 0–21),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib42) and the 21-item Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II; scores: 0–63),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib43) respectively. Higher scores on these scales indicate greater perceived stress, more severe anxiety (with cut-off points of ≥5, ≥10, and ≥15 corresponding to mild, moderate, and severe anxiety, respectively), or more severe depressive symptoms (with thresholds of 14–19, 20–28, and 29–63 indicating mild, moderate, and severe depression, respectively). All three scales have demonstrated good psychometric properties in previous studies, not only in clinical settings but also in the general population.[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib43), [44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib44), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib45)

##### Sleep quality

2.4.3.2
Given the consistent evidence of a bidirectional relationship between sleep quality and mental health,[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib46) sleep quality was assessed as an additional parameter related to mental health. The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI; scores: 0–21) was utilized to evaluate participants' sleep quality and disturbances over the preceding month.[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib47) The PSQI comprises a series of questions designed to assess multiple dimensions of sleep, including sleep duration, sleep latency, habitual sleep efficiency, and disruptions during sleep.

##### Health-related quality of life

2.4.3.3
The 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) to assess multidimensional health and well-being.[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib48) In addition to assessing mental health through psychological well-being and emotional states, the SF-36 also measured physical functioning based on limitations in daily activities, social functioning based on the impact of health on social activities, and general health perceptions based on participants’ overall view of their health. Responses were recorded using Likert scales, and scores for each domain were normalized to a scale from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better health status.

##### Resilience

2.4.3.4
The 25-item Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC; scores: 0 to 100 with higher scores denoting greater resilience) was employed to quantify participants' resilience, conceptualized as the capacity to cope with and adapt to adversity.[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib49) By measuring resilience, the CD-RISC helps paint a fuller picture of someone's mental well-being and how they might handle life's challenges.

### Statistical analysis

2.5
Prior to the execution of the primary statistical analyses, the normality of outcome variables was evaluated using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Intergroup differences in baseline participant characteristics were examined via one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For datasets encompassing multiple temporal measurement points during exercise and longitudinal changes over the 12-week intervention, three way repeated measures ANOVA was employed, considering “time” (before, during, and after exercise) and “week” (aggregated as week 1–4, 5–8, and 9–12) as within-subject factors, while “group” served as the between-subject factor to investigate main effects and interactions effects across distinct groups, enabling an investigation of temporal dynamics and intergroup differences. Physiological parameters and mental health parameters following the intervention were assessed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for baseline values. Furthermore, to gauge how training adherence influenced study outcomes, differences in changes in health and physiological parameters pre-to post-intervention among the intervention groups were calculated using the number of sessions attended as an additional covariate. In instances where significant main effects were observed, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc analyses were conducted using one-way repeated measures ANOVA and/or paired-tests to further elucidate these differences. Data are presented as means±standard deviations (SDs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Effect sizes were calculated using partial eta-squared (η 2 p) and interpreted in accordance with Cohen's benchmarks: small effect (0.01), medium effect (0.06), and large effect (0.14).[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#bib30) All statistical analyses were performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 23.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

During the 12-week intervention, significant disparity was observed in the total number of training sessions completed among the groups ([Supplementary Table S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#appsec1)). Participants in the BIT and SIT group completed an average of 59±1 sessions (completion rate >95%), which was significantly greater than the average completed by the BIT-RW group (48±8 sessions, completion rate >80%). TRIMP data, derived from the HR and session attendance, revealed significant differences in training load among the three groups, with BIT-RW exhibiting the lowest values compared to the two supervised groups. Moreover, the supervised groups showed a marked decrease in training load between the first and final four-week phases (dropping from approximately 96 to 62), whereas the BIT-RW group experienced a more modest decline (from approximately 62 to 51).

Furthermore, significant differences were observed in the number of burpees performed between the two BIT groups (refer to [Table S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#appsec1)). While both groups exhibited an increase in the number of burpees executed over the course of the intervention, the BIT group consistently performed a significantly higher number of burpees compared to the BIT-RW group at each four-week interval.

### Affective responses

3.3
The analysis of affect assessed via FS and arousal measured through the FAS during exercise over the 12-week intervention, revealed statistically significant and substantial main effects of time, week, and group, as well as significant interaction effects ([Table 2a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#tbl2a), [Table 2b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#tbl2b)). Specifically, FS scores demonstrated a significant decline from pre-exercise to post-exercise, with the lowest post-exercise affect scores being negative (-0.2 to −1.9) across all three groups at each four-week interval, except for the BIT-RW group during week 9–12, where affect scores approached neutrality (0.1±0.1) ([Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12273568#fig3)). All groups showed a progressive improvement in affect and a decline in arousal over the 12-week period. Notably, when pre-exercise values were taken into account, the BIT group reported significantly lower affect mid-exercise across all 4-week intervals and post-exercise during week 1–4 and 9–12 compared to the BIT-RW group. Additionally, the SIT group demonstrated a significant decline in affect valence during the final four-week interval, displaying lower affect scores at both mid-exercise and post-exercise compared to the other two groups. This was in contrast to their significantly higher mid-exercise affect scores during weeks 1–4 and post-exercise scores during weeks 5–8. The integration of arousal and affect valence data suggests that participants experienced distress (characterized by negative affect and high arousal) at the conclusion of training in all groups throughout the intervention. This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Exercise Science and Fitness (June 25, 2025) reporting on a randomized controlled trial (RCT) examining the real-world efficacy of equipment-free reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) using burpees in inactive males.

**Study Design & Participants:**
- 12-week randomized controlled trial with 319 inactive men (age 20.5±1.1 years, VO2max 37.7±1.4 ml/min/kg)
- Four cohorts: supervised Burpee Interval Training (BIT, n=79), unsupervised BIT in real-world conditions (BIT-RW, n=79), supervised cycling-based sprint interval training (SIT, n=82), and non-exercising control (CON, n=79)
- Participants were physically inactive young adults (BMI in normal range, VO2max below age-predicted average)
- Study conducted at universities in Tianjin, China and Macao

**Training Protocol:**
- All exercise groups performed 2×20s all-out effort sessions, 3-5 times weekly
- BIT/BIT-RW used burpees (full-body calisthenic movement: squat, plank, push-up, explosive jump)
- SIT used cycle ergometers with identical 2×20s protocol
- Sessions were extremely time-efficient (~2 minutes total including a 1-minute warm-up and 10-second passive recovery between sprints)
- Supervised groups completed ~59 sessions (>95% completion rate); BIT-RW completed ~48 sessions (>80%)

**Key Results:**
- Supervised BIT achieved 91-94% of maximal heart rate (HRmax); BIT-RW achieved ~90% HRmax
- All exercise groups showed significant physiological improvements: 6-8% body mass reduction, 8-13% VO2max increase (large effect sizes, p<0.001)
- Supervised BIT matched SIT in VO2max gains (5.0±0.6 ml/min/kg); BIT-RW showed smaller physiological benefits (3.0±0.6 ml/min/kg)
- BIT-RW showed 10% greater improvements in affective responses compared to supervised groups (p<0.05)
- Significant reductions in stress (49-61%), anxiety (37-86%), depression (14-48%), and improvements in resilience (22-27%) and quality of life (14-27%) across all exercise groups (p<0.001)
- No significant differences among exercise groups for most mental health symptom improvements, though supervised BIT and SIT showed greater resilience gains than BIT-RW
- Exercise sessions elicited distress (negative affect with high arousal) in most groups, but BIT-RW showed slight excitement (near-neutral affect with high arousal) by weeks 9-12
- In-session enjoyment (EES) was lower than post-exercise enjoyment (PACES); SIT enjoyment declined significantly by weeks 9-12 compared to BIT groups

**Conclusions:**
The study demonstrates that a 40-second equipment-free REHIT protocol using burpees improves both physical and mental health outcomes, even when implemented in unsupervised free-living settings. BIT represents an accessible and time-efficient training option for individuals with limited access to equipment or professional oversight. This is the first study to examine a burpee-based REHIT protocol over an extended intervention period in free-living conditions.

# Reduced Exertion High-Intensity Interval Training is More Effective at Improving Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Cardiometabolic Health than Traditional Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training

### Tom F Cuddy

### Joyce S Ramos

### Lance C Dalleck

Correspondence: ldalleck@western.edu; Tel.: +1-970-943-3095

Received 2019 Jan 15; Accepted 2019 Feb 3; Issue date 2019 Feb.

Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland. This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license (<http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>).

## Abstract

This study sought to determine the effectiveness of an 8 wk reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) at improving cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and positively modifying cardiometabolic health in the workplace environment. Participants (n = 32) were randomized to two groups: (1) One group (n = 16) was prescribed an 8 wk REHIT program, and (2) one group (n = 16) was prescribed moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). Cardiometabolic risk factors and CRF were measured at baseline and 8 wks. After 8 wks, changes in CRF (REHIT, 12%; MICT, 7%), systolic blood pressure (REHIT, −5%; MICT, −2%), waist circumference (REHIT, −1.4%; MICT, −0.3%), and metabolic syndrome (MetS) severity (MetS z-score: REHIT, −62%; MICT, 27%) were more favorable (*p* < 0.05) in the REHIT group relative to the MICT group. Interestingly, there was a significantly greater proportion of participants in the REHIT group (75%, 9/12) who had a favorable change in the MetS z-score (Δ > −0.60) relative to the MICT group (47%, 7/15). The main finding of the present study is that 8 wks REHIT elicited more potent and time-efficient improvements in CRF and cardiometabolic health when compared to traditional MICT. This study provides critical evidence for implementation of the sprint interval training (SIT) paradigm from the scientific literature into a real-world workplace setting.

**Keywords:** cardiometabolic risk factor, metabolic syndrome, sprint interval training, translational research

## 1. Introduction

Findings from numerous epidemiological studies clearly demonstrate that physical inactivity is associated with a higher prevalence of most cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors, including abnormal lipids, high blood pressure, metabolic syndrome, obesity, and type 2 diabetes [[1](#B1-ijerph-16-00483)]. Additionally, physical inactivity is linked with increased risk of certain forms of cancers, poor psychological health, and an overall diminished quality of life [[2](#B2-ijerph-16-00483)]. Moreover, research findings also exhibit a robust inverse relationship between physical activity levels and risk of mortality from CVD and all-causes. Last, it has been estimated that physical inactivity contributes annually to approximately 250,000 premature deaths [[3](#B3-ijerph-16-00483)]. However, despite its widespread benefits, engagement in physical activities or exercise remains scarce, primarily reported to be due to a ‘lack of time’ [[4](#B4-ijerph-16-00483)].

Over the past decade, the concept of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) has captivated the attention of the scientific community due to its superior ability to improve cardiorespiratory fitness [[5](#B5-ijerph-16-00483)] and cardiometabolic health [[6](#B6-ijerph-16-00483),[7](#B7-ijerph-16-00483),[8](#B8-ijerph-16-00483)] for a lesser weekly time-commitment relative to the current exercise guidelines [[2](#B2-ijerph-16-00483)] of moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). HIIT involves multiple (~4–10 repetitions) brief bouts (20 s–5 min) of high-intensity exercise (80%–100% peak heart rate (HRpeak)), interspersed with either rest or low-intensity workloads throughout an exercise session. Another prominent form of interval training is known as sprint interval training (SIT), which is characterized by repeated (6–10 bouts) 20–30 s all-out supramaximal sprints (>100% VO2max). This strategy enables unfit individuals to accumulate periods of vigorous to high-intensity exercise that would otherwise not be possible if executed continuously. However, one drawback to the protocols employed in the majority of previous HIIT/SIT studies [[9](#B9-ijerph-16-00483)] is that they were not actually time-efficient, with most HIIT/SIT protocols requiring a time commitment (~120 min/week) that is similar to the current recommended exercise guideline of 150 min per week of MICT. Moreover, it has also been suggested that the potential for a negative perceptual response to high-intensity exercise heightens with increasing repetition [[10](#B10-ijerph-16-00483)]. Thus, for HIIT or SIT to be a feasible option to improve public health, it must be time-efficient by specifically reducing the number of bouts (intervals) performed at vigorous to high-intensity exercise.

Recent research has demonstrated that a modified version of SIT known as reduced exertion high intensity training (REHIT), characterized by minimal sprint durations and repetitions (2 × 20 s sprints), elicits substantial cardiometabolic health benefits (i.e., CRF and glycemic control improvements) in a more time-efficient fashion relative to traditional HIIT [[11](#B11-ijerph-16-00483),[12](#B12-ijerph-16-00483)]. However, despite the reduced exercise volume evident in this REHIT protocol, its safety still remains questionable given its ‘all-out’ nature. It has therefore recently been suggested that additional future research is warranted to identify safe and effective REHIT protocols [[9](#B9-ijerph-16-00483)]. It also remains unknown how effectively the REHIT paradigm can be translated to a real-world workplace setting. Accordingly, we sought (1) to quantify the acute cardiovascular and metabolic responses to REHIT, and (2) to determine the effectiveness of 8 wk chronic REHIT at improving CRF and positively modifying cardiometabolic health in the workplace environment. It was hypothesized that: (1) An acute bout of REHIT would be a safe and effective form of SIT, and (2) chronic REHIT would lead to time-efficient improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness and cardiometabolic health.

## 2. Materials and Methods

A cohort (n = 32) of men (n = 16) and women (n = 16) were recruited from the faculty/employee population of a local university and hospital via advertisement through the university website, local community newspaper, and through word-of-mouth. Participants were eligible for inclusion into the study if they were low risk-to-moderate risk and physically inactive as defined by the American College of Sports Medicine [[13](#B13-ijerph-16-00483)]. Exclusionary criteria included evidence of cardiovascular pulmonary and/or metabolic disease. This study was approved by the Human Research Committee at Western State Colorado University. Prior to participation, each participant signed an informed consent form.

### 2.1. Chronic Responses (8 wk) to the REHIT vs. MICT

After recruitment, participants were randomized by age and sex to one of two exercise-training groups and subsequently completed baseline testing ([Figure 1](#ijerph-16-00483-f001)). Participants performed 8 wks of supervised exercise training according to one of two programs:

One group (n = 16) was prescribed an 8 wk REHIT program consisting of intense ride options performed on CAR.O.L ™. All REHIT were performed in two local workplace environments (university and hospital). One CAR.O.L ™ cycle ergometer unit was placed in each location in order for participants to perform REHIT in the workplace environment.

One group (n = 16) was prescribed 8 wk standardized MICT (5 days/wk of 30 min aerobic exercise at 50%–65% heart rate reserve—HRR).

#### Figure 1.

[![Figure 1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/40f6/6388288/fedcc16b9eb2/ijerph-16-00483-g001.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=6388288_ijerph-16-00483-g001.jpg)

![Figure 1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/40f6/6388288/fedcc16b9eb2/ijerph-16-00483-g001.jpg)

Experimental flow diagram and week-to-week exercise prescription for the days/times of training.

At baseline and post-program, participants performed a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer to determine the maximal heart rate and maximal CRF. Resting blood pressure, body composition, fasting blood lipids and blood glucose, waist circumference, and weight were assessed in order at baseline and post-program, at 48–72 h following the last training session. Collectively, these measures were obtained to compare the effectiveness of an 8 wk REHIT vs. MICT exercise training for improving cardiometabolic health. The experimental flow diagram and week-to-week exercise prescription for the days/times of training are presented in [Figure 1](#ijerph-16-00483-f001).

### 2.2. Acute Responses to REHIT

To quantify the acute cardiovascular and metabolic responses to REHIT, an Oxycon Mobile portable calorimetric measurement system and Polar F1 heart rate monitor were worn by each participant throughout two REHIT sessions performed on CAR.O.L™, a cycle ergometer unit developed by Integrated Health Partners (London, UK). The CAR.O.L ™ REHIT protocol utilises self-learning algorithms called Cardiovascular Optimisation Logic to adapt the resistance level according to participant’s weight, power output and fatigue index in every session as they get progressively fitter and stronger. Details for the REHIT ride options are as follows:

Intense ride: A 10 min REHIT ride comprised of a 3 min warmup, 20 s sprint, 3 min recovery (slow pedal), 20 s sprint, and 3 min cooldown.

The acute responses to the two REHIT were measured (and averaged) during week 4–5 of the intervention, with these testing sessions also serving as two of the actual training sessions.

### 2.3. Anthropometric Measurements

Participants were weighed to the nearest 0.1 kg on a medical grade scale and measured for height to the nearest 0.5 cm using a stadiometer. Percentage of body fat was determined via skinfolds [[13](#B13-ijerph-16-00483)]. Skinfold thickness was measured to the nearest ± 0.5 mm using a Lange caliper. All measurements were taken on the right side of the body using standardized anatomical sites (three-site) for men and women. These measurements were performed until two were within 10% of each other. Waist circumference measurements were obtained using a cloth tape measure with a spring loaded-handle. A horizontal measurement was taken at the narrowest point of the torso (below the xiphoid process and above the umbilicus). These measurements were taken until two were within 0.5 mm of each other.

### 2.4. Fasting Blood Lipid and Blood Glucose Measurement

A fasting blood sample was collected and analyzed for measurement of lipids and glucose. Participants’ skin was punctured using lancets and a fingerstick sample was collected into a heparin-coated 40 μL capillary tube. Blood was allowed to flow freely from the fingerstick into the capillary tube without milking of the finger. Samples were analysed via a Cholestech LDX System according to strict standardized operating procedures. The LDX Cholestech measured the total cholesterol, high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, triglycerides, and blood glucose in the fingerstick blood. A daily optics check was performed on the LDX Cholestech analyzer used for the study.

### 2.5. Resting Blood Pressure Measurement

The procedure for the assessment of resting blood pressure, outlined elsewhere, was followed [[13](#B13-ijerph-16-00483)]. Briefly, participants were seated quietly for 5 min in a chair with a back support with the feet on the floor and the arm supported at the heart level. The left arm brachial artery systolic and diastolic blood pressure were measured using a sphygmomanometer in duplicate and separated by 60 s. The means of the two measurements were reported for the baseline and post-program values.

### 2.6. Metabolic Syndrome z-Score

A continuous risk score assessment scale (MetS z-score) has been used previously to identify changes in metabolic syndrome (MetS) risk factors following MICT and HIIT interventions [[14](#B14-ijerph-16-00483)]. The MetS severity was presented as a sex-specific MetS z-score calculated using the following equations [[15](#B15-ijerph-16-00483)]:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| MetS z-scoremen = [(40 − HDL-C)/8 × 9] + [(TG − 150/69)] + [(FG − 100)/17 × 8] + [(WC − 102)/11 × 5] + [(MAP− 100)/10 × 1]; | (1) |

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| MetS z-scorewomen = [(50 − HDL-C)/14 × 5] + [(TG − 150/69)] + [(FG − 100)/17 × 8] + [(WC − 88)/12 × 5] + [(MAP − 100)/10 × 1], | (2) |

where FG = fasting glucose; HDL-C = high-density lipoprotein cholesterol; MAP = mean arterial pressure; TG = triglycerides; and WC = waist circumference.

### 2.7. Maximal Exercise Test

Participants were prepared for maximal exercise on the cycle ergometer (Viasprint 150P; Sensormedics Corp., Palm Springs, CA, USA) during which gas exchange data (Oxycon Mobile system) and HR (Polar Electro, Woodbury, NY, USA) were assessed. Participants completed 2 min of pedaling at 50 W as a warm-up. During exercise, power output was increased in a step like manner equal to 5 W/30 s for women and 5 W/20 s for men to elicit volitional fatigue in approximately 7–11 min. Pedal cadence was maintained at 70–90 rev/min, with volitional fatigue representing a failure to sustain a pedal cadence greater than 40 rev/min. The criteria for the attainment of maximal CRF were two out of three of the following: (1) A plateau (ΔVO2
< 150 mL/min) in VO2 with increases in workload, (2) maximal respiratory exchange ratio (RER) > 1.1, and (3) maximal HR within 15 beats/min of the age-predicted maximum (220—age).

### 2.8. Testing Sessions to Quantify Acute Cardiovascular and Metabolic Responses to REHIT

Prior to the start of the testing sessions, both the heart rate monitor and portable metabolic analyzer were attached to the participant. Participants were also familiarized with the breathing apparatus and provided an explanation of the testing instructions and precautions. Participants subsequently performed two REHIT testing sessions (i.e., the intense ride) on separate days. At the first testing session, after being connected to the Oxycon Mobile system and Polar F1 heart rate monitor, participants rested quietly for 5 min in a seated position. The last minute of breath-by-breath and heart rate (HR) data were averaged and considered to be the resting metabolic rate (VO2) and resting HR.

### 2.9. Exercise Intensity and Metabolic Calculations for Acute Responses

The individual heart rate reserve (HRR) was determined as the difference between the resting and HRmax values. Percent HRR was calculated by subtracting resting HR from the REHIT HR responses, dividing by HRR, and then multiplying the quotient by 100. Likewise, individual oxygen uptake reserve (VO2R) was quantified by taking the difference between individual resting VO2 and maximum VO2 values. Percent VO2R was calculated by subtracting resting VO2 from the REHIT VO2 responses, dividing by VO2R, and then multiplying the quotient by 100. The metabolic equivalent (MET) for REHIT was determined by dividing the REHIT VO2 by the individual resting VO2 value (i.e., 3.5 mL/kg/min). Energy expenditure (kcal/min) for the REHIT sessions were calculated by multiplying the above-calculated MET equivalent of the REHIT sessions by the individual body mass, dividing by 1000, and multiplying by the caloric equivalent for the respiratory exchange ratio or RER. An RER of 1.0 was assumed and equates to an energy cost of ~5.0 kcal/L oxygen. Means for each exercise intensity and metabolic calculation were determined using data from the two intense ride REHIT sessions.

### 2.10. Statistical Analyses

All analyses were performed using SPSS Version 25.0 (Chicago, IL, USA) and GraphPad Prism 7.0. (San Diego, CA, USA). Measures of centrality and spread are presented as mean ± SD. Primary outcome measures for the acute cardiovascular and metabolic responses to the REHIT portion of the study were the relative exercise intensity (% HRR and % VO2R), metabolic equivalents (METs), blood pressure, and energy expenditure (kcal/min). Primary outcome measures for the chronic cardiovascular and metabolic responses to REHIT and MICT were the change in cardiometabolic risk factors, including CRF, weight, waist circumference, body composition, blood lipids, blood pressure, and blood glucose, and the MetS z-score. A two-way repeated measures analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was used to examine the change in cardiometabolic factors between training groups, with the baseline value of each factor entered as the covariate and the post-intervention value as the dependent variable. To determine individual MetS z-score training responsiveness, delta values (Δ) were calculated (post-program minus baseline value) to establish the change (Δ) in the MetS z-score. The Δs in MetS z-score were compared to our calculated laboratory-specific coefficient of variability (CV) value of 0.60 [[16](#B16-ijerph-16-00483)]. Thus, for a participant to be considered a responder to overall MetS severity improvement, his/her MetS z-score change should be favorably greater than the established MetS z-score CV. Subsequently, participants were categorized as ‘1’ = responder if their Δ was greater than the laboratory-specific biological variability criterion or ‘0’ = non-responder if the Δ failed to exceed the laboratory-specific criterion. Chi-square (χ2) tests were used to analyze the incidence of responders and non-responders for the MetS z-score following the intervention separated by the treatment group (MICT and REHIT). The probability of making a Type I error was set at *p* < 0.05 for all statistical analyses.

## 3. Results

All analyzes and data presented in the results are for those participants who completed the investigation. At baseline, treatment (REHIT and MICT) groups did not differ significantly in physical or physiological characteristics. The physical and physiological characteristics for participants in both groups at baseline and 8 wks are shown in [Table 1](#ijerph-16-00483-t001). The exercise prescriptions in both treatment groups were well-tolerated for 27 of the 32 participants who completed the study. Five participants were unable to complete the study for the following reasons: Illness (n = 4) and personal reasons (n = 1). Dropout was greater in the REHIT group (n = 4) relative to the MICT group (n = 1); however, these differences can be explained by more illness in the REHIT group (n = 3) vs the MICT group (n = 1). Overall, there was excellent adherence to the total number of prescribed training sessions: REHIT group—mean, 89.2% (range, 75%–100%) and MICT group—mean, 87.8% (range, 77.1%–100%).

### Table 1.

Changes in CRF (REHIT, 12%; MICT, 7%; F[1,24] = 9.9, *p* < 0.01), systolic blood pressure (REHIT, −5%; MICT, −2%; F[1,24] = 8.1, *p* < 0.01), waist circumference (REHIT, −1.4%; MICT, −0.3%; F[1,24] = 7.132, *p* = 0.01), and MetS severity (MetS z-score: REHIT, −62%; MICT, 27%; F[1,24] = 5.9, *p* = 0.02) were more favorable in the REHIT group when compared to the MICT group ([Table 1](#ijerph-16-00483-t001)) following the 8-wk program. There were significant within-group improvements (*p* < 0.05) in CRF, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and the MetS z-score in both groups (MICT and REHIT). However, only the REHIT group showed significant reductions (*p* < 0.05) in systolic blood pressure and waist circumference.

### 3.1. Acute Cardiovascular and Metabolic Responses to REHIT

Acute cardiovascular and metabolic responses (range and mean ± SD) to the overall REHIT workout and the intense ride 2 × 20 s sprint sessions are presented in [Table 2](#ijerph-16-00483-t002). Peak heart rate for the REHIT workouts were 168 beats/min, which corresponded to a 94% HRR. Peak metabolic equivalent (METs) was 8.8, which equated to a 92.9% oxygen uptake reserve (VO2Reserve). The peak systolic and diastolic blood pressure during the REHIT sessions equated to 218 and 98 mmHg, respectively.

### 3.2. Incidence of MetS z-Score Responders and Non-Responders

The incidence of MetS z-score responders and non-responders to exercise training in both the MICT and REHIT groups are shown in [Figure 2](#ijerph-16-00483-f002). In the MICT group, 47% (7/15) of individuals experienced a favorable change in the MetS z-score (Δ > −0.60) and were categorized as responders. In the REHIT group, the incidence of individuals who experienced a favorable change in the MetS z-score were significantly (*p* < 0.05) greater when compared to the MICT group. Indeed, there was a positive improvement in the MetS z-score (Δ > −0.60) in 75% (9/12) of the individuals in the REHIT group.

## 4. Discussion

The main finding of the present study was that 8 wks of REHIT elicited more potent and time-efficient improvements in CRF and cardiometabolic health when compared to traditional MICT. Indeed, there was nearly a two-fold greater improvement in CRF in the REHIT group (12.3%) relative to the MICT group (6.9%). Additionally, reductions in systolic blood pressure in the REHIT group were three-fold greater when compared to the MICT group ([Table 1](#ijerph-16-00483-t001)) and underpinned a ~4% reduction in mean arterial pressure (MAP). Another novel finding from the present study was that REHIT elicited a nearly 1.5-fold greater incidence of cardiometabolic responders (75%) as quantified by the MetS z-score when compared to the MICT group (47%). Given that a ‘lack of time’ is the most often cited reason for not exercising regularly, this study provides preliminary evidence that extends the application of the SIT paradigm from the scientific literature into a real-world workplace setting through the CAR.O.L ™ units which are developed for self-guided and public implementation of the REHIT protocol.

Consistent with previous REHIT studies with a similar program duration (6–10 weeks) including sedentary individuals [[11](#B11-ijerph-16-00483),[17](#B17-ijerph-16-00483)], our REHIT protocol also induced a ~12% increase in CRF. This is a clinically significant finding given that a 10% increase in CRF significantly reduces the risk of mortality and morbidity by 15% [[18](#B18-ijerph-16-00483)]. Moreover, congruent with a previous finding [[19](#B19-ijerph-16-00483)], we also showed that this CRF improvement following REHIT is superior to that elicited by a five-fold larger volume MICT. In contrast, Gillen et al. [[20](#B20-ijerph-16-00483)] reported a similar CRF increase following both REHIT and MICT in sedentary individuals. The discrepancies between these results may be due to the difference in the exercise program duration. Both the present study and Ruffino et al. [[19](#B19-ijerph-16-00483)] had the same 8-week program duration, whereas participants in Gillen et al.’s study [[20](#B20-ijerph-16-00483)] only performed 6 weeks of REHIT, suggesting that a minimum of 8 weeks of REHIT is required to surpass the beneficial effect of the traditional MICT on CRF.

The specific mechanism by which REHIT can improve CRF more than MICT remains elusive. There is, however, evidence to suggest that the capacity of interval training to improve CRF more than MICT may be due to its ability to induce both central (i.e., increase in stroke volume) and peripheral adaptations (i.e., mitochondrial content/enzyme activity, and capillary density) [[21](#B21-ijerph-16-00483)]. Interestingly, Gillen et al. [[20](#B20-ijerph-16-00483)] showed no significant difference in mitochondrial content change following 6 weeks of REHIT and MICT, whereas Matsuo et al. [[22](#B22-ijerph-16-00483)] revealed significant changes in stroke volume, left ventricular mass, and resting heart rate following 8 weeks of interval training (SIT/HIIT), but not MICT. Collectively, these studies support our aforementioned hypothesis that at least 8 weeks of REHIT may be required to exceed the favorable CRF change following MICT.

The superior CRF improvement following REHIT relative to MICT in the present study was also accompanied by a similar pattern in cardiometabolic risk change, depicted as a reduction in MAP and overall MetS severity. Our MAP result is comparable with previous findings also showing a 4%–7% MAP reduction following REHIT [[17](#B17-ijerph-16-00483),[19](#B19-ijerph-16-00483)]. This is a clinically significant finding as MAP is a major independent predictor of stroke [[23](#B23-ijerph-16-00483)]. This significant decrease in MAP could partly explain the superior reduction in overall MetS severity following REHIT compared to MICT, given that MAP contributes towards the calculation of MetS severity via the MetS z-score. Moreover, the superior ability of REHIT to improve MetS severity relative to MICT is not at all surprising given that CRF has repeatedly been reported to have an inverse relationship with MetS [[24](#B24-ijerph-16-00483)]. Earnest et al. [[24](#B24-ijerph-16-00483)] reported a significantly lower MetS z-score (MetS severity) in ‘high fit’ individuals compared to less fit individuals (‘low fit’ and ‘moderate fit’). This inverse relationship may be due to the significant positive association of CRF with insulin sensitivity [[25](#B25-ijerph-16-00483)] and vascular function [[26](#B26-ijerph-16-00483)], which are both mechanisms contributing to the severity of MetS [[27](#B27-ijerph-16-00483),[28](#B28-ijerph-16-00483)]. Interval training has been reported to be more effective in improving insulin sensitivity [[7](#B7-ijerph-16-00483)] and vascular function [[6](#B6-ijerph-16-00483)] when compared to MICT. Interestingly, a previous study that utilized a similar REHIT protocol as the present study demonstrated improvements of insulin sensitivity in sedentary individuals to a similar extent as MICT [[20](#B20-ijerph-16-00483)]. This suggests that the superior improvement in MetS severity that was evident following REHIT relative to MICT could primarily be attributed to improved vascular function as reflected by a reduction in MAP. Further studies are warranted to test this hypothesis.

Although interval training has consistently been shown to confer health and fitness benefits [[6](#B6-ijerph-16-00483),[7](#B7-ijerph-16-00483)], it is often criticized to impose unpleasant sensations in previously sedentary middle-aged men and women, ultimately affecting exercise adherence and compliance [[29](#B29-ijerph-16-00483)]. However, it has also been argued that this initial appraisal is based on the traditional definition of interval training, comprising of longer exposure to vigorous or high-intensity bouts of exercise compared to more practical and scalable protocols, such as REHIT, that have been continued to be developed as reflected in the present study. Indeed, previous interval protocols shown to be effective in improving cardiometabolic health usually require at least 1–4 min exercise bouts at vigorous to high-intensity that are repeated at least 4–10 times within a session, and essentially demand a comparable weekly time commitment as the current guideline (MICT) of 150 min per week [[13](#B13-ijerph-16-00483)]. In contrast, the REHIT protocol utilized in the present study only demanded one fifth of the time commitment required by MICT, yet demonstrated superior health benefits. Indeed, our study extends the findings of others reporting good adherence to REHIT sessions [[12](#B12-ijerph-16-00483)], suggesting that REHIT may be a more practical model than previous interval training protocols and the current guideline in the prevention of cardiometabolic diseases in time-poor middle-aged sedentary individuals.

Safety is also a paramount issue when designing and implementing a HIIT program. Overall, it has been demonstrated that exercise is safe for most individuals, and exercise alone does not incite adverse cardiovascular or other untoward events [[13](#B13-ijerph-16-00483)]. Nevertheless, it has been shown that the risk of an acute myocardial infarction or sudden death during exercise is higher in adults compared to their younger counterpart; and that the greatest risk exists for those individuals with underlying or diagnosed CVD. Overall, the absolute risk of sudden death during vigorous-intensity, physical activity has been estimated to be one per year for every 15,000–18,000 people [[13](#B13-ijerph-16-00483)]. In a systematic review focused on the safety of HIIT for patients with CVD, it was found that there were no adverse cardiac or other life threatening events secondary to the prescription of HIIT [[30](#B30-ijerph-16-00483)]. Our REHIT results were consistent with these findings. Nevertheless, a key to minimizing complications during and after exercise is to identify those participants who may be at an increased risk of adverse symptoms through appropriate pre-participation screening. Participants with a clinically relevant CVD risk factor or diagnosed CVD may benefit from a medical examination and physician supervised maximal exercise test prior to participation in vigorous-intensity exercise [[13](#B13-ijerph-16-00483)]. Despite the absence of untoward events in the present study, given the near-maximal cardiovascular strain and hypertensive blood pressure responses to REHIT, these authors recommend careful pre-participation screening prior to the commencement of REHIT for previously inactive and/or risk factor burden individuals.

### Limitations

There are a few limitations to the present study that warrant further discussion. First, while participants were instructed to maintain their regular dietary intake during the 8 wk intervention, diet intake was not strictly controlled for in this study. Moreover, physical activity/sedentary behaviour outside of the training program and prescribed medications were not monitored, and thus may have influenced the current findings. Dropout was greater in the REHIT group (n = 4) when compared to the MICT group (n = 1); however, these differences appear to be explained by more illness in the REHIT group. Nevertheless, future research is needed to better ascertain whether REHIT is less-tolerable relative to MICT.

## 5. Conclusions

There is a wealth of existing research reporting that regular exercise training confers positive effects on CRF and numerous other cardiometabolic outcomes related to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Accordingly, substantial public health efforts have been aimed at promoting and increasing levels of physical activity. The main finding of the present study is that 8 wks of REHIT was safe and elicited more potent, time-efficient improvements in CRF and cardiometabolic health when compared to traditional MICT. Given that a ‘lack of time’ is the most often cited reason for not exercising regularly, this study provides critical evidence for ‘how’ to implement and translate the SIT paradigm into a real-world workplace setting. Future research is required in more diverse workplace settings beyond those examined in the present study. Additionally, the long-term adherence and effectiveness of REHIT requires scientific inquiry in order to determine its potential as a viable public health strategy. Overall, this knowledge may benefit researchers, along with exercise physiologists, health and fitness professionals, and others who design exercise programs and promote physical activity.

This is a peer-reviewed scientific study published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (February 2019) by Tom F. Cuddy, Joyce S. Ramos, and Lance C. Dalleck (corresponding author, Western State Colorado University). The study investigated whether 8 weeks of reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) is more effective than traditional moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) at improving cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and cardiometabolic health in a real-world workplace setting.

**Study Design:** 32 physically inactive, low-to-moderate risk participants (16 men, 16 women) from a university and hospital workforce were randomized into two groups: REHIT (n=16, using CAR.O.L™ cycle ergometers placed in workplace settings, performing 2×20-second all-out sprints within a 10-minute protocol) and MICT (n=16, 5 days/week of 30-min aerobic exercise at 50%-65% heart rate reserve). 27 of 32 participants completed the study (5 dropouts: 4 illness, 1 personal). Adherence was excellent (REHIT: 89.2%; MICT: 87.8%). The REHIT protocol required only one-fifth the time commitment of MICT.

**Key Results (8 weeks):**
- CRF improvements: REHIT +12% vs MICT +7% (significantly more favorable in REHIT, ~2-fold greater)
- Systolic blood pressure: REHIT −5% vs MICT −2% (3-fold greater reduction, underpinning ~4% reduction in mean arterial pressure)
- Waist circumference: REHIT −1.4% vs MICT −0.3%
- Metabolic syndrome (MetS) severity (z-score): REHIT −62% vs MICT +27%
- 75% (9/12) of REHIT participants were MetS responders (Δ > −0.60) vs 47% (7/15) in MICT group
- Both groups showed significant within-group improvements in CRF, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and MetS z-score; only REHIT significantly reduced systolic blood pressure and waist circumference

**Acute responses to REHIT:** Peak heart rate 168 beats/min (94% HRR), peak METs 8.8 (92.9% VO2 reserve), peak systolic blood pressure 218 mmHg and diastolic 98 mmHg during sessions. The REHIT protocol used the CAR.O.L™ device with Cardiovascular Optimisation Logic algorithms, consisting of a 10-min ride (3 min warmup, 20-s sprint, 3 min recovery, 20-s sprint, 3 min cooldown).

**Discussion highlights:** The ~12% CRF increase is clinically significant as a 10% CRF increase reduces mortality/morbidity risk by 15%. The study suggests a minimum of 8 weeks of REHIT is required to surpass MICT benefits on CRF (contrasting with a 6-week study by Gillen et al. showing no difference). Mechanisms proposed include central (stroke volume) and peripheral (mitochondrial content, capillary density) adaptations. The superior MetS improvement is attributed primarily to improved vascular function (reduced MAP). The authors emphasize REHIT addresses the "lack of time" barrier to exercise. Despite no adverse events, authors recommend careful pre-participation screening given the near-maximal cardiovascular strain and hypertensive blood pressure responses, especially for previously inactive individuals.

**Limitations:** Diet not strictly controlled, physical activity/medications outside program not monitored, higher dropout in REHIT group (though explained by illness). Funded by the American Council on Exercise; authors declare no conflicts of interest.

## Details and patient eligibility

About

This study will use a randomized, double-blind clinical trial to evaluate the effects of eight-week HIIT and MICT exercise programs on cardiorespiratory fitness, the testosterone/cortisol ratio, and mental health in 68 healthy, moderately active young adults aged 18 to 21. Participants will be assigned to parallel groups based on their sex and training type (HIIT men, HIIT women, MICT men, MICT women). The key metrics will be measured both before and after the intervention period to assess the impact of the different training regimens.

Full description

This randomized, double-blind clinical trial will investigate the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on cardiorespiratory fitness and symptoms of anxiety and depression in high school students.

The study will recruit 68 male and female students, aged 15-19, who are moderately inactive. Participants will be randomized into HIIT or MICT groups, stratified by gender. The 8-week intervention consists of three weekly sessions: HIIT involves 10x1-minute high-intensity intervals, while MICT consists of 30 minutes of continuous running. Cardiorespiratory fitness (measured via the Course Navette test to estimate VO₂max) and mental health symptoms (using Beck inventories) will be assessed before and after the intervention.

The primary hypothesis is that HIIT will yield greater improvements in VO₂max and greater reductions in anxiety and depression symptoms compared to MICT. Statistical analysis will employ ANOVA and related tests to evaluate changes within and between groups, with a significance level set at p<0.05. The study aims to provide evidence for designing personalized exercise programs that optimize both physical and mental health in adolescents.

args.summary:
This webpage describes a clinical trial (NCT07397702) sponsored by the Universidad de Colima, examining the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on cardiorespiratory fitness, testosterone/cortisol ratio, and mental health in young adults.

STUDY DESIGN: This is a randomized, double-blind interventional clinical trial with a parallel assignment design and basic science primary purpose. The study is "not yet enrolling" with an estimated enrollment of 76 participants (68 in one section, 76 overall). Participants are healthy, moderately active/sedentary young adults aged 18 to 21.

TREATMENT GROUPS:
- Group A (HIIT, experimental): 5-minute warm-up at 75% HRmax, then 10x1-minute high-intensity intervals at 85-90% HRmax with 1-minute recovery periods at 50-60% HRmax. Three sessions per week (75 minutes weekly), ending with cool-down walk and stretching.
- Group B (MICT, active comparator): 30 minutes of continuous running at 60-70% HRmax, three sessions per week (60 minutes weekly), ending with cool-down walk and stretching.

OUTCOMES AND METHODOLOGY: Cardiorespiratory fitness (measured via Course Navette test to estimate VO₂max) and mental health symptoms (using Beck inventories for anxiety and depression) are assessed before and after the 8-week intervention. The primary hypothesis is that HIIT will produce greater improvements in VO₂max and greater reductions in anxiety and depression symptoms compared to MICT. Statistical analysis will use ANOVA with significance set at p<0.05.

INCLUSION CRITERIA: Men and women aged 18-21, sedentary or moderately active (IPAQ ≤600 METs-min/week), physician-approved for exercise, and signed informed consent.

KEY EXCLUSION CRITERIA: Motor disabilities, pregnancy, metabolic disorders, chronic respiratory diseases, high blood pressure or arrhythmia, high-performance training participation, irregular menstrual cycles with contraceptive medication, caffeine/alcohol/tobacco use, diagnosed anxiety/depression, heavy alcohol consumption, and dietary supplement use (caffeine, nitric oxide precursors, beta-alanine, creatine, sodium bicarbonate, L-carnitine).

ELIMINATION CRITERIA: Voluntary withdrawal, less than 80% session attendance, incomplete measurements, joint/muscle injuries, and overtraining syndrome.

CONTACT: Luis Jaime Orozco Milanez, M. Sc. serves as the central trial contact.

Note: There is an inconsistency in the webpage — the header states participants are aged 18-21 while the full description mentions high school students aged 15-19. The study aims to provide evidence for designing personalized exercise programs that optimize both physical and mental health in adolescents.
