**I. TIME-EFFICIENCY EVIDENCE (Relevance to <150 and <60 min/week)**

- The 2026 T2DM meta-analysis (Zeng et al.) reported that ~78 min/week of HIIT can achieve glycemic control comparable to ~210 min/week of MICT.
- The 2019 PLOS ONE meta-analysis (Su et al.) reported HIIT sessions averaged 30.0±10.2 min versus 39.7±15.5 min for MICT — a 9.7 min per-session time saving.
- The 2023 IJERPH meta-analysis (Guo et al.) reported HIIT sessions of 9–54 min vs 15–60 min for MICT.
- The 2016 Gillen RCT showed 30 min/week of SIT produced comparable benefits to 150 min/week of MICT.
- The SIT study in *The Journal of Physiology* showed ~1 hour/week of SIT was comparable to ~5 hours/week of MICT in obese men.
- The REHIT protocol (Astorino et al., *Trials* 2026) uses only 20 min/week total (two 10-minute sessions).
- The 2022 JCEM liver fat meta-analysis (Sabag et al.) concluded HIIT elicits comparable liver fat improvements to MICT "despite often requiring less energy and time commitment."
- The 2018 Aging Clin Exp Res meta-analysis (Liu et al.) noted HIIT addresses the time barrier preventing many T2D patients from achieving recommended physical activity levels.
- The 2021 IJERPH review (Atakan et al.) notes lack of time is the most common barrier to exercise adherence, with ~1.4 billion people not meeting public health guidelines; WHO 2020 guidelines recommend 150–300 min of moderate-intensity or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise weekly.

---

**J. QUALITY, CERTAINTY, AND LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE BASE**

- The 2026 Cochrane review (Strauss et al.) rated confidence in results as low to moderate due to variation in participant responses, small study sizes with too few studies for some outcomes, and lack of blinding. All included studies examined supervised HIIT; future research should investigate unsupervised HIIT feasibility and safety. Searches covered CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and two trial registries up to 13 October 2025. No studies reported long-term outcomes such as heart attacks, strokes, or deaths.
- The 2018 T2DM meta-analysis (Liu et al.) GRADE assessment rated most outcomes "Low" or "Very low" quality; only VO2peak was "Moderate."
- The 2025 cancer survivors meta-analysis reported 4 of 12 studies with some concerns and 8 at high risk of bias; performance bias was unavoidable.
- The 2026 prediabetes meta-analysis noted most studies had "some concerns" in risk of bias; certainty for glycemic outcomes was generally low to very low; 9 of 13 studies lasted ≤2 weeks.
- The 2026 real-world HIIT meta-analysis reported substantial heterogeneity (I² up to 95%) and moderate methodological quality; mean PEDro 6.2; mean dropout 14.9%.
- The 2026 Sports Medicine network meta-analysis noted no network comparison was rated as high confidence; many studies had some concerns or high risk of bias.
- The 2022 JCEM liver fat meta-analysis downgraded HIIT vs CON liver fat evidence to LOW certainty; MICT vs CON to MODERATE; HIIT vs MICT to MODERATE.
- The 2025 LV-HIIT meta-analysis rated only 30% of studies (6 of 20) as high quality.
- The 2026 Frontiers in Physiology meta-analysis (Li et al.) noted 77.3% of studies had low risk in random sequence generation, only 40.9% low risk in allocation concealment, and 36.4% high risk in performance blinding; ~30% of studies showed high risk in at least one domain, but sensitivity analyses confirmed robust results.
- The 2026 F1000Research T2DM insulin sensitivity meta-analysis reported overall low risk of bias with good-to-excellent methodological quality across the 4 included RCTs.

**K. DIRECTIONS FOR FURTHER RESEARCH AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS**

- The 2026 T2DM meta-analysis (Zeng et al.) recommends, for T2DM patients with low HDL: HIIT at 20–30 min/session, 2–3 times/week for 8 weeks; for patients with elevated TC: short-duration HIIT (≤20 min); a cyclical training program to avoid adaptation plateau. Limitations: insufficient follow-up duration, non-standardized dietary control, HIIT protocol heterogeneity, unexplored "exercise resistance," incomplete publication bias assessment for secondary outcomes, no grey literature searched, English-language restriction.
- The 2026 Cochrane review concludes HIIT "may be an effective alternative to MICT" for sedentary populations at risk of cardiometabolic disease; larger, higher-quality RCTs with longer follow-up are needed.
- The 2025 VAT systematic review recommends tailoring HIIT to patient age, fitness, and comorbidities; gradual progression with initial supervision for older/deconditioned individuals; and hybrid supervised/home-based models to improve feasibility and adherence.
- The 2026 IJDDT NAFLD protocol calls for standardized, adequately powered trials with harmonized imaging, fibrosis, adherence, safety, and durability outcomes before HIIT can be ranked definitively against MICT or resistance training for liver fat.
- The 2025 prediabetes RCT (*Frontiers in Endocrinology*) suggests MICT may be the superior exercise option based on glucose and lipid metabolism results in prediabetic patients, in direct contradiction to other studies favoring HIIT — highlighting the outcome-specific and population-specific nature of the evidence.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: HIIT vs. MICT to Improve Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Exercise Capacity in Older Adult ---
URL: https://clinmedjournals.org/articles/ijsem/international-journal-of-sports-and-exercise-medicine-ijsem-9-256.php?jid=ijsem

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the International Journal of Sports and Exercise Medicine (2023, Vol 9:256) by Yang Yang, Cao Youxiang, Chen Jiacheng, Hu Guangxuan, Chang Bo, and Yi Xuejie, examining whether High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) is more effective than Moderate-Intensity Continuous Exercise (MICT) for improving cardiorespiratory fitness and exercise capacity in older adults.

**Methods:** The review searched five electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, and Cochrane Library) up to September 10, 2022, and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022302359). Inclusion criteria required supervised HIIT and MICT interventions, mean subject age ≥55 years, intervention duration ≥2 weeks, and exercise modalities of running, cycling, or elliptical. The search identified 6,709 articles from databases plus 3 additional manual finds; after removing 2,317 duplicates, screening titles and abstracts, and full-text review, 30 studies met inclusion criteria, involving 1,973 subjects. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool, and statistical analyses were performed using REVMAN software.

**Key Results:**
- HIIT significantly improved VO2max compared to MICT (weighted mean difference = 1.80, 95% CI: 1.25-2.35, p < 0.001), and HIIT improved VO2peak over controls (WMD = 2.97, 95% CI: 2.39-3.56, p < 0.001)
- Subgroup analysis showed the greatest effects on VO2 peak with: training period <12 weeks (WMD = 3.59), 3 sessions/week (WMD = 4.46), 20 min per intervention (WMD = 3.57), <80% intensity VO2 peak (WMD = 4.47), >4 repetitions (WMD = 4.51), >60s per training session (WMD = 3.34), and ≤90s rest time (WMD = 4.04)
- Sick patients had a larger effect on VO2 peaks in older adults compared to healthy subjects (WMDs of 3.85 vs 2.47)
- HIIT significantly improved maximal heart rate (WMD = 2.68, HIIT vs MICT), ventilation (VE/VO2), and peak power output (PPO; WMD = 16.54, HIIT vs MICT)
- 16 studies showed reduction in systolic blood pressure (WMD = -2.59) and diastolic blood pressure (WMD = -1.40) after HIIT, though SBP reduction was not statistically superior to MICT; longer interventions (≥12 weeks) showed better SBP reduction
- HIIT significantly improved 6-minute walk test (WMD = 51.60), time up and go test, METs, and peak power output

**Conclusions:** HIIT is more effective than MICT in improving cardiorespiratory fitness and exercise capacity in older adults. The optimal HIIT protocol suggested was approximately 8 × ≤60s HIIT at <80% VO2 peak with ≤90s recovery, 3 times per week for <20 minutes for <12 weeks. No serious adverse events were reported. The study aligns with ACSM recommendations of 20 minutes of vigorous exercise 3 days per week and demonstrates HIIT can achieve results in shorter time than moderate-intensity exercise. The authors note limitations including the lack of subgroup confirmation for blood pressure effects and insufficient studies on muscle area metrics.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"HIIT significantly improved VO2max (HIIT vs. MICT) (weighted mean difference = 1.80, 95% confidence interval: 1.25-2.35, p < 0.001) and maximal heart rate, ventilation maximal power output compared to the MICT protocol."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: The effects of HIIT and MICT on body fat composition and cardiopulmonary fitness in adults: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12911145

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (2026 Jan 24;18:94, doi: 10.1186/s13102-025-01519-2, PMID: 41580784, PMCID: PMC12911145) examining the effects of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) versus Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training (MICT) on body fat composition and cardiorespiratory fitness in adults. The study was conducted by Hongling Cheng (Tianjin Police Institute, China) and colleagues from the University of Birmingham (UK), Guangxi Science and Technology Normal University (China), Shanghai University of Sport, and Beijing Academy.

METHODS: The authors searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (January 1, 2000 to December 31, 2024) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing HIIT cycling's effects on fat reduction and cardiorespiratory fitness. A total of 1,326 articles were identified from databases plus 841 via citation searching; 19 RCTs met inclusion criteria, comprising 527 participants (HIIT: n=267; MICT: n=260). All studies used cycling-based interventions lasting 2–24 weeks, 3–5 sessions/week. Data were pooled using standardized mean differences (SMD) in Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 18, with subgroup analyses stratified by population (disease, obese, sedentary). GRADE assessment was performed.

KEY RESULTS:
- BMI: HIIT significantly reduced BMI overall (SMD = −0.25 kg/m², 95% CI: −0.45 to −0.06, P=0.012). Subgroup: reduced BMI in obese populations (SMD = −0.59, 95% CI: −0.84 to −0.34, P<0.001), increased BMI in disease populations (SMD = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.77, P=0.042), no effect in sedentary populations.
- Body fat percentage: No significant difference between HIIT and MICT overall (SMD = −0.17%, 95% CI: −0.39 to 0.06, P=0.160).
- Fat mass: No significant difference (SMD = −0.18 kg, 95% CI: −0.43 to 0.06, P=0.134).
- Lean body mass: No significant difference (SMD = −0.11 kg, 95% CI: −0.38 to 0.16, P=0.461).
- VO₂peak: HIIT significantly improved VO₂peak overall (SMD = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.08 to 0.44, P=0.007), with significant improvements in obese (SMD = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.45, P=0.041) and sedentary populations (SMD = 6.21, 95% CI: 4.68 to 7.74, P<0.001), but no significant effect in clinical populations.

GRADE assessment rated BMI, lean body mass, and VO₂peak as MODERATE certainty, while body fat and fat mass were rated LOW. Sensitivity analysis (leave-one-out) confirmed findings were robust; no single study exerted dominant influence.

DISCUSSION AND MECHANISMS: HIIT's BMI reduction in obese individuals may result from enhanced fat oxidation via AMPK pathway activation and increased resting metabolic rate. Increased BMI in clinical populations (diabetes, fibromyalgia) may stem from metabolic compensatory mechanisms, chronic hyperglycemia-induced inflammatory stress, compensatory eating, or exercise-induced muscle damage/tissue edema. VO₂peak improvements are attributed to cardiovascular adaptive remodeling, improved cardiac output, erythropoietin release, and mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α/NRF-1 pathway activation. Clinical populations showed no VO₂peak improvement due to disease-imposed cardiopulmonary limitations.

CLINICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: For obese individuals, HIIT on a cycle ergometer (4-min intervals at 90% VO₂peak with 3-min active recovery at 50% VO₂peak, 3–4 times/week for >12 weeks) is recommended. For those with comorbidities, modified low-intensity HIIT three times weekly with an initial 6-week shortened period is advised. For sedentary individuals, a progressive approach starting with lower-intensity HIIT (3 min at 75% VO₂peak/3 min at 50% VO₂peak) five times/week for >12 weeks, potentially extended to 24 weeks.

LIMITATIONS: Gender differences not accounted for; no age or comorbidity stratification; notable protocol variations between HIIT and MICT interventions.

CONCLUSION: HIIT cycling demonstrates comparable efficacy to MICT for improving body composition (body fat percentage, fat mass, lean body mass) in adults, while outperforming MICT in reducing BMI among obese individuals and enhancing cardiorespiratory fitness (VO₂peak) across obese and sedentary populations. Given its time efficiency, HIIT offers a viable exercise option for adults seeking fat reduction and cardiopulmonary endurance improvement.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Compared to MICT, HIIT significantly reduced BMI in obese populations (SMD = -0.59 kg/m2, 95% CI: -0.84 to -0.34, P<0.001), but slightly increased BMI in disease populations (SMD = 0.40 kg/m2, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.77, P = 0.042)."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from The American Journal of Managed Care (AJMC), published September 26, 2021, authored by Hayden E. Klein. The article reports on a review published in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine (September 3, 2021; doi:10.3389/fcvm.2021.734278) by Taylor JL, Bonikowske AR, and Olson TP, titled "Optimizing outcomes in cardiac rehabilitation: the importance of exercise intensity."

KEY FINDINGS:
- High intensity interval training (HIIT) produces greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness than moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) or low-intensity exercise for patients with heart failure and cardiovascular disease.
- Investigators recommend slowly introducing and progressing HIIT on a case-by-case basis to reduce musculoskeletal discomfort while maximizing safety, adherence, enjoyment, and physiological outcomes.
- Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a class 1 clinical practice recommendation for patients with select cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).
- Systematic reviews on coronary heart disease (2004-2011) showed exercise-based CR reduced hospitalizations by 31%, cardiovascular mortality by 26%, and all-cause mortality by 20% compared with standard medical care. However, the RAMIT (Rehabilitation After Myocardial Infarction Trial) results later questioned these benefits.
- Guidelines recommend aerobic exercise prescription based on relative indices of peak exercise capacity, including: percentage of peak workload (Wpeak), percentage of peak heart rate (%HRpeak), percentage of VO2peak, percentage of HR reserve (%HRR), and percentage of VO2 reserve (%VO2R).

STUDY DETAILS:
- Moholdt et al: HIIT improved VO2peak and HR recovery more than MICT at 6 months in post-coronary artery bypass patients; similar QOL and adiponectin improvements in both groups.
- SAINTEX-CAD and FITR Heart studies: Similar improvements between HIIT and MICT at 12 months in CAD patients for VO2peak, CVD risk factors, QOL, body composition, and physical activity; no dietary intake changes. FITR Heart Study showed HIIT numerically higher VO2peak improvement (2.9 mL/kg/min vs 1.8 mL/kg/min for MICT).
- Adherence data: FITR Heart Study reported 53% adherence for HIIT and 41% for MICT; OptimEx-Clin reported 56% for HIIT and 60% for MICT. After excluding nonadherent participants, HIIT showed greater VO2peak improvement (5.2 mL/kg/min vs 2.2 mL/kg/min for MICT).
- SMARTEX HF (HFrEF patients) and OptimEX-Clin (HFpEF patients) both showed regression of supervised training improvements at 12 months regardless of exercise intensity.
- Moholdt et al: After 5 months of home-based training, 35% of participants stopped HIIT in favor of MICT, while only 4% of MICT participants increased intensity; 74% of HIIT and 68% of MICT participants performed 3 sessions/week.

CONCLUSION: While short-duration HIIT protocols can improve peripheral mitochondrial adaptations and provide similar VO2peak improvements to MICT, longer-duration and higher-volume HIIT protocols appear superior for eliciting stroke volume and vascular adaptations, and greater VO2peak improvements. High-intensity exercise also improves VO2 at submaximal exercise, important for daily activities.

The article is categorized under Heart Failure and Payers on the AJMC site.
</summary>

The study was conducted by Katsunori Tsuji, Yosuke Tsuchiya, Hisashi Ueda, and Eisuke Ochi.

BACKGROUND: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is an effective method to improve maximal oxygen uptake (VO2 peak), but there was no definitive conclusion about the specific effectiveness of home-based HIIT. METHODS: The systematic review searched four electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Igaku Chuo Zasshi) for studies through March 25, 2023. Comparisons were made against non-exercise controls, laboratory-based HIIT, and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). The primary outcome was cardiorespiratory fitness; secondary outcomes were patient-reported outcomes. The standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was calculated, and a random-effects model was used. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, the authors systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and EBSCOhost up to February 2025. Twelve eligible RCTs were included: 7 breast cancer, 3 colorectal cancer, and 2 mixed cancer type studies. Studies were conducted in New Zealand (1), Australia (6), Canada (1), Iran (2), US (1), and Germany (1), spanning 2015-2023, with sample sizes of 7-47 participants and ages 39-75 years. Exercise durations ranged from 3-12 weeks, 2-5 days/week (mostly 3 days/week), 10-75 min/session. Meta-analysis used Cochrane's Review Manager 5.4; sensitivity analysis used Stata MP 14.0; Egger's test assessed publication bias. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420250654968.

KEY RESULTS:
- VO2 peak (primary outcome, 7 studies, 92 HIIT vs 78 MICT participants): HIIT significantly superior [SMD = 0.53, 95% CI (0.21, 0.84), Z = 3.30, P = 0.001, I² = 0%]. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness; Egger's test showed no publication bias (P = 0.75).

- Heart rate (2 studies): No significant difference [SMD = -0.55, P = 0.14].
- Resting heart rate (3 studies): No significant difference [SMD = -0.11, P = 0.63].
- Body composition: No significant differences between HIIT and MICT for body mass, total fat mass, lean body mass, fat percentage, BMI, waist circumference, or hip circumference.
- Physical function: No significant differences in Sit-to-Stand test (STS) or 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT).

RISK OF BIAS: 8 studies at high risk of bias, 4 with some concerns. Main issues included lack of blinding (performance bias), unclear randomization/allocation concealment, and unblinded outcome assessors.

DISCUSSION/CONCLUSION: HIIT appears superior to MICT in enhancing VO2 peak and cardiopulmonary function in cancer survivors, particularly breast and colorectal cancer. Both modalities produce comparable outcomes in body composition and physical function. Proposed mechanisms for HIIT's VO2 peak advantage include AMPK-PGC-1α pathway activation (mitochondrial biogenesis) and catecholamine-mediated cardiorespiratory adaptations. Limitations include small number of studies/participants, heterogeneity in intervention protocols, uneven cancer type distribution, lack of long-term follow-up, unavoidable performance bias, and absence of direct survival/recurrence analysis. --- SOURCE 1: Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1440244018309198

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (Volume 22, Issue 8, August 2019, Pages 941-947) titled "Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials." The study was conducted by Daizong Wen, Till Utesch, Jun Wu, Samuel Robertson, John Liu, Guopeng Hu, and Haichun Chen (DOI: 10.1016/j.jsams.2019.01.013).

OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of different HIIT protocols on VO2max improvements in healthy, overweight/obese, and athletic adults, based on classifications of work intervals, session volumes, and training periods.

METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Medline, and Web of Science databases were searched up to April 2018. Inclusion criteria were randomised controlled trials involving healthy, overweight/obese, or athletic adults, examining pre- and post-training VO2max/peak, with HIIT compared to control or moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) groups.

RESULTS: Of 1,190 articles initially identified, 53 studies met eligibility criteria. The degree of change in VO2max induced by HIIT varied by populations (SMD=0.41–1.81, p<0.05). Compared to control groups, even short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term HIIT (≤4 weeks) elicited clear beneficial effects (SMD=0.79–1.65, p<0.05) on VO2max/peak. However, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT displayed significantly larger effects on VO2max (SMD=0.50–2.48, p<0.05). When compared to MICT, only long-interval, high-volume, and moderate to long-term HIIT showed beneficial effects (SMD=0.65–1.07, p<0.05).

CONCLUSIONS: Short-interval (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT are effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2max, especially for the general population. To maximize training effects on VO2max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended. The study was supported by the Key Laboratory of Physical Motor Function Assessment, General Administration of Sport of China. The article has been cited 218 times and is part of the JSAMS Highlights 2018 and 2019 special issue. The authors reported no conflicts of interest.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min) and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT represent effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2 max, especially for the general population. To maximize the training effects on VO2 max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min) and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: VO2max (VO2peak) in elite athletes under high-intensity interval training: A meta-analysis ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in Heliyon (June 1, 2023) examining the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on VO2 max (VO2 peak) in elite athletes. The study, authored by Xianghua Ma, Zhenbo Cao, Zheng Zhu, Xiangru Chen, Donglin Wen, and Ziwei Cao from Shanghai University of Sport and Xi'an Physical Education University, China, was funded by the Science and Technology Department of Shaanxi Province (grant no. 2021JM-529).

METHODOLOGY: A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted across four databases (LISTA, PubMed, Web of Science, and China National Knowledge Internet) from inception to March 2022. Nine studies (8 English, 1 Chinese) met inclusion criteria, comprising 176 elite athletes (80 female) across sports including kayaking, tennis, taekwondo, triathlon, and cycling. Inclusion criteria required published experimental studies with a control group, focus on high-level (national-level competition) athletes, HIIT training period ≥3 weeks, ≥2 sessions per week, and specified training intensity. Study quality was assessed using the PEDro scale (average score 7.2/11; 6 studies low risk, 3 moderate risk). Meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.3 with weighted mean difference and 95% confidence intervals.

KEY RESULTS: Compared to conventional training (continuous training, repeated-sprint training, high-volume low-intensity training, high-intensity continuous running, sprint-interval training, moderate-intensity continuous training), VO2 max was significantly increased after HIIT (overall effect size: 0.58 [0.30, 0.87], P=0.03, I²=0.49). Significant subgroup findings included: males (0.41 [0.06, 0.76], P=0.89, I²=0%), recovery interval ≥2 min (0.44 [0.03, 0.84], P=0.99, I²=0%), recovery phase intensity ≤40% (0.38 [0.05, 0.71], P=0.96, I²=0%), control training intensity ≤75% (0.42 [0.11, 0.73], P=0.008), and taekwondo/tennis/kayaking athletes (0.99 [0.50, 1.48], P<0.0001, though with high heterogeneity I²=80%).

DISCUSSION & MECHANISMS: The study proposes that HIIT improves VO2 max through increased cardiac output (with peak stroke volume occurring during intermittent recovery periods, requiring interval durations not less than 60 seconds), enhanced recruitment of fast oxidative and glycolytic muscle fibers, increased mitochondrial enzyme activity, improved ventilation threshold, enhanced lipid oxidation, and improved cardiovascular function. HIIT intensities that showed improvement included 90-100% of HRmax, VO2 max, MAP, and other maximal parameters. --- SOURCE 3: Effect of Low Volume Sprint Interval Training on Cardiorespiratory Fitness ---
URL: https://ctv.veeva.com/study/effect-of-low-volume-sprint-interval-training-on-cardiorespiratory-fitness

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes a clinical trial (NCT07328568) conducted by California State University, San Marcos, testing the effect of low-volume sprint interval training on cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). The study is funded by a U.S. NIH Grant (R15AG093525) and is currently "Active, not recruiting."

Background: Low physical activity is linked to poor health and premature death, with 75% of adult Americans not meeting PA recommendations in 2020. Physical inactivity is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide and increases risk of 40 chronic conditions. Low maximal oxygen uptake (V̇O2max) is a stronger predictor of morbidity and all-cause mortality than smoking, hypertension, obesity, high cholesterol, and insulin resistance. Time is cited as the primary barrier to exercise, making time-efficient high intensity interval training (HIIT) an attractive alternative.

The study specifically tests "reduced exertion high intensity interval training" (REHIT), a special type of HIIT requiring only two 20-second sprints within a 10-minute session. This randomized controlled trial will recruit 60 inactive adults to complete 18-24 sessions of REHIT (2 days per week) over a 9-week period on a stationary bike, comparing changes in CRF, fuel/substrate metabolism, and psychological responses against a non-exercising control group. This sample size is threefold higher than prior work in this area, providing adequate statistical power to detect meaningful increases in V̇O2max.

Key trial details:
- Status: Active, not recruiting
- Study type: Interventional (Prevention), Randomized, Parallel Assignment, Open label
- Conditions: Healthy participants, Overweight (BMI > 25), Physical inactivity
- Treatment: High intensity interval training (Other)
- Enrollment: 60 estimated patients (2 groups: experimental REHIT group and non-exercising control/placebo comparator group)
- Ages: 18-64 years; Sex: All
- Inclusion criteria: Healthy, BMI < 35 kg/m², under 65 years old, no joint issues
- Exclusion criteria: Currently active or not weight stable, BMI > 35 kg/m², use of medications that may alter study outcomes
- Trial documents available: Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP_000.pdf) and Informed Consent Form (ICF_001.pdf)

The study has significant public health applications, as positive findings could potentially modify public health guidelines to include REHIT as a feasible alternative or adjunct to moderate or vigorous-intensity exercise in current PA recommendations.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: HIIT Improves Cardiorespiratory Fitness More Than Low-Intensity ... ---
URL: https://www.ajmc.com/view/hiit-improves-cardiorespiratory-fitness-more-than-low-intensity-exercise-review-says

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from The American Journal of Managed Care (AJMC), published September 26, 2021, authored by Hayden E. Klein. The article reports on a review published in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine (September 3, 2021; doi:10.3389/fcvm.2021.734278) by Taylor JL, Bonikowske AR, and Olson TP, titled "Optimizing outcomes in cardiac rehabilitation: the importance of exercise intensity."

KEY FINDINGS:
- High intensity interval training (HIIT) produces greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness than moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) or low-intensity exercise for patients with heart failure and cardiovascular disease.
- Investigators recommend slowly introducing and progressing HIIT on a case-by-case basis to reduce musculoskeletal discomfort while maximizing safety, adherence, enjoyment, and physiological outcomes.
- Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a class 1 clinical practice recommendation for patients with select cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).
- Systematic reviews on coronary heart disease (2004-2011) showed exercise-based CR reduced hospitalizations by 31%, cardiovascular mortality by 26%, and all-cause mortality by 20% compared with standard medical care. However, the RAMIT (Rehabilitation After Myocardial Infarction Trial) results later questioned these benefits.
- Guidelines recommend aerobic exercise prescription based on relative indices of peak exercise capacity, including: percentage of peak workload (Wpeak), percentage of peak heart rate (%HRpeak), percentage of VO2peak, percentage of HR reserve (%HRR), and percentage of VO2 reserve (%VO2R).

STUDY DETAILS:
- Moholdt et al: HIIT improved VO2peak and HR recovery more than MICT at 6 months in post-coronary artery bypass patients; similar QOL and adiponectin improvements in both groups.
- SAINTEX-CAD and FITR Heart studies: Similar improvements between HIIT and MICT at 12 months in CAD patients for VO2peak, CVD risk factors, QOL, body composition, and physical activity; no dietary intake changes. FITR Heart Study showed HIIT numerically higher VO2peak improvement (2.9 mL/kg/min vs 1.8 mL/kg/min for MICT).
- Adherence data: FITR Heart Study reported 53% adherence for HIIT and 41% for MICT; OptimEx-Clin reported 56% for HIIT and 60% for MICT. After excluding nonadherent participants, HIIT showed greater VO2peak improvement (5.2 mL/kg/min vs 2.2 mL/kg/min for MICT).
- SMARTEX HF (HFrEF patients) and OptimEX-Clin (HFpEF patients) both showed regression of supervised training improvements at 12 months regardless of exercise intensity.
- Moholdt et al: After 5 months of home-based training, 35% of participants stopped HIIT in favor of MICT, while only 4% of MICT participants increased intensity; 74% of HIIT and 68% of MICT participants performed 3 sessions/week.

CONCLUSION: While short-duration HIIT protocols can improve peripheral mitochondrial adaptations and provide similar VO2peak improvements to MICT, longer-duration and higher-volume HIIT protocols appear superior for eliciting stroke volume and vascular adaptations, and greater VO2peak improvements. High-intensity exercise also improves VO2 at submaximal exercise, important for daily activities.

The article is categorized under Heart Failure and Payers on the AJMC site.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The majority of guidelines on exercise training in CR recommend aerobic exercise prescription based on relative indices of peak exercise capacity," the authors wrote.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Sprint Interval Training Effects on Aerobic Capacity ---
URL: https://coachathletics.com.au/s/2013_Gist_SpringIntervalTrainingMeta_SportsMedicine.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review and meta-analysis titled "Sprint Interval Training Effects on Aerobic Capacity" by Nicholas H. Gist, Michael V. Fedewa, Rod K. Dishman, and Kirk J. Cureton, published in Sports Medicine (October 2013, DOI: 10.1007/s40279-013-0115-0). The study was conducted at the Department of Kinesiology, University of Georgia, with Gist affiliated with the United States Military Academy at West Point.

PURPOSE: To systematically review the literature and conduct a meta-analysis to determine the effects of sprint interval training (SIT) on aerobic capacity (VO2max).

METHODS: 
- Literature search followed PRISMA guidelines; searched PubMed, MEDLINE, and Web of Science using terms including 'sprint interval training', 'high intensity intermittent training/exercise', 'aerobic capacity', and 'maximal oxygen uptake'
- Inclusion criteria: RCTs available in English, participants randomly assigned to SIT or control group, training intensity classified as "all out," "supramaximal," "maximal," or ≥100% VO2max; SIT work:rest ratio of 30-s:4-min (3-5 min rest); laboratory assessment of VO2max/VO2peak
- 303 studies identified; 16 RCTs (318 participants) included, yielding 17 effects
- Mean participants per study: 18.7 ± 5.1; mean participant age: 23.5 ± 4.3 years
- Studies primarily used cycling (9 studies), running (6 studies), or rowing (1 study)
- Training intervention length: 4.8 ± 2.3 weeks with 2.9 ± 0.4 sessions per week
- Studies conducted in Canada, USA, UK, Australia, Iran, Denmark, and Norway
- Cohen's d effect sizes calculated; random effects model used; moderators analyzed included control group type, fitness level, intervention length, additional training, and training mode

KEY RESULTS:
- Overall effect size: small-to-moderate (Cohen's d = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10-0.55; z = 2.79, P < 0.01)
- Aggregate improvement: ~3.6 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (~8% increase) in VO2max
- Moderate-to-large effect vs. no-exercise control groups (Cohen's d = 0.69, 95% CI 0.46-0.93; z = 5.84, P < 0.01)
- No significant difference compared with endurance training control groups (Cohen's d = 0.04, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.24; z = 0.36, P = 0.72)
- Effects were heterogeneous (Q16 = 59.87; P < 0.01; I² = 74.95)
- Fail-safe number: 28 effects; funnel plot indicated no publication bias
- Inter-rater reliability: ICC (2,2) = 0.98
- Only the type of control group accounted for significant variation in the overall effect (b = -0.33; z = -3.57; P < 0.01)
- Effects not significantly different when moderating by fitness level, intervention length, inclusion of additional training, or mode of training
- Individual study effect sizes ranged from -0.39 to 1.22; 12 of 17 effects (>71%) were greater than zero

CONCLUSION: SIT improves aerobic capacity in healthy, young people. Relative to continuous endurance training of moderate intensity, SIT presents an equally effective alternative with a reduced volume of activity. The review supports the prescription of supramaximal SIT as an alternative method to improve cardiorespiratory fitness and health.

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS:
- Blair et al. estimated men who improve fitness may reduce mortality risk by 44% relative to those who remained unfit
- SIT improvements likely result from peripheral adaptations (e.g., skeletal muscle arterial-venous oxygen difference), while endurance training improves central adaptations (stroke volume, maximal cardiac output); a combination of both methods may be ideal
- Time efficiency noted: in one study, SIT group spent only 15 min (135 min including recovery) exercising vs. 630 min for endurance training, yet achieved similar improvements in oxidative capacity and exercise performance (training volume only ~10% of endurance group)
- However, rest intervals reduce time savings (e.g., six 30-s sprints with six 4-min recovery intervals = 27 min active)
- Limitations: young age (23.2 ± 4.3 years) and normal health of participants; most interventions <6 weeks; further research needed on older populations, longer-term adherence, injury rates, and various exercise modes
- Existing evidence supports SIT effectiveness in special populations: coronary artery disease patients, congestive heart failure patients, and sedentary overweight/obese individuals
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The effect size calculated for all studies indicates that supramaximal-intensity SIT has a small-to-moderate effect (Cohen's d = 0.32, 95 % CI 0.10–0.55; z = 2.79, P < 0.01) on aerobic capacity with an aggregate improvement of ~3.6 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (~8 % increase)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Effects of sprint interval training on VO2max and aerobic ... ---
URL: https://paulogentil.com/pdf/Effects%20of%20sprint%20interval%20training%20on%20VO2max%20and%20aerobic%20exercise%20performance%20-%20A%20systematic%20review%20and%20meta-analysis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Effects of Sprint Interval Training on VO2max and Aerobic Exercise Performance

### Purpose and Methods
This study (published in Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2013; accepted May 21, 2013) by Sloth, Sloth, Overgaard, and Dalgas from Aarhus University (Denmark) systematically reviewed the literature on the aerobic and metabolic effects of low-volume sprint interval training (SIT) in healthy sedentary or recreationally active adults. A systematic search was conducted across six databases (PubMed, Embase, Bibliotek.dk, SPORTDiscus, SveMed+, and PEDro) on May 7, 2012. SIT was defined as: bouts of 10–30 seconds, maximal "all-out" intensity, ≤12 repetitions per session, and recovery ≥5 times the work duration. Inclusion criteria required longitudinal designs, interventions ≥2 weeks, human subjects who were healthy sedentary or recreationally active (baseline VO2max ≤55 mL/kg/min), and RCTs, matched-controlled trials (MCTs), or noncontrolled designs.

### Study Selection
- 2,668 publications retrieved; 823 duplicates removed, leaving 1,845 unique publications
- 93 publications read in full; 74 excluded for not meeting inclusion criteria
- 19 publications (19 unique studies) identified, plus 2 additional RCTs found via reference list screening (Babraj et al., 2009; Metcalfe et al., 2011)
- Final inclusion: 21 publications representing 19 unique studies

### Key Results

**VO2max Meta-Analysis (13 studies, 238 participants):**
- Weighted mean effect size: Hedges' g = 0.63, 95% CI (0.39; 0.87), statistically significant
- VO2max increases ranged from 4.2% to 13.4%
- Homogeneity test: Q = 2.79, df = 12, P = 0.99 (homogeneity could not be rejected)
- Mean VO2max improvement after 2 weeks of SIT: 6.8%; after 4–8 weeks: 9.6%

**Aerobic and Anaerobic Performance:**
- Consistent improvements in exercise performance, with some studies reporting improvements similar to traditional high-volume endurance training
- Increases in mean and peak power during Wingate tests up to 17%
- Burgomaster et al. (2005): 100% increase in cycle endurance capacity at 80% VO2peak after six SIT sessions
- Gibala et al. (2006): 750-kJ time trial improved 10.1% with SIT vs. 7.5% with endurance training (no significant group difference despite SIT total training volume being only ~10% of ET volume)
- Macpherson et al. (2011): 2000-m time trial improved 4.6% (SIT) and 5.9% (ET) with no group difference

**Peripheral Adaptations:**
- Increased citrate synthase (CS) activity of ~11–42% across five studies
- Increased glycogen content, GLUT4 content (~25% increase persisting 6 weeks after training cessation), and increased oxidative enzyme activity (COX, MDH, SDH, PDH)
- PGC-1alpha identified as a key regulatory mechanism (increased protein content after 6 weeks; AMPK and p38MAPK signaling cascades stimulated after acute SIT)

**Central/Cardiovascular Effects:**
- Limited and equivocal evidence; some studies showed decreased submaximal heart rate; conflicting results on stroke volume
- Two studies reported no change in resting HR

**Glycemic Control and Insulin Sensitivity:**
- Four studies suggest SIT may improve glycemic control and insulin sensitivity
- Babraj et al. (2009): reduced glucose and insulin AUC following OGTT after 2 weeks of SIT
- Richards et al. (2010): improved insulin sensitivity in both men and women via hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp
- Whyte et al. (2010): in overweight/obese men, reduced fasting insulin and 23.3% higher insulin sensitivity index at 24h post-SIT (not significant at 72h)

### Training Characteristics
- Most common protocol: repeated 30-s "all-out" Wingate bicycle sprints, 3×/week, 3–7 repetitions per session, 2–5 min recovery between bouts
- Some studies used 10–15 s sprints; one used treadmill sprinting
- Intervention duration: 2–8 weeks
- SIT generally well tolerated: compliance 95–100%, low dropout rates, few non-serious adverse events

### Conclusions
1. Strong evidence supports improvement of aerobic exercise performance and VO2max following SIT
2. Solid evidence supports peripheral muscular adaptations (increased oxidative potential) as a key mechanism
3. Evidence for central cardiovascular adaptations is limited and equivocal
4. SIT may improve glycemic control and insulin sensitivity
5. Rapid adaptations occur, with some effects seen after only 2 weeks (~12 min of exercise time per week)
6. Future research needed on long-term SIT effects, underlying mechanisms, optimal work:recovery ratios, and safety in unsupervised/sedentary populations

### Health Promotion Perspective
SIT may represent a time-efficient training protocol for improving cardiovascular health and preventing type 2 diabetes, though safety concerns remain for unsupervised, unmedically-screened populations, and the motivation required for repeated "all-out" efforts is substantial.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Strong evidence support improvements of aerobic exercise performance and VO2max following SIT. A meta-analysis across 13 studies evaluating effects of SIT on VO2max showed a weighted mean effects size of g = 0.63 95% CI (0.39; 0.87) and VO2max increases of 4.2–13.4%."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: HIIT vs. SIT: What Is the Better to Improve V˙O2max? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/18/24/13120

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (IJERPH) on December 12, 2021, investigating which interval training protocol—high-intensity interval training (HIIT) or sprint interval training (SIT)—promotes greater gains in cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max/peak). The study was conducted by researchers from the University of Campinas (UNICAMP) and the Federal University of São Carlos (UFSCar) in Brazil.

METHODOLOGY: Searches were conducted in October 2021 across PubMed (MEDLINE), Scopus, and Web of Science databases. Nineteen studies comparing HIIT and SIT effects on VO2max/peak were included in the final meta-analysis. Studies were screened by two independent evaluators, and quality was assessed using the TESTEX scale. The classification by Buchheit and Laursen (2013) was used: efforts lasting less than 60 seconds were classified as SIT, while efforts lasting over 60 seconds (up to 5 minutes) were classified as HIIT. Inclusion criteria required interventions lasting at least two weeks with a minimum weekly frequency of two days. Data were analyzed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software version 3, with fixed-effects models (due to homogeneity, I²=0%), presenting results as standardized mean difference (SMD) and raw mean differences (RMD).

RESULTS: There was no significant difference in VO2max/peak gains between HIIT and SIT for the standardized mean difference (SMD = 0.150; 95% CI = −0.038 to 0.338; p = 0.119) and raw mean differences (RMD = 0.921 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; 95% CI = −0.185 to 2.028; p = 0.103). No significant heterogeneity was found (p = 0.999 for SMD and p = 1.000 for RMD), and there was no significant publication bias (Egger's test p = 0.828). Subgroup analyses showed that sex, intervention duration, and physical activity levels did not influence the main effects, and sensitivity analysis of high-quality studies (TESTEX ≥ 10) confirmed the same results.

CONCLUSIONS: HIIT and SIT are both time-efficient protocols that promote similar gains in cardiorespiratory fitness. The choice between the two protocols should be made based on the availability of time, aptitude to perform intense physical activity, and specificity of individual physical conditions. The study suggests that both protocols predominantly rely on oxidative metabolism, and both lead to high physiological stress, high recruitment of type I and II muscle fibers, and increased PGC1-α activation. The authors note that although HIIT and SIT produce similar VO2max gains, they may lead to different magnitudes of other adaptations (neuromuscular, cardiovascular, etc.). Future studies are encouraged to compare the manipulation of other training variables (recovery time, number of bouts, different exercise types) using equalized caloric expenditure or total work performed.

The article has received 25 citations and has an Altmetric score of 13, with approximately 17,291 article views.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We conclude that the literature generates very consistent data to confirm that HIIT and SIT protocols promote similar gains in cardiorespiratory fitness. Thus, for this purpose, the choice of the protocol can be made for convenience."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: The effect of low volume sprint interval training on ... ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a study protocol published in the journal Trials (Springer Nature) for a definitive randomized controlled trial examining the effect of low-volume sprint interval training (specifically reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training, REHIT) on cardiorespiratory fitness in inactive adults.

**Background and Rationale:** Low physical activity and low cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max) are major public health concerns, with over 75% of adult Americans not meeting minimum PA recommendations in 2020. Physical inactivity is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide. Traditional HIIT and SIT protocols are criticized for being too time-consuming (~66-93 min/week), too strenuous, and producing negative affective responses. REHIT, consisting of two 20-second all-out sprints within a 10-minute session, 2 days per week (20 min/week total), addresses these barriers. Prior studies show VO2max increases ~10% after 6 weeks and ~19% after 12 weeks of REHIT, with no serious adverse events observed. Improvements in VO2max of this magnitude are associated with 30% and 38% risk reductions for all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality, respectively.

**Methods:** The study will recruit 120 inactive men and women aged 18-64 years (60 controls, 60 REHIT), who are healthy, weight-stable, with BMI < 35 kg/m². Participants will be randomized 1:1 to a non-exercising control group or 12 weeks of supervised REHIT performed 2 days/week on a cycle ergometer. Primary outcome is change in VO2max (measured via indirect calorimetry using incremental cycling test), assessed at baseline, week 6, and week 12. Secondary outcomes include body composition (bioelectrical impedance analysis), substrate metabolism, cardiac output, and perceptual measures (RPE, affective valence, enjoyment), plus quality of life. Expected dropout rate is 10-15%. The study is set at California State University—San Marcos (Department of Kinesiology), with data collection beginning January 2026 over a 3-year period. PI is Dr. Todd A. Astorino; Dr. Michael Joyner (Mayo Clinic) serves as NIH-appointed Safety Officer.

**Registration and Approval:** Approved by CSU—San Marcos IRB (#2313242−2 on September 12, 2025). Registered with OSF (osf.io/wvcz4) on November 3, 2025, and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07328568) on January 8, 2026. Study design follows SPIRIT guidelines. Published 23 March 2026, Volume 27, article number 340.

**Hypotheses:** Compared to control, REHIT will produce a significant increase in VO2max and exercise fat oxidation, and will be well-tolerated, safe, and perceived as enjoyable.

**Discussion:** This study aims to provide a definitive answer on whether REHIT induces clinically meaningful improvements in VO2max and is feasible/acceptable, advancing physical activity research and potentially contributing to reduced cardiovascular disease risk factors and improved public health.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We propose a definitive randomized controlled exercise training study in a large sample of inactive adults to examine the effects of REHIT on outcomes related to cardiometabolic health in comparison to a non-exercise control group."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Comparative effects of high-intensity and sprint interval ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1668326/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review with meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Physiology (11 November 2025, Volume 16, DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1668326) comparing the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and sprint interval training (SIT) on cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and body composition, with subgroup analyses based on baseline fitness status.

**Methods:** Nine randomized controlled trials (n = 666 participants) were included, registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251016362, registered 15 March 2025). The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and the Cochrane Handbook (v6.4). Literature was searched across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and SPORTDiscus from inception to 15 March 2025. Primary outcomes were changes in VO2max/VO2peak and body fat percentage. Analysis used SMD or WMD with 95% CIs, with subgroup analyses stratified by population type (healthy/trained vs. overweight/obese). From 379 retrieved studies, 9 eligible RCTs were included. Six studies had low risk of bias and 3 had moderate risk; none had high risk. Participants were young adults aged 13±1 to 29±8 years, with interventions lasting 4-12 weeks using running or cycling protocols.

**Key Results:**
- Both HIIT and SIT significantly improved CRF (SMD = 1.54; 95% CI: 0.89–2.18; p < 0.00001) and reduced body fat mass (WMD = −3.45%; 95% CI: −5.04 to −1.87; p < 0.0001) compared to control.
- HIIT was significantly more effective than SIT in improving CRF overall (SMD = −0.80; p = 0.0005), and particularly among overweight/obese individuals (SMD = −0.97; p = 0.0004), with no significant difference between modalities in healthy/trained populations.
- SIT was more effective than HIIT in reducing fat mass among healthy or trained populations (WMD = 5.85; p < 0.00001), while no significant difference was observed in overweight/obese individuals.
- High heterogeneity (I² = 86% for CRF; I² = 84% for fat mass) was noted, likely reflecting differences in training protocols and participant characteristics.

**Conclusion:** Both HIIT and SIT effectively improve cardiorespiratory fitness and reduce body fat, but relative efficacy depends on baseline health status. HIIT appears optimal for individuals with lower fitness levels (overweight/obese), while SIT may be preferable for time-efficient fat reduction in trained populations. The study recommends tailoring interval training prescriptions to individual characteristics, with SIT particularly suitable for trained individuals due to its time efficiency and HIIT offering a more accessible option for lower-fit populations. The authors call for future research on protocol standardization and long-term outcomes across different groups.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Both HIIT and SIT are effective interventions for enhancing CRF and reducing body fat, but their relative efficacy may depend on participants' baseline health status. HIIT appears optimal for individuals with lower fitness levels, while SIT may be preferable for time-efficient fat reduction in trained populations."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Is low-volume high intensity interval training a time-efficient ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1736441/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Physiology (19 December 2025, Volume 16) examining whether low-volume high-intensity interval training (LV-HIIT) is a time-efficient strategy for improving body composition and cardiovascular health in children and adolescents. The study was registered on OSF (https://osf.io/exhjm/) and conducted following PRISMA guidelines.

METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL), and CNKI was conducted from inception to April 2025. A three-level random-effects model was used with subgroup and meta-regression analyses. LV-HIIT was defined as total session duration ≤30 minutes (including warm-up, recovery, cool-down) with total vigorous exercise time ≤10 minutes, based on the Gibala et al. (2014) framework.

RESULTS: 23 studies (996 participants, 246 females) were included — 6 on normal-weight and 17 on overweight/obese individuals. Compared with controls, LV-HIIT significantly reduced:
- BMI (g = −1.24, K=17, moderate GRADE)
- Fat mass (g = −0.99, K=8, low GRADE)
- Body fat (g = −0.89, K=11, low GRADE)
- Waistline (g = −0.42, K=7, low GRADE)
- Weight (g = −0.34, K=13, moderate GRADE)
- SBP (g = −0.37, K=10, low GRADE)

--- SOURCE 3: High-intensity interval training ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-intensity_interval_training

SUMMARY:
<summary>
High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a training protocol alternating short periods of intense or explosive anaerobic exercise with brief recovery periods until exhaustion. It differs from aerobic cardiovascular activity because it relies heavily on anaerobic energy systems. HIIT workouts typically last under 30 minutes, with high-intensity intervals ranging from 20 to 45 seconds (no longer than 75 seconds) at near-maximal effort, followed by short recovery periods. Sprint interval training (SIT) is a related but distinct method using "supramaximal" or "all-out" efforts in shorter bursts; both fall under the broader class of interval training.

A typical HIIT session includes a warm-up, repetitions of high-intensity exercise (at near-maximum effort) separated by medium-intensity recovery (about 50% intensity), and a cool-down. A typical work-to-rest ratio is 2:1 (e.g., 30–40 seconds sprinting with 15–20 seconds jogging/walking). Sessions last 4–30 minutes. Research has been primarily conducted using cycling ergometers, though running, rowing, stair climbing, and uphill walking are also effective.

Several named regimens exist:
- Peter Coe regimen (1970s): repeated fast 200-meter runs with only 30 seconds recovery, inspired by Woldemar Gerschler and Per-Olof Åstrand.
- Tabata regimen (1996): 20 seconds of ultra-intense exercise at ~170% VO2max followed by 10 seconds rest, repeated for 4 minutes (8 cycles). Tabata trained athletes 4x/week plus steady-state training for 6 weeks and achieved aerobic improvements comparable to a steady-state group (VO2max from 48 to 55 mL/(kg·min) vs. 52 to 57), plus anaerobic capacity gains. This is technically classified as SIT since it is "supramaximal."
- Gibala regimen (McMaster University): 60 seconds at 95% VO2max followed by 75 seconds rest, repeated 8–12 cycles, 3x/week, with results comparable to steady-state training 5x/week. A 2011 gentler version for sedentary people used 10 reps of 60-second bursts at 60% peak power.
- Zuniga regimen (2011, Creighton University): 30 seconds at 90% of power output at VO2max followed by 30 seconds rest, typically 10 repetitions, shown to maximize VO2 consumption and workout duration.
- Vollaard regimen (University of Stirling): argued benefits plateau after 2–3 all-out sprints, developing a 10-minute routine with two 20-second all-out cycling sprints; meta-analysis showed protocols with 6–10 sprints don't improve aerobic fitness more than "2×20-s" protocol.

Health effects:
- Cardiovascular: HIIT improves cardiovascular fitness in healthy adults (18–45), with greater VO2max improvements than traditional endurance training. In patients with lifestyle-induced chronic diseases, HIIT produced nearly double the VO2max improvement of MICT (19.4% vs. 10.3%).
- Rehabilitative: Beneficial for coronary artery disease, heart failure, and myocardial infarction survivors, improving VO2max and exercise capacity.
- Metabolic: Significantly lowers insulin resistance, modestly decreases fasting blood glucose, and increases weight loss.
- Fat oxidation: Reduces subcutaneous fat, particularly abdominal and visceral fat, with greater effects in overweight individuals. Combined with resistance training in teens (8–12 weeks), it substantially reduces waist size and body fat percentage.
- Cognitive: Elicits short-term cognitive improvements similar to aerobic exercise; a 2017 study found HIIT beneficial to cognitive control and working memory in children, mediated by the BDNF polymorphism.
- Youth: Increases muscle mass in adolescents, helps treat and prevent pediatric obesity (decreasing BMI, body fat, insulin resistance, and LDL), and improves full-body strength.

Dangers: The American College of Sports Medicine recommends consulting a doctor before starting HIIT, especially with a history of coronary heart disease. Risks include rapid blood pressure increases (potentially causing hyper-perfusion injury in sedentary adults), injury from fatigue and overtraining, and common knee/ankle sprains. Neuromuscular training and pre-strengthening are recommended.

Key research findings: A 2008 study found HIIT lowered fasting insulin 31% vs. 9% for MICT. A 2011 study found a 4×8-min regimen (4 times 8 minutes intense work with 2-minute recovery) twice weekly provided the greatest VO2max improvements (~11% after 7 weeks). A 2019 trial found HIIT improves vascular health (decreased arterial wall thickness, increased endothelial function, enhanced flow-mediated dilation, lowered pulse wave velocity). A 2019 study found higher-intensity exercise more effective for lower back rehabilitation. HIIT has also been studied as prehabilitation for men awaiting urological cancer surgery.

PARTICIPANTS: Forty-eight healthy, physically sedentary women were recruited and divided into an experimental group (EG, n=24; mean age 21.21±2.15 years, weight 61.16±8.94 kg, BMI 22.69±2.49 kg/m²) and a control group (CG, n=24; mean age 20.50±1.29 years, weight 62.0±6.65 kg, BMI 23.04±1.74 kg/m²). The EG performed a 10-week online HIIT program (3 sessions/week using the Tabata method), while the CG maintained their daily routines. Due to Spanish COVID-19 lockdown regulations, training was conducted at home using calisthenics (bodyweight) exercises without equipment. Training intensity was monitored via Borg's RPE scale (progressing from 12-13 in weeks 1-4 to 18-19 in weeks 9-10), though heart rate was not monitored. The adherence rate was 96.3%±2.2%, with no withdrawals.

RESULTS: The repeated measures ANCOVA showed significant group×time interactions for weight (p=0.001; ηp²=0.97), BMI (p=0.001; ηp²=0.35), VO2 max (p=0.001; ηp²=0.42), power output W/kg (p=0.001; ηp²=0.49), and power output W (p=0.001; ηp²=0.87). The EG showed significant weight loss (p=0.001; d=-0.96), decreased BMI (d=0.24, moderate effect, -2.72%), significant VO2 max improvement (p=0.001; d=-1.07; a 15.94% increase), and significant improvements in power output (W and W/kg). The CG showed no significant changes in any measure.

CONCLUSIONS: A 10-week online HIIT program significantly improved maximum oxygen consumption, promoted weight loss, and decreased BMI in sedentary young women during COVID-19 lockdown. HIIT is demonstrated to be a time-efficient strategy for improving body composition and cardiorespiratory fitness in sedentary populations even under restricted conditions like confinement.

LIMITATIONS: Cycle ergometer evaluation may not precisely reflect running/jumping exercise intensities; reliance on RPE without concurrent heart rate monitoring; other influencing factors not controlled; sample limited to sedentary individuals.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Effects of Sprint Interval Training on VO2max and Aerobic Exercise Performance

### Purpose and Methods
This study (published in Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2013; accepted May 21, 2013) by Sloth, Sloth, Overgaard, and Dalgas from Aarhus University (Denmark) systematically reviewed the literature on the aerobic and metabolic effects of low-volume sprint interval training (SIT) in healthy sedentary or recreationally active adults. A systematic search was conducted across six databases (PubMed, Embase, Bibliotek.dk, SPORTDiscus, SveMed+, and PEDro) on May 7, 2012. SIT was defined as: bouts of 10–30 seconds, maximal "all-out" intensity, ≤12 repetitions per session, and recovery ≥5 times the work duration. Inclusion criteria required longitudinal designs, interventions ≥2 weeks, human subjects who were healthy sedentary or recreationally active (baseline VO2max ≤55 mL/kg/min), and RCTs, matched-controlled trials (MCTs), or noncontrolled designs.

### Study Selection
- 2,668 publications retrieved; 823 duplicates removed, leaving 1,845 unique publications
- 93 publications read in full; 74 excluded for not meeting inclusion criteria
- 19 publications (19 unique studies) identified, plus 2 additional RCTs found via reference list screening (Babraj et al., 2009; Metcalfe et al., 2011)
- Final inclusion: 21 publications representing 19 unique studies

### Key Results

**VO2max Meta-Analysis (13 studies, 238 participants):**
- Weighted mean effect size: Hedges' g = 0.63, 95% CI (0.39; 0.87), statistically significant
- VO2max increases ranged from 4.2% to 13.4%
- Homogeneity test: Q = 2.79, df = 12, P = 0.99 (homogeneity could not be rejected)
- Mean VO2max improvement after 2 weeks of SIT: 6.8%; after 4–8 weeks: 9.6%

**Aerobic and Anaerobic Performance:**
- Consistent improvements in exercise performance, with some studies reporting improvements similar to traditional high-volume endurance training
- Increases in mean and peak power during Wingate tests up to 17%
- Burgomaster et al. (2005): 100% increase in cycle endurance capacity at 80% VO2peak after six SIT sessions
- Gibala et al. (2006): 750-kJ time trial improved 10.1% with SIT vs. 7.5% with endurance training (no significant group difference despite SIT total training volume being only ~10% of ET volume)
- Macpherson et al. (2011): 2000-m time trial improved 4.6% (SIT) and 5.9% (ET) with no group difference

**Peripheral Adaptations:**
- Increased citrate synthase (CS) activity of ~11–42% across five studies
- Increased glycogen content, GLUT4 content (~25% increase persisting 6 weeks after training cessation), and increased oxidative enzyme activity (COX, MDH, SDH, PDH)
- PGC-1alpha identified as a key regulatory mechanism (increased protein content after 6 weeks; AMPK and p38MAPK signaling cascades stimulated after acute SIT)

**Central/Cardiovascular Effects:**
- Limited and equivocal evidence; some studies showed decreased submaximal heart rate; conflicting results on stroke volume
- Two studies reported no change in resting HR

**Glycemic Control and Insulin Sensitivity:**
- Four studies suggest SIT may improve glycemic control and insulin sensitivity
- Babraj et al. (2009): reduced glucose and insulin AUC following OGTT after 2 weeks of SIT
- Richards et al. (2010): improved insulin sensitivity in both men and women via hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp
- Whyte et al. (2010): in overweight/obese men, reduced fasting insulin and 23.3% higher insulin sensitivity index at 24h post-SIT (not significant at 72h)

### Training Characteristics
- Most common protocol: repeated 30-s "all-out" Wingate bicycle sprints, 3×/week, 3–7 repetitions per session, 2–5 min recovery between bouts
- Some studies used 10–15 s sprints; one used treadmill sprinting
- Intervention duration: 2–8 weeks
- SIT generally well tolerated: compliance 95–100%, low dropout rates, few non-serious adverse events

### Conclusions
1. Strong evidence supports improvement of aerobic exercise performance and VO2max following SIT
2. Solid evidence supports peripheral muscular adaptations (increased oxidative potential) as a key mechanism
3. Evidence for central cardiovascular adaptations is limited and equivocal
4. SIT may improve glycemic control and insulin sensitivity
5. Rapid adaptations occur, with some effects seen after only 2 weeks (~12 min of exercise time per week)
6. Future research needed on long-term SIT effects, underlying mechanisms, optimal work:recovery ratios, and safety in unsupervised/sedentary populations

### Health Promotion Perspective
SIT may represent a time-efficient training protocol for improving cardiovascular health and preventing type 2 diabetes, though safety concerns remain for unsupervised, unmedically-screened populations, and the motivation required for repeated "all-out" efforts is substantial.
</summary>

</key_excerpts>

- Overall effect size: small-to-moderate (Cohen's d = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10-0.55; z = 2.79, P < 0.01)

- Moderate-to-large effect vs. no-exercise control groups (Cohen's d = 0.69, 95% CI 0.46-0.93; z = 5.84, P < 0.01)

- Effects were heterogeneous (Q16 = 59.87; P < 0.01; I² = 74.95)
- Fail-safe number: 28 effects; funnel plot indicated no publication bias
- Inter-rater reliability: ICC (2,2) = 0.98
- Only the type of control group accounted for significant variation in the overall effect (b = -0.33; z = -3.57; P < 0.01)
- Effects not significantly different when moderating by fitness level, intervention length, inclusion of additional training, or mode of training
- Individual study effect sizes ranged from -0.39 to 1.22; 12 of 17 effects (>71%) were greater than zero

CONCLUSION: SIT improves aerobic capacity in healthy, young people. - Blair et al. estimated men who improve fitness may reduce mortality risk by 44% relative to those who remained unfit

- Time efficiency noted: in one study, SIT group spent only 15 min (135 min including recovery) exercising vs. 630 min for endurance training, yet achieved similar improvements in oxidative capacity and exercise performance (training volume only ~10% of endurance group)
- However, rest intervals reduce time savings (e.g., six 30-s sprints with six 4-min recovery intervals = 27 min active)
- Limitations: young age (23.2 ± 4.3 years) and normal health of participants; most interventions <6 weeks; further research needed on older populations, longer-term adherence, injury rates, and various exercise modes
- Existing evidence supports SIT effectiveness in special populations: coronary artery disease patients, congestive heart failure patients, and sedentary overweight/obese individuals

Credibility of evidence (CINeMA) ranged from high to very low, attributed to limited direct comparisons and high heterogeneity (confidence: moderate for HIIT vs CON, high for RST vs CON, low for SIT vs CON).

LIMITATIONS: Inclusion of nonrandomized trials; interventions conducted alongside regular training preventing isolation of effects; reliance on VO2max/VO2peak metrics (which don't always correlate with performance in trained runners); some subgroups limited to 1–2 studies. The review also notes a plateau effect—most RST adaptations occur within the initial 6-week phase, and HIIT/SIT show gains within <2 weeks reaching plateau around 6–10 weeks.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"All three interval training methods significantly increased VO2max compared to CON, with NMA rankings: RST (NMA's g=1.04) > HIIT (NMA's g=1.01) > SIT (NMA's g=0.69) > CT (NMA's g=0.29), no significant differences existed among RST, HIIT, and SIT (p>0.05)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: The effect of low volume sprint interval training on cardiorespiratory fitness: study protocol for a definitive randomized controlled trial - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13130460

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the study protocol for a definitive randomized controlled trial (RCT) examining the effect of low-volume sprint interval training on cardiorespiratory fitness, published in Trials (2026;27:340) by Todd A. Astorino (CSU—San Marcos), Richard S. Metcalfe (Swansea University), and Niels B. J. Vollaard (University of Stirling). The study received 2025-2026 dates, was approved by CSU—San Marcos IRB (#2313242-2) on September 12, 2025, and registered with OSF (osf.io/wvcz4) on November 3, 2025, and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07328568) on January 7/8, 2026. The trial is funded by the National Institute on Aging (R15AG093525).

BACKGROUND: Physical inactivity is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide, with over 75% of adult Americans not meeting PA guidelines in 2020. V̇O2max (maximal oxygen uptake) is a stronger predictor of morbidity/mortality risk than smoking, hypertension, obesity, high cholesterol, and insulin resistance. Reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT)—a protocol of two 20-second all-out sprints within a 10-minute session—has shown V̇O2max increases of ~10% after 6 weeks and ~19% after 12 weeks across multiple studies (Table 1 lists 14 studies). REHIT is genuinely time-efficient (as low as 20 min/week), as enjoyable as MICT, and does not produce negative affective responses, addressing common criticisms of HIIT/SIT (i.e., not time-efficient, too strenuous, unpleasant). However, prior studies used small sample sizes, necessitating this definitive trial.

METHODS: This is a randomized, repeated-measures controlled trial with 120 inactive adults (60 REHIT, 60 control) aged 18-64 years, healthy, weight-stable, BMI<35 kg/m². Participants will be randomized 1:1 via computer-generated sequence by a statistician with no participant interaction. REHIT involves 2 days/week of supervised training on a cycle ergometer for 12 weeks (2 min warm-up, all-out sprint, 3 min recovery, second sprint, 4 min cool-down; sprint duration increases from 10s in week 1, to 15s in week 2, and 20s for remaining 10 weeks; resistance at 5% body mass). Primary outcome is change in V̇O2max (gold-standard incremental cycling test with continuous gas exchange, ParvoMedics True One; typical error 0.11 L/min), assessed at baseline, week 6, and week 12. Secondary outcomes include cardiac output and stroke volume (Physioflow Enduro impedance cardiograph), substrate metabolism (Frayn equations from 10-min submaximal cycling at 30/40 W), body composition (InBody bioelectrical impedance analysis), and psychological responses (RPE, affective valence, PACES enjoyment scale, self-efficacy, acceptability questionnaire, and 36-item SF-36 health-related quality of life). Sample size: n=120 total detects smallest worthwhile difference of 1.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (~4.5% V̇O2max increase, equivalent to ~8% CVD mortality risk reduction) with d=0.60, alpha=0.05, 90% power. Data analysis uses two-way mixed-model ANOVA (time × group), intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.

DISCUSSION: The study addresses criticisms of REHIT's small sample sizes and aims to provide definitive evidence on whether REHIT induces clinically meaningful V̇O2max improvements and is feasible/acceptable, with potential to reduce CVD risk factors and improve public health. Trial status: ongoing, first participant recruited December 2025, completion September 2028. Safety oversight provided by Dr. Michael Joyner (Mayo Clinic) as NIH-appointed Safety Officer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Low levels of physical activity (PA) and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) are significant issues for societal health... more than 75% of adult Americans did not meet these minimum PA recommendations" (2020 data).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Sprint Interval Training: The Research — FitCraft ---
URL: https://getfitcraft.com/science/sprint-interval-training-research

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Domenic Angelino (published July 29, 2026) provides a research-based review of Sprint Interval Training (SIT), distinguishing it from HIIT and evaluating its effectiveness against moderate continuous training (MICT).

**Core Definition:** SIT involves short all-out efforts (10-30 seconds) separated by several minutes of easy recovery. It differs from HIIT, which operates at 85-95% max heart rate for 20 seconds to 4 minutes. SIT pushes to the true ceiling for much shorter bursts.

**Key Research Findings:**
1. **Gillen & Gibala 2016 (PLOS ONE):** The landmark trial randomized 25 sedentary men (mean age 27, BMI 26) into SIT (n=9), MICT (n=10), and control (n=6) groups over 12 weeks. SIT protocol: 3x20-second all-out sprints (peak power ~500W) with 2 minutes easy recovery, totaling 10 minutes per session (1 minute of actual sprinting). MICT: 45 minutes at ~70% max HR. Weekly time: 30 min (SIT) vs 150 min (MICT) — a 5-fold difference. Both groups improved VO2 peak ~19%, insulin sensitivity ~53%, and mitochondrial content 48-49%. No statistical separation on primary outcomes.

2. **Sloth 2013 (Scand J Med Sci Sports):** Meta-analysis of 13 studies found weighted effect size g=0.63 (95% CI 0.39-0.87) on VO2max, with absolute improvements of 4.2-13.4% over 2-8 weeks.

3. **Vollaard 2017 (Med Sci Sports Exerc):** Found no additional VO2max benefit past 4-6 sprints per session. Mechanistically, peak metabolic stress saturates AMPK and PGC-1-alpha signaling pathways.

4. **MacInnis & Gibala 2017 (J Physiol):** Both SIT and endurance training drive mitochondrial biogenesis, capillary density, and plasma volume — via peak metabolic stress vs. cumulative metabolic stress respectively.

5. **Liang 2024 (PeerJ):** Pooled 169 participants. SIT and MICT reduced systolic BP similarly (~2.8 vs 3.0 mmHg), but MICT won cleanly on diastolic BP (2.1 vs 0.75 mmHg) and absolute VO2 peak (3.1 vs 1.75 mL/kg/min).

**Practical Protocol Recommendations:**
- Start with 3 sprints per session (not 6), 20-30 seconds all-out
- Rest 2-4 minutes between sprints with easy movement
- 3 sessions per week on non-consecutive days
- Cycling and rowing carry lowest orthopedic risk; running sprints highest (hamstring/Achilles injuries)
- Warm up 2-5 minutes; do not fast before SIT
- Pair with 1-2 easy zone 2 sessions weekly

**Key Takeaways:** SIT is time-efficient (not superior) to steady cardio. On markers tied to mortality risk, MICT is at least as good or better. SIT wins on time cost — 3 minutes of weekly hard work matches 150 minutes of moderate work. It is best for those with 10-minute time constraints, and should be a complement (1-2 sessions/week) for those with established training. It will not fix a low training base — 4-6 weeks of easy base work should precede all-out efforts.

**Common Misconceptions Debunked:** SIT ≠ HIIT; more sprints ≠ more adaptation; SIT is not a total replacement for steady cardio; SIT does not burn huge calories (80-150 calories per 10-min session, with EPOC adding only 6-15%).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"for these three health-relevant adaptations, 3 minutes of hard weekly work matched 150 minutes of moderate weekly work. The trial does not claim SIT is superior. It claims SIT is not inferior at a much lower time cost."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Frontiers | Effects of 6-week sprint interval training compared to traditional training on the running performance of distance runners: A randomized controlled trail ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1536287/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Physiology (Exercise Physiology section) on February 6, 2025, examining the effects of a 6-week sprint interval training (SIT) program compared to traditional training on the running performance of well-trained male distance runners.

**Study Design & Methods:**
- Twenty male distance runners (VO2max: 67.4 ± 4.5 mL/kg/min; personal best 5000m: 14'38"47 ± 00'23"46) were randomly assigned to either an intervention training (IT) group performing SIT or a control training (CT) group engaging in traditional long-distance training.
- Both groups trained twice per week for 6 weeks (12 sessions total).
- The SIT protocol consisted of 10 sets of 30-second maximal sprint runs with 3.5-minute recovery periods between sets (heart rate maintained below 70% of max during recovery), with average interval intensity around 175% of maximal aerobic speed. Each session lasted ~50 minutes including a 3-minute cooldown.
- The CT group performed traditional endurance sessions (10km runs, repetitions of 3000m, 2000m, 1500m, 1000m, and 400m runs) at 70%-85% of maximum heart rate.
- Measurements included VO2max, O2 cost, time to exhaustion (TTE), and running times for 100m, 400m, and 3000m, taken before and after the intervention.

**Key Results:**
- The IT group showed significant improvements (all P < 0.01) in TTE and running performance across 100m, 400m, and 3000m distances.
- The CT group only demonstrated significant improvement in 400m time (P < 0.01).
- The IT group exhibited superior 3000m performance compared to the CT group (P < 0.01, large effect size of 1.53).
- VO2max and O2 cost did not reach statistical significance in the IT group (P = 0.055 and 0.077 respectively), though effect sizes suggested potential effects (VO2max: small ES 0.43; O2 cost: moderate ES 0.65; TTE: moderate ES 0.77).
- IT group mean changes included: 100m time reduced by 0.20s, 400m by 0.67s, 3000m by 4.86s, and TTE increased by 0.12 min.

**Conclusions & Implications:**
The authors conclude that SIT may offer superior benefits for enhancing running performance in well-trained male distance runners, particularly in time to exhaustion and middle-to-long distance events, compared to traditional long-distance training. The study recommends incorporating 2-3 SIT sessions per week to complement traditional endurance training, enhancing both aerobic and anaerobic capacity while reducing overall training time. The authors note study limitations including small sample size, all-male participants in a narrow age range, and the relatively short 6-week intervention period.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results indicated that the IT group showed significant improvements in TTE and running performance across 100, 400, and 3000 m (all P < 0.01), while the CT group only demonstrated improvements in 400 m time (P < 0.01). The IT group exhibited superior 3000 m performance compared to the CT group (P < 0.01)."
</key_excerpts>
