ARTICLE Decreasing sprint duration from 20 to 10 s during reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) attenuates the increase in maximal aerobic capacity but has no effect on affective and perceptual responses Gulbin R. Nalçakan, Preeyaphorn Songsorn, Ben L. Fitzpatrick, Yasin Yüzbasioglu, Noel E. Brick, Richard S. Metcalfe, and Niels B.J. Vollaard Abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated that modifying the “classic” 6 × 30-s “all-out” sprint interval training protocol by incorporating either shorter sprints (6 × 10-s or 15-s sprints) or fewer sprints (e.g., 2 × 20-s sprints; reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT)) does not attenuate the training-induced improvements in maximal aerobic capacity. The aim of the present study was to determine if reducing the sprint duration in the REHIT protocol from 20 s to 10 s per sprint inﬂuences acute affective responses and the change in maximal aerobic capacity following training. Thirty-six sedentary or recreationally active participants (17 women; mean ± SD; age: 22 ± 3 years; body mass index: 24.5 ± 4.6 kg·m−2; maximal aerobic capacity: 37 ± 8 mL·kg−1·min−1) were randomised to a group performing a “standard” REHIT protocol involving 2 × 20-s sprints or a group who performed 2 × 10-s sprints. Maximal aerobic capacity was determined before and after 6 weeks of 3 weekly training sessions.
Acute affective responses and perceived exertion were assessed during training. Greater increases in maximal aerobic capacity were observed for the group performing 20-s sprints (2.77 ± 0.75 to 3.04 ± 0.75 L·min−1; +10%) compared with the group performing 10-s sprints (2.58 ± 0.57 vs. 2.67 ± 3.04 L·min−1; +4%; group × time interaction effect: p < 0.05; d = 1.06). Positive affect and the mood state vigour increased postexercise, while tension, depression, and total mood disturbance decreased, and negative affect remained unchanged. Affective responses and perceived exertion were not altered by training and were not different between groups. In conclusion, reducing sprint duration in the REHIT protocol from 20 s to 10 s attenuates improve-ments in maximal aerobic capacity, and does not result in more positive affective responses or lower perceived exertion.
Key words: V ˙ O2max, sprint interval training, SIT, Wingate sprint, affect.
Résumé : Selon des études récentes, la modiﬁcation du protocole « usuel » de l’entraînement par intervalle de sprint comprenant 6 × 30 s d’effort a ` fond de train en intégrant des sprints plus courts (6 × 10 s ou 15 s) ou moins nombreux (p. ex. 2 × 20 s; entraînement par intervalle d’intensité élevée, mais moins difﬁcile (« REHIT »)) n’atténue pas pour autant l’amélioration de la capacité aérobie. Cette étude a pour objectif de vériﬁer si la diminution de la durée du sprint dans le protocole REHIT de 20 s a ` 10 s a un effet sur les réponses affectives ponctuelles et sur la modiﬁcation de la consommation maximale d’oxygène par l’entraînement. On répartit aléatoirement 36 participants sédentaires ou actifs par loisir (17 femmes; moyenne ± écart-type; âge : 22 ± 3 ans, indice de masse corporelle : 24,5 ± 4,6 kg·m−2; consommation maximale d’oxygène : 37 ± 8 mL·kg−1·min−1) dans un groupe s’en tenant au protocole REHIT standard (2 sprints de 20 s) ou un groupe effectuant 2 sprints de 10 s. On évalue la consommation maximale d’oxygène avant et après 6 semaines d’entraînement a ` raison de 3 séances par semaine. On évalue les réponses affectives ponctuelles et la perception de l’intensité de l’effort au cours de l’entraînement. La consommation maximale d’oxygène augmente plus dans le groupe des sprints de 20 s (de 2,77 ± 0,75 a ` 3,04 ± 0,75 L·min−1; +10%) comparativement au groupe des sprints de 10 s (de 2,58 ± 0,57 a ` 2,67 ± 3,04 L·min−1; +4%; interaction groupe × temps : p < 0,05, d = 1,06). Après l’exercice, on note une amélioration positive de l’affect et de l’humeur et une diminution de la tension, de la dépression et des troubles de l’humeur; on ne note pas de modiﬁcation des affects négatifs. L’entraînement ne modiﬁe pas les réponses affectives et la perception de l’effort dans les deux groupes. En conclusion, la diminution de la durée du sprint de s a ` 10 s dans le protocole REHIT atténue l’amélioration de la consommation maximale d’oxygène et n’engendre pas plus d’affects positifs ou moins d’intensité d’effort perçue. Introduction Low maximal aerobic capacity (V ˙ O2max) is one of the strongest predictors of future chronic disease and premature mortality (Keteyian et al. 2008; Myers et al. 2002), and longitudinal studies have demonstrated that increasing V ˙ O2max substantially lowers morbidity and mortality during follow-up (Blair et al. 1995; Lee et al. 2011). Thus physical activity and/or exercise interventions that improve V ˙ O2max should be emphasised in public health guidelines (Bouchard et al. 2015; Ross et al. 2016). V ˙ O2max can be improved through moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) (Garber et al. 2011), but as perceived lack of time prevents many people from doing such exercise (Kimm et al. 2006; Korkiakangas et al. 2009; Trost et al. 2002), alternative exercise routines such as (sub)maximal high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and supra-maximal sprint interval training (SIT) have been proposed as time-efﬁcient alternative/adjunct exercise strategies (Gillen and Gibala 2014). However, the need for recovery periods in between repeated sprints diminishes the time-efﬁciency of most HIIT and SIT protocols compared with less strenuous MICT (Gillen and Gibala 2014).
The mechanisms that underpin the increases in V ˙ O2max with HIIT and SIT remain unclear (Vollaard and Metcalfe 2017), but have been proposed to rely on activation of skeletal muscle signal-ling pathways involving 5= adenosine monophosphate-activated pro-tein kinase, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (Gibala 2009), and potentially other signalling molecules such as p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (Little et al. 2011), sirtuin 1 (Guerra et al. 2010), and sirtuin 3 (Edgett et al.
2016). It has been proposed that the activation of relevant signal-ling pathways with supramaximal exercise may be reliant on achieving peak power output (Hazell et al. 2010), but we have proposed an alternative theory suggesting that activation of sig-nalling pathways could plausibly be related to rapid glycogenoly-sis associated with supramaximal exercise (Metcalfe et al. 2015). As glycogen depletion during supramaximal exercise is limited to the ﬁrst 15 s of the ﬁrst bouts of repeated “all-out” sprints (Parolin et al. 1999), we have previously proposed that more time-efﬁcient SIT protocols with fewer and/or shorter sprints may re-main effective at improving V ˙ O2max (Metcalfe et al. 2012; Vollaard and Metcalfe 2017). In recent years we have provided support for this hypothesis by demonstrating that a reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) protocol involving two 20-s all-out cycle sprints within a 10-min exercise session improves V ˙ O2max in sedentary individuals (Metcalfe et al. 2012, 2016) and patients with type 2 diabetes (Rufﬁno et al. 2017). Furthermore, REHIT may improve measures of insulin sensitivity (Gillen et al.
2014, 2016; Metcalfe et al. 2012) and blood pressure (Rufﬁno et al.
2017). With a total time-commitment of 3 × 10 min per week, the REHIT protocol appears to offer a genuinely time-efﬁcient alter-native to MICT (Vollaard and Metcalfe 2017; Vollaard et al. 2017).
The sprints in the REHIT protocol are shorter (20 s) compared with those used in most other SIT protocols (30 s). This shortened sprint duration and the concomitant lower increase in muscle metabolites (e.g., lactate, hydrogen ions) and reduction in central motor command can be expected to reduce perceived exertion (Pageaux 2016; Vollaard and Metcalfe 2017). The strong contribu-tion of phosphocreatine hydrolysis to energy demands during the ﬁrst 10 s of a 30-s Wingate sprint means that perceived exertion during this phase is relatively low, whereas the gradual switch to glycolysis as the predominant energy source (Parolin et al. 1999) is associated with severe and progressive fatigue during the latter stages of the sprint. It follows that if sprint duration in the REHIT protocol can be reduced further without affecting the associated improvements in V ˙ O2max, the protocol would be perceived as less unpleasant and more tolerable. Recent ﬁndings by Townsend et al. (2017) suggest that reducing sprint duration may attenuate negative affective responses to SIT. This in turn could potentially lead to better uptake of, and adherence to, SIT as a viable alterna-tive exercise intervention for reducing risk of noncommunicable disease (Rhodes and Kates 2015).
To date there has been little focus on the effects of sprint dura-tion in SIT protocols on associated adaptations to V ˙ O2max. Hazell and co-workers (2010) suggested that generation of peak power may be more important as a mechanism for improving V ˙ O2max than the maintenance of a high power output for a longer duration. Indeed, they observed no difference in the increase in V ˙ O2max between SIT protocols incorporating either 4–6 × 30-s or 10-s sprints (Hazell et al. 2010). This was supported by Zelt et al.
(2014) who found similar increases in V ˙ O2max with 4–6 × 30-s or 15-s sprints. Therefore, the present study aimed to determine whether reducing the sprint duration in the REHIT protocol from 20 s to 10 s per sprint affects the associated change in V ˙ O2max as well as ratings of perceived exertion and changes in affect and mood state.
Materials and methods Compliance with ethical standards The study was approved by the local University Ethics commit-tees (references: University of Stirling SSREC 888/Ulster University FC52 2016-17/Ege University 16-8.1/18), and conformed to the stan-dards set forth in the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki.
The study protocol was fully explained to all participants in writ-ten and verbal form before they were asked to provide written consent.
Participants Thirty-six apparently healthy, sedentary, or recreationally ac-tive participants (Table 1) were recruited at sites in the United Kingdom (Stirling, Derry/Londonderry) and Turkey (I ˙zmir), and randomised into a group performing the REHIT protocol as previ-ously described by Metcalfe et al. (2012) (REHIT20; n = 18, 11 men) and a group performing the same protocol but with the sprint duration reduced by 50% for each session (REHIT10; n = 18, 8 men).
Randomisation was performed using the sealed-envelope method.
Exclusion criteria were classiﬁcation as highly physically active according to the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (Craig et al. 2003), contraindications to exercise as determined using a standard physical activity readiness questionnaire (Thomas et al. 1992), clinically signiﬁcant hypertension (>140/90 mm Hg), or resting heart rate ≥100 beats·min−1. All participants were asked not to make conscious changes to their diet and physical activity pat-terns for the duration of the study.
Experimental procedures Following measurement of body mass and height, V ˙ O2max was determined using an incremental cycling test to exhaustion (Ex-calibur Sport; Lode, Groningen, the Netherlands), with breath-by-breath measurement of oxygen uptake using a calibrated online gas analyser (Oxycon Pro; Jaeger, Wurzburg, Germany. After a 2-min warm-up at 50 W, the intensity was increased by 1 W every 3 s until volitional exhaustion (failure to maintain rpm >50) de-spite verbal encouragement. V ˙ O2max was determined as the high-est value for a 15-breath rolling average, and accepted if 2 or more of the following criteria were met: (i) volitional exhaustion, (ii) a plateau in V ˙ O2 despite increasing intensity, (iii) respiratory ex-change ratio > 1.15, and (iv) maximal heart rate within 10 beats of the age-predicted maximum (i.e., 220 – age). This was the case for all participants. Because of technical difﬁculties we were unable to complete the post-training V ˙ O2max test for 1 female participant in the REHIT20 group, so V ˙ O2max data are presented for 11 men and 6 women for this group.
Following the V ˙ O2max test, participants performed a 6-week training programme involving 3 training sessions per week.
Training sessions consisted of 10 min of unloaded pedalling (Ergomedic 874e; Monark, Vansbro, Sweden), with 2 all-out cycle sprints against a resistance of 7.5% of the participant’s body weight. The ﬁrst sprint started at 2 min and the second sprint ﬁnished at 6 min. Sprint duration in the REHIT20 group increased from 10 s in the ﬁrst 3 sessions, to 15 s in sessions 4–6, and 20 s in all remaining sessions. Sprint duration in the REHIT10 group was exactly half that of the REHIT20 group in all sessions: duration increased from 5 s in the ﬁrst 3 sessions, to 7.5 s in sessions 4–6, and 10 s in all remaining sessions. Participants were asked to increase their cadence to maximal 3 s prior to the start of the sprint and to maintain the highest possible cadence throughout the sprint. Verbal encouragement was provided. A session rating of perceived exertion (RPE) score using the 6–20 Borg scale (rep-resenting the entire training session (Borg 1982)) was taken di-rectly postexercise at the last session of each training week. In addition, during the ﬁrst, fourth, seventh, and eighteenth train-ing session, the changes in psychological affect as a result of ex-ercise were assessed using the Positive and Negative Affect Scale (Watson et al. 1988) and the Brunel Mood Scale (Terry et al. 1999).
These scales were completed before and within 5 min after the exercise session. Following the ﬁnal training session, participants completed a questionnaire on the acceptability of the interven-tion, as previously used by Boereboom et al. (2016). A second V ˙ O2max test was performed on the third day after the ﬁnal training session, at a similar time as the baseline test and following iden-tical procedures.
Statistical analysis Data are presented as means ± SD. Based on a coefﬁcient of variation for the V ˙ O2max test protocol of 4% (Songsorn et al. 2016), it was calculated that 14 participants were needed in each group to be able to detect a difference in the change in V ˙ O2max of 5% between the 2 groups, with a power of 90% and  = 0.05.
Independent-sample t tests were used to determine differences between the 2 groups at baseline. Two-way mixed-model ANOVA (intervention (REHIT10/REHIT20) × trial (pretraining/post-training)) was used to determine differences in the change in V ˙O2max and body mass from baseline to post-intervention between the 2 groups.
Three-way repeated-measures ANOVA (intervention (REHIT10/ REHIT20) × training session (session 1/4/7/18) × time (pre-exercise/ postexercise)) was used to assess the effect of acute exercise on affect and mood state, and 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (intervention (REHIT10/REHIT20) × training session (session 3/6/9/12/15/18)) was used to assess the effect of acute exercise on perceived exertion. A Mann–Whitney U test was used to test for differences between the groups for intervention acceptability. Cohen’s d effect sizes are re-ported. Signiﬁcance was accepted at p < 0.05.
Results There were no signiﬁcant differences between participants in the control group and the training group for mean baseline char-acteristics (Table 1) or other variables. Of the 36 participants, 23 completed all 18 training sessions, 7 completed 17 sessions, and 6 completed 16 sessions, resulting in an overall mean adher-ence of 97% (98% for REHIT10 and 96% for REHIT20). We observed a small but signiﬁcant increase in body mass from pre- to post-intervention (main effect of time: p < 0.05), but no difference between the change in the REHIT20 group (70.3 ± 11.5 vs. 71.2 ± 11.0 kg) compared with the REHIT10 group (75.8 ± 18.7 vs. 76.2 ± 18.8 kg). There was a greater increase in V ˙ O2max in the REHIT20 group (2.77 ± 0.75 vs. 3.04 ± 0.75 L·min−1; +10%) compared with the REHIT10 group (2.58 ± 0.57 vs. 2.67 ± 3.04 L·min−1; +4%; group × time interaction effect: P < 0.05; d = 1.06; main effect of time: p < 0.001; Fig. 1).
Acute REHIT sessions were associated with a small but signiﬁ-cant increase in positive affect directly postexercise (main effect of time: p < 0.05; d = 0.23), whereas negative affect was unchanged (Table 2). There were no signiﬁcant time × session interaction effects for affect, and no signiﬁcant differences were observed between the changes in the REHIT10 and REHIT20 groups. Signif-icant exercise-induced improvements with small effect sizes (d = 0.11–0.21) were observed for the mood states tension, depression, vigour (main effect of time: p < 0.01 for each), and total mood disturbance (main effect of time: p < 0.05), but there were no signiﬁcant changes for anger, fatigue, or confusion (Fig. 2). Again, no differences were observed between training sessions, nor be-tween the REHIT10 and REHIT20 groups. Ratings of perceived ex-ertion scores averaged between 13–15 (“somewhat hard” to “hard”), with no signiﬁcant differences between the groups or between training sessions (Fig. 3). Following the ﬁnal training session, both REHIT programmes were deemed acceptable by the majority of participants (Fig. 4), with no signiﬁcant differences between the protocols. Speciﬁcally, on average participants in both groups agreed with the statements that they believed that their ﬁtness had improved, that they would do HIT again, that they would recommend HIT to others, and that they enjoyed HIT.
They were neutral about the statement that HIT was more de-manding than expected, and on average disagreed with the state-ments that the physical strain or travelling involved with HIT interfered with their life, and that HIT was a time burden.

Discussion The present study aimed to determine whether a REHIT protocol with 10-s sprints could be equally effective at improving V ˙O2max com-pared with a protocol involving 20-s sprints. Unlike previous studies that found no difference in the increase in V ˙O2max between 2–4 weeks of 4–6 × 30-s sprints versus 10 (Hazell et al. 2010) or 15-s sprints (Zelt et al. 2014), we observed signiﬁcantly greater improvements in V ˙O2max with 2 × 20-s versus 2 × 10-s sprints. As acute affective re-sponses and perceived exertion were not affected by sprint duration, we conclude that in protocols with very few sprints the sprint dura-tion should be longer than 10 s.
The increase in V ˙ O2max we observed in response to our original 2 × 20-s REHIT protocol is similar to what we have reported in our previous studies (Metcalfe et al. 2012, 2016). This increase is impor-tant as low V ˙ O2max is strongly linked to poor health and increased risk of premature morbidity (Keteyian et al. 2008; Myers et al.
2002). As the prevalence of physical inactivity remains high world-wide (Hallal et al. 2012), there is an urgent need to establish alter-native exercise interventions that are (i) effective at improving V ˙ O2max and (ii) acceptable to populations that are currently un-willing or unable to adhere to recommended levels of MICT. In an attempt to address the commonly reported barrier to exercise of perceived lack of time (Kimm et al. 2006; Korkiakangas et al. 2009; Trost et al. 2002), we previously developed the genuinely time-efﬁcient REHIT intervention (Metcalfe et al. 2012). REHIT has a total time-commitment of 3 × 10 min per week and is associated with acceptable session RPEs (“somewhat hard”) (Metcalfe et al.
2012). Nonetheless, there remains a need to establish whether the REHIT protocol can be made shorter and/or easier to enhance the likelihood of sedentary populations taking up and adhering to this exercise routine. We have recently provided preliminary data suggesting that a minimum of 2 sprint repetitions within a train-ing session is required to improve V ˙ O2max (Songsorn et al. 2016, 2017; Vollaard et al. 2017). Reducing the sprint duration in the REHIT protocol would do little to reduce the total training time (the bulk of each training session is spent on the low-intensity Table 2. However, in the present study we demonstrate that reducing the sprint duration from 20 s to 10 s attenuates the efﬁcacy of the REHIT protocol at improving V ˙O2max, and we therefore propose that the original protocol involving 20-s sprints remains the protocol of choice.
The exact physiological stimuli and molecular signalling path-ways responsible for the rapid improvements in V ˙ O2max associ-ated with HIIT and SIT protocols remain unclear (Vollaard and Metcalfe 2017). As long as this is the case, establishing the shortest and/or easiest exercise interventions associated with health ben-eﬁts such as improved V ˙ O2max remains a matter of trial and error, involving studies examining a variety of protocol modiﬁcations.
Previous work by the groups of Hazell (Hazell et al. 2010) and Gurd (Zelt et al. 2014) suggested that the sprint duration in SIT protocols can be substantially reduced from that used in the “classic” 4–6 × 30-s SIT protocol popularised by Gibala’s group (Burgomaster et al.
2005). On the basis of these results it was suggested that genera-tion of peak power is a key stimulus for improving V ˙ O2max. Our present data suggest that this is not the case, at least not when the number of sprint repetitions is kept low (2 repetitions). The evi-dence to date points to a need to repeat all-out sprints of a sufﬁ-cient duration (e.g., 2 × 20 s) or number (e.g., 4–6 × 10 s) to achieve clinically meaningful increases in V ˙ O2max. The reasons why cer-tain combinations of sprint repetitions and sprint duration lead to differences in the effectiveness of the protocols in improving V ˙ O2max will remain unclear until we have a more detailed under-standing of the mechanisms responsible for the increase in V ˙ O2max associated with very low volume SIT protocols (Vollaard and Metcalfe 2017).
This is the ﬁrst study to provide data on the acute effects of REHIT on affective responses and mood state. We demonstrate that reducing the sprint duration in the REHIT protocol from 20 s to 10 s does not reduce session RPEs, nor does it lead to more positive affective responses or changes in mood state at postexer-cise. This is important, because a criticism of SIT protocols has been that all-out sprints are too strenuous for untrained individ-uals: it has been suggested that performing all-out sprints re-quires too much motivation (which many sedentary populations lack), and is likely to evoke negative affect that may lead to sub-sequent avoidance of further exercise (Hardcastle et al. 2014).
However, the evidence on which this criticism is based is conten-tious (Jung et al. 2015), and our data suggest that REHIT is not associated with the negative affective responses described by Hardcastle et al. (2014).
Exercise interventions can only improve health if performed regularly, and therefore exercise protocols leading to a smaller increase in V ˙ O2max could still be deemed acceptable if they were substantially less strenuous and associated with less negative af-fect. However, we demonstrate that acute exercise in a REHIT session is not associated with an increase in negative affect or a disruption of mood state directly after exercise, and that neither reducing the sprint duration from 20 s to 10 s nor regularly per-forming REHIT sessions (i.e., training) modiﬁes the acute re-sponses. Our ﬁnding that REHIT does not result in negative affect directly postexercise is in contrast to longer SIT protocols with more sprints (Townsend et al. 2017). Conversely it is in line with Townsend’s ﬁnding that shorter and, if sprint duration is kept constant, fewer sprints have less of an impact on affective re-sponses. Nonetheless, our data should be interpreted with caution given that affective responses and changes in mood state were only assessed on completion of the exercise session, i.e., 5 min following the second sprint. Previous studies that have applied continuous exercise have shown that affective responses to exer-cise above the ventilatory threshold follow an inverse U-shaped curve: affect decreases (and may become negative) during exer-cise, but then rebounds quickly upon exercise cessation and mood state may then be enhanced in the immediate postexercise period (Ekkekakis et al. 2008). Future studies should determine whether negative affect is present at any point during the 10-min exercise session. Still, that REHIT may be associated with positive affective responses immediately postexercise is in direct contrast to classic SIT (4–6 × 30-s sprints) (Saanijoki et al. 2015) and at the very least suggests that any potential negative responses will be short-lived.
In conclusion, our present study shows that reducing the sprint duration in the REHIT protocol from 2 × 20 s to 2 × 10 s attenuates improvements in V ˙ O2max, but does not impact perceived exertion, acute affective responses or mood state. Our ﬁndings further sup-port the use of the original REHIT protocol consisting of 2 × 20-s sprints, and strengthens our contention that REHIT represents an efﬁcacious, time-efﬁcient, and acceptable alternative to classic SIT and MICT for improving health and reducing risk of future mor-bidity and premature mortality.

This is a scientific research article from Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism (Vol. 43, 2018, pp. 338-344) examining whether reducing sprint duration in the reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) protocol from 20 seconds to 10 seconds affects maximal aerobic capacity (VO2max) improvements, affective responses, and perceived exertion.

STUDY DESIGN: Thirty-six sedentary or recreationally active participants (17 women; mean age 22 ± 3 years; BMI 24.5 ± 4.6 kg/m²; VO2max 37 ± 8 mL/kg/min) were recruited at sites in the UK (Stirling, Derry/Londonderry) and Turkey (Izmir) and randomised into two groups: REHIT20 (2 × 20-s sprints; n=18) and REHIT10 (2 × 10-s sprints; n=18). Both groups performed 6 weeks of training, 3 sessions per week, with each session consisting of 10 minutes of unloaded pedalling with 2 all-out cycle sprints against a resistance of 7.5% of body weight. Sprint durations were progressively increased from 10s→20s (REHIT20) and 5s→10s (REHIT10). VO2max was measured via incremental cycling test to exhaustion before and after training. Affective responses (Positive and Negative Affect Scale, Brunel Mood Scale) and session RPE (Borg 6-20 scale) were assessed during training.

KEY RESULTS:
- VO2max increased significantly more in the REHIT20 group (+10%; 2.77 ± 0.75 to 3.04 ± 0.75 L/min) compared with the REHIT10 group (+4%; 2.58 ± 0.57 to 2.67 ± 0.57 L/min) (group × time interaction: p < 0.05; d = 1.06).
- Positive affect and vigour increased post-exercise, while tension, depression, and total mood disturbance decreased; negative affect remained unchanged.
- Affective responses and perceived exertion (RPE averaging ~13-15, "somewhat hard" to "hard") were NOT different between groups and not altered by training.
- Overall adherence was 97% (98% for REHIT10, 96% for REHIT20).
- Both protocols were deemed acceptable by participants, with no significant differences in acceptability ratings.

CONCLUSIONS: Reducing sprint duration in the REHIT protocol from 20s to 10s attenuates improvements in VO2max and does NOT result in more positive affective responses or lower perceived exertion. The authors conclude that in protocols with very few sprints, sprint duration should be longer than 10 seconds, supporting the original REHIT protocol of 2 × 20-s sprints as the protocol of choice. This is the first study to provide data on acute effects of REHIT on affective responses and mood state, and it contrasts with criticism of SIT protocols as being too strenuous for untrained individuals (Hardcastle et al. 2014). The findings support REHIT as an efficacious, time-efficient (3 × 10 min per week), and acceptable alternative to classic SIT and moderate-intensity continuous training.

# REHIT Workout: The 10-Minute Protocol That Raises VO2 Max

By Cristian Serb · Updated July 27, 2026

![Women sprinting on stationary bikes during an indoor cycling session](/public/blog/rehit-workout.webp "Women sprinting on stationary bikes during an indoor cycling session")  [![](/public/peakvo2-app-icon.svg) Run these workouts on your iPhone, or hands-free on Apple Watch. Get PEAKVO2](https://apps.apple.com/app/apple-store/id6532617265?pt=72776&ct=article-top&mt=8) 

**REHIT (reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training) is the shortest evidence-backed cardio workout there is: a 10-minute session containing just two all-out 20-second sprints on a bike, done three times a week. In the original controlled trial, six weeks of REHIT raised VO2 max by 15 percent in men and 12 percent in women, from 30 minutes of total weekly exercise ([Metcalfe et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22124524/)).**

If the [Norwegian 4x4](/blog/norwegian-4x4-protocol/) is the heavyweight of VO2 max training, REHIT is the minimalist: it asks the least total time and the least suffering per session of any protocol with published results. Here is what the research actually shows, the exact workout, and where its limits are.

## What a REHIT Session Looks Like

The whole session fits in about 10 minutes on a stationary bike:

1. **2 to 3 minutes easy pedaling** to warm up (light resistance, conversational).
2. **Sprint 1: 20 seconds all-out.** Not hard, not "9 out of 10": genuinely maximal, against high resistance, like your life depends on it.
3. **3 to 4 minutes easy pedaling** to recover.
4. **Sprint 2: 20 seconds all-out.**
5. **2 to 3 minutes easy pedaling** to cool down.

That is the entire workout: two sprints, roughly 40 seconds of real work, done three times a week. The original study built up to it, starting with 10-second sprints in week one and 15-second sprints in weeks two and three before settling at 20 seconds, which is a sensible on-ramp if you are new to all-out efforts.

A bike is the right tool for this. All-out running sprints from a standing start carry real hamstring risk and take seconds to reach full power; on a bike against resistance you are at maximal effort almost instantly, safely.

## What the Research Shows

REHIT comes out of Niels Vollaard's lab at the University of Bath, built on a simple question: how little high-intensity work still produces adaptation?

**The original trial** put 29 sedentary adults through six weeks of the protocol above. VO2 max rose 15 percent in men and 12 percent in women, and insulin sensitivity improved 28 percent in men, all from 10-minute sessions that participants rated as only moderately hard (RPE 13 of 20), which is the "reduced exertion" in the name ([Metcalfe et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22124524/)).

**Why only two sprints?** A meta-analysis across 34 sprint-training studies found that adding more sprints per session did not produce bigger VO2 max gains; if anything, the trend pointed the other way ([Vollaard et al., 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28079707/)). The first all-out sprint appears to trigger most of the signal (rapid glycogen breakdown and strong sympathetic activation); repeating it twenty times adds fatigue faster than it adds adaptation.

**Why 20 seconds?** A follow-up study cut the sprints from 20 to 10 seconds and the VO2 max improvement shrank measurably, without the sessions feeling any easier ([Nalçakan et al., 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29172029/)). Twenty seconds is the studied dose; the app protocol below uses exactly that.

**Does it work outside the lab?** In type 2 diabetes patients, REHIT improved VO2 max more than five 30-minute moderate walking sessions per week, on a fraction of the time ([Ruffino et al., 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28121184/)).

## REHIT vs Tabata vs Norwegian 4x4

All three are intervals; they occupy different points on the time-versus-dose curve.

| REHIT | Tabata | Norwegian 4x4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Session length | ~10 min | ~14 min with warm-up | ~38 min |
| Hard work per session | 40 seconds | 4 minutes | 16 minutes |
| Intensity | All-out sprints | All-out intervals | 90-95% of max HR |
| Documented VO2 max gain | 12-15% in 6 weeks (untrained) | Large, in athletes | 7.2% in 8 weeks (trained) |
| Best for | Minimal time, getting started | Short sessions, conditioned athletes | Maximum stimulus, structured training |

The honest framing: the spectacular REHIT percentages come from sedentary beginners, who improve fast on almost any stimulus; the [4x4's 7.2 percent](/blog/norwegian-4x4-protocol/) was measured in already-trained subjects. If you are starting from the couch or your week is genuinely full, REHIT is the highest return per minute in the literature. As fitness grows, the ceiling of 40 weekly seconds of work arrives, and protocols with more time at high intensity, like the 4x4 or [Tabata](/blog/tabata-vs-norwegian-4x4/), take over. Many people run both: REHIT on crowded weeks, 4x4 in focused blocks.

## How to Run REHIT (Without Buying a Special Bike)

REHIT is marketed hard by makers of AI exercise bikes that cost as much as a used car. You do not need one: the protocol is two timed sprints on any stationary bike with adjustable resistance, and the timing is the only thing that needs automating.

PEAKVO2 has the protocol built in as **REHIT 2x20**, a 9-minute guided session: the app walks you through warm-up, counts down each 20-second sprint with a full-screen color change and haptic cues, and paces the recoveries. Start it, put the phone on the handlebars or wear the watch, and give the two sprints everything.

Two practical notes. First, all-out means all-out: the protocol's entire effect hangs on those 40 seconds being genuinely maximal, so set the resistance high enough that you cannot hold the sprint past 20 seconds. Second, if you are untrained, older, or have any cardiovascular risk factors, get medical clearance before adding all-out sprints; they are the most intense thing you can do on a bike.

Track the result the same way as any VO2 max training: your [Apple Watch cardio fitness score](/blog/improve-apple-watch-cardio-fitness/), [Fitbit](/blog/fitbit-vo2-max/), or [Whoop](/blog/whoop-vo2-max/) will show the trend, or test yourself with the [VO2 max calculator](/tools/vo2-max-calculator/) every 4 to 8 weeks.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does REHIT stand for?

Reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training. The name comes from the research goal: keeping the proven VO2 max stimulus of sprint training while cutting the number of sprints to the minimum that still works, which turned out to be two per session.

### How is REHIT different from HIIT?

Dose. A typical HIIT session accumulates many hard intervals (Tabata: eight, a 4x4: sixteen hard minutes); REHIT uses exactly two all-out 20-second sprints inside an otherwise easy 10-minute ride. Research found that adding more sprints per session did not increase the VO2 max gain, which is the insight REHIT is built on.

### Does REHIT really work?

In controlled trials, yes: 12 to 15 percent VO2 max improvement in six weeks in sedentary adults, plus a 28 percent insulin sensitivity improvement in men, from three 10-minute sessions a week. The caveat: those subjects started untrained. The fitter you are, the less 40 seconds of weekly work can move, and longer protocols take over.

### Do I need a special AI bike for REHIT?

No. The studied protocol is two timed all-out sprints on an ordinary stationary bike with enough resistance. What you need is the timing and the honesty to sprint maximally; an interval app with countdowns and haptic cues handles the first part.

### How many times a week should I do REHIT?

Three sessions per week is the studied frequency, on non-consecutive days. Because each session contains only 40 seconds of true work, recovery demand is low, but the sprints only work if they stay genuinely all-out, so do not stack them daily.

### Can I do REHIT by running instead of cycling?

Cycling is strongly preferred. All-out efforts from a standing start are hard on hamstrings when running, and it takes seconds to reach full power on foot; on a bike against high resistance you are at maximal output almost immediately and safely. If you have no bike, hill sprints are the safer running approximation.

3 INTRODUCTION As perceived lack of time is commonly reported as a barrier to exercise (Trost et al. 2002), there is a need to identify time-efficient exercise interventions for reducing the risk of inactivity-related noncommunicable diseases. Sprint interval training (SIT; repeated ‘all-out’ sprints of 20-30 s) aims to provide a time-efficient alternative to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) (Vollaard & Metcalfe 2017), but the total training time commitment of the ‘classic’ SIT protocol (4-6 x 30-s ‘all-out’ sprints (Burgomaster et al. 2005)) is greater than that of American recommendations for vigorous exercise (~90 min/week vs. 75 min/week (Garber et al. 2011)). It has previously been shown that the training time commitment of the classic SIT protocol can be substantially reduced while remaining efficacious at improving key health markers such as maximal aerobic capacity (V̇O2max), insulin sensitivity and blood pressure (Gillen et al. 2016; Metcalfe et al. 2012; Ruffino et al. 2017). The reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training (REHIT) protocol (Metcalfe et al. 2012) consists of two 20-second ‘all-out’ sprints within an otherwise low-intensity 10-minute exercise session. As long as the associated health benefits are not affected, reducing the total volume of sprint exercise in a SIT protocol could be expected to enhance the uptake of, and adherence to, SIT (Reljic et al. 2019). Reducing sprint duration only has a small effect on overall training time requirement, and we have previously demonstrated that, in the REHIT protocol, performing 10-second ‘all-out’ sprints is less effective at improving V̇O2max compared to 20-second sprints (Nalcakan et al. 2018). Conversely, reducing the number of sprint repetitions in a SIT session has a large effect on overall training time-commitment, as this also reduces the number of relatively lengthy recovery periods. In a recent meta-analysis, we demonstrated that performing as few as 2 sprint repetitions within a SIT session is sufficient for improving V̇O2max, with no apparent added benefit of performing additional sprints (Vollaard et al. 2017). Apart from sprint duration and number of sprint repetitions, a final approach to reducing the total volume of sprint exercise in a SIT protocol is to reduce the training frequency. A small number of Page 3 of 15 Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by UNIVERSITY OF BRIGHTON on 02/27/20. For personal use only.
4 studies investigating the effects of repeated sprint training (RST; repeated ‘all-out’ sprints of <20 s) (Adamson et al. 2014) and high-intensity interval training (HIIT; repeated (sub-)maximal sprints of ≥60 s) (Stavrinou et al. 2018) have demonstrated significant improvements in V̇O2max with just 2 training sessions/week for 8 weeks, but to the best of our knowledge, the effect of training frequency on improvements in V̇O2max in response to SIT has not yet been studied. Similar to REHIT, most commonly studied SIT protocols involve a training frequency of 3 sessions/week (Vollaard et al. 2017). It is possible that a lower training frequency would enhance uptake of, and adherence to, an exercise routine. Conversely, a higher training frequency could be expected to result in greater improvements in key cardiometabolic health markers. Thus, the aim of the present study was to determine the effect of training frequency (2, 3 or 4 sessions/week) on changes in V̇O2max in response to 6 weeks of REHIT in inactive individuals. We hypothesised that a greater training frequency would increase the magnitude of adaptations, with the greatest improvements with a training frequency of 4 sessions/week. Page 4 of 15 Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by UNIVERSITY OF BRIGHTON on 02/27/20. For personal use only.
5 MATERIALS AND METHODS Participants Apparently healthy, inactive participants were recruited at 4 sites in the UK (Derry/Londonderry, Stirling, Swansea, Worcester), and randomised into groups performing the REHIT protocol as previously described by Metcalfe et al. (2012), but involving either 2 (REHIT2), 3 (REHIT3) or 4 (REHIT4) training sessions per week. Randomisation was performed using the sealed envelope method. Exclusion criteria were classification as highly physically active according to the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), contraindications to exercise as determined using a standard physical activity readiness questionnaire (PAR-Q), clinically significant hypertension (>140/90 mm Hg), or resting heart rate ≥100 beats·min-1. Forty-nine participants volunteered to take part, but 7 participants dropped out of the study (REHIT3: n=3 (reasons: lack of time for all); REHIT4: n=4 (unrelated medical issue, pregnancy, lack of time)). Characteristics of the remaining participants are shown in Supplementary Table S1 (Worcester: n=18, Stirling: n=9, Swansea: n=9, Ulster: n=6). Participants were asked not to change their normal diet and/or physical activity patterns for the duration of the study. The study received University Ethics approval (NICR(17/18-16); 2016-111). All participants provided written consent after full written and verbal explanation of the study protocol.
Experimental Procedures An incremental cycling test to exhaustion was used to determine V̇O2max (Excalibur Sport, Lode, Groningen, the Netherlands; CV: ~4%). An online gas analyser was used to measure oxygen uptake (Oxycon Pro, Jaeger; Jaegar Vyntus, Vyaire Medical Products; Cortex Metalyzer, Cortex; Quark C-PET, Cosmed). Participants were requested not to perform strenuous exercise and/or to consume caffeine or alcohol on the day prior to testing, and to drink a pint of water in the morning before testing. The test started with a 5-min warm-up (50 W), after which the intensity was increased by 1 W every 3 s until volitional exhaustion. V̇O2max was determined as the highest value of a 15-breath rolling Page 5 of 15 Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by UNIVERSITY OF BRIGHTON on 02/27/20. For personal use only.
6 average, and accepted if ≥2 of the following criteria were met: 1) volitional exhaustion, 2) RER>1.15, and 3) maximal heart rate within 10 beats of the age-predicted maximum (i.e. 220-age). This was the case for all participants. Participants subsequently performed six weeks of REHIT consisting of 2, 3 or 4 exercise sessions per week. REHIT sessions involved 10 min of unloaded cycling interspersed with 2 all-out sprints against a resistance of 7.5% of the participant’s body mass (Ergomedic 874e, Monark, Sweden). Sprint duration was 10 s in week 1, 15 s in week 2, and 20 s in the remaining 4 weeks. The first sprint finished at 2 min and the second sprint finished at 7 min. A questionnaire on the acceptability of the intervention (Boereboom et al. 2016) was completed after the last exercise session. The post-training V̇O2max test was scheduled 3 days following the last training session. Data on RPE and acute changes in affect in response to REHIT training sessions was collected, but this data is presented in a previous publication (Songsorn et al. 2019). Statistical analysis Data are presented as mean±SD. To detect differences in the change in V̇O2max between the three groups with an effect size of f=0.5, power of 80% and α=0.05, at least 12 participants were required in each group. Two-way mixed model ANOVA (group (REHIT2/REHIT3/REHIT4)) × time (pre/post)) was used to determine differences between the groups for ΔV̇O2max and for Δbody mass. A Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to determine differences between the three groups for intervention acceptability. Significance was accepted at p<0.05. Page 6 of 15 Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by UNIVERSITY OF BRIGHTON on 02/27/20. For personal use only.
7 RESULTS Overall mean adherence (% of prescribed training sessions completed) was not significantly different between the three groups (99% for REHIT2, 98% for REHIT3, 99% for REHIT4). No significant changes from pre- to post-intervention were observed for body mass (REHIT2: 84.5±20.7 vs. 84.5±20.6 kg; REHIT3: 70.6±15.9 vs. 71.1±16.0 kg; REHIT4: 79.3±7.8 vs. 78.8±7.3 kg). There was a significant improvement in absolute V̇O2max (+8.7%; main effect of time: p<0.001), but no significant group*time interaction effect, indicating similar improvements in the 3 groups (REHIT2: +10.2%, REHIT3: +8.1%, REHIT 4: +7.3%; Figure 1). Acceptability of the 3 REHIT interventions was good (Supplementary Table S2). On average, participants’ responses indicated that they thought REHIT was enjoyable, that is wasn’t a time-burden, that the physical strain and traveling involved with REHIT did not interfere with their life, that they would continue doing REHIT, and that they would recommend REHIT to others. Participants did tend towards agreeing that REHIT was more demanding than expected. There were no significant differences between the 3 groups for any of the responses. Page 7 of 15 Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by UNIVERSITY OF BRIGHTON on 02/27/20. For personal use only.
8 DISCUSSION To date the vast majority of studied SIT protocols have used a training frequency of 3 sessions/week, but to the best of our knowledge, no papers have studied if, or justified why, this would be the ‘optimal’ training frequency (e.g. either the lowest training volume to achieve a given mean improvement in V̇O2max, or the training dose with the greatest mean improvement in V̇O2max). Thus, the present study aimed to determine the effect of training frequency (2, 3 or 4 sessions/week) on changes in V̇O2max in response to 6 weeks of REHIT in inactive individuals. For the first time, we demonstrate that performing 2 REHIT sessions per week for 6 weeks is sufficient to significantly improve V̇O2max, and that performing 3 or 4 sessions/week does not significantly augment the magnitude of improvement. Thus, similar to the number of sprints within a SIT session (Vollaard et al. 2017), the total volume of sprint exercise per week does not appear to be a main driver of adaptations to V̇O2max for SIT. This finding is important, because lack of time is commonly reported as a barrier to exercise (Kimm et al. 2006; Korkiakangas et al. 2009; Trost et al. 2002), and reducing the number of training sessions per week from 3 to 2 has a large effect on the total required time commitment. The lack of a significantly greater improvement in V̇O2max with 3 or 4 REHIT sessions/week compared to 2 sessions/week is contrary to our hypothesis. A greater training volume is generally expected to enhance adaptations (Church et al. 2007), but it appears that a low dose of REHIT (2 sessions/week) is sufficient to stimulate the mechanisms by which REHIT induces improvements in V̇O2max to a similar extent as with higher doses (3 or 4 sessions/week). Some support for our finding comes from a recent study by Stavrinou et al. (2019), who reported that improvements in V̇O2max with twice-weekly HIIT (10 x 60 s cycling at ~83% of peak power) are not significantly different from those with the same protocol performed three times/week.
It remains unknown whether greater training frequencies (>4 sessions/week) could increase the magnitude of improvements in V̇O2max, or whether a lower training frequency (1 session/week) would be sufficient. This will need to be established in future studies. Page 8 of 15 Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by UNIVERSITY OF BRIGHTON on 02/27/20. For personal use only.
9 There are a number of limitations to our study that need to be highlighted. Firstly, although we did not observe a significant difference in the magnitude of improvements in V̇O2max between REHIT protocols performed 2, 3 or 4 times/week, the study was not powered to test for statistical equivalence of the improvements. Secondly, we did not stratify the groups in any way, so we cannot exclude potential confounding effects of for example sex or baseline V̇O2max, nor can we exclude a possible confounding effect through the use of different gas analysers in our multi-centre approach. Thirdly, we only studied the effect of training frequency on changes in V̇O2max, so it remains unknown whether training frequency may affect adaptations for other important health markers such as blood pressure, insulin sensitivity, or body composition. args.summary: This is a scientific research paper (randomised-controlled trial) investigating the effect of REHIT (reduced-exertion high-intensity interval training) frequency on maximal aerobic capacity (V̇O2max) in inactive individuals. The study, published in Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism, involved 42 inactive participants (13 women; mean±SD age: 25±5 y, V̇O2max: 35±5 mL·kg-1·min-1) recruited from 4 UK sites (Derry/Londonderry, Stirling, Swansea, Worcester). Participants were randomised into three groups performing REHIT at either 2, 3, or 4 sessions/week for 6 weeks. REHIT sessions consisted of 10 minutes of unloaded cycling interspersed with two all-out sprints against 7.5% of body mass resistance (10s sprints in week 1, 15s in week 2, 20s in weeks 3-6). Results showed no significant difference in V̇O2max improvements between groups (2 sessions/week: +10.2%; 3 sessions/week: +8.1%; 4 sessions/week: +7.3%), with overall significant improvement in absolute V̇O2max (+8.7%; p<0.001). Adherence was high (98-99% across groups), no significant changes in body mass, and intervention acceptability was good. The authors conclude that 2 sessions/week is sufficient for REHIT to improve V̇O2max, and that reducing training frequency from 3-4 to 2 sessions/week does not attenuate improvements. This is contrary to the authors' hypothesis that higher frequency would produce greater improvements. Limitations include the study not being powered to test statistical equivalence, lack of stratification for confounding variables (sex, baseline V̇O2max, different gas analysers), and only V̇O2max being studied (not blood pressure, insulin sensitivity, or body composition). The finding supports the notion that the total weekly sprint exercise volume is not a main driver of V̇O2max adaptations in SIT, and is important given that lack of time is a commonly reported barrier to exercise.

The most common HIIT prescription was 4×4-minute intervals at 85-95% of maximum/peak heart rate, interspersed with 3 minutes of active recovery at 60-70% HRmax/peak, three times per week for 12-16 weeks. Brachial artery FMD improved by 4.31% following HIIT and 2.15% following MICT, resulting in a significant mean difference of 2.26% (p<0.05, I²=68%). When the 2-week outlier study was removed, the mean difference increased to 2.45%.

KEY FINDINGS:
- HIIT improved FMD more than MICT (pre vs. post: 5.14% to 9.45% for HIIT; 5.12% to 7.27% for MICT)
- No change in GTN-mediated (vascular-independent) dilation in either group, indicating FMD improvements reflect endothelial-level restoration
- HIIT had greater tendency to positively affect cardiorespiratory fitness (14-46% vs. 5-16% improvement), traditional CVD risk factors, oxidative stress, inflammation, and insulin sensitivity
- Longer-interval HIIT (4×4 min) appeared more effective than shorter-interval HIIT (1-min bouts)
- PGC-1α protein increased 47-138% following HIIT, with no change in MICT groups
- No significant between-group differences in body fat reduction, hsCRP, or shear rate
- 4×4 HIIT significantly reduced ambulatory systolic blood pressure more than MICT (12 vs. 4.5 mmHg)

CONCLUSION: HIIT is more effective than MICT at improving brachial artery vascular function, potentially due to its greater influence on CRF, CVD risk factors, oxidative stress, inflammation, and insulin sensitivity. The review suggests 4×4 HIIT (three times per week for at least 12 weeks) is a powerful exercise form to enhance vascular function, though variability in secondary outcomes and small sample sizes limit the findings.

LIMITATIONS: Most participants were on medications known to improve vascular function; four studies came from the same laboratory in Norway; substantial heterogeneity was detected (I²=68%).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Brachial artery FMD improved by 4.31 and 2.15 % following HIIT and MICT, respectively. This resulted in a significant (p<0.05) mean difference of 2.26 %."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1440244018309198

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (Volume 22, Issue 8, August 2019, Pages 941-947) titled "Effects of different protocols of high intensity interval training for VO2max improvements in adults: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials." The study was conducted by Daizong Wen, Till Utesch, Jun Wu, Samuel Robertson, John Liu, Guopeng Hu, and Haichun Chen (DOI: 10.1016/j.jsams.2019.01.013).

OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of different HIIT protocols on VO2max improvements in healthy, overweight/obese, and athletic adults, based on classifications of work intervals, session volumes, and training periods.

METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Medline, and Web of Science databases were searched up to April 2018. Inclusion criteria were randomised controlled trials involving healthy, overweight/obese, or athletic adults, examining pre- and post-training VO2max/peak, with HIIT compared to control or moderate intensity continuous training (MICT) groups.

RESULTS: Of 1,190 articles initially identified, 53 studies met eligibility criteria. The degree of change in VO2max induced by HIIT varied by populations (SMD=0.41–1.81, p<0.05). Compared to control groups, even short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term HIIT (≤4 weeks) elicited clear beneficial effects (SMD=0.79–1.65, p<0.05) on VO2max/peak. However, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT displayed significantly larger effects on VO2max (SMD=0.50–2.48, p<0.05). When compared to MICT, only long-interval, high-volume, and moderate to long-term HIIT showed beneficial effects (SMD=0.65–1.07, p<0.05).

CONCLUSIONS: Short-interval (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min), and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT are effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2max, especially for the general population. To maximize training effects on VO2max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min), and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended. The study was supported by the Key Laboratory of Physical Motor Function Assessment, General Administration of Sport of China. The article has been cited 218 times and is part of the JSAMS Highlights 2018 and 2019 special issue. The authors reported no conflicts of interest.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Short-intervals (≤30 s), low-volume (≤5 min) and short-term (≤4 weeks) HIIT represent effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2 max, especially for the general population. To maximize the training effects on VO2 max, long-interval (≥2 min), high-volume (≥15 min) and moderate to long-term (≥4–12 weeks) HIIT are recommended."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: VO2max (VO2peak) in elite athletes under high-intensity interval training: A meta-analysis ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10279791

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in Heliyon (June 1, 2023) examining the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on VO2 max (VO2 peak) in elite athletes. The study, authored by Xianghua Ma, Zhenbo Cao, Zheng Zhu, Xiangru Chen, Donglin Wen, and Ziwei Cao from Shanghai University of Sport and Xi'an Physical Education University, China, was funded by the Science and Technology Department of Shaanxi Province (grant no. 2021JM-529).

METHODOLOGY: A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted across four databases (LISTA, PubMed, Web of Science, and China National Knowledge Internet) from inception to March 2022. Nine studies (8 English, 1 Chinese) met inclusion criteria, comprising 176 elite athletes (80 female) across sports including kayaking, tennis, taekwondo, triathlon, and cycling. Inclusion criteria required published experimental studies with a control group, focus on high-level (national-level competition) athletes, HIIT training period ≥3 weeks, ≥2 sessions per week, and specified training intensity. Study quality was assessed using the PEDro scale (average score 7.2/11; 6 studies low risk, 3 moderate risk). Meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.3 with weighted mean difference and 95% confidence intervals.

KEY RESULTS: Compared to conventional training (continuous training, repeated-sprint training, high-volume low-intensity training, high-intensity continuous running, sprint-interval training, moderate-intensity continuous training), VO2 max was significantly increased after HIIT (overall effect size: 0.58 [0.30, 0.87], P=0.03, I²=0.49). Significant subgroup findings included: males (0.41 [0.06, 0.76], P=0.89, I²=0%), recovery interval ≥2 min (0.44 [0.03, 0.84], P=0.99, I²=0%), recovery phase intensity ≤40% (0.38 [0.05, 0.71], P=0.96, I²=0%), control training intensity ≤75% (0.42 [0.11, 0.73], P=0.008), and taekwondo/tennis/kayaking athletes (0.99 [0.50, 1.48], P<0.0001, though with high heterogeneity I²=80%).

DISCUSSION & MECHANISMS: The study proposes that HIIT improves VO2 max through increased cardiac output (with peak stroke volume occurring during intermittent recovery periods, requiring interval durations not less than 60 seconds), enhanced recruitment of fast oxidative and glycolytic muscle fibers, increased mitochondrial enzyme activity, improved ventilation threshold, enhanced lipid oxidation, and improved cardiovascular function. HIIT intensities that showed improvement included 90-100% of HRmax, VO2 max, MAP, and other maximal parameters. HIIT also improves anaerobic capacity (~12% improvement) through enhanced glycolysis capacity, muscle buffering capacity, and fast-twitch muscle development.

LIMITATIONS: Only 9 articles were included; 4 did not divide subjects by gender; 7 studies had small samples (<10 subjects); and HIIT regimens varied significantly across studies in exercise style, interval time, intensity, and duration.

CONCLUSIONS: HIIT shows superiority over conventional training methods in improving VO2 max and aerobic capacity in elite athletes. This is the first meta-analysis of HIIT effects specifically in elite athletes. Practical implications include that coaches should select HIIT forms according to training purpose, and athletes should undergo both aerobic and anaerobic training. Recovery intensity and duration of HIIT play important roles in cardiopulmonary function of endurance athletes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Compared to that with conventional training, VO 2 max was significantly increased after HIIT (overall: 0.58 [0.30, 0.87], I 2=0.49, P=0.03; males: 0.41 [0.06, 0.76], I 2=0%, P=0.89)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Effects of Low-Volume High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) on Fitness in Adults: A Meta-Analysis of Controlled and Non-Controlled Trials ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4072920

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in Sports Medicine (2014 Apr 18; 44(7):1005-1017; DOI: 10.1007/s40279-014-0180-z; PMCID: PMC4072920; PMID: 24743927) by Matthew Weston, Kathryn L Taylor, Alan M Batterham, and Will G Hopkins, titled "Effects of Low-Volume High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) on Fitness in Adults: A Meta-Analysis of Controlled and Non-Controlled Trials."

**Objective:** To estimate meta-analysed mean effects of low-volume HIT on aerobic power (VO2max in an incremental test) and sprint fitness (peak and mean power in a 30-s Wingate test).

**Methods:**
- Five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, BIOSIS, Web of Science) searched for original research up to January 2014
- Inclusion criteria: fitness assessed pre/post-training, training ≥2 weeks, repetition duration 30–60 s, work/rest ratio <1.0, maximal or near-maximal intensity, adults >18 years
- Final dataset: 55 estimates from 32 trials for VO2max (11 controlled), 23 estimates from 16 trials for peak sprint power (3 controlled), 19 estimates from 12 trials for mean sprint power (3 controlled)
- Effects analysed as percentages via log transformation; mixed-model meta-regression (SAS Proc Mixed) with fixed effects including study type, sex, training status, baseline fitness, and training parameters
- Probabilistic magnitude-based inferences using standardized thresholds (0.2, 0.6, 1.2 for small, moderate, large)
- 550 potentially eligible studies initially screened; typical protocol was 4–6 × 30-s all-out efforts with ~4 min recovery

**Key Results:**
- Mean low-volume HIT protocol (13 training sessions, 0.16 work/rest ratio) in controlled trials produced a likely moderate improvement in VO2max of active non-athletic males (6.2%; 90% CL ±3.1%)
- Possibly moderate improvements in VO2max: sedentary males (10.0%; ±5.1%), active non-athletic females (3.6%; ±4.3%); likely small increase for sedentary females (7.3%; ±4.8%)
- Effect on VO2max of athletic males was unclear (2.7%; ±4.6%)
- A possibly moderate additional increase was likely for subjects with a 10 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ lower baseline VO2max (3.8%; ±2.5%)
- Modifying effects of sex and exercise dose were unclear
- Comparison of HIT with traditional endurance training was unclear (−1.6%; ±4.3%)
- Unexplained variation between studies: 2.0% (SD)
- Meta-analysed effects of HIT on Wingate peak and mean power were unclear
- No evidence of publication bias in funnel plot analyses

**Conclusion:** Low-volume HIT produces moderate improvements in the aerobic power of active non-athletic and sedentary subjects. More studies are needed to resolve unclear modifying effects of sex and HIT dose on aerobic power and the unclear effects on sprint fitness.

**Background context:** The authors note that HIT is considered one of the most effective means of improving cardiorespiratory and metabolic function. They compare their findings to prior meta-analyses (Sloth et al. reporting standardized effect 0.63; Gist et al. reporting 0.69 vs. no-exercise controls and 0.04 vs. endurance-training controls). The study excluded HIT research using longer intervals (1–4 min) at high but not maximal intensity with work:rest ratio ≥1.0, acknowledging this as a limitation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A mean low-volume HIT protocol (13 training sessions, 0.16 work/rest ratio) in a controlled trial produced a likely moderate improvement in the VO2max of active non-athletic males (6.2%; 90% confidence limits ±3.1%), when compared with control."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: VO 2 max Trainability and High Intensity Interval Training in ... ---
URL: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0073182

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PLOS ONE scientific research article titled "VO2max Trainability and High Intensity Interval Training in Humans: A Meta-Analysis" by Bacon AP, Carter RE, Ogle EA, and Joyner MJ (2013). The study challenges the notion that some individuals have limited or non-existent "trainability" (ability to increase VO2max) in response to endurance training.

The researchers analyzed 37 studies published in English from 1965-2012 that used interval training (IT) or combined interval and continuous training (CT). Inclusion criteria required: ≥3 healthy sedentary/recreationally active humans under 45 years old, training duration of 6-13 weeks, ≥3 days/week, ≥10 minutes of high intensity work, ≥1:1 work/rest ratio, and results reported as mean ± SD or SE. A random effects model was used due to heterogeneity (I²=70).

KEY FINDINGS:
- 334 subjects (120 women) from 37 studies, grouped into 40 distinct training groups
- Mean increase in VO2max of 0.51 L·min⁻¹ (95% CI: 0.43-0.60 L·min⁻¹; p<0.001)
- Standardized effect size of 0.86 SDs (95% CI: 0.72-0.99 SDs)
- A subset of 9 studies with longer intervals (3-5 min) showed even larger changes (~0.8-0.9 L·min⁻¹) with marked responses in ALL subjects
- Trim and Fill analysis suggested potential publication bias (adjusted estimate: 0.37 L·min⁻¹), but Rosenthal's fail-safe N was 4531, indicating the findings are robust
- Fixed effects model sensitivity analysis: 0.45 L·min⁻¹ (95% CI: 0.41-0.49 L·min⁻¹)

CONTEXT: This contrasts with the Heritage Study (Bouchard et al.), which used 20 weeks of moderate continuous training and found a mean VO2max increase of only ~0.4 L·min⁻¹, with 7% of subjects showing gains of 0.1 L·min⁻¹ or less (suggesting "non-responders"). The authors argue that trainability biology should be evaluated using regimens designed to maximize physiological adaptations (high intensity, ~90% VO2max), not just public health guideline-style training.

The "Hickson protocol" (10 weeks, 6 days/week, alternating interval training at near-VO2max intensity and high-intensity continuous running) produced the largest improvements. The authors caution that the extreme arduousness of such programs may make them unrealistic for the general population, but conclude that the idea that some humans are genetically incapable of increasing VO2max should be re-evaluated with standardized IT/IT-CT programs.

LIMITATIONS: Retrospective analysis, wide variability in training programs, ~2/3 of subjects were likely Caucasian young men, no genetic data, and potential publication bias. The article was published September 16, 2013, edited by Conrad P. Earnest (University of Bath), with funding from NCATS, the Mayo Foundation, and the Caywood Professorship.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The main finding of this meta-analysis is that interval training produces improvements in VO2max slightly greater than those typically reported with what might be described as adult fitness based continuous training even though many of the studies were of short duration with limited training sessions per week."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 5: Comparison of different interval training methods on athletes’ oxygen uptake: a systematic review with pairwise and network meta-analysis ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13102-025-01191-6

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a scientific research article titled "Comparison of different interval training methods on athletes' oxygen uptake: a systematic review with pairwise and network meta-analysis," published on 02 July 2025 in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (Volume 17, article number 156). The study was authored by Qiushi Yang, Junli Wang, and Dongyang Guan, and is registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023435021). The article has received 11k accesses and 8 citations.

OBJECTIVE: To examine the effect size and ranking of training effects for high-intensity interval training (HIIT), sprint interval training (SIT), and repeated sprint training (RST) on athletes' VO2 max through network meta-analysis, and to investigate the effects of training program protocols of the three methods through pairwise meta-analysis and meta-regression.

METHODS: A systematic search of four databases (Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus) was conducted on April 1, 2025. A total of 51 eligible studies (1,261 athletes) were included, evaluating direct/indirect effects of HIIT, SIT, RST versus continuous training (CT) and conventional training (CON). A frequentist network meta-analysis (using the netmeta package in R) quantified effect sizes (Hedges' g) and probabilistic rankings (P-scores), while three-level meta-regression modeled dose-response relationships. Methodological quality was assessed using the 11-item PEDro scale, with scores ranging from 4 to 7 (fair-to-good).

RESULTS: All three interval training methods significantly increased VO2 max compared to CON, with NMA rankings: RST (g = 1.04) > HIIT (g = 1.01) > SIT (g = 0.69) > CT (g = 0.29). No significant differences existed among RST, HIIT, and SIT (p > 0.05). CT's effect was not significant (g = 0.29, p = 0.11). Subgroup analyses showed HIIT efficacy was moderated by athlete level, whereas SIT improvements were influenced by intervention duration, training frequency, and training mode. For SIT, the running mode (g = 2.44) produced greater increases than cycling (g = 0.69) or rowing (g = 0.49) modes. Meta-regression identified inverted U-shaped relationships for HIIT, with peak benefits at 140 s work duration and a work-to-recovery ratio of 0.85. For SIT, improvements were not significant when recovery durations exceeded 97 s.

CONCLUSIONS: RST, HIIT, and SIT all enhance VO2 max in athletes, with RST demonstrating the strongest probabilistic efficacy. Optimal protocols include 3-6 weeks of running-based HIIT (140 s work, 165 s recovery) or SIT (≤ 30 s sprints, < 97 s recovery) at 3 sessions per week. Conducting RST 3 sessions a week for two weeks is sufficient to achieve improvements.

The network meta-analysis included 10 study designs with 62 pairwise comparisons, showing moderate heterogeneity (τ² = 0.13, I² = 36%). The between-design inconsistency test showed no statistical significance (Q = 3.05, p = 0.88), supporting the transitivity hypothesis. Credibility assessment (CINeMA) ranged from high to very low confidence, primarily due to limited direct comparisons and high heterogeneity. Confidence was moderate and high for HIIT and RST respectively versus CON, low for SIT versus CON, and very low for RST versus CT due to no direct comparisons.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"All three interval training methods significantly increased VO2 max compared to CON, with NMA rankings: RST (NMA's g = 1.04) > HIIT (NMA's g = 1.01) > SIT (NMA's g = 0.69) > CT (NMA's g = 0.29), no significant differences existed among RST, HIIT, and SIT (p > 0.05)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Frontiers | Comparative effects of high-intensity and sprint interval training on cardiorespiratory fitness and body composition: a systematic review with meta-analysis ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1668326/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review with meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Physiology (11 November 2025, Volume 16, DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1668326) comparing the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and sprint interval training (SIT) on cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and body composition, with subgroup analyses based on baseline fitness status.

**Methods:** Nine randomized controlled trials (n = 666 participants) were included, registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251016362, registered 15 March 2025). The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and the Cochrane Handbook (v6.4). Literature was searched across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and SPORTDiscus from inception to 15 March 2025. Primary outcomes were changes in VO2max/VO2peak and body fat percentage. Analysis used SMD or WMD with 95% CIs, with subgroup analyses stratified by population type (healthy/trained vs. overweight/obese). From 379 retrieved studies, 9 eligible RCTs were included. Six studies had low risk of bias and 3 had moderate risk; none had high risk. Participants were young adults aged 13±1 to 29±8 years, with interventions lasting 4-12 weeks using running or cycling protocols.

**Key Results:**
- Both HIIT and SIT significantly improved CRF (SMD = 1.54; 95% CI: 0.89–2.18; p < 0.00001) and reduced body fat mass (WMD = −3.45%; 95% CI: −5.04 to −1.87; p < 0.0001) compared to control.
- HIIT was significantly more effective than SIT in improving CRF overall (SMD = −0.80; p = 0.0005), and particularly among overweight/obese individuals (SMD = −0.97; p = 0.0004), with no significant difference between modalities in healthy/trained populations.
- SIT was more effective than HIIT in reducing fat mass among healthy or trained populations (WMD = 5.85; p < 0.00001), while no significant difference was observed in overweight/obese individuals.
- High heterogeneity (I² = 86% for CRF; I² = 84% for fat mass) was noted, likely reflecting differences in training protocols and participant characteristics.

**Conclusion:** Both HIIT and SIT effectively improve cardiorespiratory fitness and reduce body fat, but relative efficacy depends on baseline health status. HIIT appears optimal for individuals with lower fitness levels (overweight/obese), while SIT may be preferable for time-efficient fat reduction in trained populations. The study recommends tailoring interval training prescriptions to individual characteristics, with SIT particularly suitable for trained individuals due to its time efficiency and HIIT offering a more accessible option for lower-fit populations. The authors call for future research on protocol standardization and long-term outcomes across different groups.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Both HIIT and SIT are effective interventions for enhancing CRF and reducing body fat, but their relative efficacy may depend on participants' baseline health status. HIIT appears optimal for individuals with lower fitness levels, while SIT may be preferable for time-efficient fat reduction in trained populations."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Comparative effects of high-intensity and sprint interval training on cardiorespiratory fitness and body composition: a systematic review with meta-analysis ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12643836

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review with meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Physiology (2025) comparing the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and sprint interval training (SIT) on cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and body composition, with subgroup analyses based on participants' baseline health status.

**Background and Objective:** Both HIIT and SIT are recognized for time efficiency and health benefits, but it was unclear how baseline fitness levels influence their differential effects. The study aimed to compare HIIT vs. SIT on CRF and body fat mass, stratified by population health status.

**Methods:** Nine randomized controlled trials (n = 666) were included. Primary outcomes were changes in VO2max/VO2peak and body fat percentage. Data were synthesized using SMD or WMD with subgroup analyses stratified by population type (healthy/trained vs. overweight/obese). The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251016362; registered 15 March 2025) and followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Literature was searched across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and SPORTDiscus from inception to March 15, 2025. Quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (6 studies low risk, 3 moderate risk, none high risk). Training durations ranged from 4-12 weeks; modalities included running and cycling.

**Key Results:**
- Both HIIT and SIT significantly improved CRF (SMD = 1.54; 95% CI: 0.89–2.18; p < 0.00001) and reduced body fat mass (WMD = −3.45%; 95% CI: −5.04 to −1.87; p < 0.0001) vs. control.
- HIIT was more effective in improving CRF in overweight/obese individuals (SMD = −0.97; p = 0.0004), while no significant difference was observed between modalities in healthy/trained populations.
- SIT was more effective in reducing fat mass among healthy/trained populations (WMD = 5.85; p < 0.00001), while no significant difference was seen between HIIT and SIT in overweight/obese individuals (WMD = 0.27; p = 0.59).
- HIIT showed a large effect size on CRF (SMD = 2.04) vs. SIT's moderate effect size (SMD = 1.06), though subgroup difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.14).
- No high-risk bias studies were identified; high heterogeneity (I² = 86% for CRF, 84% for fat mass) was noted.

**Conclusions:** Both HIIT and SIT are effective for enhancing CRF and reducing body fat, but relative efficacy depends on baseline health status. HIIT appears optimal for individuals with lower fitness levels (overweight/obese), while SIT may be preferable for time-efficient fat reduction in trained populations. The study recommends tailoring interval training prescriptions to individual characteristics. SIT may be challenging in terms of tolerability and safety for individuals with compromised cardiorespiratory function, while HIIT's structured nature may be more feasible and sustainable for overweight/obese populations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Both HIIT and SIT significantly improved CRF (SMD = 1.54; 95% CI: 0.89–2.18; p < 0.00001) and reduced body fat mass (WMD = −3.45%; 95% CI: −5.04 to −1.87; p < 0.0001) compared to control."
</key_excerpts>
