# Research Report: HIIT, MICT, and Hybrid Protocols for Cardiorespiratory Fitness (VO2max/VO2peak) in Adults Aged 30-70 with Limited Weekly Training Time

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. Tavily search: "meta-analysis HIIT vs MICT cardiorespiratory fitness VO2max adults 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022"; "high-intensity interval training moderate continuous training meta-analysis VO2peak effect size 95% CI randomized controlled trial"
2. Tavily search: "low-volume high-intensity interval training sprint interval training VO2max randomized controlled trial meta-analysis 2019 2020 2021"; "sprint interval training cardiorespiratory fitness meta-analysis effect size time-efficient"
3. Tavily search: "low-volume high-intensity interval training meta-analysis Sultana 2019 VO2max cardiorespiratory fitness"; "sprint interval training meta-analysis VO2max healthy adults 2020 2021 effect size time-efficient exercise"
4. Tavily search: "Gillen 2016 low-volume interval training VO2max six 20-second sprints randomized trial"; "time-efficient exercise 1-minute high intensity interval training VO2max randomized trial 2019 2020 adults"
5. Tavily search: "Gillen 2019 randomized trial low-volume high intensity interval training 1 minute hard cycling VO2max sedentary"; "Metcalfe reduced exertion high intensity interval training REHIT two 20 second sprint VO2max randomized controlled trial 12 weeks"
6. Tavily search: "Wen 2019 meta-analysis HIIT VO2max long interval high volume 4-12 weeks recommendation"; "interval training combined continuous training hybrid protocol VO2max middle aged adults randomized trial 2020 2021 2022"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### A. META-ANALYSES: HIIT vs. MICT on Cardiorespiratory Fitness

**A1. Yang Yang et al. (2023) – HIIT vs. MICT in Older Adults**
- Source: International Journal of Sports and Exercise Medicine, 2023, Vol 9:256; systematic review and meta-analysis by Yang Yang, Cao Youxiang, Chen Jiacheng, Hu Guangxuan, Chang Bo, Yi Xuejie.
- Methods: Searched PubMed, Embase, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, Cochrane Library up to September 10, 2022; PROSPERO registration CRD42022302359. Inclusion: supervised HIIT and MICT, mean age ≥55 years, duration ≥2 weeks, exercise modalities running/cycling/elliptical. 30 studies, 1,973 subjects. Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool; REVMAN software.
- **Key results:**
  - HIIT significantly improved VO2max vs MICT: **WMD = 1.80, 95% CI: 1.25–2.35, p < 0.001**
  - HIIT improved VO2peak over controls: **WMD = 2.97, 95% CI: 2.39–3.56, p < 0.001**
  - Subgroup analysis (greatest effects on VO2peak): training period <12 weeks (WMD = 3.59); 3 sessions/week (WMD = 4.46); 20 min per intervention (WMD = 3.57); <80% intensity VO2peak (WMD = 4.47); >4 repetitions (WMD = 4.51); >60s per training session (WMD = 3.34); ≤90s rest time (WMD = 4.04)
  - Sick patients had larger effect on VO2peak vs healthy subjects (WMDs 3.85 vs 2.47)
  - HIIT significantly improved maximal heart rate (WMD = 2.68, HIIT vs MICT), ventilation (VE/VO2), and peak power output (PPO; WMD = 16.54, HIIT vs MICT)
  - 16 studies showed reduction in systolic BP (WMD = -2.59) and diastolic BP (WMD = -1.40) after HIIT, though SBP reduction not statistically superior to MICT; longer interventions (≥12 weeks) showed better SBP reduction
  - HIIT significantly improved 6-minute walk test (WMD = 51.60), time up and go test, METs, peak power output
- Conclusion: HIIT more effective than MICT in improving cardiorespiratory fitness and exercise capacity in older adults. Optimal HIIT protocol suggested: ~8 × ≤60s HIIT at <80% VO2peak with ≤90s recovery, 3 times/week for <20 minutes for <12 weeks. No serious adverse events reported. Aligns with ACSM recommendations of 20 minutes vigorous exercise 3 days/week.

**A2. Cheng et al. (2026) – HIIT vs. MICT on Body Fat and Cardiopulmonary Fitness in Adults**
- Source: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2026 Jan 24;18:94, doi: 10.1186/s13102-025-01519-2, PMID: 41580784, PMCID: PMC12911145. Authors: Hongling Cheng (Tianjin Police Institute) and colleagues from University of Birmingham (UK), Guangxi Science and Technology Normal University, Shanghai University of Sport, Beijing Academy.
- Methods: Searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science (Jan 1, 2000–Dec 31, 2024) for RCTs assessing HIIT cycling vs MICT on fat reduction and cardiorespiratory fitness. 1,326 articles + 841 via citation searching; 19 RCTs, 527 participants (HIIT: n=267; MICT: n=260). All cycling-based, 2–24 weeks, 3–5 sessions/week. SMD pooling in Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 18; GRADE assessment.
- **Key results (VO2peak):**
  - HIIT significantly improved VO2peak overall: **SMD = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.08–0.44, P=0.007**
  - Obese populations: SMD = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.01–0.45, P=0.041
  - Sedentary populations: **SMD = 6.21, 95% CI: 4.68–7.74, P<0.001**
  - Clinical populations: no significant effect
- Other results: BMI reduced overall (SMD = -0.25 kg/m², 95% CI: -0.45 to -0.06, P=0.012); reduced in obese (SMD = -0.59, 95% CI: -0.84 to -0.34, P<0.001); increased in disease populations (SMD = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.03–0.77, P=0.042); no effect in sedentary. Body fat %, fat mass, lean body mass: no significant differences between HIIT and MICT.
- GRADE: BMI, lean body mass, VO2peak MODERATE certainty; body fat and fat mass LOW. Sensitivity analysis (leave-one-out) confirmed robustness.
- Clinical recommendations: Obese individuals – HIIT on cycle ergometer (4-min intervals at 90% VO2peak with 3-min active recovery at 50% VO2peak, 3–4 times/week for >12 weeks). Comorbidities – modified low-intensity HIIT three times weekly with initial 6-week shortened period. Sedentary – progressive approach starting with lower-intensity HIIT (3 min at 75% VO2peak/3 min at 50% VO2peak) five times/week for >12 weeks, potentially extended to 24 weeks.
- Limitations: gender differences not accounted for; no age or comorbidity stratification; notable protocol variations.

**A3. Tsuji et al. (2023) – Home-Based HIIT**
- Source: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, Dec 5, 2023, Vol 15, article 166. Authors: Katsunori Tsuji, Yosuke Tsuchiya, Hisashi Ueda, Eisuke Ochi.
- Methods: Searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Igaku Chuo Zasshi through March 25, 2023. RCTs of home-based HIIT in adults regardless of disease. HIIT defined as multiple repetitions of short bursts (≤4 min) of high-intensity (≥80% HRmax); MICT defined as prolonged moderate-intensity (40-70% HRmax) continuous exercise. 15 studies (12 in quantitative meta-analysis); 5 healthy adults, 10 patients. PROSPERO CRD42021260812. PRISMA 2020.
- **Key results:**
  - Home-based HIIT superior to non-exercise controls: **SMD 0.61, 95% CI: 0.21–1.02**
  - No significant difference between home-based HIIT and lab-based HIIT: SMD -0.35, 95% CI: -0.73 to 0.03
  - No significant difference between home-based HIIT and MICT: SMD 0.34, 95% CI: -0.05 to 0.73
- Context note: "An improvement in VO2peak of 1 ml/kg/min can reduce all-cause mortality risk by 9%."

**A4. Frontiers in Physiology (2025) – HIIT vs. MICT in Cancer Survivors**
- Source: Frontiers in Physiology, June 13, 2025, doi: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1594574. Systematic review and meta-analysis. PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD420250654968. Searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, EBSCOhost up to February 2025. 12 RCTs (7 breast cancer, 3 colorectal, 2 mixed), studies from New Zealand, Australia, Canada, Iran, US, Germany (2015-2023), sample sizes 7-47, ages 39-75, durations 3-12 weeks, 2-5 days/week (mostly 3), 10-75 min/session.
- **Key result (VO2peak, 7 studies, 92 HIIT vs 78 MICT):** HIIT significantly superior: **SMD = 0.53, 95% CI (0.21–0.84), Z = 3.30, P = 0.001, I² = 0%**. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness; Egger's test no publication bias (P = 0.75).
- Subgroups: Breast cancer (5 studies, 100 subjects) SMD = 0.39, P = 0.06 (not significant); colorectal cancer (2 studies, 70 subjects) SMD = 0.74, P = 0.004 (significant).
- No significant differences in heart rate, resting heart rate, body composition, Sit-to-Stand, or 6MWT.
- Risk of bias: 8 studies high risk, 4 some concerns (blinding, randomization/allocation concealment, unblinded outcome assessors).

**A5. Conceição et al. (2026) – HIIT vs. MICT in Heart Failure**
- Source: Respiratory Medicine, Vol 253, Article 108662, March 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.rmed.2026.108662. Authors: Lino Sergio Rocha Conceição, Mansueto Gomes-Neto, Camila Souza Gama Rocha, Acauã Oliveira Coelho, Vitor Oliveira Carvalho (Universidade Federal de Sergipe, Brazil). PROSPERO: CRD42025636762. Searched PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Central, PEDro up to April 2025. 18 studies included. HIIT defined as 70-85% peak VO2, 75-90% max HR, or Borg 14-16; MICT as 40-69% peak VO2, 55-74% max HR, or Borg 12-13.
- **Key result:** HIIT improved VO2peak by **1.49 mL/kg/min (95% CI: 0.74–2.24; I²=61.2%; N=682)** compared to MICT overall.
- **Critical caveat:** "our subanalysis of isocaloric exercise protocols according to the left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) showed no statistical significance between HIIT and MICT exercise training groups."
- No significant differences in HRQoL; HIIT improved 6MWD in HFrEF patients vs MICT.
- Conclusion: HIIT superiority disappears when protocols are matched for isocaloric conditions and LVEF is considered. Limited number of isocaloric HFpEF studies precludes definitive conclusions for that subgroup.

**A6. Medicine (Baltimore) 2026 – HIIT vs. MICT in Healthy Elderly**
- Source: Medicine (Baltimore), published January 9, 2026, PMC12795074, PMID: 41517714. Systematic review and meta-analysis. PROSPERO CRD420251037775. Searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar through March 2025. 16 RCTs (n=1,434). Random-effects model; WMD effect size.
- Context: "After age 30, VO2max declines 5-15% per decade, reaching up to 50% decline by age 70."
- **Key results:**
  - MICT (12 studies, n=535): significantly improved VO2max: **MD = 1.22, 95% CI: 0.90–1.53, P<.01, I² = 0%**
  - HIIT (11 studies, n=483): more pronounced improvement: **MD = 1.62, 95% CI: 1.10–2.13, P<.01, I² = 0%**; some publication bias (Egger P=.003), trim-and-fill corrected MD = 1.48
  - Direct comparison (7 studies, n=610): HIIT significantly superior: **MD = 1.17, 95% CI: 0.52–1.82, P<.01, I² = 70%**
- Optimal protocols: HIIT: >3 to <6 months duration, 4 sessions/week, 21–39 minutes/session. MICT: >3 to <6 months, 3 sessions/week, ≥60 minutes/session. HIIT showed significant improvements even within ≤3 months (MD = 2.56); MICT required mid-cycle periods. MICT at 4×/week significantly declined in effectiveness (MD = 0.20), likely due to fatigue accumulation.
- Conclusion: Both improve cardiorespiratory function in elderly; HIIT yields more favorable results. MICT suitable for long-term training in tolerant individuals; HIIT better for short-term interventions in those able to tolerate high-intensity exercise.

**A7. Milanović, Sporiš & Weston (2015) – HIT vs. Continuous Endurance Training**
- Source: Sports Medicine, 2015, DOI: 10.1007/s40279-015-0365-0. Authors: Zoran Milanović, Goran Sporiš, Matthew Weston. 28 controlled trials, 723 participants, healthy adults aged 18-45 (mean age 25.1 ± 5 years; initial fitness 40.8 ± 7.9 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹).
- Key results (magnitude-based inference):
  - Endurance training vs no exercise: possibly large beneficial effect on VO2max (4.9 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; ±1.4); additional moderate increases for younger subjects (2.4) and longer interventions (2.2); small improvement for lower baseline fitness (1.4)
  - HIT vs no exercise: likely large beneficial effect (5.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; ±1.2); likely moderate greater increases for lower baseline fitness (3.2) and longer interventions (3.0); small lesser effect for longer HIT repetitions (-1.8)
  - HIT vs endurance training: possibly small beneficial effect for HIT (1.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; ±0.9), with small additional improvements for longer HIT repetitions (2.2), older subjects (1.8), longer interventions (1.7), greater work:rest ratio (1.6), lower baseline fitness (0.8)
- Conclusion: Both elicit large improvements in VO2max in healthy young to middle-aged adults; gains greater following HIT vs endurance training.

**A8. Ramos, Dalleck, Tjonna, Beetham & Coombes (2015) – HIIT vs MICT on Vascular Function**
- Source: Sports Medicine, DOI 10.1007/s40279-015-0321-z. 7 randomized trials, 182 patients (heart failure, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, CAD, type 2 diabetes, post-menopausal women, obese adults). Mean PEDro score 7.29/10. Most common HIIT prescription: 4×4-minute intervals at 85-95% max/peak heart rate, 3 minutes active recovery at 60-70% HRmax/peak, 3×/week for 12-16 weeks.
- Brachial artery FMD improved 4.31% (HIIT) vs 2.15% (MICT): significant mean difference 2.26% (p<0.05, I²=68%); when 2-week outlier removed, mean difference increased to 2.45%.
- HIIT had greater tendency to positively affect cardiorespiratory fitness (14-46% vs 5-16% improvement). Longer-interval HIIT (4×4 min) appeared more effective than shorter-interval HIIT. PGC-1α increased 47-138% following HIIT, no change in MICT. 4×4 HIIT significantly reduced ambulatory systolic BP more than MICT (12 vs 4.5 mmHg).

**A9. Weston, Taylor, Batterham & Hopkins (2014) – Low-Volume HIIT**
- Source: Sports Medicine, April 18, 2014, DOI: 10.1007/s40279-014-0180-z. Meta-analysis of controlled and non-controlled trials.
- Key finding: "Low-volume HIT produces moderate improvements in the aerobic power of active non-athletic and sedentary subjects and on Wingate peak and mean power." Authors note more studies needed to resolve unclear modifying effects of sex and HIT dose.

**A10. Sultana et al. (2019) – Low-Volume HIIT**
- Cited via Semantic Scholar listing: "Low-volume HIIT is a time-efficient treatment for increasing fitness but not for improving body composition."

**A11. Wen et al. (2019) – HIIT protocol recommendations**
- Cited via Semantic Scholar listing: "For maximizing VO2max training effects, long-interval (≥2min), high-volume (≤15min), and moderate to long-term (4-12 weeks) HIIT are recommended."

### B. SPRINT INTERVAL TRAINING (SIT) META-ANALYSES

**B1. Sloth, Sloth, Overgaard & Dalgas (2013) – SIT Effects on VO2max and Aerobic Performance**
- Source: Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2013. Aarhus University, Denmark. Systematic search of 6 databases May 7, 2012. SIT defined as: bouts of 10–30 seconds, maximal "all-out" intensity, ≤12 repetitions/session, recovery ≥5× work duration. Inclusion: healthy sedentary or recreationally active (baseline VO2max ≤55 mL/kg/min), interventions ≥2 weeks. 21 publications (19 unique studies).
- **Key results:**
  - VO2max meta-analysis (13 studies, 238 participants): **Hedges' g = 0.63, 95% CI (0.39–0.87)**, statistically significant; VO2max increases ranged 4.2%–13.4%; Q = 2.79, df = 12, P = 0.99 (homogeneity not rejected)
  - Mean VO2max improvement after 2 weeks of SIT: 6.8%; after 4–8 weeks: 9.6%
  - Gibala et al. 2006: 750-kJ time trial improved 10.1% with SIT vs 7.5% with endurance training (no significant group difference despite SIT total training volume only ~10% of ET volume)
  - Macpherson et al. 2011: 2000-m time trial improved 4.6% (SIT) and 5.9% (ET), no group difference
  - Citrate synthase activity increased ~11–42% across five studies; GLUT4 increased ~25% persisting 6 weeks after training cessation
  - Most common protocol: repeated 30-s all-out Wingate sprints, 3×/week, 3–7 reps/session, 2–5 min recovery; durations 2–8 weeks
  - Compliance 95–100%, low dropout, few non-serious adverse events
  - Rapid adaptations: some effects after only 2 weeks (~12 min of exercise time per week)
- Conclusions: Strong evidence for VO2max and aerobic performance improvement following SIT; solid evidence for peripheral muscular adaptations; central cardiovascular evidence limited and equivocal.

**B2. Gist, Fedewa, Dishman & Cureton (2013) – SIT Effects on Aerobic Capacity**
- Source: Sports Medicine, October 2013, DOI: 10.1007/s40279-013-0115-0. University of Georgia; United States Military Academy at West Point. PRISMA; searched PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science. 16 RCTs (318 participants), 17 effects. Mean age 23.5 ± 4.3 years. Training length 4.8 ± 2.3 weeks; 2.9 ± 0.4 sessions/week. Cycling (9), running (6), rowing (1).
- **Key results:**
  - Overall effect size: small-to-moderate: **Cohen's d = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10–0.55; z = 2.79, P < 0.01**; aggregate improvement ~3.6 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (~8% increase)
  - Moderate-to-large effect vs no-exercise controls: **Cohen's d = 0.69, 95% CI 0.46–0.93; z = 5.84, P < 0.01**
  - No significant difference vs endurance training controls: **Cohen's d = 0.04, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.24; z = 0.36, P = 0.72**
  - Heterogeneity: Q16 = 59.87, P < 0.01, I² = 74.95; no publication bias (funnel plot); fail-safe number 28
- Conclusion: "SIT improves aerobic capacity in healthy, young people. Relative to continuous endurance training of moderate intensity, SIT presents an equally effective alternative with a reduced volume of activity."
- Time efficiency note: In one study, SIT group spent only 15 min (135 min including recovery) exercising vs 630 min for endurance training, yet achieved similar improvements; training volume only ~10% of endurance group. However, rest intervals reduce time savings (e.g., six 30-s sprints with six 4-min recovery intervals = 27 min active).
- Limitations: young age (23.2 ± 4.3 years), normal health, most interventions <6 weeks; further research needed on older populations, long-term adherence.

**B3. Yang, Wang & Guan (2025) – Network Meta-Analysis of HIIT, SIT, RST in Athletes**
- Source: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, open access. Authors: Qiushi Yang, Junli Wang, Dongyang Guan. Received Aug 22, 2024; accepted May 21, 2025. PROSPERO CRD42023435021. 51 studies (1,261 athletes), 62 pairwise comparisons. Frequentist network meta-analysis (Hedges' g, P-scores); three-level meta-regression.
- **Key results (NMA rankings vs CON):** RST (g=1.04) > HIIT (g=1.01) > SIT (g=0.69) > CT (g=0.29, not significant). No significant differences among RST, HIIT, SIT (p>0.05). Heterogeneity τ²=0.13, I²=36%; no publication bias (Egger p=0.42).
- Optimal protocols: 3–6 weeks of running-based HIIT (140 s work, 165 s recovery) or SIT (≤30 s sprints, <97 s recovery) at 3 sessions/week. HIIT peak benefits at 140 s work duration and work:recovery ratio 0.85 (140 s work/165 s recovery). For SIT, improvements not significant when recovery durations exceeded 97 s. RST: 2 weeks at 3 sessions/week sufficient.
- Plateau effect: most RST adaptations occur within initial 6-week phase; HIIT/SIT show gains within <2 weeks, plateauing around 6–10 weeks.
- Note: This is in athletes (Tier 2–5), not the general adult population of interest, but provides protocol dose-response data.

### C. INDIVIDUAL RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS (RCTs)

**C1. Gillen et al. (2016) – Twelve Weeks of SIT vs MICT**
- Source: PLoS ONE 11(4): e0154075, published April 26, 2016. Authors: Gillen JB, Martin BJ, MacInnis MJ, Skelly LE, Tarnopolsky MA, Gibala MJ (McMaster University).
- Design: 27 sedentary men (age 27±8y; BMI 26±6 kg/m²), randomized to SIT (n=9), MICT (n=10), non-training control (n=6). 12 weeks, 3 sessions/week.
  - SIT: 3×20-second all-out cycle sprints (~500W) interspersed with 2 min cycling at 50W; sessions 10 min including warm-up/cool-down (~1 min intense exercise per session, 3 min per week, 30 min total weekly time commitment)
  - MICT: 45 min continuous cycling at ~70% maximal heart rate (~110W); sessions 50 min (~150 min/week)
- **Key results:**
  - VO2peak increased by 19% in both training groups (SIT: 32±7 to 38±8; MICT: 34±6 to 40±8 ml/kg/min; p<0.001 for both); absolute change ~6 ml/kg/min (~1.7 METs)
  - Insulin sensitivity (CSI): +53% after SIT (4.9±2.5 to 7.5±4.7, p=0.002); +34% after MICT (5.0±3.3 to 6.7±5.0, p=0.013)
  - Citrate synthase maximal activity +48% after SIT (p<0.0001), +27% after MICT (p=0.004); GLUT4 increased ~50% both groups
  - Body fat percentage decreased after both SIT (p=0.011) and MICT (p=0.011); body mass unchanged
- **Conclusion (verbatim):** "Twelve weeks of brief intense interval exercise improved indices of cardiometabolic health to the same extent as traditional endurance training in sedentary men, despite a five-fold lower exercise volume and time commitment." This is the longest direct comparison of SIT and MICT to date. Authors suggest training intensity, rather than volume, may be the more critical determinant of improvements in CRF and mitochondrial content. SIT requires high motivation and is not suited for everyone.

**C2. Arboleda-Serna et al. (2022) – Low-Volume HIIT vs MICT in Overweight Women**
- Source: Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness, Vol 20, Issue 2, April 2022, pages 108-112. Authors: Víctor H. Arboleda-Serna, Fredy A. Patiño-Villada, Deiber A. Pinzón-Castro, Elkin F. Arango-Vélez. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03300895.
- Design: 35 overweight women randomized to HIIT (n=16) or MICT (n=19); 24 exercise sessions on grass sports field. HIIT: 15 bouts of 30 s at 90-95% HRmax. MICT: 30 min continuous at 65-75% HRmax.
- **Key result:** Difference between HIIT and MICT post-intervention on VO2max was NOT statistically significant: **0.8 ml/kg/min, 95% CI: -1.0 to 2.7, p=0.37**. No significant differences in body fat % or HRQoL.
- Conclusion: Low-volume HIIT showed no quantitative advantage over MICT in this population.

**C3. Dalsaniya, Kundariya & Tekchandani (2025) – 12-Week HIIT RCT in Sedentary Adults**
- Source: Journal of Heart Valve Disease, Vol 30, Issue 8, August 2025, pages 67-70 (open access). Authors from GMERS Medical College, Gandhinagar, India.
- Design: 40 sedentary adults aged 25-45; HIIT (n=20) vs control (n=20). HIIT: 4 supervised sessions/week of 4×4-min cycling at 85-90% HRmax with 3-min active recovery, 10-min warm-up, 5-min cooldown.
- **Key results:** VO2max in HIIT group increased significantly from 32.1 ± 3.8 to 39.5 ± 4.2 mL/kg/min (p<0.001), ~23% improvement; control no change (32.8 ± 4.0 to 33.1 ± 3.9, p=0.411). Fasting glucose decreased (102.4±6.2 to 94.3±5.9 mg/dL, p<0.01); total cholesterol -12.5%; triglycerides -15.2%; HDL-C +8.1%. No dropouts or adverse events.
- Note: This RCT is not randomized against MICT (control was sedentary), and age range is 25-45.

**C4. Hu, Chen, Nie, Shi & Kong (2025) – Equipment-Free REHIT RCT**
- Source: Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness, Vol 23, Issue 4, October 2025, pages 317-327, DOI: 10.1016/j.jesf.2025.06.006. Open access.
- Design: 12-week RCT, 319 inactive men (age 20.5±1.1 years, VO2max 37.7±1.4 ml/min/kg). Four cohorts: supervised burpee-based REHIT (BIT; n=79), unsupervised real-world BIT (BIT-RW; n=79), supervised cycling SIT (n=82), non-exercising control (n=79). Exercise groups performed 2×20s all-out sessions 3-5 times weekly.
- **Key results:** Supervised BIT achieved 91%-94% HRmax vs ~90% BIT-RW. All exercise groups: 6%-8% body mass reduction, **8%-13% VO2max increase (η²p=0.7-0.8, p<0.001)**. Supervised BIT matched SIT in VO2max gains (5.0±0.6 ml/min/kg); BIT-RW showed smaller physiological benefits (3.0±0.6 ml/min/kg) but 10% greater improvements in affective responses (p<0.05). Significant reductions in stress (49-61%), anxiety (37-86%), depression (14-48%); improvements in resilience (22-27%) and QoL (14-27%).
- Conclusion: A 40-s equipment-free REHIT protocol using burpees improves physical and mental health even unsupervised. Note: participants were young (mean 20.5 years).

### D. REDUCED-EXERTION HIGH-INTENSITY INTERVAL TRAINING (REHIT) – VERY LOW VOLUME (<60 MIN/WEEK)

**D1. Metcalfe et al. (2018) – REHIT Sprint Duration (20s vs 10s)**
- Source: Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism, Vol 43, 2018, pp. 338-344. UK (Stirling, Derry/Londonderry) and Turkey (Izmir).
- Design: 36 sedentary/recreationally active participants (17 women; mean age 22±3 years; BMI 24.5±4.6 kg/m²; VO2max 37±8 mL/kg/min). REHIT20 (2×20-s sprints; n=18) vs REHIT10 (2×10-s sprints; n=18). 6 weeks, 3 sessions/week, 10 min unloaded pedalling with 2 all-out sprints against 7.5% body weight resistance. Sprint durations progressed.
- **Key results:** VO2max increased significantly more in REHIT20 (+10%; 2.77±0.75 to 3.04±0.75 L/min) vs REHIT10 (+4%; 2.58±0.57 to 2.67±0.57 L/min) (group × time interaction p<0.05; **d = 1.06**). Affective responses and RPE (~13-15) NOT different between groups. Adherence 97%.
- **Conclusion (verbatim):** "In protocols with very few sprints, sprint duration should be longer than 10 seconds," supporting original REHIT protocol of 2×20-s sprints. Supports REHIT as efficacious, time-efficient (3×10 min per week), and acceptable alternative to classic SIT and MICT.

**D2. Vollaard group REHIT Frequency Study (2 vs 3 vs 4 sessions/week)**
- Source: Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism (randomized controlled trial).
- Design: 42 inactive participants (13 women; mean±SD age 25±5 y, VO2max 35±5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) from 4 UK sites. Randomised to REHIT at 2, 3, or 4 sessions/week for 6 weeks. REHIT = 10 min unloaded cycling with two all-out sprints against 7.5% body mass resistance (10s week 1, 15s week 2, 20s weeks 3-6).
- **Key results:** No significant difference in VO2max improvements between groups (2/week: +10.2%; 3/week: +8.1%; 4/week: +7.3%), overall significant improvement in absolute VO2max (+8.7%; p<0.001). Adherence 98-99%; no significant body mass changes.
- **Conclusion (verbatim):** "A training frequency of 2 sessions/week is sufficient for REHIT to improve V̇O2max," and reducing frequency from 3-4 to 2 sessions/week does not attenuate improvements. Contradicts the hypothesis that higher frequency produces greater improvements. Supports the notion that total weekly sprint exercise volume is not a main driver of VO2max adaptations in SIT.

**D3. Metcalfe et al. (2012) – Original REHIT Trial (cited in PeakVO2 blog)**
- Six weeks of REHIT raised VO2max by **15% in men and 12% in women** in sedentary adults, from ~30 minutes of total weekly exercise; plus 28% insulin sensitivity improvement in men.
- Research from Niels Vollaard's lab at University of Bath established only two sprints are needed (a meta-analysis found adding more sprints didn't increase gains); 20 seconds is the optimal sprint duration.

**D4. Astorino, Metcalfe & Vollaard (2026) – Definitive REHIT RCT Protocol**
- Source: Trials, 2026;27:340. Published March 23, 2026. Funded by National Institute on Aging (R15AG093525). CSU—San Marcos; IRB #2313242-2 (Sept 12, 2025); OSF osf.io/wvcz4; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07328568.
- Design: 120 inactive adults (60 REHIT, 60 control), aged 18-64, healthy, weight-stable, BMI<35 kg/m². REHIT: 2 days/week, 12 weeks (2 min warm-up, all-out sprint, 3 min recovery, second sprint, 4 min cool-down; sprint duration 10s week 1, 15s week 2, 20s weeks 3-12; resistance 5% body mass). Primary outcome: change in VO2max at baseline, week 6, week 12. First participant recruited December 2025; completion September 2028.
- Background (verbatim): REHIT has shown "V̇O2max increases of ~10% after 6 weeks and ~19% after 12 weeks across multiple studies (Table 1 lists 14 studies)." REHIT is genuinely time-efficient (as low as 20 min/week), as enjoyable as MICT, does not produce negative affective responses. Prior studies used small sample sizes, necessitating this definitive trial. Sample size n=120 detects smallest worthwhile difference of 1.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (~4.5% VO2max increase, equivalent to ~8% CVD mortality risk reduction) with d=0.60, alpha=0.05, 90% power.
- Context: "V̇O2max is a stronger predictor of morbidity/mortality risk than smoking, hypertension, obesity, high cholesterol, and insulin resistance." "In 2020, 75% of adult Americans did not meet PA recommendations." "Physical inactivity is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide, increasing the risk of 40 chronic conditions."
- Note: Traditional HIIT and SIT protocols criticized for being too time-consuming (~66-93 min/week), too strenuous, and producing negative affective responses.

**D5. REHIT comparison to other protocols (PeakVO2 blog)**
- REHIT compared to Tabata and Norwegian 4×4 protocols; REHIT's percentages come from untrained beginners, while 4×4's 7.2% gain was measured in trained subjects. REHIT outperformed five weekly 30-minute moderate walking sessions in type 2 diabetes patients (Ruffino et al., 2017). Cycling strongly preferred over running due to hamstring injury risk with standing-start running sprints.

### E. KEY CONTEXTUAL / MECHANISTIC FINDINGS

**E1. Taylor, Bonikowske & Olson (2021) – Optimizing Outcomes in Cardiac Rehabilitation (as reported by Klein, AJMC, Sept 26, 2021)**
- Original: Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine, Sept 3, 2021, doi:10.3389/fcvm.2021.734278.
- HIIT produces greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness than MICT or low-intensity exercise for patients with heart failure and CVD. Recommend slowly introducing/progressing HIIT case-by-case.
- Key RCT data cited:
  - FITR Heart Study: HIIT numerically higher VO2peak improvement (2.9 mL/kg/min vs 1.8 mL/kg/min for MICT); adherence 53% (HIIT) vs 41% (MICT). After excluding nonadherent participants, HIIT showed greater VO2peak improvement (5.2 vs 2.2 mL/kg/min)
  - OptimEx-Clin: adherence 56% (HIIT) vs 60% (MICT)
  - SAINTEX-CAD and FITR Heart: similar improvements between HIIT and MICT at 12 months in CAD patients for VO2peak, CVD risk factors, QOL, body composition, physical activity
  - Moholdt et al: HIIT improved VO2peak and HR recovery more than MICT at 6 months post-CABG; after 5 months home-based training, 35% stopped HIIT in favor of MICT, only 4% of MICT participants increased intensity; 74% of HIIT and 68% of MICT performed 3 sessions/week
  - SMARTEX HF (HFrEF) and OptimEX-Clin (HFpEF): both showed regression of supervised training improvements at 12 months regardless of exercise intensity
- Conclusion: While short-duration HIIT can improve peripheral mitochondrial adaptations and provide similar VO2peak improvements to MICT, longer-duration and higher-volume HIIT protocols appear superior for stroke volume and vascular adaptations and greater VO2peak improvements.

**E2. WOD-Science (2026) – Minimum Effective Dose for Maintaining VO2max (Hickson studies)**
- Two classic 1980s studies by Robert Hickson:
  - Study 1 (volume reduction): After 10-week block (~20% VO2max improvement), reducing training to 26 min/day (33% reduction) or 13 min/day (67% reduction) while keeping intensity and frequency constant → both groups COMPLETELY maintained VO2max gains
  - Study 2 (intensity reduction): Reducing intensity by 33% or 67% while maintaining frequency and duration → VO2max DROPPED by 4-10% within first 5 weeks, dose-response (67% reduction → 10% drop)
- **Conclusion: The single most important training component for MAINTAINING endurance capacity is INTENSITY, not volume or frequency.** Athletes can drastically cut training volume (e.g., 6 sessions to 1-2/week, ~66% reduction) as long as intensity stays HIGH (80-90% max HR). This supports the premise of time-efficient high-intensity protocols.

**E3. Data Driven Athlete (2017) – VO2max Training Context**
- ~50% of untrained VO2max baseline from genetic/environmental factors; remaining 50% from training response.
- Hickson Protocol (long intervals): 6×5-min near-maximal with 2 min rest, 3×/week → average 44% (16.8 mL/kg/min) VO2max increase in initially untrained participants.
- Ronnestad Protocol (short intervals): 2 sessions/week of 30s all-out with 15s recovery for 10 min, repeated 3 times with 3-min rests → larger relative VO2max improvements in trained cyclists.
- Practical: both long (3-8 min) and short (30s) intervals work; limit VO2max workouts to 2/week max; 4-6 week training blocks.

**E4. Roadman Cycling Podcast (2024) – Low Cadence Training (Hebisz & Hebisz, PLOS ONE, Nov 2024)**
- 24 well-trained female cyclists aged 17-20; 8 weeks identical polarized plans; only difference was cadence (50-70 RPM vs freely chosen ~80 RPM).
- VO2max improved 8.7% (low-cadence) vs 4.6% (control), p=0.02; Maximum Aerobic Power 8.1% vs 3.0%, p=0.03.
- Note: This is a trained athlete population, not directly applicable to the 30-70 age group, but relevant for protocol design.

### F. KEY EXISTING GAPS, INCONSISTENCIES AND FLAGS

1. **Population age gap:** The strongest SIT/low-volume evidence (Gillen 2016; Metcalfe 2018; Vollaard frequency study; Hu 2025) was conducted in young adults (mean ages ~20-27). The 30-70 age range is covered mainly by HIIT vs MICT meta-analyses in older adults (Yang 2023; Medicine 2026), but very-low-volume REHIT/SIT data specifically in the 30-70 age group is sparse. The Astorino 2026 trial (ages 18-64) is ongoing and aims to fill this gap (completion September 2028).
2. **The <60 min/week subgroup:** Direct RCT evidence with protocols genuinely under 60 min/week exists mainly via REHIT (2×20-s sprints, ~20-30 min/week: Metcalfe 2012, Metcalfe 2018, Vollaard frequency study) and Gillen 2016 SIT (~30 min/week time commitment). All are in younger adults. No published RCT specifically targeting the 30-70 age group with <60 min/week was found in this search; the Astorino 2026 trial (ages 18-64, 20 min/week) is the closest, currently active.
3. **Isocaloric matching caveat:** Conceição et al. 2026 found that HIIT's VO2peak superiority over MICT disappears when protocols are matched for isocaloric conditions and LVEF is considered — an important contradictory finding within the literature. Only a limited number of isocaloric HFpEF studies exist.
4. **Arboleda-Serna 2022** found no significant difference between low-volume HIIT and MICT in overweight women (0.8 ml/kg/min, 95% CI: -1.0 to 2.7, p=0.37), contradicting meta-analytic findings favoring HIIT. This is an individual RCT flag.
5. **Hybrid HIIT + MICT protocols:** No dedicated published RCT or meta-analysis of combined/hybrid HIIT+MICT protocols on VO2max in the 30-70 age range was identified in this search. This appears to be a genuine gap in the literature. The Gist 2013 discussion notes that a combination of SIT and endurance training "may be ideal" (SIT improvements likely from peripheral adaptations, endurance training from central adaptations), but this is speculative.
6. **Clinical populations:** Cheng 2026 found no VO2peak benefit of HIIT over MICT in clinical populations (disease-imposed cardiopulmonary limitations). Cancer survivor meta-analysis (2025) showed HIIT superiority (SMD 0.53), but 8 of 12 studies at high risk of bias.
7. **Adherence/compliance concerns:** Taylor 2021 reports adherence data from FITR Heart (53% HIIT vs 41% MICT) and OptimEx-Clin (56% HIIT vs 60% MICT); Moholdt found 35% of HIIT participants stopped in favor of MICT during home-based training. Long-term drop-off in HIIT adherence is a known limitation. REHIT literature claims high adherence (96-99%) and no negative affective responses, but most REHIT studies are short (6 weeks).
8. **Publication bias:** Medicine 2026 meta-analysis detected publication bias for HIIT (Egger P=.003), though trim-and-fill confirmed stability (corrected MD = 1.48).
9. **Age-related decline context:** "After age 30, due to the natural decline in physiological function and reduced physical activity, VO2max decreases by 5% to 15% every decade. By the age of 70, this decline can reach up to 50%." (Medicine 2026).

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

**A. OVERVIEW: THE COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS QUESTION**

The literature comparing HIIT versus MICT on cardiometabolic outcomes in adults is extensive but marked by important contradictions. Across multiple meta-analyses, the most consistent finding is that HIIT and MICT produce broadly similar improvements in glycemic control (HbA1c, fasting glucose, HOMA-IR), blood pressure, and most blood lipids, while HIIT shows a consistent superiority for cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max/VO2peak) and, in some analyses, HDL cholesterol and certain adiposity outcomes. Several sources explicitly note that where HIIT shows advantages, the clinical significance of the improvements is limited, and the certainty of evidence is often low to moderate.

---

**B. GLYCEMIC OUTCOMES (HbA1c, Fasting Glucose, HOMA-IR, Fasting Insulin)**

**B.1. Meta-analytic evidence: No significant difference between HIIT and MICT for glycemic control**

- A 2026 meta-analysis of 21 RCTs (792 participants with type 2 diabetes, mean intervention 13.35 weeks) by Zeng, Zhu, Yang & Wang (Beijing Sport University), published in *Frontiers in Endocrinology* (DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2026.1876685), found **no significant differences between HIIT and MICT** for HbA1c (SMD 0.00), fasting blood glucose (SMD 0.04), or HOMA-IR (SMD −0.11). The authors explain comparable glycemic effects by noting both modalities activate the skeletal muscle AMPK–GLUT4 axis for insulin-independent glucose uptake. The study also reported that approximately 78 min/week of HIIT can achieve glycemic control comparable to ~210 min/week of MICT.

- A 2022 meta-analysis by Mateo-Gallego et al., published in *Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice* (Vol. 190, Article 109979), covering 32 articles (19 trials in the meta-analysis) in type 1 and type 2 diabetes, found that **HIIT vs. control (CON) significantly reduced fasting glucose by 13.3 mg/dL (p<0.001), HbA1c by −0.34% (p<0.001), insulin by −2.27 UI/L (p=0.003), and HOMA-IR by −0.88 (p=0.005)**. However, these reductions were **NOT significantly different when comparing HIIT with MICT** (p=0.140 for glucose, p=0.315 for HbA1c, p=0.520 for insulin, and p=0.389 for HOMA-IR). HIIT did significantly increase VO2max versus MICT (0.22 L/min, p=0.025 absolute; 0.97 ml/kg/min, p=0.045 relative). BMI decrease was similar after both protocols. This was reported as the first meta-analysis including all types of clinical trials examining HIIT effects on glucose metabolism in both T1DM and T2DM.

- A 2018 meta-analysis by Liu et al., published in *Aging Clinical and Experimental Research* (Vol. 31, Issue 5, p. 575; DOI: 10.1007/s40520-018-1012-z; PMID: 30097811; PMCID: PMC6491404), of 13 trials (345 patients with type 2 diabetes) found that compared to MICT, HIIT produced a significant reduction in **HbA1c (MD −0.37%, 95% CI −0.55 to −0.19, P<0.0001)** and body weight (MD −1.22 kg, 95% CI −2.23 to −0.18, P=0.02) and BMI (MD −0.40 kg/m², 95% CI −0.78 to −0.02, P=0.04). However, **no significant differences were found for fasting glucose, HOMA-IR, or HDL cholesterol vs MICT**. Fasting insulin decreased significantly from baseline (SMD −0.46) but not versus MICT. GRADE assessment rated most outcomes as "Low" or "Very low" quality, mainly due to inconsistency and imprecision; only VO2peak outcomes were rated "Moderate."

- A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis in *F1000Research* (Vol 15:836), examining HIIT vs MICT on insulin sensitivity in adults with T2DM (4 RCTs, n=162; adults aged 30–70), found **no statistically significant between-group differences** for any post-intervention outcome: HbA1c (SMD −0.52, p=0.42), HOMA-IR (SMD −0.14, p=0.67), fasting insulin (SMD −0.05, p=0.91), fasting blood sugar (SMD −0.29, p=0.18), and BMI (SMD −0.37, p=0.27). Heterogeneity was moderate-to-high for some outcomes (I²=42–84%). Included RCTs were Pandey et al. (2017), Winding et al. (2018), Findikoglu et al. (2023), and Niyazi et al. (2024), with interventions lasting 11–12 weeks.

- A 2026 meta-analysis of 13 RCTs in adults with prediabetes, published in *Frontiers in Endocrinology* (DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2026.1837386), found: **HbA1c: no significant difference between HIIT and MICT (MD 0.08%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.26; very low certainty)**; **FBG: MICT showed a small but significant advantage over HIIT (MD 0.12 mmol/L, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.22; very low certainty)**; **2hPG (post-challenge glucose): HIIT showed a significant advantage over MICT (MD −0.16 mmol/L, 95% CI −0.28 to −0.04; low certainty)**. The authors concluded that in prediabetes, HIIT may be more favorable for post-challenge glycemic control and cardiorespiratory fitness, whereas MICT may offer a modest advantage for fasting glucose. Notably, 9 of 13 included studies lasted ≤2 weeks, so effects may reflect short-term responses.

**B.2. Meta-analytic evidence from umbrella review and low-volume HIIT**

- A 2026 umbrella review (reported by The Cardiology Advisor, based on a systematic review/meta-analysis published in *Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism*, searching 3 databases up to August 15, 2024, encompassing 76 unique primary studies with 2,954 distinct participants; 9 of the reviews included only RCTs) found that **HIIT significantly improved glycemic control and enhanced cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF)** in T2DM, with WMD increases in CRF of 3.35 to 6.38 mL/kg/min. Compared to MICT, HIIT provided **similar or superior benefits across most cardiometabolic outcomes**, though CRF improvements were consistently greater with HIIT (WMD 1.68–4.12 mL/kg/min). The authors concluded the umbrella review "provides comprehensive and up-to-date evidence supporting the efficacy of HIIT in improving glycaemic control compared with non-active CON groups and conventional exercise regimens such as MICT in individuals with T2DM."

- A 2025 meta-analysis of "practical models of low-volume HIIT" (LV-HIIT) by Lu et al., published in *Frontiers in Endocrinology* (23 January 2025, DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2025.1481200), included 20 RCTs (738 participants; mean age 20–58 years; 16 HIIT and 4 SIT protocols; LV-HIIT defined as ≤15 min of intense training within sessions ≤30 min, with <30s all-out sprints for SIT). Results: **LV-HIIT vs. CON significantly improved fasting glucose (MD −16.63 mg/dL; 95% CI −25.30 to −7.96; p<0.001) and HbA1c (MD −0.70%; 95% CI −1.10 to −0.29; p<0.001)**, with greater improvements in overweight/obese or T2D participants; T2D was a significant moderator of FPG effects (p=0.006). **LV-HIIT vs. MICT showed no differences in FPG, FPI, HbA1c, or HOMA-IR (p>0.05), but LV-HIIT was more effective in improving insulin sensitivity (SMD −0.40; 95% CI −0.70 to −0.09; p=0.01)**. No significant effects on fasting insulin (FPI) or HOMA-IR were seen in the main analysis vs CON. The authors note that two SIT-based LV-HIIT studies showed no improvements, suggesting protocols with extremely low volumes may be insufficient.

- A 2021 evidence-based review by Atakan et al., published in *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health* (18(13):7201; doi: 10.3390/ijerph18137201), provides historical context: the 1996 Tabata study showed HIIT (43 min/week) was more effective than MICT (300 min/week) at upregulating both oxidative and glycolytic energy systems; the 2006 Gibala landmark study showed SIT produced similar improvements to MICT in time-trial performance despite ~90% less training volume (630 kJ vs. 6500 kJ); and the 2010 Little study designed practical low-volume HIIT (8–12 × 60 s at ~100% PPO) that improved mitochondrial capacity, PGC-1α, sirtuin 1, and mitochondrial transcription factor A. HIIT is reported to increase PGC-1α, mitochondrial biogenesis markers, citrate synthase, muscle buffer capacity, and insulin sensitivity.

**B.3. Individual RCT evidence on glycemic control**

- A 12-week RCT (Research Square preprint, rs-7199864) in 90 adults aged 40–65 with metabolic syndrome (HIIT: 4×4-minute intervals at 85–95% HRmax, 3x/week, ~30–35 min sessions; MICT: 60–70% HRmax, 45-min sessions, 5x/week; 78 completers, 13.3% attrition) found **HIIT showed superior FBG reductions (−0.68 mmol/L males, −0.67 females) and HbA1c reductions (−0.72% males, −0.51% females), all statistically significant (p<0.05), while MICT showed modest, non-significant changes**. HIIT also reduced BMI (−1.56 males, −1.42 females kg/m²), ALT (−9.3 males, −10.4 females U/L), and uric acid (−38.9 males, −39.3 females µmol/L), all p<0.001. Exercise adherence was 89.2% (HIIT) and 91.4% (MICT); no exercise-related adverse events.

- A 2020 RCT by Sogaard et al. published in *Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism* (J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2020; 105(8):e2941–e2959; DOI: 10.1210/clinem/dgaa345; PMID: 32492705) randomized 31 inactive adults with obesity (age 31±6 years; BMI 33±3 kg/m²) to 12 weeks (4 sessions/week) of HIIT (10 × 1-minute at 90% HRmax; ~25 min/session; ~150 kcal) or MICT (45 min at 70% HRmax; ~250 kcal), with body weight maintained by design. **Peripheral insulin sensitivity (hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp) was ~20% greater the day after the final exercise session versus pretraining (P<0.01), with NO difference between HIIT and MICT. When participants abstained from exercise for 4 days, insulin sensitivity returned to pretraining levels in both groups.** Hepatic glucose production and antilipolytic sensitivity to insulin were unaffected by either modality. No changes were observed in blood pressure, HbA1C, cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose, insulin, CRP, IL-6, hepatic fat, or visceral fat in the absence of weight loss. The authors conclude the insulin-sensitizing effects of both HIIT and MICT are mediated primarily by factors stemming from the most recent exercise session(s) rather than adaptations that accrue over time.

- A 2016 RCT by Gillen et al., published in *PLoS ONE* 11(4): e0154075, randomized 27 sedentary men (age 27±8 y; BMI 26±6) to 12 weeks of SIT (3×20-second all-out sprints within 10-minute sessions, 3x/week; 30 min/week total) or MICT (45 min continuous cycling at ~70% HRmax, 3x/week; 150 min/week total). **Insulin sensitivity (CSI from IVGTT) increased by 53% after SIT (4.9±2.5 to 7.5±4.7, p=0.002) and 34% after MICT (5.0±3.3 to 6.7±5.0, p=0.013).** VO2peak increased 19% in both groups. Citrate synthase maximal activity increased 48% (SIT) and 27% (MICT); GLUT4 increased ~50% in both groups. The authors concluded 3 minutes of sprinting per week within a 30-minute weekly time commitment improved cardiometabolic health indices to the same extent as 150 minutes per week of endurance training.

- A randomized trial in *The Journal of Physiology* (Obese SIT study, Liverpool John Moores University) in 16 young obese men (age 25±1 yr, BMI 34.8±0.9) compared 4 weeks of MICT (40–60 min cycling at ~65% VO2peak, 5x/week) versus constant-load SIT (4–7 intervals at 200% Wattmax, 3x/week; ~1 hour/week vs ~5 hours/week). **Both SIT and MICT equally increased VO2peak (MICT 10%, SIT 13%) and the Matsuda insulin sensitivity index (MICT 24%, SIT 11%)**, with no significant differences between modalities on any measured variable. Both increased muscle microvascular eNOS content, reduced endothelial NOX2 content, increased capillary density, and reduced central artery stiffness (cPWV) and augmentation index.

**C. BLOOD PRESSURE (Systolic and Diastolic)**

**C.1. Meta-analytic evidence**

- The 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* meta-analysis by Li et al. (PMC12605200; DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1669941; 21 RCTs, 1,066 participants aged 46–67 with chronic diseases) found: **DBP significantly reduced (SMD −0.23, 95% CI −0.39 to −0.08, p<0.01, I²=0.0%)**; **SBP NOT significantly reduced (SMD −0.14, 95% CI −0.38 to 0.11, p>0.05, I²=59.3%)**. European studies showed significant SBP reduction (SMD −0.43) while non-European studies did not (SMD −0.02). Exploratory analysis suggested sprint interval training and short-interval HIIT produced greater lipid improvements, while long-interval HIIT showed more consistent blood pressure effects.

- The 2026 Cochrane review (Strauss JA et al., *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews* 2026, Issue 3, Art. No. CD013617; DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD013617.pub2; 58 studies, 2,075 inactive adults; searches up to 13 October 2025) found: **Compared to no exercise, HIIT probably improves VO2max and reduces waist size, but no clear differences were found for systolic blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, or triglycerides. Compared to MICT, HIIT may improve fitness slightly, but no clear differences were found for blood pressure, waist size, waist-to-hip ratio, or triglycerides.** Evidence on systolic blood pressure was described as "very uncertain." No adverse events were reported, though it is unclear if studies actively monitored for them.

- A 2026 network meta-analysis published in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine* (DOI: 10.1136/bjsports-2025-111474; 31 RCTs, 1,345 people, 67 exercise types; reported via Medical Xpress) found that, compared with no exercise: combined exercise training reduced 24-hour systolic BP by 6.18 mmHg, **HIIT by 5.71 mmHg**, aerobic exercise by 4.73 mmHg. Average diastolic BP reductions: combined training 3.94 mmHg, aerobic exercise 2.76 mmHg, **HIIT 4.64 mmHg**, Pilates 4.18 mmHg. Aerobic exercise showed the most consistent reductions in ambulatory BP both day and night. The authors recommend "aerobic (continuous or interval training) or combined training as primary evidence-based interventions for reducing 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure in adults with hypertension."

- A 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis in *Sports Medicine* (Hu et al., published 18 August 2026; 159 RCTs, n=10,821, adults ≥45 years) found all exercise modalities significantly reduced SBP and DBP versus control. **Circuit-based training (CBT) showed the largest estimated SBP reduction (MD −13.52 mmHg; 95% CrI −18.59 to −8.44), followed by combined training (CT), HIIT, MICT, dynamic resistance training, and isometric exercise.** Higher baseline SBP was associated with greater reductions (β=−2.49 mmHg per 10-mmHg increase). Dose-response analysis revealed a nonlinear association, with the largest model-estimated reduction around 1200 METs-min/week. No network comparison was rated as high confidence.

- A 2025 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (500 participants) in sedentary populations, published in *Frontiers in Physiology* (DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1702247), found significant improvements with HIIT vs control: **SBP (MD −5.02 mmHg, 95% CI −7.29 to −2.76, P<0.0001, I²=0%)**; **DBP (MD −2.43 mmHg, 95% CI −4.08 to −0.79, P=0.004, I²=37%)**; pulse wave velocity (MD −0.28 m/s, 95% CI −0.56 to −0.01, P=0.04); flow-mediated dilation (SMD 1.12, 95% CI 0.32–1.92, P=0.006, I²=79%).

- A 2026 meta-analysis of real-world HIIT by Stefanovic et al., published in *Sports* (2026, 14(7), 311; 31 studies, 25 RCTs, 1,119 participants, mean age 34, range 20–70), found pre-post reductions in **SBP of −4 mmHg and DBP of −3 mmHg (both p<0.001)**. HIIT was superior to passive controls for VO2max/peak (6.9 mL/kg/min) and waist circumference (−2.9 cm), and superior to active controls (e.g., MICT) only for VO2max/peak (1.1 mL/kg/min).

- A 2026 meta-analysis of 21 RCTs in T2DM (Zeng et al., *Frontiers in Endocrinology*, DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2026.1876685) found no significant differences between HIIT and MICT for systolic BP (SMD −0.11) or diastolic BP (SMD −0.11).

- The 2026 prediabetes meta-analysis (*Frontiers in Endocrinology*, DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2026.1837386) found no significant between-group differences for SBP (MD 0.77 mmHg) or DBP (MD 0.40 mmHg) between HIIT and MICT.

**C.2. Individual RCT evidence on blood pressure**

- In the 12-week metabolic syndrome RCT (Research Square rs-7199864), all groups showed mild SBP/DBP reductions but no significant between-group differences (all p>0.3). HIIT males achieved −6.31 mmHg SBP (described as a clinically meaningful trend).

- In the 12-week prediabetes RCT (*Frontiers in Endocrinology*, 2025, DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2025.1614149; 71 participants aged 45–59; HIIT 10×1-min at 75–90% HRpeak, 30 min; MICT 50 min at 55–70% HRpeak; 3x/week): both groups significantly reduced SBP (P<0.001; no between-group difference, P=0.398). **MICT was significantly better than HIIT at reducing DBP (P=0.011, large effect size).**

**D. BLOOD LIPIDS (Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, Triglycerides)**

**D.1. HDL cholesterol — HIIT advantage in some meta-analyses**

- The 2026 T2DM meta-analysis (Zeng et al., *Frontiers in Endocrinology*, DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2026.1876685) found **HIIT demonstrated a significant advantage in improving HDL (SMD 0.44, 95% CI 0.06–0.82, p=0.023, I²=73.7%)**, while no significant differences were found for total cholesterol (SMD −0.22), triglycerides (SMD −0.22), or LDL (SMD −0.04). Subgroup analyses identified optimal HIIT conditions for HDL improvement: moderate session duration (20–30 min: SMD 0.64, p=0.002), weekly frequency ≤3 sessions (SMD 0.56, p=0.009), intervention duration ≤8 weeks (SMD 0.43, p=0.048) — described as an inverted U-shaped dose-response. Short-duration HIIT (≤20 min/session) significantly reduced TC (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −1.04 to −0.13) versus MICT, while moderate and long durations showed no effect. Publication bias: significant asymmetry for TC (Egger's test p=0.017). Mechanistic explanations include HIIT's HDL benefit linked to hepatic apolipoprotein A-I synthesis and ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux, and short-duration HIIT's TC reduction linked to AMPK activation and HMG-CoA reductase inhibition.

- The 2026 middle-aged/elderly meta-analysis (Li et al., *Frontiers in Physiology*, PMC12605200) found **HDL-C significantly improved (SMD 0.41, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.71, p<0.01, I²=76.8%)**; **TG significantly reduced (SMD −0.68, 95% CI −1.20 to −0.16, p<0.05, I²=90.7%)**, with significant regional differences (non-European SMD −0.45; European SMD −0.11, non-significant). Intervention duration was a significant moderator for HDL (9–16 weeks: SMD 0.43, significant).

- A 2024 adolescent meta-analysis (Wang et al., *Physiology & Behavior*, Vol. 275; 12 studies, 468 participants, mean age 15.19±4.35) found HIIT improved HDL (SMD −0.47, 95% CI −1.11 to 0.17 — note the negative SMD reported) and concluded HIIT was superior to MICT across body weight, BMI, fat mass, SBP, DBP, VO2max, triglycerides, TC, LDL, HDL, glucose, and insulin. **Glucose (SMD −1.53, 95% CI −2.93 to −0.13) and VO2max (SMD 0.56, 95% CI 0.20, 0.93) showed significant improvements.**

- A 2025 meta-analysis on diabesity (Al-Mhanna et al., *Diabetology & Metabolic Syndrome*, Vol. 17, Issue 1, Article 406; DOI 10.1186/s13098-025-01974-4; 18 RCTs, 504 patients with T2DM and obesity, mean age 55.0±11.8, mean BMI 31.0±6.9) found significant improvements with HIIT vs standard treatment in: body mass (SMD −0.36 kg), BMI (SMD −0.57 kg/m²), waist-to-hip ratio (SMD −1.68), fasting blood glucose (SMD −0.64 mmol/L), HbA1c (SMD −1.08%), fasting insulin (SMD −0.79 mIU/L), HOMA-IR (SMD −0.95), LDL (SMD −0.64 mg/dL), triglycerides (SMD −0.64 mg/dL), and total cholesterol (SMD −0.66 mg/dL).

**D.2. LDL and total cholesterol — HIIT advantage in some analyses**

- A 2023 meta-analysis by McCormick, Mamikunian & Thorp, published in *International Journal of Exercise Science* (Vol. 16, Issue 3, pp. 791–813; DOI 10.70252/WGFU4000), examined blood lipids in nondiabetic overweight/obese young adults (BMI>25, ages 18–30; 8 studies, mean PEDro 5.8). **Compared to CON, HIIT significantly decreased LDL (−12.14 mg/dL, p<0.00001) and total cholesterol (−9.27 mg/dL, p=0.003), without significantly affecting HDL or triglycerides. Compared to MICT, HIIT significantly decreased LDL (−6.23 mg/dL, p=0.05) and total cholesterol (−7.85 mg/dL, p=0.02).** The authors concluded HIIT is superior to MICT and CON in improving LDL and total cholesterol in this population.

- The 2018 T2DM meta-analysis (Liu et al., *Aging Clinical and Experimental Research*) found HIIT significantly reduced **LDL cholesterol (MD −0.25 mmol/L, 95% CI −0.46 to −0.04, P=0.02)** versus MICT, but no significant differences for total cholesterol or HDL.

- The 2019 PLOS ONE meta-analysis by Su et al. (DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0210644; 22 studies, 620 overweight/obese adults) found both HIIT and MICT significantly reduced TC (SMD 0.467 and 0.488). **HIIT significantly reduced LDL (SMD 0.445) but MICT did not (SMD 0.287). No significant effects of either intervention on TG, HDL, FBG, or insulin.** HIIT sessions averaged 30.0±10.2 min versus 39.7±15.5 min for MICT — a time saving of 9.7 min per session. HIIT with interval durations ≥2 min significantly increased VO2max vs MICT (SMD 0.444, 95% CI 0.037–0.851, P=0.032).

- The 2026 real-world HIIT meta-analysis (Stefanovic et al., *Sports* 14(7):311) found significant pre-post reductions in total cholesterol (−9 mg/dL), LDL (−10 mg/dL), and triglycerides (−8 mg/dL), but no significant effects on HDL, fasting glucose, insulin, or HOMA-IR.

- The 2023 meta-analysis by Kramer et al., published in *Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness* (Vol. 21, Issue 4, pp. 385–394; DOI: 10.1016/j.jesf.2023.09.002; 11 RCTs using DEXA), found **no significant difference between HIIT and continuous aerobic training (CAT) in reducing %BF (MD −0.55%, 95% CI −1.42 to 0.31; p=0.209)** or abdominal visceral fat (SMD −0.05, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.19; p=0.997), but HIIT showed greater benefits in VO2max, fasting blood glucose, and total cholesterol.

**D.3. Contradictory/negative findings on lipids**

- The 2019 PLOS ONE meta-analysis (Su et al.) found no significant effects of either HIIT or MICT on TG, HDL, FBG, or insulin in overweight/obese adults.
- The 2018 T2DM meta-analysis (Liu et al.) found no significant difference for total cholesterol or HDL versus MICT.
- The 2026 Cochrane review found no clear differences between HIIT and MICT for triglycerides.
- The 2026 prediabetes meta-analysis found limited lipid evidence with no clear superiority of HIIT over MICT.

**E. ADIPOSITY MEASURES (Body Fat %, Waist Circumference, Visceral Fat, Liver Fat)**

**E.1. Body fat percentage and waist circumference — meta-analyses**

- A 2023 meta-analysis by Guo et al., published in *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health* (March 8, 2023; PMC10048683; PMID 36981649; 29 RCTs, 807 participants aged 18–60), found **HIIT was significantly superior to MICT for waist circumference (MD −0.96 cm), percent fat mass (MD −0.48%), and VO2peak (SMD 0.19)**. No significant differences were found for body mass, BMI, fat mass, fat-free mass, or blood pressure. **Subgroup analyses revealed HIIT's advantages in WC, PFM, and VO2peak were significant in younger adults (18–45 years) but not middle-aged (45–60 years). HIIT was more effective for obese participants, and HIIT performed >3 times/week and >6 weeks produced greater benefits.** HIIT sessions were 9–54 min vs 15–60 min for MICT. Study quality was moderate (PEDro mean 5.72±0.83); attendance 90.24%.

- A 2023 meta-analysis by Khodadadi et al., published in *Journal of Clinical Medicine* (2023, 12(6):2291; DOI: 10.3390/jcm12062291; 36 RCTs, 1,130 participants aged 18–57), found HIIT (all modalities) significantly reduced **body fat % (WMD −1.53%, 95% CI −2.13 to −0.92, p=0.001, I²=86.7%)** and **fat mass (WMD −1.86 kg, 95% CI −2.55 to −1.18, p=0.001, I²=63.3%)**, and improved fat-free mass (WMD 0.51 kg, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.95, p=0.025, I²=0%). Overground running produced the largest BF% reduction (WMD −2.80%, 95% CI −3.89 to −1.71). No significant BF% reduction was seen in participants with BMI>30. Cycling increased FFM (WMD 0.63 kg, 95% CI 0.17 to 1.09, p=0.007); treadmill running did not significantly reduce FM (WMD −1.10 kg, p=0.210). Training >8 weeks, ≥3 sessions/week, with work intervals ≤60 s separated by ≤90 s active recovery were most effective. GRADE certainty: FFM high, FM medium, BF% low.

- The 2018 Maillard et al. meta-analysis (39 studies, 617 subjects, reported via Scribd) found HIIT significantly reduced total, abdominal, and visceral fat mass. **Running was more effective than cycling at reducing total and visceral fat; intensity >90% peak heart rate was more successful for whole-body fat reduction, while lower intensities were more effective for abdominal and visceral fat; CT and MRI were required to detect abdominal/visceral fat loss.**

- The 2026 Cochrane review found: compared to no exercise, HIIT probably reduces waist size slightly but has little/no effect on waist-to-hip ratio; **HIIT vs MICT: no clear differences for waist size (MD 0.06 cm, 95% CI −1.49 to 1.62; 15 studies, 407 participants) or waist-to-hip ratio**.

- A 2025 meta-analysis in overweight/obese adolescents (*Frontiers in Physiology*, DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1636792; 16 RCTs, 473 participants) found **HIIT was significantly superior in reducing body fat percentage (MD −0.74, 95% CI −1.44 to 0.04, P=0.04, I²=40%)**, with no significant differences for body weight (MD 0.29), BMI (MD 0.06), fat-free mass (MD 1.19), SBP (MD 1.18), or DBP (MD −0.46). Subgroup analysis showed MICT was more effective than HIIT in reducing waist circumference when running was the modality (MD 2.81, 95% CI 0.36–5.26, P=0.02).

- The 2025 cancer survivors meta-analysis (*Frontiers in Physiology*, DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1594574; 12 RCTs, ages 39–75) found **no significant differences between HIIT and MICT for body mass, total fat mass, lean body mass, fat percentage, BMI, waist circumference, or hip circumference**, while HIIT was superior for VO2peak (SMD 0.53, 95% CI 0.21–0.84, P=0.001, I²=0%).

- The 2026 real-world HIIT meta-analysis (Stefanovic et al.) found borderline non-significant body weight reduction (−1.0 kg, p=0.059), BMI −0.4 kg/m² (p=0.041), body fat −1.5%, waist circumference −1.7 cm.

**E.2. Visceral adipose tissue (VAT)**

- A 2025 systematic review by Delgado, Delgado & Burns, published in *International Journal of Exercise Science* (Dec 2025; 18(5):1321; PMID 41368564), examined HIIT effects on VAT in T2D. Five RCTs (138 participants, mean ages 52–62, all overweight/obese; 8–12 weeks; 3x/week; session durations 4–12 minutes) met criteria. **Four of five trials reported significant reductions in VAT after thrice-weekly cycling HIIT. The one negative study (Findikoglu et al.) controlled for energy expenditure and found no significant VAT reduction. All five HIIT interventions showed significant HbA1c reductions.** Notable liver fat reductions: Cassidy et al. found a 39% relative reduction in liver fat; Sabag et al. and Winding et al. also noted liver fat reductions. The authors state HIIT consistently outperformed MICT in reducing visceral fat, likely due to greater EPOC, increased mitochondrial biogenesis, and enhanced fat oxidation. Adherence averaged ~85%. PEDro scores 6–8/9. A meta-analysis was not conducted due to clinical heterogeneity.

- The 2023 Kramer et al. meta-analysis (*Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness*; 11 RCTs using DEXA) found **no significant difference between HIIT and continuous aerobic training for abdominal visceral fat (SMD −0.05, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.19; p=0.997)**.

- The 2025 prediabetes RCT (*Frontiers in Endocrinology*, DOI: 10.3389/fendo.2025.1614149) found **MICT was superior to HIIT in reducing visceral adipose area (P=0.043) and body fat rate (P=0.030)**; lean mass and muscle mass decreased significantly more in the HIIT group (P=0.01, Cohen's d ≈ 0.9, large effect). TG decreased significantly more in MICT (P=0.006). VO2peak increased in both groups (HIIT +2.13±4.94; MICT +1.63±3.40 ml/kg/min) with no between-group difference (P=0.647).

**E.3. Liver fat (hepatic steatosis)**

- A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis by Sabag et al., published in *The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism* (Vol. 107, No. 3, pp. 862–881), examined HIIT vs MICT on liver fat in adults with NAFLD. Nineteen RCTs (745 participants; 67% male; mean age 53±10 years; BMI 30.9±4.4; liver fat 11.5±6.2%) used MRI-based techniques (1H-MRS or MRI). Results: **HIIT vs control reduced liver fat by −2.85% (95% CI −4.86 to −0.84, P=0.005, LOW-certainty evidence); MICT vs control reduced liver fat by −3.14% (95% CI −4.45 to −1.82, P<0.001, MODERATE-certainty evidence); HIIT vs MICT showed no significant difference (−0.34%, 95% CI −2.20 to 1.52, P=0.721, MODERATE-certainty evidence)**. Effect sizes: HIIT vs CON g=−0.59; MICT vs CON g=−0.47; HIIT vs MICT g=−0.05. Neither total weekly exercise volume in minutes (P=0.89) nor exercise-related energy expenditure (P=0.23) was significantly related to liver fat changes. **The authors concluded HIIT elicits comparable improvements in liver fat to MICT despite often requiring less energy and time commitment.**

- A 2024 network meta-analysis in *Scientific Reports* (Vol. 14, Article 6212; 43 RCTs, 2,070 NAFLD patients: aerobic n=779, resistance n=159, HIIT n=160, combined AT+RT n=96) ranked modalities: **AT+RT was best for TC (SUCRA 71.7), TG (SUCRA 96.8), and LDL-C (SUCRA 86.1); AT was best for ALT (SUCRA 83.9) and HDL-C (SUCRA 72.3); RT was best for AST (SUCRA 81.7)**. Recommended prescription: AT+RT at least 3x/week, 50 min/session, for 10 weeks. The review assessed blood biomarkers, not direct liver steatosis imaging.

- A 2026 systematic review (protocol-ready meta-analysis) by Sawant, Motimath & Chivate, published in *IJDDT* (Vol. 16, Issue 59s, pp. 634–643; DOI: 10.25258/ijddt.16.59s.77), on HIIT for NAFLD/NASH/MASLD reviewed 18 studies (15 interventional + 3 systematic reviews; 551 participants; trials 8–16 weeks, 3x/week). Key findings: HIIT largely reduced liver fat (MRI, proton MRS, CAP, ultrasound); ALT and AST often improved, especially in high metabolic risk populations; benefits were often observed without clinically meaningful weight loss; energy-matched comparisons suggested exercise dose is a major determinant of liver-fat response, with HIIT offering comparable benefit in shorter time. **Fibrosis outcomes remained least certain; evidence that HIIT reverses fibrosis should be considered preliminary. GRADE certainty: liver fat reduction = moderate; ALT/AST = low-moderate; liver stiffness/fibrosis = low; insulin resistance = moderate; adverse events = low-moderate.** This is explicitly a protocol-ready meta-analysis, NOT a completed pooled analysis.

- A 2022 RCT by Stine et al. (PMC10287833; cited by 100), "Modified high-intensity interval training reduces liver fat and improves cardiac function in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: A randomized controlled trial," found modified HIIT reduced liver fat (intrahepatic lipid by 37% vs 20% for MICT per the AMPED trial page; HIIT reduced liver fat by 16.6% per the same source).

- The Nature Index topic summary on "Exercise Interventions in Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease" reports: a 2017 *Scientific Reports* study comparing resistance training, HIIT, and MICT over 12 weeks in sedentary obese men with NAFLD found all regimens achieved similar hepatic fat reductions, but only HIIT improved liver stiffness and restored Kupffer cell phagocytic function. A 2023 Sports Medicine position statement (Exercise and Sport Science Australia) confirmed 150–240 min/week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise reduces hepatic steatosis by 2–4%, with HIIT offering comparable benefits. A 2024 JHEP Reports deep phenotyping study using HIIT in MASH patients demonstrated a 10% increase in cardiorespiratory fitness and transcriptomic shifts favoring adipose tissue beiging, despite no histological regression.

- The AMPED trial (NCT04987879, Milton S. Hershey Medical Center/NIDDK; adults 18–69 with NAFLD/NASH, sedentary <90 min/week, BMI>30) is testing aerobic exercise doses of 750 and 1,000 MET-min/wk. Supporting evidence cited: aerobic exercise decreased liver fat by 21% in 4 weeks; HIIT reduced intrahepatic lipid by 37% vs 20% for MICT; a 12-week HIIT program reduced liver fat from 11% to 8%; regular exercise (≥5x/week) reduced risk of new fatty liver disease by 14% and increased resolution likelihood by 40%.

- A qualitative study nested within an Australian RCT (ACTRN12616000305426) in 12 participants with biopsy-confirmed NASH (mean age 57±10, mean BMI 39.4±7.3; 100% metabolic syndrome, 92% hypertension, 75% T2DM) undergoing 12 weeks of supervised HIIT (4×4-min at 85–95% HRmax, 3x/week) found supervised session attendance >90% with full adherence, but self-directed HIIT adherence was poor (33% dropout overall). The qualitative findings are reported in *Journal of Clinical and Translational Hepatology* (2023;11(5):1050-1060; doi: 10.14218/JCTH.2022.00091S).

**F. HYBRID HIIT + MICT AND COMBINED PROTOCOLS**

- A 13-week ACE-sponsored RCT by Dalleck, Keeling, Weatherwax, Ramos & Green (reported at ACE Fitness, "Does Combining MICT and HIIT Yield Greater Health Benefits?") randomized 54 inactive adults (ages 21–55) to (1) non-exercise control, (2) individualized MICT+HIIT program (ACE IFT Model, HIIT: eight 60-second intervals at 100% VO2max separated by 150 s light recovery), or (3) standardized MICT (ACSM guidelines). **100% of MICT+HIIT participants were "responders" for metabolic syndrome z-score versus only 56.25% in MICT-only (43.75% were non-responders). For VO2max, 100% of MICT+HIIT were responders versus 68.75% in MICT-only.** Changes in VO2max and MetS z-score were significantly more favorable in the MICT+HIIT group. Adherence was 90% (MICT-only) and 91% (MICT+HIIT). Both exercise groups significantly improved percent body fat and waist circumference.

- A 2026 network meta-analysis in *British Journal of Sports Medicine* found combined aerobic+resistance training was associated with the largest 24-hour SBP reduction (6.18 mmHg) among modalities, slightly ahead of HIIT (5.71 mmHg).

- The 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis in *Sports Medicine* found circuit-based training (CBT) had the largest SBP reduction (MD −13.52 mmHg; 95% CrI −18.59 to −8.44), followed by combined training (CT), HIIT, MICT, dynamic resistance training, and isometric exercise. CBT showed a peak effect at approximately 580 METs-min/week (lower range of WHO recommendations).

- A 2024 RCT in sedentary young women (*Journal of Sports Sciences*, DOI: 10.1080/02640414.2024.2363708; 42 women aged 18–25, 8 weeks, 3x/week) compared high-intensity circuit training (HICT, body-weight based) vs traditional cycling HIIT vs control. **Total cholesterol and leptin significantly decreased only in the HICT group; HICT improved lean mass, upper/lower limb strength, and balance; HIIT improved only lower limb strength. The control group showed significant increases in triglycerides, weight, BMI, and fat mass.** Compliance was 93.8% (HICT) and 93.5% (HIIT).

- The Stanford University trial NCT05513300 (HIIT vs MICT in sedentary adults, 12 weeks + 4-week follow-up, ages 18+, BMI>18 and <40, sedentary <1 hour structured exercise/week) is examining changes in cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength, body composition, and multiomics profile.

---

**G. LOW-VOLUME HIIT AND SPRINT INTERVAL TRAINING (SIT) VARIANTS**

- A study protocol by Astorino et al., published in *Trials* (2026, Vol. 27, Article 340; DOI: 10.1186/s13063-026-09647-x), describes a definitive RCT of reduced-exertion HIIT (REHIT: two 20-second all-out sprints within a 10-minute session, 2 days/week = 20 min/week) in 120 inactive adults aged 18–64. Prior studies cited show VO2max increases of ~10% after 6 weeks and ~19% after 12 weeks of REHIT, with no serious adverse events. Improvements of this magnitude are associated with 30% and 38% risk reductions for all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality, respectively. Traditional HIIT/SIT protocols are criticized for requiring ~66–93 min/week, being too strenuous, and producing negative affective responses.

- The RunRepeat.com meta-analysis (Rizzo, March 26, 2024; ~75 studies comparing SIT, HIIT, MICT) reported: **SIT resulted in a 39.95% higher reduction in body fat percentage than HIIT and a 91.83% higher reduction than MICT; SIT participants exercised 60.84% less time than HIIT and 71.17% less than MICT over ~9.8 weeks; SIT produced a 2.31% body fat reduction vs HIIT's 1.64% and MICT's 1.2%; SIT spent 81.46% less time doing high-intensity work than HIIT.** Average protocols: SIT = 8 sprints of 27.6 s at RPE 10 with 2 min 44 s rest; HIIT = 8 intervals of 2 min 24 s at RPE 7 with 2 min 8 s rest; MICT = 40 min 32 s at RPE 4. (Note: This is a secondary/aggregator source, not a peer-reviewed journal publication.)

- The 2025 LV-HIIT meta-analysis (Lu et al., *Frontiers in Endocrinology*) found LV-HIIT more effective than MICT for insulin sensitivity (SMD −0.40; 95% CI −0.70 to −0.09; p=0.01), with no differences in FPG, FPI, HbA1c, or HOMA-IR. FPG decreased with each additional second of interval duration (β=−0.10; p=0.046). Two SIT-based LV-HIIT studies showed no improvements, suggesting extremely low volumes may be insufficient.

- The 2026 middle-aged/elderly meta-analysis (Li et al.) exploratory analysis suggested sprint interval training and short-interval HIIT produced greater lipid improvements, while long-interval HIIT showed more consistent blood pressure effects.

- The 2016 Gillen RCT (PLoS ONE) demonstrated that SIT with a five-fold lower exercise volume and time commitment (30 vs 150 min/week) produced comparable improvements in insulin sensitivity, VO2peak, and mitochondrial content to MICT in sedentary men.

- The 2016 (published) SIT study in *The Journal of Physiology* showed constant-load SIT (~1 hour/week) was equally effective to MICT (~5 hours/week) for aerobic capacity, insulin sensitivity, muscle capillarization, and endothelial enzyme balance in young obese men.

**H. QUALITY OF LIFE / PSYCHOSOCIAL OUTCOMES (Contextual)**

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis by a group in *Scientific Reports* (Vol. 13, Article 13915; 25 studies, 23 in meta-analysis; CVD patients) found no statistically significant differences between HIIT and MICT for quality of life (SMD 0.21, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.61, P=0.290), physical component summary (SMD 0.10, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.23, P=0.128), mental component summary (SMD 0.07, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.20, P=0.25), depression (SMD −0.08, 95% CI −0.40 to 0.25, P=0.646), or anxiety (WMD 0.14, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.84, P=0.694). HIIT significantly improved PCS in the coronary artery disease subgroup and was superior for physical role, vitality, and social function. Background context: the AHA introduced HIIT to cardiac rehabilitation in 2007; HIIT has been shown to improve mitochondrial biogenesis, insulin sensitivity, glucose regulation, HDL cholesterol, and blood pressure.

**I. TIME-EFFICIENCY EVIDENCE (Relevance to <150 and <60 min/week)**

- The 2026 T2DM meta-analysis (Zeng et al.) reported that ~78 min/week of HIIT can achieve glycemic control comparable to ~210 min/week of MICT.
- The 2019 PLOS ONE meta-analysis (Su et al.) reported HIIT sessions averaged 30.0±10.2 min versus 39.7±15.5 min for MICT — a 9.7 min per-session time saving.
- The 2023 IJERPH meta-analysis (Guo et al.) reported HIIT sessions of 9–54 min vs 15–60 min for MICT.
- The 2016 Gillen RCT showed 30 min/week of SIT produced comparable benefits to 150 min/week of MICT.
- The SIT study in *The Journal of Physiology* showed ~1 hour/week of SIT was comparable to ~5 hours/week of MICT in obese men.
- The REHIT protocol (Astorino et al., *Trials* 2026) uses only 20 min/week total (two 10-minute sessions).
- The 2022 JCEM liver fat meta-analysis (Sabag et al.) concluded HIIT elicits comparable liver fat improvements to MICT "despite often requiring less energy and time commitment."
- The 2018 Aging Clin Exp Res meta-analysis (Liu et al.) noted HIIT addresses the time barrier preventing many T2D patients from achieving recommended physical activity levels.
- The 2021 IJERPH review (Atakan et al.) notes lack of time is the most common barrier to exercise adherence, with ~1.4 billion people not meeting public health guidelines; WHO 2020 guidelines recommend 150–300 min of moderate-intensity or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise weekly.

---

**J. QUALITY, CERTAINTY, AND LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE BASE**

- The 2026 Cochrane review (Strauss et al.) rated confidence in results as low to moderate due to variation in participant responses, small study sizes with too few studies for some outcomes, and lack of blinding. All included studies examined supervised HIIT; future research should investigate unsupervised HIIT feasibility and safety. Searches covered CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and two trial registries up to 13 October 2025. No studies reported long-term outcomes such as heart attacks, strokes, or deaths.
- The 2018 T2DM meta-analysis (Liu et al.) GRADE assessment rated most outcomes "Low" or "Very low" quality; only VO2peak was "Moderate."
- The 2025 cancer survivors meta-analysis reported 4 of 12 studies with some concerns and 8 at high risk of bias; performance bias was unavoidable.
- The 2026 prediabetes meta-analysis noted most studies had "some concerns" in risk of bias; certainty for glycemic outcomes was generally low to very low; 9 of 13 studies lasted ≤2 weeks.
- The 2026 real-world HIIT meta-analysis reported substantial heterogeneity (I² up to 95%) and moderate methodological quality; mean PEDro 6.2; mean dropout 14.9%.
- The 2026 Sports Medicine network meta-analysis noted no network comparison was rated as high confidence; many studies had some concerns or high risk of bias.
- The 2022 JCEM liver fat meta-analysis downgraded HIIT vs CON liver fat evidence to LOW certainty; MICT vs CON to MODERATE; HIIT vs MICT to MODERATE.
- The 2025 LV-HIIT meta-analysis rated only 30% of studies (6 of 20) as high quality.
- The 2026 Frontiers in Physiology meta-analysis (Li et al.) noted 77.3% of studies had low risk in random sequence generation, only 40.9% low risk in allocation concealment, and 36.4% high risk in performance blinding; ~30% of studies showed high risk in at least one domain, but sensitivity analyses confirmed robust results.
- The 2026 F1000Research T2DM insulin sensitivity meta-analysis reported overall low risk of bias with good-to-excellent methodological quality across the 4 included RCTs.

---

**K. DIRECTIONS FOR FURTHER RESEARCH AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS**

- The 2026 T2DM meta-analysis (Zeng et al.) recommends, for T2DM patients with low HDL: HIIT at 20–30 min/session, 2–3 times/week for 8 weeks; for patients with elevated TC: short-duration HIIT (≤20 min); a cyclical training program to avoid adaptation plateau. Limitations: insufficient follow-up duration, non-standardized dietary control, HIIT protocol heterogeneity, unexplored "exercise resistance," incomplete publication bias assessment for secondary outcomes, no grey literature searched, English-language restriction.
- The 2026 Cochrane review concludes HIIT "may be an effective alternative to MICT" for sedentary populations at risk of cardiometabolic disease; larger, higher-quality RCTs with longer follow-up are needed.
- The 2025 VAT systematic review recommends tailoring HIIT to patient age, fitness, and comorbidities; gradual progression with initial supervision for older/deconditioned individuals; and hybrid supervised/home-based models to improve feasibility and adherence.
- The 2026 IJDDT NAFLD protocol calls for standardized, adequately powered trials with harmonized imaging, fibrosis, adherence, safety, and durability outcomes before HIIT can be ranked definitively against MICT or resistance training for liver fat.
- The 2025 prediabetes RCT (*Frontiers in Endocrinology*) suggests MICT may be the superior exercise option based on glucose and lipid metabolism results in prediabetic patients, in direct contradiction to other studies favoring HIIT — highlighting the outcome-specific and population-specific nature of the evidence.
